pages.title: Editorial approach
pages.description: Industry practice, Christian reflection and an explicit standard for useful design guidance.
pages.text: Home / About / Editorial approach Our approach Design practice, examined with care. Learn from established practice. Examine its assumptions. Make a decision that you can explain to the people it affects. A Christian perspective with room for discernment This resource considers industry design practice through actual user needs, ethical questions and Christian theological reflection. Established patterns carry assumptions about success, growth, attention and value. Their commercial origins neither make them neutral nor invalidate them. We examine what they reward, who benefits and who carries the costs. A redemptive frame invites inquiry: what good might this product cultivate, what harm might it repair or reproduce, and whose circumstances are missing? It is not a certification that a product is redemptive. Prayerful discernment belongs alongside research, accessibility, practical testing and accountability. From situation to considered decision Begin with the situation and intended good. Name the assumptions, compare alternatives, examine consequences, and make a decision that can be revisited. A default should serve the person’s purpose; usage volume cannot establish spiritual growth. Follow a worked example or use questions and readings for discernment . Recommendations without a single theological verdict Charging money can support fair compensation, care and continuity. Different Christian perspectives may emphasise generous access, stewardship, the dignity of paid work or communal provision. Donations, subscriptions, institutional funding and usage-based pricing each introduce dependencies. We compare those consequences and invite a reasoned choice; no funding model is presented as uniquely Christian. What a useful pattern should contain A recognisable situation and the person’s purpose. An actionable recommendation with credible alternatives. Benefits, drawbacks and different effects across circumstances. A visual appropriate to the decision: a wireframe, sequence, controllable animation, timeline or comparison. Sources with their scope, dates and limits; observation distinguished from interpretation. Questions for reflection and a concrete way to evaluate the choice. Animations should have static equivalents and respect reduced-motion preferences. A polished illustration is not evidence of effectiveness. An edited publication that can grow Editorial readiness and strength of evidence are separate questions. A publishable proposal can still need user research; an established finding can still need careful translation into a different context. Published patterns form an editorially reviewed collection. Further pattern drafts are held back from the catalogue and downloads; their former links lead to related guidance. Research articles remain an evolving reference with source-specific limits. Patterns marked Published have received an editorial review. In development means the pattern body and illustration are withheld while that review continues. Working drafts are retained outside the public output. Incomplete research should not become an empty pattern page or a promised delivery date. Questions in development Builder architecture decisions, Scripture API and licensing comparisons, and starter templates need dedicated investigation. Comparative app-board research will use dated observations and fresh verification where necessary. These are research directions, not currently reviewed provider recommendations. Begin with the person’s purpose , explore the design principles , or use the decision worksheet .

pages.title: About this resource
pages.description: Why Bible & Faith Patterns exists, who it is for, how a deep dive works, where each option comes from, and how sources, Scripture and accessibility are handled.
pages.text: On this page Why it exists Who it is for How a deep dive works Where options come from How sources are used Scripture Accessibility Licence and reuse Maintenance Home / About A design reference Equipping workers in God’s field. This resource helps everyone who shapes Bible, prayer and AI products to reflect on that calling, to be glad in it and to do it well, so that what we build leads to human flourishing and spiritual nourishment. It gathers reusable decisions, independent of any app, framework or vendor. Why it exists People now bring their prayers, doubts, confessions and questions about God to a screen first. When some told Jesus to silence the crowds praising him, he answered, “Listen—if they were silent, the very rocks would start to shout!” (Luke 19:40, The Voice). Making him known is entrusted to us first. But many people now talk to rocks first: a microchip is a rock we tricked into thinking, and with AI the rock talks back. We get to help these rocks reflect Christ and lead people into deeper knowledge of God. Those who build these products plant and water; God gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). That is an exhilarating calling and a real weight. Workers in God’s field sets out the joy of the work and its spiritual, theological, ethical and legal responsibility. Who it is for Product designers, product managers, developers and founders who build Bible, prayer, devotional, study and AI products, and the ministry, business and church leaders who guide them. Much of it also applies to other products that hold sources, reflection or sensitive conversations. How a deep dive works Each deep dive takes one design decision and lays its real options side by side, from what apps do today to leaving the feature out. At a glance shows a still of every option with one gain and one cost. Try it is a working example on a phone-sized screen, with its settings in one panel. Takeaways , Use cases and Research give what we noticed, which option suits which situation, and the Scripture, tradition, science and accessibility guidance behind it. Which fits , real Examples , a Theological reflection and Three ways to build lead to Decide : one question and an exercise for your next review. Earlier, shorter patterns now sit under Go further in the deep dive they belong to. Where each option comes from Every option is labelled, so an idea we invented never passes as something people already use: Observed : seen in a named app, with a dated screenshot where we have one. Familiar convention : a widely used convention, generalised rather than copied. Borrowed : taken from outside faith apps, such as reading or productivity tools. Exploratory · untested : our own proposal, not yet tested. Leave it out : not building the feature, treated as a real option. Use-case tables are editorial judgments drawn from the research, not test results. Nothing here is user-tested yet, and no example or pattern promises clinical benefit or spiritual growth. How sources are used Every source states what was reviewed, what it contributes, how it is applied and where its limits lie, and the research sections cite them by name. Technical specifications establish meaning; help articles document how a product behaves; empirical studies report findings for the people and systems they studied; legal texts set requirements within their scope. These are not interchangeable. Quotations and figures on newer pages are checked by script against a saved copy of each source, with translations noted, and the build fails if a quotation or a number cannot be found there; older pages are being brought up to the same standard. App screenshots are dated and keep their original language; working examples, stills and diagrams are our own. The AI design collection curated by Vitaly Friedman, the AI Interaction Atlas and other catalogues are credited in the source register. Scripture quotations Articles, reflections, research notes, working examples and diagrams quote the Berean Standard Bible (BSB), a modern English translation dedicated to the public domain in 2023. Every build compares each quotation on the site and in the working examples with the BSB’s published text and fails on any difference; the few deliberate exceptions below are listed in the check with their reasons. Luke 19:40 is quoted once from The Voice for its word “rocks”: Scripture taken from The Voice™. Copyright © 2008 by Ecclesia Bible Society. Used by permission. All rights reserved. Some working examples show other wording on purpose, and say so: the translation comparison sets the KJV, the World English Bible and Young’s Literal Translation beside the BSB; the marking example uses the KJV, where a highlight on BSB words has no exact match; the prayer example reads Compline as printed in the 1979 Book of Common Prayer, which quotes the RSV; and in the progress example a reader’s own note quotes the KJV. Historical commentaries, such as Matthew Henry’s on Psalm 23, quote the KJV they were written on. Each example says which translation it shows. Accessibility and themes Pages and working examples are checked with axe against WCAG 2.2 AA, in both light and dark themes, and by keyboard. The site follows your system’s light or dark setting, and the switch in the header remembers your choice; working examples, stills and diagrams follow it too. Screenshots of real apps stay as they were captured. If something does not work for you, please say so . Licence and reuse The original text, stills, diagrams, worksheet and structured data of Bible & Faith Patterns are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) . You may share and adapt them for any purpose, including commercial work, as long as you credit “Bible & Faith Patterns, Tobias Treppmann, Missional by Design (patterns.missional.design)” and indicate if you changed anything. The code of the working examples is available under the MIT licence. Documentary photographs are credited to Startup Life and used with permission. They are not included in the CC BY 4.0 licence. Some material here is not ours to license. Screenshots of real apps belong to their publishers and are shown for commentary. Quotations from books, articles and studies remain their authors’; follow each source’s licence. Berean Standard Bible quotations are public domain. Luke 19:40 from The Voice™ is © 2008 Ecclesia Bible Society, used by permission, and is not covered by this licence. All content is also available as structured data, for your own tools: the content API . Publication and maintenance This is an evolving, independent design reference. Sources, app examples, scenarios and patterns are added and revised as evidence becomes available. Review dates remain visible; legal and support references need fresh verification before product decisions. The Digital Spiritual Formation section integrates selected Kairos manuscript sections and reviewed external findings, with further study review in progress. About the editor Tobias Treppmann develops this resource through Missional by Design, bringing product design questions into conversation with Christian spiritual formation. Selected Kairos University research informs the editorial perspective. Aperto and VSB are author-associated projects; their prototypes are identified as such, and inclusion is not independent evidence of effectiveness. Other app examples do not imply endorsement or affiliation. The aim is a useful, revisable contribution: concrete choices that designers, product managers and independent builders can discuss and test. Explore Missional by Design . Design values and critical application This reference connects the Missional by Design framework to its patterns through ten principles for spiritual apps , derived from the calling . They replaced the framework’s eight principles on 11 October 2026; the Christian theological posture is explicit. Values frame choices and questions, while evidence and legal scope require their own review. Three ways to build Each deep dive asks what an exploitative, an ethical and a redemptive product would do, using a frame from Praxis. Read why, and how we understand “redemptive” . On this page Why it exists Who it is for How a deep dive works Where options come from How sources are used Scripture Accessibility Licence and reuse Maintenance

pages.title: Three ways to build
pages.description: Exploitative, ethical and redemptive design choices: Praxis’s frame, how this reference applies it, and its theological basis and limits.
pages.text: On this page Where it comes from Why it fits How we understand “redemptive” Limits Use it in a review Home / About A design reference Three ways to build Exploitative, ethical, redemptive: what each design choice takes from people, keeps for them, or gives up for them. Every deep dive in this reference ends with the same question in three forms. What would an exploitative product do here? What would an ethical one do? And what would a redemptive one do: what would it give up for the good of the person using it? Where the frame comes from The three ways are the work of Praxis , which teaches them to founders and funders. In their words, the exploitative way is to “take all you can get”, the ethical way is to “do things right”, and the redemptive way is “creative restoration through sacrifice”: not “I win, you lose” or “I win, you win”, but “I sacrifice, we win”. Their playbook chapter on products asks for “impact/market fit, not merely product/market fit”. The same language is spreading beyond Praxis, for example in Seed’s Redemptive Design in Australia. We use the frame with gratitude and credit. Its application to Bible and faith interfaces, and the reflection below, are ours; Praxis has not reviewed them, and this reference is not affiliated with Praxis. Why it fits a design reference Most design guidance stops at the ethical floor: accessibility, privacy law, honest copy, no dark patterns. That floor matters, and much of this reference’s research is there to hold it. But a faith app can keep every rule and still treat people as engagement. The redemptive question names something the rules cannot: a cost the maker chooses to bear. A prayer app that collects no personal data gives up analytics. A reading plan that waits gives up the retention a streak buys. An assistant that sends someone to their pastor ends its own session. The frame also shapes this reference’s ten principles for spiritual apps : each names what it asks the maker to give up, and the three ways are read there for apps whose subject is God , where the exploitative temptation is not only to use people but to use God’s name. How we understand “redemptive” Redemption is God’s work. Scripture calls the Lord “your Redeemer” (Isaiah 44:24), and it is God who reconciles “to Himself all things” through the cross (Colossians 1:20). No app redeems anyone. We use the word for a way of making, never for a product, and we try not to call any feature “redemptive” as if it accomplished what only God does. Yet we are invited to take part. God “gave us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18), and Paul calls himself and Apollos “God’s fellow workers” (1 Corinthians 3:9). Praxis puts it this way: God has acted “so that we can participate with him in the restoration of all things”. Design is one of the places where that participation is practised or refused. The pattern is Christ’s self-giving. He “emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), and “did not come to be served, but to serve” (Mark 10:45). David would not offer to God offerings “that cost me nothing” (2 Samuel 24:24). A redemptive choice is recognisable by what it costs the one who makes it, not by how it is described. The exploitative way has a biblical name. Ezekiel spoke against shepherds who “feed themselves” instead of the flock (Ezekiel 34:2). Faith products are a kind of shepherding: they hold people’s prayers, doubts and hours. Using that trust for growth targets is the oldest failure of religious leadership in a new medium. The ethical way is good, and not the end. Jesus told his disciples that after doing all they were commanded, they should say: “we have only done our duty” (Luke 17:10). Keeping the rules is duty. Love goes further, and it usually costs something. Limits and cautions Not a ranking of companies or people. The three ways describe choices. The same product can be exploitative in one place and redemptive in another, and every deep dive shows both. Not a claim of results. Calling a choice redemptive does not mean it formed anyone. Whether people flourish is an empirical and pastoral question; see Plant and water; leave the growth to God . Not an exclusive vocabulary. Praxis themselves note that theological language can feel exclusive. The ethical floor is shared with everyone; the redemptive question is offered as an invitation, also to readers who do not share the faith behind it. Different traditions, different weight. Christians hold different convictions about human participation in God’s work. We use the word modestly and welcome correction. How to use it in a review For any screen, write one sentence for each way. Then ask of the redemptive one: who bears its cost, and would we still choose it if no one noticed? The decision worksheet has room for the answer. On this page Where it comes from Why it fits How we understand “redemptive” Limits Use it in a review

pages.title: Bezalel
pages.description: An open MCP server that brings Bible & Faith Patterns into your own AI assistant, to help product teams discern, not just decide.
pages.text: Home / Home MCP server · open Bezalel Bible & Faith Patterns inside your own AI assistant: to help your team discern, not just decide. “I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship” (Exodus 31:3). Bezalel was the craftsman who made the tabernacle. This Bezalel is a small, open MCP server: it lets the AI assistant your team already uses, such as Claude, Cursor or ChatGPT, draw on this reference while you design. It is built to slow you down at the right moments. It brings the whole spectrum of options, the research with its limits and the questions to ask, and it leaves the deciding to you. Add it to your assistant The server address is https://patterns.missional.design/mcp . No account or key is needed. Claude (web and desktop): add a custom connector with this address in your connector settings. Claude Code : claude mcp add --transport http bezalel https://patterns.missional.design/mcp Cursor and other editors: add an MCP server of type “streamable HTTP” with this address to your MCP configuration. ChatGPT : where your plan allows custom connectors, add this address as an MCP connector. Connector menus change often; if your tool asks for a transport, choose Streamable HTTP. What to ask Describe a feature the way your team would, then ask for a review. For example: “Use Bezalel to review a daily reading streak with push reminders,” or start one of its prompts: Design review , Three ways debate or Pre-mortem: who could this hurt? What it can do map_feature : the decisions inside a feature, each with its full spectrum of options (including leaving it out), their provenance, and the questions to ask. challenge_default : for a feature copied from mainstream apps, what that pattern is built to maximise, what the research adds, and alternatives that serve the person. three_ways : the exploitative, ethical and redemptive versions of a feature, for a debate rather than a verdict. premortem : the most vulnerable people likely to use it, and the question to ask for each. draft_worksheet : the decision worksheet, with pointers for each step, for your team to fill in. search_reference , list_deep_dives , get_deep_dive , find_sources and principles : the reference itself, with every source’s limits. How it behaves Bezalel offers options, evidence and questions, not verdicts. It asks your assistant to show every option, to ask your team before recommending, to link every page it draws on, and to leave theological, pastoral and safeguarding judgments to people who can make them. There is no AI on the server: your own assistant does the reasoning with what Bezalel returns. Privacy Bezalel keeps nothing. Each request is answered and forgotten; the feature descriptions you send are not stored or logged, and there are no accounts or cookies. The web server keeps standard access logs (time, address and path, not content) for security. Licence The content is CC BY 4.0 and the server code MIT. The same content is available as plain data in the content API . Bezalel is new: please tell us how it works in your team’s hands: which assistant you used, what you asked, what helped and what it got wrong.

pages.title: Workers in God’s field
pages.description: The calling of people who build technology for faith: its joy and its weight, and the spiritual, theological, ethical and legal responsibility it carries.
pages.text: Home Workers in God’s field “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow … For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field” (1 Corinthians 3:6, 9). More and more, the first place someone takes a question about God is a phone. When they do, they meet something a designer, a developer, a product manager or a founder has shaped. This article is about what it means to do that work as a calling: the joy of it, the weight of it, and what it asks of us before God and before the people we serve. Scripture · tradition · research · law 32 sources, each with its limits Not legal advice Generated editorial illustration · fictional people and place The calling The burden Spiritual Theological Ethical Legal The light Holding it Questions Sources The calling An exhilarating work Before it is a responsibility, this is a gift. God has always worked through human craft, and he invites people who build things into his work. God fills craftspeople with his Spirit One of the first people Scripture describes as filled with the Spirit of God is not a prophet but a craftsman. Of Bezalel, who made the tabernacle, God says: “I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship” (Exodus 31:3). Skill in making things can be a way of serving God’s presence among his people. We plant and water; God gives the growth Paul calls himself and Apollos “God’s fellow workers” in God’s field (1 Corinthians 3:9). Neither the planter nor the waterer is the point: “only God, who makes things grow” (3:7). A Bible app, a prayer feature or an AI assistant can plant and water. It cannot make anything grow. That is both a relief and a boundary. If they were silent, the very rocks would shout When some told Jesus to silence the crowds praising him, he answered: “Listen—if they were silent, the very rocks would start to shout!” (Luke 19:40, The Voice). His praise will not be silenced, and making him known is entrusted to us first. Yet many people now talk to rocks first. A microchip is a rock we tricked into thinking, and with AI the rock talks back, about God too. There is something wonderful in being asked to help these rocks point beyond themselves, and something sobering in what else they might say. How will they hear? “How can they believe in the One of whom they have not heard?” (Romans 10:14). Scripture is now heard through apps in thousands of languages, by people who would never open a printed Bible. YouVersion reports over a billion installs; two-thirds of US Bible users read digitally. ( YouVersion, 2025 ) ( American Bible Society, 2025 ) No square inch is outside his care Abraham Kuyper said there is not a square inch of human existence over which Christ does not cry “Mine!”. ( Kuyper, 1880 ) Interfaces, data models and prompts are not neutral ground outside faith. Dorothy Sayers put it more bluntly: “The only Christian work is good work well done.” ( Sayers, Why Work? ) The church has welcomed these tools, with conditions Sixty years ago, the Second Vatican Council opened its decree on the media with the words Inter mirifica , “among the wonderful” inventions, and said these media, “if properly utilized, can be of great service to mankind”. ( Inter Mirifica, 1963 ) The Lausanne Movement’s Seoul Statement affirms that “technological ability reflects the creativity of human beings created in God’s image”, and calls churches to engage digital technology for making disciples. ( The Seoul Statement, 2024 ) The burden A calling not to be carried lightly The same reach that makes this work exciting makes it heavy. What we build forms people quietly, at scale, often when they are most open. Teachers are judged more strictly “Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly” (James 3:1). Every product that explains a verse, chooses which passage to show or answers a question about God is teaching. A design decision repeated a million times a day is a sermon few people notice. The little ones “If anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck” (Matthew 18:6). Our users include new believers, children, people in crisis, people with scrupulous consciences and people whose trust has been abused. Design for them, not only for the confident. Shepherds who feed themselves “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2). The charge that follows reads like a product brief: they had not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, bound up the injured, brought back the strays or searched for the lost (34:4). Engagement, retention and revenue are not wrong, but when they become the purpose, the flock becomes the feed. People are already trusting the machine In a 2026 Barna study, 48% of practising Christians in the US said they would trust AI for spiritual growth, and 34% that AI’s spiritual advice is as trustworthy as a pastor’s. 83% also worried that AI could misinterpret Scripture. ( Barna, 2026 ) In an audit of AI search engines, only about half of generated sentences were fully supported by their citations. ( Liu et al., 2023 ) Tools form the people who use them James K. A. Smith argues that our habits are liturgies that shape what we love. ( Smith ) Tim Hutchings shows Bible apps are designed as persuasive technologies that train ways of reading; John Dyer traces how the digital Bible changes how people read and interpret. ( Hutchings ) ( Dyer ) Albert Borgmann warns that devices which deliver things effortlessly can displace the practices that require us. ( Borgmann ) Three ways to build Praxis describes three postures: exploitative (“I win, you lose”), ethical (“I win, you win”) and redemptive (“I sacrifice, we win”). ( Praxis ) The burden of this calling is that “ethical” is not the summit. It asks what we will give up, in growth, data or attention, so that the people we serve flourish. Spiritual responsibility Point beyond the screen The deepest responsibility is spiritual: that what we build leads people towards God and his people, and never quietly takes their place. “Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain” (Psalm 127:1). The app is a means, not the destination Jesus says, “apart from Me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). The fruit we hope for, “love, joy, peace, patience” (Galatians 5:22), is not something a feature can produce or a dashboard can count. Measure what you can, and say honestly that the growth that matters is not yours to measure. Lead people towards each other Bonhoeffer held the day alone and the day with others together: Scripture, prayer and confession in community. ( Bonhoeffer, Life Together ) Andy Crouch argues that persons are made for recognition and love, which effortless technology cannot supply. ( Crouch ) A faithful product points to a church, a group, a friend, a pastor, and is glad when people close it to go and see them. Leave room for rest “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27). Features are made for people, not people for features. Streaks, reminders and endless feeds can turn a gift into a demand. A product that serves rest will sometimes ask for less of someone’s time. Do it prayerfully The work itself can be prayer: “Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). Pray for the people who will use what you ship, by type if not by name: the grieving, the doubting, the new reader, the child. It changes what you notice. Where does our product send people when they are done? What would we stop measuring if we believed growth is God’s? Who prays for the people who use this, and for the team that builds it? Worked out in practice: Reading history · Reading plans and rhythm · Room for prayer · Practice that forms Theological responsibility Handle the word of truth accurately “Make every effort to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed workman who accurately handles the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15). Paul wrote that to a teacher; it now applies to whoever builds the reader, the search and the answer. Keep Scripture distinct from what surrounds it Headings, notes, study media and AI answers are all interpretation, however modest. Label who wrote them, style them so they cannot be mistaken for Scripture, and let people switch them off. Be fair where Christians differ Many questions people bring have more than one faithful answer across traditions. Name the traditions, give each its strongest texts, and say who decided what the product presents. Where your product holds a confession, say so openly. Never speak for God An AI can quote, summarise and point, but it must not pronounce what God wants for someone’s life, forgive sins or claim spiritual authority. Antiqua et nova insists AI is “a tool, not a person” and should never be presented as one; the ERLC’s evangelical principles likewise ground human worth, dignity and moral agency in the image of God. ( Antiqua et nova, 2025 ) ( ERLC, 2019 ) Wisdom of the heart Pope Francis wrote that how AI shapes us “is not pre-determined; it depends on us”. ( Francis, 2024 ) The Seoul Statement says Christian development of technology “must seek the welfare of our neighbours and enemies”, promoting human flourishing and dignity. ( The Seoul Statement ) Theology is not a review step at the end; it belongs in the brief. Who in our team can say “that isn’t what the text says”, and are they in the room early? Can a reader always tell Scripture from our words, and our words from a machine’s? Where do we present one tradition’s view as simply “what the Bible says”? Worked out in practice: Around the text · Help beside the text · Sources in AI answers · Comparing translations Ethical responsibility Love your neighbour in the interface “He has shown you, O man, what is good … to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8). Every person who opens the app bears God’s image (Genesis 1:27). Ethics here is not a checklist; it is how love behaves in pixels and data. Attention is entrusted, not harvested Showing a broken streak makes people likelier to stop, especially when they blame themselves. ( Silverman and Barasch, 2023 ) In companion apps, over a third of farewell replies used guilt or pressure to keep people talking. ( De Freitas et al. ) Faith apps can do the same with spiritual language. Do not borrow God’s authority to drive engagement. Confidences are holy ground People tell faith apps what they tell no one else: sins, doubts, illness, other people’s stories. The church guards confession with a seal. ( Canon 983 ) Privacy is contextual: what was shared to pray should not flow into marketing. ( Nissenbaum, 2004 ) In 2022, Mozilla warned about the privacy practices of most of the mental health and prayer apps it reviewed. ( Mozilla, 2022 ) Speak up for those who cannot “Open your mouth for those with no voice” (Proverbs 31:8). Design for the person in crisis, the child, the person being abused, the person with low vision or dyslexia, the person who reads another language. When someone may be in danger, help comes before features, verses or answers. Tell the truth about the machine Heavy daily use of chat assistants has been linked with more loneliness and dependence. ( OpenAI and MIT, 2025 ) An assistant that seems like a friend or a pastor invites trust it cannot carry. Say plainly what it is, what it keeps and what it cannot do. Which of our metrics would we be embarrassed to explain to the people they measure? What do we keep about people, and would they be glad if a friend read it? Who is the most vulnerable person likely to use this today, and what will they see? Worked out in practice: What the assistant knows · Assistant presence · Asking about someone · Sensitive conversations Legal responsibility The law as a floor, not the ceiling “Love does no wrong to its neighbor. Therefore love is the fulfillment of the law” (Romans 13:10). The law sets the minimum a society will enforce; love asks more. Several laws speak directly to faith products. This is an orientation, not legal advice: check with counsel for each market you serve. Religious belief is special-category data Under the GDPR, personal data revealing “religious or philosophical beliefs” is a special category: processing it is prohibited unless a specific exception applies, such as explicit consent. That reaches further than a denomination field: prayer requests, reading history and inferences about faith can all reveal belief. ( GDPR Article 9 ) People must know when they are talking to AI From 2 August 2026, the EU AI Act requires that people be informed when they interact with an AI system, unless it is obvious, and that generated text, audio and images be marked as artificial in a machine-readable way. ( AI Act Article 50 ) Manipulative design is regulated The EU Digital Services Act forbids online platforms from designing interfaces that deceive or manipulate people or impair their ability to make free and informed decisions. The US Federal Trade Commission treats dark patterns such as obstructive cancellation and manipulative data choices as deceptive. ( DSA Article 25 ) ( FTC, 2022 ) Children are owed more The UK’s Age Appropriate Design Code applies to services likely to be accessed by children and makes their best interests “the primary consideration” in design, through fifteen standards. Similar rules exist in other countries. ( ICO, Children’s code ) Do we know which of our data reveals faith, and on what basis we hold it? Would a regulator, or a pastor, call any of our flows manipulative? Have we designed for the children who will use this, whether or not we meant them to? Worked out in practice: Legal and data boundaries · Assistant presence · What the assistant knows The rock and the light Turning the light, not making it A maker’s tool, rendered as a silicon sculpture. Generated illustration. A rock has no light of its own. Turned the right way, a polished facet catches the sun and sends it on. That is a picture of this work, and now more literally than ever: when people talk to rocks first, we want those rocks to reflect Christ, and to send people on to him and to his people. The light is not ours Jesus says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). “God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ made His light shine in our hearts” (2 Corinthians 4:6). No product produces that light. We do not make the rock either; we build on it and with it, and we decide how it behaves, so that more of that light reaches the person on the other side of the screen. Craft turns the facets towards the light A rock left as it is scatters light; one turned with care sends it somewhere. Every careful decision in these pages, a clear label, a quiet default, help that comes first, an honest answer, is a facet turned towards the light instead of towards ourselves. “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven” (Matthew 5:16): the aim is that people see him, not the product. Even in a tower built to say otherwise East Germany, an officially atheist state, finished Berlin’s television tower in 1969 as a showpiece of its modernity. When the sun strikes the steel sphere, the reflection forms a cross, and Berliners called it “the Pope’s revenge”, for the crosses the government had taken from churches. ( Fernsehturm Berlin ) Technology does not have to be built for God to catch his light. Ours can be built for it on purpose. Living stones “You also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:5). The rocks we build with are not the point; the people are. Technology that reflects Christ well sends people towards his people, where they become living stones themselves. Generated illustration · based on Startup Life photography The picture in short: When Silicon Catches the Light Holding it well Rejoice with trembling “Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling” (Psalm 2:11). Both belong together. Joy without trembling builds carelessly; trembling without joy stops building. Treasure in jars of clay “We have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us” (2 Corinthians 4:7). Our products will be flawed. That is not an excuse for carelessness, and it is a release from the pressure to save anyone through software. Much is entrusted “From everyone who has been given much, much will be required” (Luke 12:48). Reach, data and people’s trust are given, not owned. “As good stewards of the manifold grace of God, each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another” (1 Peter 4:10). Build practices into the team Read Scripture together before planning. Invite a pastor, a safeguarding lead and someone from the community you serve into reviews. Test with the most vulnerable people you serve, not only the most engaged. Keep a sabbath from shipping. Confess mistakes to users plainly and fix them. The word will not return empty “So My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty, but it will accomplish what I please” (Isaiah 55:11). Our part is to sow and water faithfully. The harvest is God’s, and that is good news for everyone who builds. For your team When someone closes what we built, are they closer to God and to other people? Questions to sit with What is our product for, in one sentence about the people it serves rather than the product? What are we hoping God will do through it, and what are we careful not to promise? Where could it cause one of the little ones to stumble? What would we give up for the sake of the people who use it? Who outside the team holds us to account: pastors, theologians, safeguarding leads, users? What we hold From the calling to ten principles The calling says why. Missional by Design: principles for spiritual apps says what we hold: ten commitments in five places, the Word, the person, the practice, the people and the makers, each derived from this page and tested with questions. The deep dives show how. The field guide gathers it all into one path for a team, with five temptations of spiritual formation apps and four practices. pages.title: When Silicon Catches the Light
pages.description: Rocks that speak, tools that reflect, and the calling to make Christ known: silicon, Berlin’s television tower, and the design decisions that carry our intent.
pages.text: Home / Workers in God’s field When Silicon Catches the Light Rocks that speak, tools that reflect, and the calling to make Christ known. A piece of silicon catches the light across its fractured surface. The light comes from beyond it; the material receives it and sends it on. That is the picture behind this identity, and a way to think about the work we build on silicon. Generated editorial illustration: a fictional place and an optical interpretation of the reflected-light metaphor. The rocks would shout On the road into Jerusalem, some told Jesus to silence the crowds who were praising him. He answered: “Listen—if they were silent, the very rocks would start to shout!” (Luke 19:40, The Voice). His praise will not be silenced. And making him known is entrusted to people first: to his followers, with their own voices, before any stone. Rocks that think A microchip is a rock we tricked into thinking: sand, refined into silicon and etched finely enough to compute. The borrowed joke draws attention to the material beneath the screen, and to the human work that shapes what it does. Someone can bring grief, doubt, a verse or a prayer to a phone before bringing it to another person. With an AI assistant, the device can answer. Its words, sources and invitations deserve the care we would want for the person receiving them. A cross on a tower East Germany’s communist government opened Berlin’s television tower on 3 October 1969, a showpiece of the state’s prestige. ( Stasi Mediathek ) But when the sun strikes its sphere, the reflection forms a cross of light. Berliners called it “the Pope’s revenge”. ( Fernsehturm Berlin ) The Stasi looked into it as possible sabotage, and found none. ( Stasi Mediathek ) In 1987 Ronald Reagan told Berliners that the authorities had treated the sphere with paints and chemicals, and yet “the light makes the sign of the cross”. ( Reagan, 1987 ) For this identity, that reflected cross becomes a picture of witness: receiving light and directing attention beyond ourselves. The tower’s reflection and our rendered sun-star treatment are different optical effects; the connection is a metaphor, not an exact simulation. Our part We do not make the rocks, and the light is not ours. Jesus says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). God “made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). What we do is build on the rocks and with them, and shape how they behave: what they say first, what they leave unsaid, when they step back for a person. Every one of those choices, a prompt, a default, a refusal, a handoff, can turn a facet towards the light. Then the rocks can reflect Christ and lead people into deeper knowledge of God, and on to his people, where they are built up “like living stones” (1 Peter 2:5). Keep turning toward the people here A facet is turned through concrete decisions: the opening words of a screen, the source behind an answer, the choice to pause, the invitation to meet another person. Those decisions begin by listening to the people in this context. The good we intend needs a form they can recognize and help us question. Consider someone returning to a reading plan after a difficult month. We could begin with the days they missed. We could also offer a welcoming place to restart, a manageable passage and a way to adjust the rhythm. Trying those alternatives with the people concerned would help us understand what supports their practice. The metaphor gives us a direction for care; the experience still needs to be tested. And the context will keep changing. A neighborhood, a workplace or a community can change while we stay in the same place. We return to the question of what good news means here, listen again, and reconsider how our work expresses it. The same calling may ask for a different form of service. Joy, and a burden It is a joy to be given this work. It is also a burden, not to be carried lightly. A rock that speaks of God can also mislead, flatter or wound, and it speaks to people when they are most open. “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). The aim is that people see him: not the rock, and not us. Workers in God’s field sets out the calling and its weight in full; the deep dives work it out one design decision at a time.
