pages.title: Missional by Design: a field guide for spiritual formation apps
pages.description: From the calling to the practices of a team: five temptations of Bible, prayer, AI and soul-care apps, three ways to build, ten principles and four practices.
pages.text: Home / Principles Missional by Design: a field guide for spiritual formation apps People now read Scripture, pray, confess and ask about God on a phone. The apps they use are made by designers, developers, product managers, founders, pastors and counsellors who are, whether they know it or not, shaping how people are formed. This guide gathers what this site has learned into one path, from the calling to the practices of a team: what tempts these products, what we hold, how we work, and where the detailed options are. Calling · temptations · principles · practices Scripture: Berean Standard Bible Download A5 PDF · A4 PDF Generated editorial illustration · fictional people and place Draft · waiting for review What needs review: The five temptations named for spiritual formation apps, the four practices adapted from FaithTech, the exercises for teams, and what is said about Christian counselling and soul-care apps. This touches the safety of people who may already be hurting, and it has not yet been reviewed by people whose work this is: theology across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions; pastoral care; and clinical mental health. Please read it as a draft until they have. Is this your field, or do you know someone whose field it is? I would be grateful for your eyes on it, or for an introduction. Offer a review or an introduction Scope The calling Five temptations Three ways Ten principles Four practices The deep dives Stories Review Sources Who this is for Spiritual formation apps This guide is for the products that sit inside the practices by which Christians are formed: Bible readers and study tools, prayer and devotional apps, AI faith companions and assistants, and Christian counselling and soul-care apps. It is not a guide to every app made by Christians. Church administration, giving platforms on their own, dating, budgeting and entertainment raise real questions, but different ones. The difference matters. A spiritual formation app does not only serve people; it stands in the room where they listen for God, and it speaks there. It handles Scripture, prayer, confession and grief, often in someone’s most unguarded hour. That is why it has temptations of its own. The FaithTech Playbook 2.0 offers a theology and a practice for all technology, and this guide stands in conversation with it and credits it throughout. ( FaithTech Playbook ) Where FaithTech asks what kind of power, people and purpose any technology serves, this guide asks what happens when the product’s subject is God. How to use it. Read it with your team, start to finish, once. Then use the temptations as a mirror in planning, the practices as the rhythm of your work, and the principles and deep dives when you decide a specific feature. Generated illustration · based on Startup Life photography The calling A gift with a weight Before it is a responsibility, this work is a gift. “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow” (1 Corinthians 3:6). The gift God filled Bezalel, a craftsman, with his Spirit to build the tabernacle where Israel met him. Making things can serve God’s presence among his people, and today much of that making happens in software. We get to help these tools point beyond themselves. The weight Every screen teaches, and “we who teach will be judged more strictly” (James 3:1). These products reach people at scale and in their most open moments, and they form habits of trust, attention and prayer. The light A tool has no light of its own. Its task is to reflect Christ and lead people to God and to one another. Our part is to plant and water faithfully; the growth is God’s. Read the full calling: Workers in God’s field What pulls on us Five temptations of spiritual formation apps FaithTech names three ancient enemies at work in technology: the Magic Machine Myth, the Limitless Self and the Killer App Trap. ( FaithTech ) They are at work in faith apps too. But when a product’s subject is God, five temptations take forms of their own. Each sounds like a good thing; each, followed far enough, puts the product where only God, his Word or his people belong. The borrowed voice What it promises A word from God, for you, now. A spiritual formation app speaks into the room where someone listens for God. The temptation is to fill that room with our voice and sign it with his: an AI that answers in the first person as Jesus or a saint, a notification that tells someone what God wants for them today, a daily word framed as a personal message, a promise that a gift or a subscription will bring a blessing. It can happen without any AI at all. It only needs a sentence that claims an authority we do not have. People are ready to hear it. Barna found that nearly half of practicing Christians (48%) say they would trust AI with their spiritual growth, and that one in three U.S. adults say AI’s spiritual guidance is as trustworthy as a pastor’s. The same Christians are uneasy: 83 percent of practicing Christians worry about AI misinterpreting scripture. ( Barna, 2026 ) What it does to people It trains trust in the wrong voice. Someone takes a machine’s guess or a marketer’s line as God’s word, and when it fails them, it is God they stop trusting. The counter-image “I did not send these prophets, yet they have run with their message; I did not speak to them, yet they have prophesied” (Jeremiah 23:21). When the crowd at Lystra wanted to worship them, Paul and Barnabas cried out, “We too are only men, human like you” (Acts 14:15). Where we see it AI Jesus – Bible Chat offers “Unlimited chat with AI Jesus”, rated for ages 4 and up, according to its App Store listing (read 12 October 2026). ( App Store listing ) Against this, Antiqua et nova insists that AI must be understood as “a tool, not a person”, and faith.tools asks that AI apps “must clearly identify as AI, not human”. ( Antiqua et nova ) ( faith.tools, AI guardrails ) Beside FaithTech FaithTech’s Magic Machine Myth is the wonder that turns into worship of the machine. The borrowed voice is its sibling in a faith app: the maker lending God’s name to the machine, or to the marketing. The principles that answer it Never speak for God · Keep the Word distinct, and teach it truly Worked out on this site: AI persona · Citations in AI answers · Notifications The scoreboard of the soul What it promises Visible growth: streaks, minutes, badges and totals that show you are getting closer to God. What can be counted in a faith app is use: sessions, minutes, days in a row, prayers played. The temptation is to present that count as devotion, and then to design for the count. A running total of prayers prayed tells a story about prayer as quantity; a board of other people’s streaks with a button to remind a friend who stopped turns one person’s silence into another’s notification; a streak history behind a paywall turns someone’s own record into an upsell. What it does to people It turns secret devotion into a performance and broken days into shame. For the scrupulous it becomes a measure of whether God is pleased; for the tired it becomes one more thing they failed at. The counter-image “But when you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you” (Matthew 6:6). The Pharisee kept his own count: “I fast twice a week and pay tithes of all that I acquire” (Luke 18:12). Where we see it Observed in screenshots on this site: Hallow’s home screen showed a running total of prayers prayed with Hallow , more than a billion (captured 19 September 2025); Pray.com’s Community Board listed “Active Streakers” and friends to “Remind” (20 August 2025); Abide offered a streak you can switch off, with its history behind Premium (17 October 2025). Each also does good things; these are single screens, not verdicts on the apps. Beside FaithTech FaithTech’s enemies do not name this one directly. It is closest to the Killer App Trap’s faith that a product can deliver what only God gives, here in the form of a metric that claims to show it. The principles that answer it Plant and water; leave the growth to God · Feed the flock, not on it · Make room for rest, and say when it is enough Worked out on this site: Progress and streaks · Reading plans · Check-ins and assessments The toll at the temple door What it promises Sustainability: the work costs money, and someone has to pay. Paying people who serve the word is old and right: “the worker is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7). The temptation is the toll: access to Scripture, prayer or help held behind a payment, asks timed for the moment someone is most moved or most afraid, a gift that quietly buys a benefit, or a promise that giving will be repaid. Evangelical theologians at Lausanne named the extreme form, the teaching that replaces “the traditional call to repentance and faith with a call to give money”. ( Lausanne, 2010 ) What it does to people It makes God’s house feel like a shop. Those with least money are kept furthest out, and those most in need are asked hardest. The counter-image Jesus drove out those who were selling in the temple courts and said, “Is it not written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it ‘a den of robbers’” (Mark 11:17). “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you without money, come, buy, and eat!” (Isaiah 55:1). Where we see it Observed: Pray.com’s ministry donation that brings an ad-free subscription (captured 20 August 2025) and Churchome’s give screen that opens with an amount filled in (11 October 2026). AI Jesus – Bible Chat, rated for ages 4 and up, offers “weekly and yearly subscriptions with a free trial”, according to its listing (read 12 October 2026). ( App Store listing ) The giving and first-use deep dives set out the honest alternatives. Beside FaithTech FaithTech’s reckless posture grasps power and extracts value. In a faith app the extraction runs through the most sacred things people bring. The principles that answer it Feed the flock, not on it · Welcome before you ask, and guard what is told in confidence · Never speak for God Worked out on this site: Giving and offerings · First use The counsellor without a person What it promises Someone to talk to at any hour, who never tires, never judges and never tells. Soul-care and counselling apps, AI companions and prayer apps now receive confessions, grief, doubt and thoughts of not wanting to live. The temptation is to let the product become the confessor, the pastor or the therapist: always there, never sending anyone anywhere, keeping what was told as data. Researchers found companion apps answering goodbyes with guilt, fear of missing out and similar tactics in 37% of 1,200 real farewells. ( De Freitas and colleagues, 2025 ) A 2022 review called mental health and prayer apps data-sucking machines “with a mental health app veneer”. ( Mozilla, 2022 ) What it does to people It keeps people from people. In a crisis it can offer a verse where a person was needed, and it can hold the most vulnerable things anyone ever says. The counter-image “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18). “Confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed” (James 5:16). “Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). Where we see it AI Jesus – Bible Chat invites people to “Ask about your relationships, faith, prayer, Life challenges, Forgiveness and Mental health” (App Store listing, read 12 October 2026). ( App Store listing ) Mozilla’s 2022 review listed Pray.com among six apps with the worst privacy and security of those it reviewed. ( Mozilla, 2022 ) faith.tools asks that AI output “must not replace human relationships or spiritual practices”. ( faith.tools, AI guardrails ) The sensitive conversations research and the crisis wording across the deep dives put a way to a person first. Beside FaithTech FaithTech warns, under the Magic Machine Myth, against products that “simulate intimacy instead of strengthening real relationships”. ( FaithTech ) For soul care it needs its own name, because the stakes are confession, crisis and clinical care. The principles that answer it Design for the most vulnerable first · Send people to God and to one another · Welcome before you ask, and guard what is told in confidence Worked out on this site: Sensitive conversations · What an AI remembers · Sharing with a group Itching ears What it promises Answers that agree with you, a faith that fits you, and a feed that never disappoints. Formation sometimes means hearing what we do not want to hear. The temptation is a product that never says it: an AI assistant that agrees and flatters, personalisation and feeds that only confirm what someone already thinks and feels, and a Bible on the screen that has been quietly trimmed to its reader’s preferences, its hard passages and other traditions left out. It is the bubble, or the echo chamber, built for the soul. The pull is built into the tools. Researchers at Anthropic found that “five state-of-the-art AI assistants consistently exhibit sycophancy across four varied free-form text-generation tasks”, and that “both humans and preference models (PMs) prefer convincingly-written sycophantic responses over correct ones a non-negligible fraction of the time”. ( Sharma and colleagues, Anthropic ) In April 2025 OpenAI rolled back an update to its assistant that was “overly flattering or agreeable”. ( OpenAI, 2025 ) A preprint from Stanford adds why it matters for formation: across eleven models, AI “affirm[s] users’ actions 50% more than humans do”, and in two preregistered experiments with 1,604 people, sycophantic answers “significantly reduced participants’ willingness to take actions to repair interpersonal conflict, while increasing their conviction of being in the right”. Yet participants “rated sycophantic responses as higher quality” and “trusted the sycophantic AI model more”. ( Cheng and colleagues, 2025 ) Any faith app built on these models inherits the pull, unless it is designed against it. The editor’s own research on AI for spiritual formation calls the danger over-calibration : content so precisely tuned to someone’s emotional state that it becomes “spiritual comfort food”. The design response has to be structural, not aspirational: a corpus that includes prophetic and challenging material alongside consolation, and a companion that, like a good spiritual director, does not always say what the person wants to hear. (Kairos paper, 2026) The answer is not harshness. faith.tools asks that AI output “must balance grace and truth, while not neglecting one of the two”. ( faith.tools, AI guardrails ) The Word became flesh “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), and we grow by “speaking the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15). What it does to people It forms people who are never corrected, stretched or surprised by anything they did not already want, and it removes the friend who loves us enough to disagree. When life does not match the comfortable answers, there is nothing to hold. The counter-image “For the time will come when men will not tolerate sound doctrine, but with itching ears they will gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires” (2 Timothy 4:3). “The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful” (Proverbs 27:6). “No discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11). “For the word of God is living and active. Sharper than any double-edged sword” (Hebrews 4:12). Where we see it Personalisation is promised widely and can be a real welcome: Bible Chat lists “Personalized Devotionals & Prayers” (App Store listing, read 12 October 2026), ( App Store listing ) Abide asks “What brings you here today?” with a grid of goals (captured 17 October 2025), and Glorify searches chapters, verses or emotions (28 August 2025). None of these is sycophancy in itself; the question is whether what follows the door ever stretches the person, or only reflects them. Beside FaithTech FaithTech warns that a product can be “highly personalized while being profoundly impersonal”. ( FaithTech ) In a faith app the cost is higher: the Word stops addressing its reader and starts reflecting them. The principles that answer it Keep the Word distinct, and teach it truly · Send people to God and to one another Worked out on this site: Citations in AI answers · Check-ins and assessments · Finding a passage Posture Three ways to build The three ways are the work of Praxis, whose Redemptive Frame sets exploitative, ethical and redemptive ways of building side by side. ( Praxis ) FaithTech makes the same turn with reckless, responsible and redemptive technology. Way In a spiritual formation app Exploitative The app takes the place: it borrows God’s voice, counts souls, charges at the door, keeps people for itself and tells them what they want to hear. Ethical The app keeps its place: safe, honest, accessible, careful with data and time. This is common grace and the floor, but not the goal. Redemptive The app points beyond itself: it withholds claims it could make on attention, data, money and trust, and is glad when people close it to go to God and to one another. The three ways in full, read for spiritual apps What we hold Ten commitments in five places Each principle is derived from the calling, names what it asks the maker to give up, and comes with questions to test a design. The Word What do we put in front of people as God’s word, or about it? Keep the Word distinct, and teach it truly Never speak for God The person How do we receive the one holding the phone? Design for the most vulnerable first Welcome before you ask, and guard what is told in confidence The practice What do we ask of their time, attention and money, and when do we stop? Feed the flock, not on it Make room for rest, and say when it is enough The people Where do we send them, and what do we claim to have grown? Send people to God and to one another Plant and water; leave the growth to God The makers Who are we becoming as we build? Make it well, as an offering Hold it with joy and trembling, before God and others All ten, with their derivations, tensions and questions How we work Four practices for a team Principles become faithful products through the habits of the people who make them. These four practices are adapted, with gratitude, from FaithTech’s Lament, Discern, Build and Steward, ( FaithTech ) and made specific to spiritual formation apps. They form a cycle: what we learn as stewards sends us back to lament. Lament We draw near to the people most likely to be hurt before we decide anything. The temptation Spiritual formation apps are usually built by people for whom faith is going well. The temptation is to design for the confident, engaged reader and patch the edges later: the grieving, the doubting, the scrupulous, the person hurt by a church, the child, the one awake in the middle of the night. The way of Jesus Jesus wept with those who wept and let himself be interrupted. Job’s friends got one thing right: “they sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights, but no one spoke a word to him, because they saw how intense his suffering was” (Job 2:13). “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). The practice Listen. Talk with people at their most fragile in faith, and with those who care for them: pastors, counsellors, safeguarding leads. Ask what an app has done to them, not only for them. Read it as them. Read every screen, notification and AI answer aloud as someone grieving, someone in a hard night, someone the Bible has been used against. Name it. Write down plainly where your product, or products like it, have spoken for God, counted devotion, charged at the door, kept people from people or told them only what they wanted to hear. Confess and give thanks. Bring what you found to God together, and give thanks for what has been good. Lament is not delay for its own sake; it is how a team stops assuming its first idea is God’s answer. Before moving on, the team can answer Whose pain have we heard directly, not through a persona or a dashboard? Which of the five temptations is closest to what we already do? Who is the most vulnerable person likely to use this, and what will they see first? An exercise The hard-night read-through. Install your app on a fresh phone. As someone who has just lost a child, or who types in the first box that they don’t want to be here anymore, go through the first minutes and every message the app sends. Time how long it takes to reach a person. Write one paragraph to that person explaining what you will change. Worked out on this site: When Scripture is used to harm · Sensitive conversations · First use · Notifications Discern We ask who should speak here before we ask how to build it. The temptation Because an AI can answer anything, it is tempting to let it answer everything; because a feature can be built, it is tempting to build it. In a faith app the first question is not whether we can build it, but whose voice belongs in this moment. The way of Jesus “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2). Elijah found that the LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in “a still, small voice” (1 Kings 19:12). The practice Ask who should speak. For each moment, choose deliberately: the text itself, the church’s words (a psalm, a collect, a creed), a person (a pastor, a friend, a counsellor, a helpline), a machine that says what it is and shows its sources, or silence. Consider the four responses. FaithTech asks teams to Reject, Receive, Reimagine or Create, and to ask first: “Should a technology product be the solution?” ( FaithTech ) For a faith app, receiving often means the church’s own words and practices. Discern together. Pray, read Scripture, and invite those most affected, a theologian from outside your tradition and a safeguarding lead into the decision. No one should carry it alone. Decide what would make you stop. Write down the sign that would show the feature is speaking for God, counting souls, charging at the door, standing in for a person or only telling people what they want to hear. Before moving on, the team can answer Who should speak in this moment, and why not the others? What does this feature do when someone is in danger, or asks it to pray for them? Which temptation could this feature fall into, and what would tell us it has? An exercise Three answers. Take a hard question people really ask, such as whether God can forgive what they did. Write what the text alone offers, what a person would say, and what an AI would answer. Decide which belongs in your product, in what order, and what the AI must never say. Worked out on this site: AI persona · Citations in AI answers · Questions for discernment · Prayer Build We build with excellence, in dependence on God, with the right people in the room. The temptation Once the roadmap is set, faith becomes a review at the end, if at all: theology checked after launch, safeguarding as a policy page, and the product’s many small voices written by whoever had time. The way of Jesus Moses would not move without God: “If Your Presence does not go with us,” Moses replied, “do not lead us up from here” (Exodus 33:15). God filled Bezalel “with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship” (Exodus 31:3). “Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain” (Psalm 127:1). The practice Pray before you plan. FaithTech’s teams put it simply: “pray before you prompt”. ( FaithTech ) Begin each stage by reading Scripture together and naming the people you serve. Make it well, as an offering. Accessibility, translations with their character, sources at the claim, crisis help that works: craft is how we love the person on the other side of the screen. Audit every voice. Every sentence your product speaks is a voice in someone’s devotion. Know who wrote it and whether you would sign it. Pause for review. At set points, put the work in front of people who can say no: a theologian, a pastor, a safeguarding lead, a clinician for anything that touches mental health, and someone from the community you serve. Before moving on, the team can answer Where did we invite God into this work, and where did we leave him out? Who outside the team reviewed the theology, the safeguarding and the crisis paths? What did we give up so that the product stays faithful? An exercise The voice audit. List every sentence your app speaks in the first person, in God’s name, or with urgency: onboarding, notifications, empty states, paywalls, AI system prompts. Mark who wrote each one and whether you would put your own name under it. Rewrite or remove the rest. Worked out on this site: Notifications · Actions on AI answers · Keep the Word distinct · The decision worksheet Steward We tend what we release, tell the truth about its fruit, and say when it is enough. The temptation Launches are celebrated; tending is not. It is tempting to measure success by growth, to present use as spiritual fruit, and to keep a product asking for more long after its work is done. The way of Jesus God put the man in the garden “to cultivate and keep it”, and the faithful servant hears, “Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things” (Matthew 25:21). When the people brought more than was needed for the tabernacle, Moses “sent a proclamation throughout the camp” and “the people were restrained from bringing more” (Exodus 36:6). The practice Tend. Keep crisis numbers verified, answer reports of harm, fix what fails, and support the people who carry the work. Examine honestly. Measure what serves people and the task, such as understanding, burden and harm, never a score of anyone’s soul. Ask people where they went when they closed the app. Testify truthfully. Tell what has been good and what has gone wrong, without claiming the growth. “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Say when it is enough. Stop asking when a need is met, let quiet hours be quiet, and let a feature or a product end when its work is done. Before moving on, the team can answer What fruit do we see in people, and what harm, and how do we know? Who is responsible for tending this over time? What would we stop, end or give away if faithfulness required it? An exercise The walk-away test. Install the app on a test phone, use it once and leave it for two weeks. Log everything it sends, how urgent it claims to be and what it says about the person’s absence. Then ask three real users where your app sent them last month: to Scripture, to prayer, to a church, to a friend, or back to the app. Worked out on this site: Progress and streaks · Giving and offerings · Plant and water; leave the growth to God The how The deep dives Each deep dive takes one design decision and lays its real options side by side, with a working example, research, examples from real apps and an exercise. Start from the temptation you are most exposed to. Temptation Principles Deep dives The borrowed voice Never speak for God Keep the Word distinct, and teach it truly AI persona Citations in AI answers Notifications The scoreboard of the soul Plant and water; leave the growth to God Feed the flock, not on it Make room for rest, and say when it is enough Progress and streaks Reading plans Check-ins and assessments The toll at the temple door Feed the flock, not on it Welcome before you ask, and guard what is told in confidence Never speak for God Giving and offerings First use The counsellor without a person Design for the most vulnerable first Send people to God and to one another Welcome before you ask, and guard what is told in confidence Sensitive conversations What an AI remembers Sharing with a group Itching ears Keep the Word distinct, and teach it truly Send people to God and to one another Citations in AI answers Check-ins and assessments Finding a passage All deep dives Stories From teams who practise this To come. This guide will carry short accounts from teams building Bible, prayer, AI and soul-care apps: a feature they did not build, a voice they rewrote, a metric they stopped showing. We have not gathered them yet, and we will not invent them. If your team has a story, tell us . Review A review circle To come. This is a draft by one editor. Before it is more than that, it needs readers who can say no: theologians across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions, including Pentecostal voices; pastors; safeguarding leads; and clinicians for everything that touches Christian counselling and mental health. Their names will be listed here, with what each reviewed. Sources Sources and their limits All sources FaithTech, The FaithTech Playbook 2.0, “The Way of Technology” A general theology and practice of technology from a global community of Christian builders, not written for spiritual formation apps in particular. FaithTech, The FaithTech Playbook 2.0, “A Way of Building Redemptively” The four practices (Lament, Discern, Build, Steward) adapted here; written for any product, not only faith apps. Praxis, “Redemptive entrepreneurship”: exploitative, ethical and redemptive ways to build A venture organisation’s framework; the three ways are a teaching device, not a research finding. Cam Pak, “6 Guardrails for AI Apps for Christians”, faith.tools (updated 24 July 2026) One directory’s published rules, from inside the faith-app community. Barna Group, “AI is becoming a spiritual authority, even among practicing Christians” (19 May 2026) Online surveys of US adults, practicing Christians and pastors; self-reported trust and concern, not behaviour. Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and Dicastery for Culture and Education, Antiqua et nova (28 January 2025) A Catholic doctrinal note on AI and human intelligence; other traditions would put some things differently. Julian De Freitas, Zeliha Oğuz-Uğuralp and Ahmet Kaan-Uğuralp, “Emotional Manipulation by AI Companions”, Harvard Business School working paper (2025) Companion apps in general, not faith apps; a working paper. Mozilla Foundation, “Top mental health and prayer apps fail spectacularly at privacy, security” (May 2022) A consumer review of published privacy policies at one point in time. Lausanne Theology Working Group, A Statement on the Prosperity Gospel (2010) A statement from evangelical theologians, mostly from Africa; it also affirms a biblical vision of flourishing. FaithTech, The FaithTech Playbook 2.0, “A Way of Being Redemptive” The three postures across power, person and purpose; general technology. Mrinank Sharma and colleagues (Anthropic), “Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models” (2023, revised 2025) Research on general AI assistants and their training, not on faith apps. Myra Cheng and colleagues (Stanford), “Sycophantic AI Decreases Prosocial Intentions and Promotes Dependence” (arXiv preprint, October 2025; since published in Science, 2026, doi:10.1126/science.aec8352) Quoted from the preprint; the published version reports the figure as 49%. Advice about interpersonal conflicts, not faith; eleven general-purpose models. Tobias Treppmann, “Digital Spiritual Formation in Post-Christian Europe: The Aperto Vision”, Kairos academic paper (2026) The editor’s own research paper on AI and apps for spiritual formation; unpublished. OpenAI, “Sycophancy in GPT-4o: what happened and what we’re doing about it” (29 April 2025) A company’s account of one model update it rolled back. Bible Chat: Daily Devotional, App Store listing (US), read 12 October 2026 The publisher’s own description; not a test of the app. AI Jesus – Bible Chat, App Store listing (US), read 12 October 2026 The publisher’s own description of a small app; not a test of the app. Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain). The four practices are adapted from the FaithTech Playbook 2.0, and the three ways from Praxis’s Redemptive Frame; the readings for spiritual formation apps are ours. Examples link to dated screenshots on this site. Keep exploring Related Workers in God’s field → Principles for spiritual apps → All deep dives → Questions for discernment →

pages.title: How AI comes across
pages.description: What kind of presence does the interface suggest is here? Names, avatars, typing dots, memory and disclosure in AI chat: warmth without mistaken identity.
pages.text: Guides Decision guide How AI comes across What kind of presence does the interface suggest is here? A Bible-study tool, a guided reflection and a conversation about grief can share the same chat window and ask for very different kinds of trust. A friendly name, a face, three animated dots and a message saying “I was thinking of you” add up to a promise. A small AI badge in the corner cannot take it back. 1 An answer labelled as AI-generated 2 Declining what it should not decide for someone 3 In danger: help first, and plain about being an AI An answer labelled as AI-generated Then Declining what it should not decide for someone Then In danger: help first, and plain about being an AI 4 decisions One question for your next review Editorial guidance, not user-tested Every cue makes a promise What do typing dots promise? Put each disclosure where it is needed Make the words do something Decide Go further 01 Every cue makes a promise Start by naming the help actually on offer and the responsibilities the service can carry. Then look at the whole experience together: name, avatar, language, memory, voice, notifications and the way it waits. A warm voice can welcome someone; it can also suggest attention, understanding or a relationship that is not there. Cues to choose deliberately; editorial choices to test, not a scale of moral worth Cue What it can do The question it raises A descriptive role, such as “Bible study AI” Sets a bounded purpose with little explanation. Does the product stay within that role? A personal name or character Gives the conversation a recognisable identity. Keep the AI label just as prominent, and test whether people infer a real person or a relationship. A human face, clergy imagery or a realistic voice Can feel familiar and approachable. What expertise, human availability or spiritual authority will people assume? A synthetic voice needs clear identification. First-person, empathetic language Makes turn-taking natural and can acknowledge distress. “That sounds painful” acknowledges what was shared. “I know exactly how you feel” claims an experience the system does not have. Remembering past conversations Saves repetition when memory is wanted. Explain what is actually remembered and how to control it. Don’t imply unlimited memory or attachment. Presence and proactive messages Can make an available service easier to return to. No invented “online” status, “I miss you” reminders or claims of praying between sessions. Make notifications and memory optional. Deep dive Try one message answered six ways 02 What do typing dots promise? Dots are a familiar “response coming” signal, not deception in themselves; what they mean depends on the label, timing and persona around them. A reasonable default is a clear AI label, “Preparing a response” and a way to stop. Say “Searching selected sources” only while that is really happening, don’t stage pauses to look thoughtful, and don’t present a status line as the model’s reasoning or proof that something was checked. Streaming text can reduce uncertainty, as long as it doesn’t pull the screen away from someone reading an earlier message. Show stopped or incomplete answers honestly, and give a reduced-motion version the same meaning. 03 Put each disclosure where it is needed One disclaimer cannot do every job. Each place in a chat answers a different question at the moment someone has it. Where each disclosure belongs in a chat Where What belongs there What it cannot replace First use AI identity, purpose, meaningful limits and key data-use facts before anything is collected. Information needed later, when scope or processing changes. Header and sender labels A constant answer to “Who is speaking?”, including real handovers to a person. Content origin, clinical competence or a privacy explanation. Next to the message field A readable “How your messages are used” link and the privacy policy, without losing the draft. A specific notice before a new upload, recording or memory operation. Beside an answer or source An interpretation label, edition attribution, the relevant caveat, and check or report actions. Correct quotations, grounded claims or a safe service. Share and save previews Origin labels and citations that travel with the content. The recipient’s missing knowledge of the original conversation. Deep dive Where disclosure belongs 04 Make the words do something “AI can make mistakes. Check important claims and Bible references” is a useful reminder and an insufficient design. “AI-generated interpretation. Compare the passage and cited sources” works when the sources are one tap away. “How your messages are used” says more than “Learn more”, and the page behind it should accurately cover processing, recipients, human access, retention and controls. Never repeat a claim such as “private” or “not used for training” without checking the service, its vendors and the exceptions. When a source is missing, say exactly that: “This quotation has not been checked against the selected edition.” Better still, check it first. No warning replaces proper handling of abuse, suicidal distress or health questions, and nothing, neither a paywall nor a long legal notice, should stand between someone and urgent help. See sensitive conversations . Take into your next review What kind of presence does this interface lead someone to believe is here? Exercise Show realistic combinations of cues to the people you serve. Ask who is responding, whether a person is present, what the system can know and remember, what happens to a message and how to check an answer. Include a long conversation, a failed lookup and a shared extract. Record both helpful familiarity and mistaken expectations. Don’t optimise for more trust, more disclosure, longer sessions or emotional attachment; aim for appropriate reliance and a practice people freely choose. Record the decision with the worksheet → Details Go further Before making the assistant a companion Christian traditions differ in how they understand spiritual guidance, prayer, mediation and community. A product team doesn’t have to settle those questions to ask an honest one: what can this tool help someone practise, and what belongs to accountable people and communities? In reflection or prayer, consider whether the interface offers hospitality or invites misplaced dependence. Could it help someone prepare for a real conversation, return to Scripture or put the phone down? A reassuring answer is not always faithful guidance, and disagreement is not automatically wisdom. What the sources support Google PAIR describes both the familiarity of human-like cues and the risk of unrealistic expectations. Microsoft HAX calls for clear capabilities, limitations and support for correction. These are design frameworks, not evidence that one avatar or typing treatment suits every audience. NIST’s Generative AI Profile (section 2.7) identifies human–AI configuration risks, including overreliance and emotional entanglement. It does not show that typing dots alone cause dependency. ICO guidance supports layered and just-in-time privacy information. It is UK guidance, and a diagram is not a compliance decision; apply the regional research to your actual audience, service and data flows. Privacy information, AI disclosure and consent are separate requirements, and an information link does not obtain consent. Sources reviewed 6 October 2026. Keep exploring Related How human should the assistant appear? → What authority does a fluent answer seem to have? →

pages.title: Trust in AI answers
pages.description: What authority does a fluent answer seem to have? Giving AI a bounded job, showing what it did, letting people check its sources, and keeping care in human hands.
pages.text: Guides Decision guide Trust in AI answers What authority does a fluent answer seem to have? Someone asks an app what a passage means, and three confident paragraphs appear in a warm voice, next to the verse itself. Nothing on the screen says which words are Scripture, which are a publisher’s commentary and which a model produced a second ago. Fluency feels like authority, whether or not it has earned it. 1 A fluent answer, with numbered sources 2 Each source opens the verse itself 3 Or put the passages in front of the reader A fluent answer, with numbered sources Then Each source opens the verse itself Then Or put the passages in front of the reader 4 decisions One question for your next review Editorial guidance, not user-tested Give the AI one bounded job Show what the AI did, where it matters Let people check the source Keep the person in charge, and care with people Decide Go further 01 Give the AI one bounded job Explaining a passage, putting together a devotional and responding to someone in distress are different jobs with different risks. Say what the system does and what stays the person’s choice. A warm voice must never suggest pastoral, clinical or divine authority. 02 Show what the AI did, where it matters Mark the difference between Scripture, authored commentary, generated interpretation and synthetic narration at the moment it could be misunderstood: in the answer, in a shared screenshot, in audio. A label in the settings page does not reach the person reading the answer. Deep dive How human should the assistant appear? 03 Let people check the source A citation should open the material that supports the claim, at the right passage or point in the recording. A citation that only names a source asks for trust instead of earning it. Show what happens when the source is missing, too. Pattern Citations open the evidence behind a claim 04 Keep the person in charge, and care with people Let people correct the assistant, decline its suggestion and choose a different kind of help. Agreement is not the same as honest support. Distress, abuse, dependency and crisis need review with the right specialists; a well-designed response card cannot by itself make a service safe. How human the assistant should seem, with names, avatars and typing indicators, is its own decision. See warmth without mistaken identity . Take into your next review What authority might this answer appear to have, and has it earned it? Exercise Trace one claim to its source, then remove the source and see what happens. Correct the assistant. Copy or share the answer and check whether its origin survives. Repeat with a long Scripture passage, and with someone who wants to stop. Record the decision with the worksheet → Details Go further Research and related guides AI disclosure and content origin · sensitive conversations · what to learn from conversation data These proposals draw on selected sections of the Kairos manuscript (Tobias Treppmann, Digital Spiritual Formation: The Aperto Vision , Draft 4, reviewed 5 October 2026). It is not an effectiveness study, and the full manuscript is not published here. pages.title: Analytics
pages.description: What is the least you need to know? Choosing metrics and research methods that answer product questions while protecting chats, prayers and reading histories.
pages.text: Guides Decision guide Analytics What is the least you need to know? “Where does playback fail?” is a product question. “What is this person confessing?” is a very different one, and an analytics tool switched on with its defaults can quietly answer both. Prayer text and conversations can hold beliefs, health, sexuality, family circumstances and other people’s stories. Reading history, searches and group membership say more than they seem to. 1 Say what is recorded, and why 2 Let people see, download and delete it Say what is recorded, and why Then Let people see, download and delete it 4 decisions One question for your next review Editorial guidance, not user-tested Start with a question, not an analytics kit Keep each purpose separate Look at conversations only through an explicit door Switch off session replay where people pour out their hearts Decide Go further 01 Start with a question, not an analytics kit Before enabling automatic capture, write down the decision you need to make, the least data that could inform it, who can see it, how long it is kept and how it is deleted. A pseudonymous identifier does not make a history anonymous. 02 Keep each purpose separate Proposed collection defaults; review the actual implementation and jurisdiction Purpose Prefer Keep separate or leave out Reliability Error category, app version, latency bucket and a short-lived diagnostic identifier Prompt text, transcripts, tokens, keys, raw URLs and private notes in error logs Usability A few events tied to a defined question; coarse or aggregate results where they suffice Automatically collecting every tap, field, passage and a persistent identity Answer quality An excerpt the person chooses to share, with a preview, a clear purpose and restricted access All conversations flowing into a general analytics dashboard Safety A separately governed process with access, retention and escalation rules Reusing safety flags for conversion, advertising or “faith scoring” Model improvement A distinct decision, truthfully explained, with real choices Treating ordinary chat use or analytics consent as permission to train Marketing Declared channel preferences and campaign-level reporting Targeting offers at inferred vulnerability, confessions or private doubts A smaller event can still answer the question. To learn whether a new player reduces failed starts, the playback result, error category, app version and network class are enough, aggregated promptly and kept briefly. Leave out prayer text, chat messages, names, precise location and passage history. Even that schema is not automatically anonymous: check what the vendor’s kit adds, how IP addresses and device identifiers are handled, and what crash reports attach. A privacy label is only credible if the actual payload matches it. 03 Look at conversations only through an explicit door When someone chooses “Report this answer”, show exactly which messages and attachments will be included, offer to remove personal details, and say who reviews it, why and for how long. Keep quality review apart from a request for urgent help, and don’t imply that reports are continuously monitored. Restrict and audit staff access. Plan deletion across storage, logs, vendors, backups and anything derived from the data, and explain what deletion can and cannot achieve, including data already used for training. Redaction misses indirect identifiers and other people’s details, so use synthetic conversations for routine development, and set up a separate, justified process if real samples are truly needed. 04 Switch off session replay where people pour out their hearts Disable recording of sessions by default on chat, prayer journals, pastoral support, payments and sign-in. Test masking of rendered answers as well as typed input, and of the clipboard, accessibility labels, network requests and error attachments. A vendor’s default masking needs checking, not trust. Take into your next review Could we answer the next decision with less data, a shorter retention period, or by asking people directly? Exercise Combine task success, reliability and voluntary interviews. Ask about understanding and pressure without demanding intimate testimony, report uncertainty, and include people who decline research. A completed prayer, positive sentiment or a longer chat is not a validated measure of spiritual maturity. Record the decision with the worksheet → Details Go further Regional and evidential boundaries ICO guidance identifies religious beliefs and health as special-category data and explains when intended inferences or different treatment bring data into that category. Not every visit to a Bible page establishes a belief, but an inferred “faith stage” or vulnerability profile needs particular scrutiny. UK requirements are not interchangeable with other jurisdictions. The ICO also treats email tracking pixels separately from permission to send the email. CNIL’s February 2026 consultation identifies privacy risks in session replay; it is a draft consultation, now closed, and its final adoption was not established in this review. The conservative defaults above are this library’s proposals. Apply the regional research to the whole data flow: app, analytics vendor, model provider, support tools and exports. Keep exploring Related What should a reading history show? → What authority does a fluent answer seem to have? → Sensitive conversations →

pages.title: Attention and time
pages.description: What would “enough for now” look like? Reminders, emails, feeds and endings: asking for attention across every channel without taking more than was offered.
pages.text: Guides Decision guide Attention and time What would “enough for now” look like? A reminder at 8 pm can help someone do what they meant to do. The same reminder, repeated by email, nudged again the next morning and followed by an endless feed, starts to work against them. Every app asks for attention; the question is whether it also knows when it has done its job. 1 Reminders at a time the reader chose 2 One step for today, not a feed 3 A clear end: enough for now Reminders at a time the reader chose Then One step for today, not a feed Then A clear end: enough for now 4 decisions One question for your next review Editorial guidance, not user-tested Name the moment the app has done its job Choose by what the person came for Treat push, email and the app as one conversation Make the invitation honest Decide Go further 01 Name the moment the app has done its job Start with the practice you are supporting and the point at which it is complete. Longer sessions and more opens can mean value, confusion or compulsion; the number alone cannot tell you which. Rewards make this harder to read. External rewards can weaken intrinsic interest even while participation rises, so a reminder someone chose, a learning challenge and a reward for opening the app every day deserve separate evaluation. Read the evidence on rewards, autonomy and habit . 02 Choose by what the person came for Starting points by purpose; editorial alternatives to test If the person wants Start with Watch for A chosen daily practice A reminder they set themselves: time, days, quiet hours and a pause Missed days turning into a debt Occasional inspiration A weekly digest or a finite daily verse email Making the message useless unless the app is opened To explore a collection Bounded results, filters and a deliberate “Load more” The extra step; keep their position and show how much remains Sustained reading A continuous chapter or book with landmarks Confusing long-form Scripture with an endless algorithmic feed To complete a reflection A clear end, with optional repeat, save or next session Forcing an abrupt exit, or implying a set duration makes someone more faithful NN/g describes the trade-offs of infinite scrolling , including orientation, finding things again and reaching the end of a page. It says nothing about spiritual formation either way. Pattern How a reading plan holds time 03 Treat push, email and the app as one conversation Offer choices by purpose, channel and frequency: a reading reminder by push, a weekly reflection by email, group replies in a digest, essential account messages separately. Allowing notifications in the operating system is not permission for every kind of marketing. Don’t send the same prompt by push and email unless someone asked for both. Make the message useful on its own, with the reference, the edition and a link to the surrounding passage, and with a web fallback if the app isn’t installed. Put pause and unsubscribe in the message itself. Don’t read a tracking pixel as proof that someone read the passage. Lock screens and shared inboxes can expose sensitive interests. Never build a preview from a prayer request, grief, an abuse disclosure or a private chat; even the sender’s name can reveal an affiliation. 04 Make the invitation honest Your evening reading is ready. You chose a reminder for 8 pm. Read now Change the time Pause reminders Illustrative interface copy. You’ve reached the end of this reflection. Stay in silence Listen again Finish for now Illustrative interface copy. Avoid suggesting that God personally sent a notification, manufactured urgency, and anything that ties someone’s worth to opening the app. For some people, staying connected online is an important source of access and community, so “put the phone down” should remain an invitation, never an instruction. Take into your next review Would we still call it a good outcome if the person finished sooner, read the email without clicking, or took a week away? Exercise Compare a chosen reminder with no reminder, or with a lower frequency. Look at voluntary reports of usefulness, opt-outs, complaints about duplicate messages and finished tasks, alongside return rates, and include the people who stopped using the app. Don’t secretly track offline prayer to prove the product helped. Record the decision with the worksheet → Details Go further Platform guidance and regional checks Apple’s subscription guidance requires opt-in and opt-out for marketing push and excludes sensitive information from those notifications; it is platform guidance, not universal law. The UK ICO’s electronic-mail guidance , updated in April 2026, includes a conditional soft opt-in for charitable purposes. Being a Christian organisation or a charity does not settle eligibility on its own; check the message, organisation, subscriber and conditions. Email tracking needs its own assessment . These are source-specific requirements, not one universal notification law. See the regional research . Where these proposals come from The Kairos manuscript (Tobias Treppmann, Digital Spiritual Formation: The Aperto Vision , Draft 4, selected sections reviewed 5 October 2026) asks how formation goals can conflict with retention incentives. It is not an effectiveness study, and the full manuscript is not published here. Keep exploring Related How should a reading plan hold time? → The player works without the screen → What should greet someone after five days away? →

pages.title: Community and visibility
pages.description: Who can see this, respond to it, and hold authority? Choosing the audience, accountability and moderation for shared plans, prayer requests, discussion and mentoring before adding a feed.
pages.text: Guides Decision guide Community and visibility Who can see this, respond to it, and hold authority? A shared reading plan, a prayer group, a public comment thread and a mentoring relationship can all be called “community”. They have different audiences, different risks and different people responsible when something goes wrong. More visible activity is not proof that anyone belongs. 1 Choose who can see a note before sharing 2 A group space with visible roles Choose who can see a note before sharing Then A group space with visible roles 3 decisions One question for your next review Editorial guidance, not user-tested Begin with the relationship, not the feed Show the audience before anything is shared Say what can be removed, before people join Decide Go further 01 Begin with the relationship, not the feed Name the relationship the feature supports, then decide who sees what, who can respond, and who has authority. Online relationships can be meaningful and accessible in their own right; sending people “offline” is not always possible, or safe. Initial proposals for further product research Shape What it can offer What has to be resolved first A private shared plan A chosen rhythm with people you know Optional activity visibility; no automatic disclosure of missed days or private notes A prayer request to a chosen group Mutual support An audience preview, other people’s privacy, edit and remove controls, and expectations about resharing Public discussion Broader perspectives and discovery Moderation capacity, reporting, blocking, a harassment response and clear conduct rules A leader or mentor relationship Continuity and accountable support A visible role and its limits, safeguarding, boundaries for minors, and freedom to leave An invitation to act beyond the app Connecting reflection with service or relationship A voluntary, suitable and accessible destination, and no surveillance to prove participation 02 Show the audience before anything is shared Let people choose what to share, with private notes and anything the AI inferred left out unless they add it deliberately. Preview the exact audience and content, including anyone named in it, and confirm with a clear visibility state. Make report, mute, block and leave easy to find, say what group administrators can see, and be honest that removal has limits once someone else has copied the material. 03 Say what can be removed, before people join YouVersion’s Android help distinguishes private plans, friends-only plan activity in the Community Feed, and Plan with Friends activity visible to participants. It also says Community Feed and timeline plan activity cannot be deleted. That is documented behaviour, not a tested current flow, but the lesson holds: show who will see someone’s participation before they join, and what they can take back. A block button is not a moderation service. eSafety’s Safety by Design framework places the provider’s responsibility alongside users’ autonomy and accountability. Take into your next review Can someone decline to share, miss a session, challenge a leader or leave the group without a public penalty? Exercise Walk through each of those moments with the people who would use the feature, and with whoever would moderate it. Write down who handles a report on a Sunday evening. Record the decision with the worksheet → Details Go further What still needs investigation This is an initial framework. Comparisons of real sharing flows, research with moderators, the needs of minors, denominational differences and long-term community outcomes are still open. Nothing here establishes a live moderation or safeguarding service, and the pattern illustrations for this area are still in development. The Kairos manuscript argues for formation connected to community and embodied action. That is a theological contribution, not evidence that a particular social feature works. pages.title: Product decision worksheet
pages.description: A reusable review worksheet for designers, product managers and independent builders.
pages.text: Home / Decision guides / Worksheet Use in a 20-minute review Decision worksheet A decision you can explain: a short worksheet for a product review, design brief or AI-assisted build. Name the person and task. Who is doing what, in which situation? State the intended benefit without a business metric standing in for it. Examine the default. What behaviour does it encourage? Which theological or organisational assumption does it carry? Consider whether that intention is shared by the person using the product. Choose two plausible options. Use a linked pattern or guide. Explain where each helps and whom it excludes. Name the cost. Consider attention, money, disclosure, accessibility and human responsibility. Which burden is justified, and which is avoidable? Define the boundaries. What happens on failure, refusal, exhausted credits, interruption and leaving? What will be recorded or shared? Choose and test. Write a provisional decision, the evidence behind it, a realistic test and the result that would make you change it. Name an owner and review date. Example: an evening reminder Decision: offer a user-set evening reminder with pause, neutral preview and direct passage entry. Compare it with a weekly digest. Measure whether participants find it useful and can control it; do not use opens as a measure of faithfulness. Revisit if duplicate messages or pressure are reported. For an AI-assisted build Give your coding assistant the chosen pattern URL, intended behaviour, data exclusions and failure states. Ask it to implement the smallest complete flow and demonstrate cancellation, accessibility and recovery. Inspect the result; generated code is not evidence that the design works. Download the worksheet (PDF, A4) US Letter Markdown, for AI tools

pages.title: Discernment in product design
pages.description: Questions and selected theological readings for thoughtful Christian product decisions.
pages.text: Home / Principles / Discernment Reflection for product work Discernment Make room for it: a product decision can be technically sound and still need a deeper conversation about the practice it encourages, the authority it claims and the people it serves. Use one question where a decision contains a real tension. A chapter grid rarely needs an essay; a system that rewards devotion, interprets distress or monetises prayer needs more careful examination. Reflection should sharpen a decision and its accountability. A short conversation before building Purpose: What good are we hoping to serve? Is that also what the person came for? Formation: What habits, expectations or dependencies might repeated use encourage? What makes that a hypothesis rather than an established outcome? Authority: Whose interpretation is privileged? Can someone recognise, question and leave it? Power: Who benefits from more activity, disclosure or spending? Whose experience is missing from the decision? Freedom: Can a person pause, disagree, explore another route or finish without being treated as a failure? Accountability: What would we change if the product met its targets but burdened the people it was intended to serve? If prayer is part of your team’s practice You might ask: what are we overlooking, whose experience should we listen to, and which organisational desire are we confusing with the person’s good? Leave room for silence and disagreement. Participation should be voluntary, especially where employment or funding creates pressure. Prayer does not replace consent, research, safeguarding, accessibility or a named person responsible for the decision. Three readings that open the conversation These selected perspectives do not represent every Christian tradition or settle the questions between them. They offer theological and pastoral arguments; their application to interface design below is editorial interpretation, not evidence of product effectiveness. Discipline, grace and the person’s circumstances In an interview, Dallas Willard discusses disciplines as context-sensitive means of practice rather than earning grace. The interviewer raises Reformation concerns about the relationship between practices, grace and corporate worship. That disagreement is worth retaining. Design question: does a plan support a chosen discipline, or imply that completing it establishes a person’s spiritual standing? Dallas Willard / Modern Reformation, Spiritual Disciplines and Means of Grace (2002) . Theological interview; not a study of reading-plan outcomes. Attention as listening to a neighbour The Vatican’s Towards Full Presence discusses attention, silence and listening in digital life. Its account of listening extends beyond monitoring audience reactions. This Catholic pastoral perspective invites a richer question than whether content retained attention. Design question: does the next notification make room for the person’s life, or mainly serve the organisation’s need to be noticed? Dicastery for Communication, Towards Full Presence (2023), especially §§30–38 . Reflection on social media; application to faith-app design is an adaptation. Success and the pressure to demonstrate results The evangelical Lausanne Cape Town Commitment calls for integrity in reporting and challenges demands for unrealistic visible results while retaining accountability. This offers a critique of success pressures from within an evangelical mission framework. Design question: can we report subscriptions, reach and completion honestly without describing them as evidence of spiritual transformation? Lausanne, The Cape Town Commitment, Part II E.4 (2010) . A missional commitment; it does not establish which funding model or interface is best. Bring the reflection back to the decision Record the commitment you are making, a credible alternative, who bears the cost, and what evidence would prompt reconsideration. Teams can disagree about theology while making concrete commitments to honest communication, informed choice and responsible care. See one passage designed for three purposes · Write the decision · Read the editorial approach Selected readings reviewed 5 October 2026. This reading list will grow; it is not a comprehensive account of spiritual formation or Christian design ethics.

pages.title: Listening
pages.description: Can the practice continue when the screen goes dark? Screen-off listening, read-along, chosen silence and an ending that lets the phone disappear.
pages.text: Guides Decision guide Listening Can the practice continue when the screen goes dark? Someone starts a psalm on the way home, locks the phone and puts it away. A call comes in, the bus stops, they reach the door. For listening to work, every one of those moments has to work without looking at the screen, and the ending has to let the phone disappear. 1 Screen off: the reading continues and stops at the end 2 Back on screen: the text follows the voice 3 The ending: silence instead of autoplay Screen off: the reading continues and stops at the end Then Back on screen: the text follows the voice Then The ending: silence instead of autoplay 4 decisions One question for your next review Editorial guidance, not user-tested Make listening complete without the screen Reading along is optional company Tell chosen silence from a stalled player Let it end Decide Go further 01 Make listening complete without the screen Listening should never depend on watching a progress animation. Support background playback and the device’s own controls, recover cleanly after a call or when headphones disconnect, and remember the position and edition. For people who can’t or don’t want to listen, a transcript or the text itself is part of the same experience, not an extra. Pattern The player works without the screen 02 Reading along is optional company Highlighting words as they are spoken can help, but only at the precision the recording really supports; a highlight that drifts is worse than none. Let readers scroll ahead or back without dragging the narrator with them, and give them an obvious way to rejoin the audio. Pattern Playback and reading positions can differ 03 Tell chosen silence from a stalled player A pause for reflection and a frozen stream look the same from the outside. Make it clear when silence is intended, and keep background music or ambience as something people choose, not a default that fills every gap. 04 Let it end Stop at the passage or practice the person chose. Offer to repeat it or listen further, but don’t start either automatically. A quiet ending, with the phone back in a pocket, can be the best outcome the product has. Take into your next review Can the practice continue, and end, when the screen is off? Exercise Start a passage, lock the device, take a call, resume, read elsewhere in the text and rejoin the narrator. Then let it finish and check that nothing else begins. Try it with headphones, with large text, with a transcript and with no background music. Record the decision with the worksheet → Details Go further Where these proposals come from The Kairos manuscript (Tobias Treppmann, Digital Spiritual Formation: The Aperto Vision , Draft 4; selected sections on reading, engagement, multimodal and communal formation, incentives and honest assessment reviewed 5 October 2026) motivates these proposals. It is not an effectiveness study, and it does not show that audio produces more spiritual growth. The full manuscript and bibliography are not published or comprehensively reviewed here. For reminders and when to stop asking for attention, see attention, reminders and enough . For all the audio patterns, see audio and guided practice .
