pages.title: One passage, three purposes
pages.description: Compare three Bible-app design briefs and the assumptions behind their interface choices.
pages.text: Home / Start here / Worked example Purpose before pattern One passage, three purposes A useful interface begins with what someone is trying to do. Compare three briefs for Luke 15:1–7—the same passage, with different reasons to open it. These are illustrative design briefs, not findings from a user study. The same person could move between all three. Each brief offers a starting decision to test, rather than a universal rule. Receive a shared passage · Prepare a group conversation · Investigate an interpretation 01 · Illustrative brief Receive a shared passage “A friend sent me this. I want to read it and consider why it matters.” Open Luke 15:1–7 Read or listen Reflect, explore or finish A starting decision Open the passage directly, with the translation named and an easy route to its wider context. Give the passage a visible ending. Keep listening and text-size controls within reach. The assumption to examine A bounded passage can make beginning manageable. It also embodies an editorial choice about where meaning begins and ends. Name that boundary; let the reader read before and after it. When to choose differently A chapter-first reader may better serve someone following along elsewhere. A guided question may help a newcomer, but should not require an answer or assume personal disclosure. Agency and a meaningful ending Avoid turning the ending into an automatic next devotion, streak prompt or chat invitation. Offer “Read the surrounding passage” when it helps; leaving can be a successful outcome. A realistic test Ask someone unfamiliar with this interface to open the shared link, identify the edition, find the surrounding text and finish. Can they explain what was Scripture and what was commentary? Compare passage-focused reading → 02 · Illustrative brief Prepare a group conversation “We will discuss this passage together. I need to prepare, then find my place quickly.” Open the group passage Read and prepare notes Return during discussion A starting decision Keep the agreed passage stable. Offer discreet verse anchors, personal notes and a reliable return after opening a cross-reference. Make note privacy explicit. The assumption to examine The organiser’s selection gives the group a shared starting point; it can also give one person substantial control over the questions and interpretation. Preparation and participation should not require public progress. When to choose differently For live follow-along, a quick book/chapter picker may matter more than a resource panel. A newcomer may need help finding the passage; a facilitator may need several sources. Offer these routes without assigning permanent roles from usage history. Agency and a meaningful ending Keep “my preparation” separate from “share with the group.” Do not publish a private question, completion state or prayer request as the default outcome of preparing. A realistic test Rehearse opening a second passage and returning while someone is speaking. Then ask participants to explain which notes others can see. Include a person joining without preparation. Compare chapter navigation by situation → 03 · Illustrative brief Investigate an interpretation “I want to understand a disputed reading before teaching or forming a conclusion.” Frame the question Compare text and sources Record a provisional conclusion A starting decision Offer comparison, inspectable sources and notes that preserve reference and edition. Keep the original question and a return path visible as the reader follows evidence. The assumption to examine More available resources do not guarantee greater understanding. A default commentary, translation or AI summary can privilege a tradition while appearing neutral. Make provenance and editorial selection discoverable. When to choose differently Side-by-side panes can help on a wide screen; verse-by-verse comparison may work better on a phone. Interlinear detail answers some language questions but is not a substitute for contextual interpretation. Agency and a meaningful ending Allow sustained investigation without an imposed devotional ending. Also make it possible to stop and record what remains uncertain. An application prompt should invite reflection, not force a moral lesson from every research session. A realistic test Ask a reader to compare two interpretations, inspect what supports one claim, and return to the original question. Observe lost context and mistaken attribution; do not use time spent as evidence of insight. Compare parallel reading options → What changes—and what remains The passage is unchanged. The prominence of navigation, notes, comparison, guidance and the next invitation changes with the task. Accessibility, accurate attribution, reader control and a route to context remain important in each brief. Is activity standing in for faithfulness? In this resource, performance spirituality names the risk of treating frequency, volume, completion or consistency as proof of faithfulness or spiritual growth. It does not mean that daily reading, sustained study or an annual Bible plan is wrong. These can be freely chosen and meaningful disciplines. The design question is whether one practice becomes an unexamined requirement for everyone. A completion badge, an uninterrupted reading surface and a single-passage page each carry assumptions. None proves its reader has grown spiritually. Ask what this product intends to support, whether the person shares that intention, and what experience would challenge the design. Take this into a product review Name a real situation and the good the product is intended to serve. Identify what the default encourages, makes difficult or leaves out. Compare a credible alternative—including a quieter or smaller intervention. State what people can choose, decline, change or finish. Record the evidence, theological commitments and unresolved judgments separately. Test the practical consequences with people in the situation, including those who opt out. Use the decision worksheet · Explore the theological questions · Find another purpose

pages.title: Finding passages
pages.description: How does someone find the passage they are looking for? Reader controls, browsing, typed references, combined search fields and book order, as one journey into Scripture.
pages.text: Guides Decision guide Finding passages How does someone find the passage they are looking for? Someone hears a reference in a sermon. Someone else remembers a story but not where it is. A third person only came for today’s reading and needs no catalogue at all. All three deserve a clear way in, and they don’t need the same controls. 1 Reading Mark 3 when a friend mentions John 3 2 Every book in one view 3 Then the chapter 4 Or type the reference straight away Reading Mark 3 when a friend mentions John 3 Then Every book in one view Then Then the chapter Then Or type the reference straight away 4 decisions One question for your next review Editorial guidance, not user-tested Where does navigation start? Follow the whole journey, not just the picker When one field does several jobs Book order is a decision too Decide Go further 01 Where does navigation start? On the reading page, the label at the top already makes promises. A single “Mark 3 · KJV” control is the most compact, but people have to guess what tapping it changes. Separate reference and translation controls make two frequent actions distinct: changing the edition should keep the passage, and changing the passage should keep the edition. Separate book, chapter and translation controls give the fastest access to a known level, as long as long book names don’t squeeze the targets. Some readers hide navigation behind a gesture to keep the page quiet, as Mere Bible’s chapter rail does. That needs a visible, accessible way to open it as well. A bounded passage with a quiet “Read in context” link is a legitimate choice too, when the task is one reflection rather than open reading. 02 Follow the whole journey, not just the picker A chapter grid is one step in a longer path: know where you are, choose a route, pick a destination, open it, and be able to get back. A chapter control should skip choosing the book again; cancelling should leave the reader exactly where it was. “Back to where I was” and “Previous chapter” are different actions and deserve different controls. Verses are optional precision. Don’t require a verse to open a chapter, but when someone does choose one, open the chapter at that verse and mark it briefly, so they can see where they have landed. Try it Four ways to reach a passage, with switches for tap or review, book grid and verse step 03 When one field does several jobs One search field can filter book names, recognise a typed reference and suggest passages with AI. These can share an input, but they are different kinds of answer: a recognised reference is a destination, and an AI suggestion is a proposal. Label results by what they are, and only promise text search if the product actually searches the text. The trigger matters. In the Video Study Bible prototype, book filtering is instant and local, a complete reference resolves locally, and other input asks the AI for suggestions after a short pause, so even a half-typed book name leaves the device. Automatic suggestions save a step but add latency, cost and privacy questions; an explicit “Find related passages” action gives people more control. Either way, keep local results useful offline and don’t let a slow answer replace what the person is now typing. Pattern One field for browsing, references and AI discovery 04 Book order is a decision too Start from the chosen edition’s actual books and order. Not every Bible has the same 66 books, and the same position in a list is not the same book in another edition. Edition order supports familiarity; alphabetical order helps find a known name but changes with language; genre groups can help exploration if the headings explain the classification. Colour can reinforce a group label, never replace it. When someone switches edition, keep the book and reference wherever a valid mapping exists. If the book or verse is missing or numbered differently, say so and offer a clear destination rather than silently opening whatever sits at the same index. Pattern Book and chapter pickers: list, grid or drill-down? Take into your next review What does this person already know, and where should this action take them? Exercise Before choosing controls, try the journey with people. Ask them to follow a spoken reference, find an unfamiliar book, open a precise verse, switch to an edition with different books, and get back to where they started. Include long book names, enlarged text, a keyboard and a screen reader, offline use and a reference that does not exist. Note wrong destinations, abandoned searches and lost places, and whether people understood what they opened. Speed is useful evidence; it is not a measure of spiritual formation. Record the decision with the worksheet → Details Go further Starting points by situation Starting points to test with the people you serve Situation Start with Watch for Following a spoken reference Visible location, predictable book order, quick chapter access and optional verse entry Too many confirmation steps; losing the group’s passage while exploring Finding an unfamiliar book Full names, local aliases, search and clearly named groups Abbreviations and assumed knowledge of the canon Comparing distant passages for study Direct reference entry, recent destinations and a back trail Recents replacing book order; back confused with previous chapter Continuing to read Resume the current place, with the next chapter named at the end Making someone choose the book again just to continue Reading one daily passage Open that passage directly, with optional wider context Turning a complete encounter into pressure to keep browsing What we saw in VSB, Mere Bible and Dwell VSB. A review of the author’s prototype on 6 October 2026 found separate book, chapter and translation actions in the reader header, and one adaptive search field. That field filters book names immediately, resolves complete references locally and requests AI passage suggestions after 450 ms for other input; book matches and suggestions can appear together. The code review did not establish exact verse-text search or a sourced inline answer. It is a local code review, not a device test or user study. Mere Bible (formerly NeuBible; the publisher listing confirms the rename). Contributed screenshots show a vertical chapter rail beside the text, and a book list that expands a chapter grid inside the chosen book. Still images do not establish the gesture, or when a scrubbed chapter becomes the destination. Capture date and build are unverified. Dwell. Its release announcement documents a book and chapter picker. A dated capture is still needed before describing its reported genre colours. Book identifiers follow the USFM catalogue , which includes deuterocanonical and additional books; identifiers do not prescribe one display order or genre taxonomy. Whom does the arrangement welcome? A browser quietly reveals the reader a team imagines: someone who knows the order, recognises abbreviations, reads consecutive chapters or starts with a question. None of these describes everyone, or every faithful encounter with Scripture. Ask together whose knowledge the arrangement assumes, and whether someone can find enough context without being pushed into more activity. In a prayerful review, consider how the interface could welcome a newcomer while respecting an experienced reader’s practice. Keep exploring Related How should someone get to a passage? → One field for browsing, references and AI discovery → A reference opens at a deliberate destination → Choose a translation with enough context → How do readers move to the next chapter? →

pages.title: Purposes and reading situations
pages.description: Find Bible and faith-app patterns by the person’s current purpose and circumstances.
pages.text: Home / Start here / Purposes Find a relevant pattern Start from a purpose Start with the person’s purpose. Choose the situation closest to your product decision. These are overlapping purposes, not types of people or stages of spiritual maturity. The same person may listen during a commute, follow a guided reflection in the evening and prepare to teach at the weekend. Receiving, following guidance and directing one’s own reading can each serve a meaningful purpose. More interaction is not automatically better engagement. See the same passage designed for three purposes . Compare the assumptions before choosing a pattern. Before choosing: consider familiarity with Scripture, language and literacy, disability and access needs, available time, connectivity, emotional circumstances and whether the device is shared. These conditions can change which option helps. Receive and listen A commute, a rest or a hands-free encounter with Scripture. Reduce visual demands while preserving control over pace, repetition and stopping. Listening is not a lesser form of engagement. 17 · Audio and guided practice The player works without the screen Support listening as a complete mode of use. Research-informed design proposal 18 · Audio and guided practice Playback and reading positions can differ Follow the narration without forcing the reader to follow every movement. Research-informed design proposal Receive today’s reading A daily passage, watchword, lectionary reading or devotional chosen by others. Offer a clear starting point without requiring enrolment. Receiving a reading can be an active choice; explain its origin and keep an archive separate from a backlog. 76 · Reading and Scripture A bounded passage with a route to wider context Choose the reading unit by the task while keeping its boundaries and context visible. Research-informed design proposal 17 · Audio and guided practice The player works without the screen Support listening as a complete mode of use. Research-informed design proposal Follow the church year Today’s observance, a season or preparation for a service. Name the calendar and community it belongs to. Help people enter the practice without turning the church year into a personal backlog. 92 · Habits and spiritual formation Orient within a liturgical calendar Make the tradition, date and observance clear before offering readings or prayer. Research-informed design proposal 93 · Habits and spiritual formation Make room for prayer Compare a prayer text, a guided sequence and a quiet space without requiring personal input. Research-informed design proposal Follow a practice A chosen reading rhythm, devotional or guided reflection. Provide orientation without turning an interruption into debt. Make the schedule and the freedom to change it clear. 20 · Audio and guided practice Choose a devotional format Compare a continuous reading, a sequence of cards and a chaptered audio session. Research-informed design proposal 93 · Habits and spiritual formation Make room for prayer Compare a prayer text, a guided sequence and a quiet space without requiring personal input. Research-informed design proposal 39 · Habits and spiritual formation A flexible reading rhythm Help someone choose a reading rhythm—and adjust it when life changes. Proposed hypothesis Explore a question A reader wants to understand a word, passage or competing explanation. Keep evidence and context available. An answer should not quietly replace the reader’s question with the system’s agenda. 49 · Reading and Scripture A reference opens at a deliberate destination Choose the content scope, landing position and temporary cue separately. Research-informed design proposal 78 · Study and annotations Citations in AI answers A citation is a route to supporting material, with source type and limitations visible. Research-informed design proposal Read independently Someone chooses their own passage, pace and depth. Support sustained reading and easy return. Independence should not require dismissing a stream of recommendations. 76 · Reading and Scripture A bounded passage with a route to wider context Choose the reading unit by the task while keeping its boundaries and context visible. Research-informed design proposal 03 · Reading and Scripture Footnotes without losing place Inspect a note and return to the exact reading anchor. Research-informed design proposal Study and prepare A teaching task, close comparison or theological investigation. Support comparison and durable notes while keeping edition, source and interpretation distinct. 76 · Reading and Scripture A bounded passage with a route to wider context Choose the reading unit by the task while keeping its boundaries and context visible. Research-informed design proposal 78 · Study and annotations Citations in AI answers A citation is a route to supporting material, with source type and limitations visible. Research-informed design proposal Engage with others A shared reading practice, discussion or prayer. Make the audience and participation expectations explicit. A shared rhythm need not mean public progress. 39 · Habits and spiritual formation A flexible reading rhythm Help someone choose a reading rhythm—and adjust it when life changes. Proposed hypothesis 40 · Habits and spiritual formation Return without shame Make it easy to pick up a reading practice after time away. Proposed hypothesis When the purpose changes Compare daily offerings, bounded plans and self-directed reading . Content selection, commitment, calendar and progress are separate design choices. Let a listener open the text, a guided reader explore wider context, and a researcher return to quiet reading without losing their place. Do not infer a permanent persona from one session. These routes are editorial proposals. Read the engagement framework and research limits , or work through reading plans and pressure .

pages.title: Context around the passage
pages.description: How much context does a reader need around the passage? Choosing the reading unit, landing in the right place, and keeping Scripture, notes and explanations distinct.
pages.text: Guides Decision guide Context around the passage How much context does a reader need around the passage? A daily reflection, a reference looked up mid-conversation and a sermon in preparation can all begin at Mark 3:5. The first wants one passage and some quiet. The second wants to land on the right verse. The third wants the whole chapter, two translations and the notes. The same verse needs three different screens. 1 A single verse: an easy way in 2 The passage it belongs to 3 The whole chapter, when context matters A single verse: an easy way in Then The passage it belongs to Then The whole chapter, when context matters 3 decisions One question for your next review Editorial guidance, not user-tested Choose the reading unit by the task Land in the right place, and keep it Keep Scripture, notes and explanations distinct Decide Go further 01 Choose the reading unit by the task A bounded passage suits a focused encounter: a devotional, a shared verse, a reflection that should be allowed to end. Continuous text suits sustained reading. Close study needs comparison, notes and room. None of these is the serious one; they serve different moments, sometimes for the same person on the same day. Whatever the unit, keep wider context one deliberate step away. A bounded passage without a route to its chapter quietly decides how much of the story someone is allowed to see. Pattern A bounded passage with a route to wider context 02 Land in the right place, and keep it When someone opens a reference, show where they have landed: scroll to the verse and mark it briefly. Keep that anchor when they change translation, open a footnote or come back from somewhere else. Losing someone’s place is one of the quickest ways to make a reading app feel careless. Pattern A reference opens at a deliberate destination Getting to the passage in the first place is its own journey; see how someone finds the passage they are looking for . 03 Keep Scripture, notes and explanations distinct Let people preview a note before a study panel takes over the screen. When notes appear, say whose they are: the translators’ footnotes, a publisher’s commentary and an AI-generated explanation carry different kinds of authority and should never look like the text itself. Comparing translations works differently on a phone and a desk. A side-by-side layout that suits a laptop can crowd a small screen; alternating verses or a second pane on demand may serve better. Pattern Parallel reading chooses a useful arrangement Take into your next review What does this person need to understand or find, right now? Exercise Ask one person to open a shared passage, change translation, look at a footnote and return. Ask another to compare two editions while preparing to teach. Watch for lost places, labels people misread and context they went looking for and could not find. Getting around easily is not yet evidence that anyone understood what they read; ask about that separately. Record the decision with the worksheet → Details Go further What the research says, and what it doesn’t The Habits and Hermeneutics of Digital Bible Readers Published abstract reviewed; author discussion reviewed separately. Population and study context limit how far this transfers. An abstract-level review does not establish causal effects or a preferred passage length. Americans’ Bible reading (August 2024 survey, published 2025) Methods and reading-approach results reviewed. US online self-report with a weighted sample of 1,200; the approach question was limited to the 1,137 who had read any Bible, and multiple selections were allowed. For engagement measures and their limits, see reading research . For a real comparison layout, look at YouVersion’s two editions with independent selectors . Keep exploring Related A bounded passage with a route to wider context → A reference opens at a deliberate destination → Footnotes without losing place → Adjust reading settings without losing the passage → Parallel reading chooses a useful arrangement →

pages.title: Coming back after a break
pages.description: What should greet someone after five days away? Choosing a reading rhythm, designing the return after a break, and deciding what an app should remember.
pages.text: Guides Decision guide Coming back after a break What should greet someone after five days away? Someone opens your app after five days. They may have been caring for a parent, reading on paper, or simply losing interest. You don’t know which, and you don’t need to. What the screen shows first will either help them carry on or quietly ask them to explain themselves. 1 Away for five days: reminders pause instead of nagging 2 Back again: a welcome and the obvious next step 3 If needed: change the schedule without penalty 4 Reading again, with the plan in quiet view Away for five days: reminders pause instead of nagging Then Back again: a welcome and the obvious next step Then If needed: change the schedule without penalty Then Reading again, with the plan in quiet view 6 decisions One question for your next review Editorial guidance, not user-tested A daily practice is worth supporting What is the structure for? Does it need to be a plan at all? Make the way back obvious Carry the purpose through the whole journey What should the app remember? Decide Go further 01 A daily practice is worth supporting Regular time with Scripture and prayer is one of the oldest Christian practices: the person who meditates on God’s law “day and night” (Psalm 1:2), Daniel praying three times a day “just as he had done before” (Daniel 6:10), Jesus praying “while it was still dark” (Mark 1:35). Evangelical and historic traditions alike treat these disciplines as means of grace and as training, not as a way of earning God’s favour. Grace is not opposed to effort, it is opposed to earning. Dallas Willard, The Great Omission Research points the same way, with care. Regular religious practice is associated with better wellbeing and health, mostly in studies of church attendance. Habit research adds something every plan should know: missing one day does not undo a habit, but showing someone a broken streak makes them more likely to stop. So helping people keep a rhythm they chose is a good thing to build. The decisions below are about doing it without making the app the measure of anyone’s faithfulness: who chose the commitment, who can see it, and what it says on the day after a miss. Research note Practice that forms, features that pressure: theology, habits, health and consent 02 What is the structure for? A church group following a seasonal reading needs a common date: everyone should arrive on Sunday having read the same passage. Someone reading through a Gospel alone only needs the next chapter. Both are real commitments, and they need different support. Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat Sun Dated plan Everyone reads the same passage by the same day. Fits A group, a church season, a lectionary Luke 13 14 15 16 Sequence The next chapter, whenever the person next reads. Fits Reading a book through alone 4 days a week Weekly rhythm A number of days chosen by the person, no dates. Fits Setting time aside without deadlines Luke 15:11 Saved place Just where they stopped. No plan at all. Fits People who know what they want to read Pattern Choose a reading rhythm 03 Does it need to be a plan at all? Receiving a passage chosen by a community or an editor can be a deliberate practice, not a passive one. A daily verse, the Moravian Daily Texts , a lectionary reading and an authored devotional are different traditions, though. Say who chose the reading and keep Scripture separate from commentary. Let yesterday’s reading stay available without becoming overdue. Four decisions are easy to tangle, and each can be made separately. A daily devotional can record nothing at all; a chosen plan can show progress without a deadline. Who chooses the reading? The reader A church An editor A lectionary Is there an end? A finite plan Ongoing Do dates matter? Shared dates Own pace What does the app record? Nothing Saved place Completion Days 04 Make the way back obvious The welcome can be simple. Show where they stopped, offer the obvious next step, and keep changing the schedule as a quieter option. The welcome A quieter option Illustrative screens for a dated group plan, in the style of the working examples. A proposal, not a tested design. Keep notes where they were. Leave reminders paused until the person chooses otherwise. If they skip ahead, keep the earlier sessions as unread rather than failed, and don’t treat opening a passage as reading it. Nobody should have to account for their absence to find the next step. Pattern Compare return screens 05 Carry the purpose through the whole journey A reusable screen needs a reason that survives being copied. For this worked example: help someone return to a reading commitment they chose, while preserving their place and their freedom to change it. This is a proposed design intent, not evidence that the flow achieves it. That purpose changes more than the welcome. Reminders stay paused after the break; the return offers the saved passage and, for a dated group, today’s shared passage; schedule changes preserve notes and unread sessions; the reading screen keeps the text central; history records only what the person actually marks as read. A different team should be able to explain these decisions before reusing the screens. Compare complete alternatives For an individual, compare a sequence with no deadline against a dated plan whose dates can move. For a group, compare resuming at the saved place against joining today’s shared reading while keeping earlier passages available. Neither choice should silently mark the missing readings complete. Working example Try the reading rhythms before and after a break Explore something the defaults overlook Try a return screen led by a person’s saved question or note, with the relevant passage beneath it. It may support continuity of attention better than a calendar does. Keep the ordinary resume option available, and ask readers whether showing a personal note unexpectedly would feel helpful or intrusive. This is an alternative to explore, not a recommendation already supported by research. Review the experience, not only the screen Ask someone to return after five days, find their place, change the pace, read and explain what was recorded and who can see it. Include someone who chooses to pause or leave. Check whether reminders remain under their control and whether the group date is clear. Observe confusion and listen for pressure; more opens alone cannot establish that the experience served them well. Write down what would change the decision: lost notes, unclear group timing, accidental completion or a return that people experience as a demand to catch up. Keep an owner and a review date with the implementation. Print the worked example and review worksheet (PDF) This application takes inspiration from Katie Dill’s invitation to carry intent through systems and use new tools to explore better possibilities. The reading-return proposal and evaluation questions are our own. Talk context: Lenny & Friends Summit . 06 What should the app remember? Each kind of record answers a different question. Only the last is about consistency, which is useful to someone who asked for it and heavy for someone who didn’t. What each record answers Record Answers Useful to Saved place “Where was I?” Everyone Completion “What’s left in this plan?” Someone in a finite plan Shared date “Where is the group?” Groups and churches Streak, calendar or chart “How consistent have I been?” Only people who asked for it Scale matters too. Measured against the whole Bible, a good first month is about 2% of it, which can make a beginner feel they have barely started. Views that start from the reader’s own first week, or from a plan they chose, give progress a size they can see. Try it Nine ways to show a reading history, before and after a break Take into your next review When someone comes back, what will they see first, and does it help them read? Exercise Open your current return screen together and pick one situation: someone continuing alone, or someone rejoining a dated group. Then finish this sentence: when someone returns, we will offer ___ because they are trying to ___. We will keep ___ and make it possible to ___. Ask people in that situation to resume, change their schedule and say who can see what. Notice where they hesitate, and listen to the ones who decide not to restart. If prayer is part of your team’s practice, you might ask whose circumstances you have overlooked in wanting to help. Participation should be voluntary. Record the decision with the worksheet → Details Go further Plans, catch-up and pressure: what we know Tobias Treppmann recounts a conversation with one Bibel TV user who preferred reading the same plan there, because YouVersion’s display of days behind felt guilt-inducing to him. This is a paraphrased personal report, not a direct quotation, a comparative study or a claim about the publisher’s intentions. The date and app version were not recorded. YouVersion’s Android documentation describes Catch Me Up , which shifts the schedule without marking sections complete; it is unavailable for Plans with Friends. A recovery option and a reader’s experience of pressure can both be true. Test its visibility and wording rather than assuming either settles the matter. Treppmann reports that Bibel TV data favours shorter plans; the figures, period and definition of “popular” were not available for this review, so this remains a reported observation. No verifiable primary-source abandonment rate for annual YouVersion plans was found. Starts, continued use and completion measure different things, and an unfinished plan does not show that someone stopped reading the Bible. Behavioural design: benefits and unintended effects · when rewards can undermine motivation · reading research Discipline, grace and success The research note on practice and formation gathers the theology, pastoral writing, habit psychology and health research behind this guide. Daily reading and annual plans can be meaningful, freely chosen disciplines; there is no need to weaken that commitment to make room for other circumstances. The difficulty comes when a product treats one rhythm as the measure of everyone’s faithfulness. A completed session tells us about an action recorded in the app, not the whole story of someone’s attention, understanding or life with God. Dallas Willard’s interview on disciplines and grace explores practices in relation to a person’s circumstances, and his interviewer raises questions about corporate worship and the means of grace; the exchange invites reflection without settling the matter for every tradition. The Cape Town Commitment (Part II E.4) calls for truthful reporting and challenges unrealistic demands for visible results. For a product team that becomes a practical question: can we describe reading activity honestly without presenting it as proof of transformation? These are theological perspectives. The interface recommendations here are editorial proposals to test, not measured effects of a reading schedule. Other practices need other forms A daily observance, a mixed-media devotion and a time of prayer ask for different interfaces. Compare liturgical calendar views , reading, card and audio formats and dedicated prayer surfaces . For reminders outside the reading itself, see attention and reminders . Keep exploring Related How should a reading plan hold time? → What should a reading history show? →

pages.title: Pricing and access
pages.description: Who pays for a faith app, and for what? What a Bible or faith app really costs, how ministries and businesses pay for it, and where the money can strain trust.
pages.text: Guides Decision guide Pricing and access Who pays for a faith app, and for what? A free Bible app is paid for by someone: donors, a church or ministry budget, investors, advertisers, or a team giving its time. A paid app is paid for by the people who use it. Neither arrangement is more faithful than the other. The question for both is whether people can see the exchange, and whether it fits the relationship the app invites. 1 Say what is always free, and what pays for it 2 Show AI costs before they are charged Say what is always free, and what pays for it Then Show AI costs before they are charged 5 decisions One question for your next review Editorial guidance, not user-tested What it actually costs Commercial and ministry models both make trade-offs Put the paywall at a boundary people understand AI makes the cost of each person different Questions worth sitting with Decide Go further 01 What it actually costs Scripture text and audio. Most modern translations are licensed from their publishers, often with conditions on offline storage, quotation length, audio and use in AI systems. Public-domain texts avoid fees but still need careful editing and formatting. Design and development. Building is the start. Operating-system updates, accessibility, app-store requirements and bug fixes continue for as long as the app exists. Infrastructure. Hosting, sync, streaming audio, backups and security grow with every person who uses the app. AI. Model use is usually billed per token and varies by person. See the section on credits below. People. Support, moderation, safeguarding, editorial and theological review are ongoing costs that are easy to leave out of a plan. Store fees. Apple and Google take a commission on in-app purchases, commonly 15% or 30% depending on the programme. Being honest about these costs, with your team, your funders and the people you serve, makes the rest of the decisions easier to explain. Start by writing down what will always be available without payment, what costs money, and what people keep if they stop paying or the product closes. 02 Commercial and ministry models both make trade-offs Original decision framework; what works depends on the service and the people it serves Model Works well when Watch for Ministry or donor funded A community wants broad, free access and can sustain it Donor priorities shaping the product, fundraising inside devotional moments, and variable AI costs that grow faster than giving. Subscription Ongoing content, service or operating costs create ongoing value Paywalls around essentials, renewals people did not expect, and cancellation made harder than signing up. One-time purchase A defined resource or edition has lasting value “Lifetime” promises that outlast the funding to keep the app running. Free with paid extras A useful core can stay free while costly features are paid Upgrade prompts in reading, prayer or moments of distress. Credits or usage limits AI or audio generation costs vary widely by person Units nobody can predict, and running out at the wrong moment. Church or organisation licence A group pays for its members Who can see participation, and what members keep when they leave. Funding must not give leaders access to private content. Advertising Rarely a good fit for reading and prayer Attention and data incentives that pull against the purpose of the app. 03 Put the paywall at a boundary people understand Let the person understand the feature and price before collecting intimate input or beginning a paid task. Present included capabilities, recurring total, trial end, renewal and any minimum commitment. Show a real decline or free route if one exists. Confirm the selected plan in the platform purchase flow; handle pending payment, restored purchases and an existing subscription. Show entitlement and the next billing date in settings, with a direct management route. On cancellation or expiry, explain when access ends and which saved work remains readable or exportable under its licence. Keep emergency contacts and basic safety information reachable when credits run out. Do not present a conversion offer as the response to suicidal distress or an abuse disclosure. This is an editorial service boundary, not a claim that unlimited AI use must be free. The FTC’s 2022 dark-pattern report summary identifies hidden terms, obstructive cancellation and manipulative data choices. It is a design reference, not a statement that a particular later subscription rule is currently in force. Apple’s subscription guidance provides platform-specific purchase and management expectations. 04 AI makes the cost of each person different Most model providers bill per token, so every conversation, long context, retrieved passage and retry has a cost, and generated audio is billed separately. A heavy user can cost many times what a light one does. That is why AI features push products towards credits, limits or higher prices, and why “unlimited” is a promise worth checking against the bill. Model tokens measure processing units; product credits are a pricing abstraction. Neither inherently corresponds to one verse, one answer or one minute of audio. Explain your conversion and its uncertainty. Hidden history, tools and retries can change cost. Illustrative flow · example units, not market prices Create a 5-minute audio reflection Estimated 2–4 credits. Maximum 4 credits for this request. 12 available. Review sources → Confirm generation → Show actual charge and remaining balance. Implement the promised cap; a warning alone is not enforcement. Define partial output, failed generation, user cancellation, retries, refunds and reservation release. Disclose expiry, rollover, top-up price and auto-recharge separately. If estimates cannot be bounded, offer a smaller predictable task. Some tools let people connect their own AI provider key instead. Today that suits a small technical audience, because most people do not have a key; if you offer it, say plainly who is billed and where requests go. 05 Questions worth sitting with “The worker is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7) and “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew 10:8) are both quoted in debates about charging for ministry. Both come from Jesus sending out his disciples, and Christian traditions apply them differently. Neither settles your pricing, but together they hold a real tension worth discussing as a team. Who is the customer, and who is being served? Are they the same people? Scripture is available free in many forms. What exactly are you asking people to pay for? If the money ran out next year, what would happen to people’s notes, plans and audio? Which source of money would you turn down because of what it would ask of the product? Take into your next review What will always be free, what costs money and why, and what do people keep if they stop paying? Exercise Before purchase, ask someone to explain what they will pay today and later, what is included and how to leave. Then test a failed generation, exhausted credits and cancellation. Track billing confusion, refunds and support load alongside revenue. Do not infer generosity or faith from spending. Decision to record: what will always be free, what costs money and why, and what people keep if they stop paying. Record the decision with the worksheet → Details Go further Sources and their limits Apple’s subscription guidance sets platform expectations for purchase and management; it is not universal law. The FTC’s 2022 dark-patterns report describes hidden terms, obstructive cancellation and manipulative data choices; it is a design reference, not a statement that any later subscription rule is in force. Keep exploring Related Suggest, confirm and act → Visible work and recoverable failure → Support access accounts for monitored devices → What is the least you need to know? →

pages.title: Design for the moment someone reaches for God
pages.description: A design reference for the people who build Bible, prayer and AI products: the real options side by side, with the Scripture, practice and research behind every choice.
pages.text: For designers, product teams and builders Design for the moment someone reaches for God. A reading at 6 a.m. A prayer typed at midnight. A question asked of an AI about what a verse means. This is a design reference for the people who build those moments: the real options side by side, with the Scripture, practice and research behind every choice. Explore the patterns Start with a decision → Generated editorial illustration · fictional people and place The calling “Listen—if they were silent, the very rocks would start to shout!” Luke 19:40, The Voice™ · Copyright © 2008 by Ecclesia Bible Society. Used by permission. All rights reserved. Jesus said this when he was told to silence the crowds who were praising him. Making him known is entrusted to us first. But many people now talk to rocks first. A microchip is a rock we tricked into thinking, and with AI the rock talks back: people ask it about God before they ask anyone else. Those of us who build on these rocks, and shape how they behave, get to help them reflect Christ and lead people into deeper knowledge of God and life with his people. It is an exhilarating calling, and also a burden, and this resource is here to help you carry it well. Read: Workers in God’s field → Or the short version: When Silicon Catches the Light Generated illustration · based on Startup Life photography How we compare options Every choice sits on a spectrum See the options side by side, and choosing one becomes a conscious choice against the others. Where options form a scale, we lay them out as one. This is how much Scripture a reading screen shows at once. Less text at once More text at once 1 One word at a time + Total focus, no lost place − No looking back 2 One verse at a time + Slow, meditative, memorable − Context out of sight 3 One verse in focus + Attention with context − Moving text needs control 4 One passage + A natural beginning and end − Boundaries are editorial 5 Whole chapter + The story stays whole − Long on a phone Explore how much text at once → Deep dives Start with a pattern Each deep dive has stills of every option, a working example, takeaways, the research behind it and one question to take into your next review. How much text at once One word, a verse, a passage or a whole chapter? 5 options · 5 app examples · research Borrowed Observed Familiar convention Numbers, headings and notes How much should surround the text? 7 options · 2 app examples · research Familiar convention Observed Bible audio How should Scripture be heard: as text, voice or read-along? 5 options · 5 app examples · research Leave it out Familiar convention Observed AI persona How human should the assistant seem? 6 options · 6 app examples · research Familiar convention Exploratory · untested Observed AI memory What should the assistant know and keep? 5 options · 2 app examples · research Familiar convention Observed Borrowed Leave it out Translations One at a time, side by side or verse by verse? 5 options · research Observed Familiar convention All patterns → How a pattern page works From first look to a decision At a glance Stills of every option, side by side, with one gain and one cost each. Try it A working example on a phone-sized screen, with the controls in one panel. Takeaways What we noticed, in a few headlined points. Research Scripture and tradition, practice today, science and accessibility, with every source and its limits. Decide One question and an exercise for your next design review. What it rests on Theology, practice and evidence Scripture and tradition How the church has read, prayed and practised, with Scripture quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. Practice that forms → Practice today How people actually use Bible and faith apps, from surveys, studies and dated screenshots of real apps. App examples → Science Reading, habit, motivation and wellbeing research, with each study’s limits stated. Research notes → Care, law and access Crisis support, privacy, AI regulation and accessibility guidance that shape what is responsible. Crisis support in AI chat → Where options come from Where each option comes from Each option says where it comes from, so an idea we invented never passes as something people already use. Observed Seen in a named app, with a dated screenshot where we have one. Familiar convention A widely used convention, generalised rather than copied. Borrowed Taken from outside faith apps, such as reading or productivity tools. Exploratory · untested Our own proposal. Untested. Leave it out Not building the feature, treated as a real option. Decision guides Or start from a situation 5-minute route Context around the passage How much context does a reader need around the passage? Choosing the reading unit, landing in the right place, and keeping Scripture, notes and explanations distinct. What does this person need to understand or find? 5-minute route Trust in AI answers What authority does a fluent answer seem to have? Giving AI a bounded job, showing what it did, letting people check its sources, and keeping care in human hands. What authority might a fluent answer appear to have? 7-minute guide Finding passages How does someone find the passage they are looking for? Reader controls, browsing, typed references, combined search fields and book order, as one journey into Scripture. What does this person know already—and where should this action take them? All guides → In your own tools Bring it into your AI assistant Bezalel is an open MCP server. Add patterns.missional.design/mcp to Claude, Cursor or ChatGPT, describe a feature, and it brings the options, the research and the questions into your work, while leaving the deciding to your team. Meet Bezalel → Make a thoughtful decision, together What good should this feature serve? Who carries its costs? What would change your mind? For your next review Use the decision worksheet for a design review, a product brief or an AI-assisted build. The ten Missional by Design principles for spiritual apps offer a Christian perspective to examine, question and apply. Open the decision worksheet → Created by Tobias Treppmann as part of Missional by Design , for fellow workers. This is editorial guidance, not yet user-tested, and every page says what its evidence can and cannot show.

pages.title: Actions on AI answers
pages.description: Copy, share, try again, report: which belong? Four options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Actions on AI answers Copy, share, try again, report: which belong? Under every answer, AI apps now offer a row of icons: copy, share, save, read aloud, try again, make it simpler, branch, double-check, thumbs up and down, report a legal issue. Each one makes a promise about where the answer goes, who sees the feedback and what the model did. In a Bible app, a shared answer can also be mistaken for Scripture. Each action is a chance to send people back to the text, or away from it. 4 working options 2 app examples 4 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Actions on AI answers At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further At a glance Four action bars, side by side 1 Every action in a row Borrowed + Everything one tap away − Fourteen unlabelled icons Try it → 2 Three, then More Borrowed + The common three, clearly − Rating is one tap further Try it → 3 Actions on the passages Observed + Scripture is what travels − Harder to keep the answer Try it → 4 No action bar Leave it out + A quiet, reflective screen − No way to report problems Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try four ways to act on an answer One answer about rest, four ways of offering actions on it. Try copying, sharing, rating and asking what the assistant did, and watch what each action says it will do. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Every action in a row · Borrowed 2. Three, then More · Borrowed 3. Actions on the passages · Observed 4. No action bar · Leave it out Option 1 Every action in a row Borrowed 2 Three, then More Borrowed 3 Actions on the passages Observed 4 No action bar Leave it out Borrowed 1. Every action in a row Borrowed from general AI apps: Gemini (good/bad, share and export, double-check, modify, report legal issue), ChatGPT (copy, read aloud, branch in new chat, try again) and Claude (copy, try again, thumbs with an issue type). Try this Without tapping, guess what each icon does. Then try Make it simpler, Read aloud and Report. + Makes easier Everything is one tap away for people who use it often. − Costs Fourteen unlabelled icons scroll off the side of a phone, and the ones that matter most look the same as the rest. Ask your team Which three of these would your readers miss? Borrowed 2. Three, then More Common in chat and content apps: the main actions visible, the rest in a menu with labels. Try this Open More: actions are grouped as Keep, Change, Check and Tell us. Try Branch, then come back. + Makes easier Copy, share and sources are easy to find, and the rest are labelled in words. − Costs Rating, branching and reporting take one more tap, so they are used less. Ask your team What do you lose if fewer people rate or report answers? Observed 3. Actions on the passages Observed in BibleAI, where each passage card has its own Bookmark and Share (see the citations page); generalized here. Try this Share a passage card and read what is shared. + Makes easier What people save and pass on is Scripture with its reference, not generated interpretation. − Costs The answer itself can’t be copied, rated or reported from here, so the team learns less about where it fails. Ask your team Should your app make the answer or the passage the thing that travels? Leave it out 4. No action bar Leave the bar out: the answer is just text, and people select it to copy. Try this Try to share or rate the answer. + Makes easier A quieter screen with nothing to tap, which can suit reflective use. − Costs Copying loses the AI label and references, nobody can report a problem, and the team hears nothing. Ask your team Where else would people go to tell you an answer was wrong? i The same answer appears in every option. Actions are simulated: nothing is copied, shared, sent or stored, and read-aloud playback is shown rather than spoken, but each action shows the screen or message it would give. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Two or three actions, the rest behind More Ten unlabelled icons are a puzzle on a phone. Most people need two or three actions; the rest are easier to understand as labelled rows behind “More”. What travels matters most A copy or share should carry the label and the references, so whoever receives it can tell generated interpretation from Scripture or a pastor’s words. Making the passage, not the answer, the thing people save and share is stronger still. Changing the answer needs care Try again can become shopping for the doctrinal answer someone hoped for, so keep every version visible and the original first. Simpler and shorter versions help readers at different levels. Checking quotations against the edition catches misquoted verses but cannot judge the interpretation. Feedback and “thinking” need honesty Thumbs should say who reads them and whether they train models. A list of steps should describe what the service actually did, such as searching and checking quotations, not present the model’s reasoning as proof. A report button needs a named owner and a response time. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Every action in a row 2 Three, then More 3 Actions on the passages 4 No action bar Reading an answer once Nothing in the way of the text Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit Sending it to a friend or group The label and references travel with it ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit Poor fit Keeping it for later study Saved apart from their own notes ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit Poor fit The answer looks wrong A way to check or report, with a named owner ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Wanting it simpler or shorter A new version that keeps the original ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Screen readers or large text Few, labelled actions Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition Holding answers lightly Test, then keep what is good “Test all things. Hold fast to what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Checking a quotation, comparing versions and reporting a problem are ways of testing; saving and sharing are ways of holding fast, and should carry what was tested. Research and guidance What each action promises Icons need words Few icons are recognised by everyone, and labels revealed on hover do not work on touch screens. Label the actions people need, and put the rest in a labelled menu. D Aurora Harley Say what feedback does Human–AI interaction guidelines ask products to make clear what the system can do, how well, and what happens when people correct it. Thumbs that train a model and thumbs read by a pastor are different promises. S Microsoft HAX Toolkit S Google Regenerating can become shopping Assistants sometimes favour agreeing over accuracy; trying again until the answer agrees compounds it. Keep the original first and every version visible. S Anthropic researchers S ITdaily Checking changes trust People trust cited answers more, even with random citations, and less once they check. A check action that opens the verses builds the right kind of trust. R Yifan Ding et al. Overreliance is a known risk NIST lists overreliance among the risks of human–AI configuration. Actions that make an answer easier to keep and spread than to question add to it. S NIST Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If Answers are mostly read and occasionally kept Start with Copy, share and sources visible, everything else behind More If The team depends on feedback to improve answers Start with Keep rating visible, and say clearly what happens to it If The product exists to lead people into the text Start with Put bookmark and share on the passages instead of the answer If Reflective use, with little to do afterwards Start with No bar, but keep a way to report problems These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. BibleAI · iOS app · device model not recorded Bookmark and Share on each passage card User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Spark Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded An AI label and thumbs at the end of the results User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What doing is for “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only” (James 1:22). Reading Scripture leads outward: to prayer, to obedience, to other people. The disciples on the road to Emmaus, their hearts burning, went straight back to Jerusalem to tell the others (Luke 24:32–33). Where Christians differ Christians share Scripture in many ways: verse cards, tracts, social media, a text to a friend. Some traditions encourage personal sharing; others prefer that teaching come through the church. All would distinguish the word of God from commentary on it. What follows for design “Let him who has My word speak it truthfully. For what is straw compared to grain?” (Jeremiah 23:28). Let the passage, not the generated text, be what people save and share, and label everything else. The best actions lead out of the app: read the whole passage, pray, talk to someone. In conversation with Albert Borgmann, Technology and the Character of Contemporary Life (1984) urged using technology to support focal practices rather than supplant them; the best action ends the session and begins the practice. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Life Together (1939) saw Scripture as received in community; sharing a passage with a friend is closer to that than sharing generated text. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Generated text shared as if it were Scripture; prompts to keep chatting. Ethical Does no harm Label generated text and keep Scripture distinct from it. Redemptive Gives something up for them Offer actions that lead away from the app: read the passage, pray, talk to someone. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review Which actions does this product need, and what does each one carry with it? Exercise Ask three people to name every icon before tapping it. Then copy and share an answer and look at what arrives on the other end, and ask each person who they think reads their thumbs down. Make the text easier to keep and share than the answer about it. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further Edge cases to design for Decide which actions this product needs. Keep two or three visible and put the rest behind “More”. Copy and share carry the AI label and references; saving to notes keeps AI answers apart from the reader’s own words; feedback says who sees it and whether it trains models; try again and simpler versions keep the original and let people compare, because regenerating until a preferred doctrinal answer appears is a real risk; checking quotations compares every quotation with the edition; “what the assistant did” lists real operations rather than private reasoning; reporting routes to a person with a stated response time. Consider putting actions on the Scripture objects instead, so the passage, not the generated text, is what travels. What tends to go wrong Icon-only rows without accessible names; a copy that drops the AI label; thumbs that silently feed training; “thinking” presented as proof of correctness; a report button with no stated owner; sharing generated interpretation as if it were Scripture. How to test it Ask people to say what each icon does before tapping it. Copy and share an answer and check what the recipient sees. Rate an answer and ask who they think will read the rating. Compare a full row with three actions plus “More” for findability and errors. Sources and their limits Editorial design proposal. Editorial review, not user validation. Send feedback or report a problem with Gemini Apps Help article reviewed 7 October 2026 · Google help documentation; current interface and options may differ by platform and region. Learn about responses from Gemini Apps Help article reviewed 7 October 2026 · Google help documentation; double-checking against web search is not the same as checking quotations against a Bible edition. ChatGPT now allows you to branch conversations News report reviewed 7 October 2026 · Secondary news report, not OpenAI documentation; interface details may have changed. Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses Help article reviewed 7 October 2026 · Anthropic help documentation; does not describe every response action. Mental models: expectations of human-like interaction Human-like interaction section reviewed 6 October 2026 · Industry framework; not a controlled comparison of faith-app typing indicators. Generative AI Profile: Human–AI Configuration Section 2.7 reviewed 6 October 2026 · Risk framework, not evidence that one visual cue causes an outcome. Icon usability Article reviewed · Practitioner guidance from usability testing, not a controlled study. Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction Official guideline overview reviewed · General guidelines; disclosure alone does not establish accuracy, safety or spiritual benefit. Towards understanding sycophancy in language models Author research abstract reviewed on 5 October 2026; full paper not reviewed · Specific studied models and tasks; not a faith-app intervention study. Citations and trust in LLM generated responses Abstract reviewed · An online experiment with general questions; effects in religious study may differ. Faith and interpretation What travels beyond the conversation matters. A shared answer may be read as Scripture, as the church’s teaching or as a friend’s counsel. Letting the passage, rather than the generated text, be the thing people save and share keeps the Bible and its interpretation distinct.
