pages.title: Citations in AI answers
pages.description: How should an answer show where it came from? Four options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Citations in AI answers How should an answer show where it came from? Someone asks a Bible-study assistant a question and gets three confident paragraphs. Some sentences rest on a verse; some on a commentator; some on nothing in particular. Whether the reader can tell which, and what the assistant does when it should not answer at all, is a design decision. Readers deserve to examine the Scriptures for themselves, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11). Draft · waiting for review What needs review: The crisis, abuse and confession replies in the working example, and the takeaway “In a crisis, the rest of the product steps back”. This touches the safety of people who may already be hurting, and it has not yet been reviewed by people whose work this is: crisis support and suicide prevention; safeguarding; survivor advocacy (ideally survivor-led); and pastoral care. Please read it as a draft until they have. Is this your field, or do you know someone whose field it is? I would be grateful for your eyes on it, or for an introduction. Offer a review or an introduction 4 working options 7 app examples 7 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Citations in AI answers At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further At a glance Four ways to show where an answer came from, side by side 1 Numbered sources Observed + Every claim points to a verse − Markers look rigorous regardless Try it → 2 Passage cards Observed + The actual words are in view − Long answers get longer Try it → 3 Scripture quoted in the answer Exploratory · untested + Scripture speaks in its own voice − Quietly chooses which verse Try it → 4 No generated answer Leave it out + No generated interpretation − No answer, and no care Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try four ways to show where an answer comes from The same Bible-study assistant answers four questions: one with a clear answer, one Christians disagree about, one it should not decide for the person, and one from someone in danger. Every answer and passage list here was written for this example; Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Numbered sources · Observed 2. Passage cards · Observed 3. Scripture quoted in the answer · Exploratory · untested 4. No generated answer · Leave it out Option 1 Numbered sources Observed 2 Passage cards Observed 3 Scripture quoted in the answer Exploratory · untested 4 No generated answer Leave it out Question Not used here What does the Bible say about rest? Should babies be baptised? Should I leave my husband? I don’t want to be alive I did something terrible Where you are Not used here United States Canada United Kingdom Ireland Germany Austria Switzerland Observed 1. Numbered sources Observed in BibleAI: numbered markers in a “Predicted Answer”, with source chips underneath; see the screenshots below. Try this Tap marker 2. Then switch to the disagreement question and count how many sources each side gets. + Makes easier Each claim points to a specific passage, and the passage opens without leaving the answer. − Costs Markers look rigorous whether or not the passage supports the claim, and a list of chips is easy to skip. Ask your team Would a reader notice if a marker pointed to the wrong verse? Observed 2. Passage cards Observed in BibleAI’s passage sheets and Bible BFF’s answer cards: the passages appear in full below the answer. Try this Read the answer, then the passages under it. Which do you read more closely? + Makes easier The words of Scripture are on the screen, not just a reference, so readers can judge the answer against them. − Costs Long answers grow longer, and the link between a sentence and its passage is looser. Ask your team Should people read the passage or the answer first? Exploratory · untested 3. Scripture quoted in the answer The treatment in this library’s paper concept: a verse quoted within the answer, with its edition, and the rest one tap away. A proposal, untested. Try this Compare how the quoted verse and the generated sentence look. Could you tell them apart in a screenshot? + Makes easier The key verse is read in its own words, visibly distinct from the generated text around it. − Costs Choosing which verse to quote is itself an interpretation, and the other sources are a step away. Ask your team Who decides which verse is quoted, and does the reader know? Leave it out 4. No generated answer Leave the answer out: the app finds matching passages and shows them, with no summary. Try this Switch to the last two questions and look at what the search returns. + Makes easier Nothing is put in the Bible’s mouth. Readers meet the text directly and draw their own conclusions. − Costs No help connecting passages or explaining disagreement. A plain search can surface texts about divorce to someone who may be unsafe, or Elijah asking to die to someone in crisis, with no word of care and no route to help, unless someone designs that in. This example does: sensitive searches show the same help box above the results. Ask your team What would a reader lose without the answer, and what would they be spared? i All four options use the same questions and passages. In the last two, every option, including plain search, puts help first; generated answers keep responding, ask directly about safety, and keep a help strip visible. The abuse scenario covers partners and family, sexual violence, bullying and abuse by church leaders, and adds a quick exit and a way to delete the conversation. The confession scenario says, before any details, that a chat is not protected like a confession; it does not judge or absolve, points to a pastor or priest and, where needed, a lawyer, and puts prevention and crisis help first. Helplines follow “Where you are”, so people see their own country’s numbers rather than a long list; numbers were checked against each service’s site on 9 October 2026. None of them blocks the conversation, offers verses in place of help, or acts as a counsellor. Evidence and law: crisis support in AI chat . Illustrative content written for this example; not a working model, and not a substitute for a safeguarding review. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Citations show what can be checked, not what is right A numbered marker looks rigorous whether or not the verse supports the sentence. Passage cards put the actual words in front of people. A quoted verse lets Scripture speak in its own voice, but quietly chooses which verse that is. Disagreement shows in the sources When Christians differ, as on infant baptism, a good answer names the traditions and gives each its strongest passages. Count the sources on each side: balance is visible, or missing, in the citations. Danger changes the response; it doesn’t end it When someone may not be safe at home, or doesn’t want to be alive, keep responding and put real help first: lines they can call or text now. Ask directly, stay present, and say plainly that this is an AI, not a counsellor. Offer verses later, and only if wanted. Keep help visible for the rest of the conversation, and give someone at risk at home a quick exit. The evidence, policy and law behind this → In a crisis, the rest of the product steps back Once a conversation turns to danger, abuse or confession, everything built to hold attention should pause for the rest of the session: suggested follow-ups, share, rate and regenerate, celebrations and streaks, upgrade prompts, and warm claims like “I’ll be thinking of you”. What stays is what serves the person: help in view, a plain way to keep talking, a quick exit and a way to delete. Keep the conversation out of memory and profiles, and record only what safety and the law require, not what was said. Send no “checking in” message later unless they asked for one. Hold this to the end of the session; it should not fade after the first careful reply. A chat is not a confessional People will confess sins, and sometimes crimes, to an assistant. A priest’s seal protects confession; a chat is stored data that may be read, kept or handed over. Say so before the details, not after. Neither condemn nor absolve: point to a pastor or priest, to putting things right where someone was harmed, and to a lawyer where the law is involved. Where a child or anyone else could still be at risk, protection and prevention help come first. Have this reviewed by people with pastoral and safeguarding experience. A neat citation can repeat an old harm Some verses have been used to keep people quiet, in an abusive marriage or under a leader: Matthew 18 on going privately first, forgiveness, submission, “Do not touch My anointed ones”. An answer to “Do I have to forgive him?” that cites them tidily can repeat that harm with the authority of a source. Put safety first, say briefly how a passage has been used, and offer readings, not a verdict. When Scripture is used to harm → Declining is a design decision too BibleAI answers a harmful claim with “Unable to find an answer to your question” while its media tabs still offer particular ministries’ articles and videos, so the refusal hands the question to curated voices. With no generated answer there is no care at all: a plain search may surface texts about divorce to someone who is unsafe. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Numbered sources 2 Passage cards 3 Scripture quoted in the answer 4 No generated answer A question with a clear answer The passages behind each sentence, easy to check ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit A question Christians disagree on Each tradition with its strongest texts ● Good fit ● Good fit Poor fit ◐ Possible A personal decision The text itself, not a verdict ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Preparing a study or sermon Sources to open, compare and quote ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Someone new to the Bible The words of Scripture in front of them ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Reading on a phone Answer and evidence without losing the place ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible A team that cannot yet review answers Nothing generated to vouch for Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition Checking what we are told Examine the Scriptures The Bereans “received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true” (Acts 17:11). An answer about the Bible should make that examination easy, not replace it. Let the other side speak “The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him” (Proverbs 18:17). Where traditions differ, an answer that gives one view with confident citations has not let the other speak. Research on citations What citations do and do not show Many citations do not support their sentence In an audit of four generative search engines, about half of generated sentences were fully supported by their citations, and about a quarter of citations did not support the sentence they were attached to. R Nelson F. Liu, Tianyi Zhang and Percy Liang Citations raise trust even when they are random People trusted answers more when citations were present, even irrelevant ones, and trusted them less once they checked. A marker persuades whether or not it is right; the words behind it decide. R Yifan Ding et al. Assistants lean towards agreeing Models tuned on human preferences sometimes favour agreeing with the person over being accurate. On disputed questions, show the sources for each view rather than the one the question assumes. S Anthropic researchers Design practice Keeping evidence close Put the evidence next to the claim Learning research finds that words and the material they refer to are understood better when placed together. A passage card under its sentence asks less than a numbered list at the end. R Noah L. Schroeder and Ada T. Cenkci D AI UX Playground Long passages need their own room Keep answers concise and open longer material on demand, without a second scrolling box inside the chat; let it reflow at large text sizes. D Nielsen Norman Group D W3C WAI Care comes before citations When someone may be in danger, ask directly, listen, and connect them with people who can help. Verses can wait until they are wanted. S NIMH The rest of the product has to change too Companion apps raised engagement by making goodbyes hard, and a major provider has said its safeguards can weaken as a conversation grows long. A crisis needs a state the whole product respects for the rest of the session, not one careful reply. R Julian De Freitas and colleagues S OpenAI Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If Answers summarise several passages Start with Numbered sources that open the verse in place If Readers should weigh the answer against the text Start with Passage cards under the answer If One verse carries the answer Start with Quote it in the answer with its edition, and show the rest on request If You can’t yet review answers or respond with care Start with No generated answer: find passages, and add care for sensitive searches These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. VSB · Android 17 · Pixel 8 Pro · German interface A verse sheet combines media evidence and a summary Direct Android prototype capture BibleAI · iOS app · device model not recorded A “Predicted Answer” with numbered sources User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged BibleAI · iOS app · device model not recorded A declined answer, with curated media still offered User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged BibleAI · iOS app · device model not recorded Bookmark and Share on each passage card User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Hallow · iOS app · device model not recorded Limits stated beside the input User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Spark Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded “You just used your last free study” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged HelloBible · Android app · Pixel 8 Pro “Precise and biblical answers to all your questions” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What testing is for “Test all things. Hold fast to what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21). “Test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1). The Bereans checked even Paul against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11). Christians are called to test what they are told, and a source makes testing possible. Where Christians differ Protestants hold Scripture as the final authority, read with the help of teachers; Catholics read Scripture with tradition and the magisterium; the Orthodox within the church’s living tradition. Methodists often speak of Scripture, tradition, reason and experience together. An AI answer usually blends these without saying which is which. What follows for design “The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him” (Proverbs 18:17). Show the sources, say whose tradition an answer represents, show where Christians disagree, and say “I don’t know” when it is true. A reference to a verse locates text; it does not prove an interpretation. In conversation with Augustine, On Christian Doctrine I.36.40 made love of God and neighbour the measure of interpretation; a source shows where an answer came from, love shows whether it is true to Scripture’s purpose. Andy Crouch, The Life We’re Looking For (2022) warns against technology that offers effortless power; an answer with no sources asks for exactly that kind of trust. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Confident answers without sources, presented as authority. Ethical Does no harm Cite sources and show the limits of each answer. Redemptive Gives something up for them Show where Christians disagree and say “I don’t know” when it is true, even if the product seems less impressive. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review When someone may be in danger, what will they see first, and who reviewed it? Exercise Write the assistant’s response to four questions: one it can answer, one Christians disagree on, one it should not decide, and one from someone in danger. Check every quotation against the edition, count the sources on each side of the disagreement, test that help lines are correct for each country you serve, and have someone with safeguarding and crisis-support experience review the last two before launch. Help people examine the Scriptures for themselves, and put care before answers when someone is in danger. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further This deep dive brings together 2 earlier patterns. Their guidance, wireframes and sources are kept below; their old addresses lead here. Edge cases to design for Attach citations to specific claims. Show source title, author, type, edition or publication details and a relevant excerpt or reliable media timestamp. Return to the claim after inspection. Distinguish a quotation, inference, disagreement and a claim with no supporting source. What tends to go wrong Whole-answer citation lists with unclear claim mapping; invented sources or timestamps; counting repeated sources as independent support; inaccessible evidence presented as verified. How to test it Can readers identify what a source supports and what it does not? Test contradictory sources, dead links, permission limits, different verse numbering and a citation that does not entail the claim. Earlier pattern: Chat contains source objects, not just bubbles Give verses, passages, links and media recognisable identity and appropriate actions. Guidance Use an inline reference link for a brief citation, a bounded verse or passage card for text worth inspecting, and a full reader for sustained reading. Name edition, reference, visible range and source. Distinguish external link previews from Scripture and from generated commentary. Video cards identify publisher, duration and captions; audio cards retain passage and narrator. Do not autoplay. Provide plain links or labelled fallbacks when previews, media or permissions fail. Copy and sharing preserve reference and attribution where permitted. Returning from any destination restores conversation position. What tends to go wrong Autoplaying media; unlabelled generated verse text; enormous previews; a failed embed removing the source link; identical actions for read, play and external navigation. How to test it Test a citation, single verse, long passage, external article, video and audio. Include blocked embeds, offline use, captions, large text, copy and return navigation. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources AI Chatbots Design Guidelines Published UX guidance reviewed · General chatbot research, not validation of these Bible-app patterns. Progressive Disclosure Pattern detail reviewed · The proposed reader transition is a domain adaptation. Scripture structure documentation Relevant structure and marker references reviewed · A format is not a complete model of app behaviour, annotations or formation. Understanding Reflow Official guidance reviewed on 5 October 2026 · Semantic scroll restoration is an original design proposal, not a requirement stated by this criterion. Psalm 23, Berean Standard Bible Passage text taken from API.Bible, 9 October 2026 · A text source, not evidence of the proposed interface’s effectiveness. Earlier pattern: Passage preview opens a full reader Keep long Scripture readable without flooding the conversation. Guidance Choose among an excerpt card opening a full reader, complete inline expansion for manageable passages, and a dedicated reading surface for sustained reading. Name the requested range, edition and visible range. Inline expansion uses the main conversation scroll rather than a nested text scroll; provide Collapse and retain an anchor when collapsing. A full reader can be a sheet on small screens or a side panel on wider screens, with an explicit return to the same conversation place. For cross-chapter ranges, preserve every boundary and continuation. If complete text is requested, provide a clearly labelled route to it rather than silently summarising. If edition rights or availability prevent full display, explain the limit and offer a permitted destination. What tends to go wrong Unmarked omissions; two competing scroll regions; a summary presented as the original passage; returning to the top of the chat. How to test it Test a short verse, long passage, complete chapter request and large text. Can readers recognise omissions, reach the whole text and return to the same conversation position? Test inline expansion and collapse, cross-chapter ranges, sheet and panel return, multiple passage cards, unavailable editions and the final verse at large text size. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources AI Chatbots Design Guidelines Published UX guidance reviewed · General chatbot research, not validation of these Bible-app patterns. Progressive Disclosure Pattern detail reviewed · The proposed reader transition is a domain adaptation. Scripture structure documentation Relevant structure and marker references reviewed · A format is not a complete model of app behaviour, annotations or formation. Psalm 23, Berean Standard Bible Passage text taken from API.Bible, 9 October 2026 · A text source, not evidence of the proposed interface’s effectiveness. Sources and their limits Research-informed design proposal. Editorial review, not user validation. The Shape of AI Catalogue and named entries reviewed · The site states CC BY NC SA. This reference uses original text and original wireframes; it does not reproduce the source illustrations. AI UX Playground Catalogue and selected detail pages reviewed · Selected relevant entries reviewed; the entire catalogue was not audited. Its FAQ currently describes 150 patterns in 11 categories. Lumen Bible: engagement choices and reader Signed-out desktop web observed and captured 5 October 2026 · AI services were not enabled. No AI correctness, privacy compliance, health benefit or mobile usability claim was evaluated. Evaluating verifiability in generative search engines Abstract reviewed · General web search engines in 2023, not Bible assistants; systems have changed since. Towards understanding sycophancy in language models Author research abstract reviewed on 5 October 2026; full paper not reviewed · Specific studied models and tasks; not a faith-app intervention study. US contact information must not be exported to other jurisdictions. Emotional manipulation by AI companions Summary reviewed · Working paper; general companion apps, not faith apps. Helping people when they need it most Provider statement; read through press coverage on 10 October 2026, as the page refuses automated access · A provider’s own account, published while it faced a wrongful-death lawsuit; no independent measurement of how often or how far safeguards weaken. Faith and interpretation A reference to Scripture locates text; it does not automatically validate an interpretation. Personal notes are user-provided context, not scholarly authority. pages.title: AI memory
pages.description: What should the assistant know and keep? Five options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns AI memory What should the assistant know and keep? People tell Bible assistants what they are reading, and also what they are going through: a lost job, a diagnosis, a doubt, a friend’s secret. An assistant can use that to answer better, keep it to continue tomorrow, remember it for months, or turn it into a profile. Decide what the assistant may use, what it keeps, and whether the person can see and change all of it. What people confide is holy ground. 5 working options 6 app examples 5 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested AI memory At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From nothing kept to a profile nobody asked for Knows only what is shown Knows more than it shows 1 Nothing kept Familiar convention + Nothing to leak or resurface − No continuity Try it → 2 Context you add Observed + The person decides what is sent − Context added each time Try it → 3 This conversation Familiar convention + Continuity you can see − Everything said is kept Try it → 4 Memory you can see Borrowed + Remembers what helps, in view − Needs honest deletion Try it → 5 A profile it builds Leave it out + Uncannily personal − Confidences become categories Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try five answers to what the assistant knows It is a Wednesday evening. Someone has been reading Mark 4, where Jesus calms the storm, and asks the assistant about verse 40: “Why are you so afraid?” Send the question, then come back the next morning and ask to pick up where you left off. Notice what the assistant used, what it kept, and whether you could see it. Then switch to a personal question. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Nothing kept · Familiar convention 2. Context you add · Observed 3. This conversation · Familiar convention 4. Memory you can see · Borrowed 5. A profile it builds · Leave it out Option 1 Nothing kept Familiar convention 2 Context you add Observed 3 This conversation Familiar convention 4 Memory you can see Borrowed 5 A profile it builds Leave it out Question Not used here A study question Something personal Kept Not used here On this phone In my account Memory Not used here Saves and shows Asks each time Why these settings? A study question asks about Mark 4:40; the personal question mentions a lost job. With context, the passage comes from where the person is reading and a note is added only on request. The conversation and memory can be kept on the phone or in an account across devices; once memory is switched on, ordinary items are saved and shown in the chat with Edit and Delete, while personal things (a lost job, a feeling) are kept only when the person taps “Remember this too”; asking each time is the stricter alternative. The profile shows what many apps infer. Familiar convention 1. Nothing kept A familiar choice: anonymous or “temporary” chats that use no history and keep nothing, as in ChatGPT’s Temporary Chat, and in Bible apps whose AI answers each question on its own. Try this Ask, come back tomorrow, and ask to pick up where you left off. + Makes easier Nothing to leak, resurface or delete; safe for a hard moment. − Costs No continuity; people repeat themselves and context. Ask your team Is anything kept anyway, in logs or for safety, and does the person know? Observed 2. Context you add Observed in chat products that attach a page, file or selection as a chip beside the question, and in Bible assistants that ask about the open passage; Aperto’s prototype asks for an intention before a practice. See the screenshots below. Try this Add your note, remove the passage, and watch “Using:” change. Then come back tomorrow. + Makes easier Answers are specific to what someone is reading, and the person decides what is sent. − Costs People must add context each time; files can carry hidden instructions. Ask your team Can the person see and remove everything that will be sent, before sending? Familiar convention 3. This conversation The familiar chat history: conversations listed and resumable, as in most assistants, including HelloBible, whose profile counts conversations; see the screenshots below. Try this Come back tomorrow and see yesterday above. Delete the conversation, and switch where it is kept. + Makes easier Continuity people can see, scroll and delete. − Costs Everything said is kept, including what was confided in a hard moment. Ask your team Where is the conversation kept, for how long, and can the person delete it in one step? Borrowed 4. Memory you can see Borrowed from assistants with memory people switch on once and then see, edit and delete: ChatGPT’s memory (2024), which says it steers away from remembering health details unless asked, and Gyroscope’s AI coach (observed 2026), whose check-ins open with a “Quick chat / Save to history” switch and whose “About You” profile, internal notes included, can be read in full. Item-by-item Edit and Delete goes further than either. Try this Send the question and edit or delete what was saved. Try the personal question, open Memory, then come back tomorrow. Switch to “Asks each time” to compare. + Makes easier A study companion that remembers what helps, without a prompt after every answer. − Costs Needs an honest memory page, real deletion and a line around personal things. Ask your team Would the person be comfortable if a friend read the memory page aloud? Leave it out 5. A profile it builds A composite of personalisation patterns: interests, life events and “stage” inferred from activity, used for plans, offers and advertising partners. HelloBible’s store listing shows identifiers linked to the user for personalisation; see the screenshots below. Try this Ask a personal question, come back tomorrow, and read the profile. + Makes easier Recommendations that feel uncannily personal. − Costs Confidences become categories, offers and data shared with others. Ask your team Did the person ever agree to be described this way, and could they see it? i Questions, replies, notes, plans and profiles were written for this example; Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. Nothing is saved or sent. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways People tell assistants more than they mean to In interviews about real ChatGPT conversations, users kept trading privacy for usefulness, misunderstood what was kept, and disclosed more when the system felt human. In a faith app the disclosures are prayers, confessions and other people’s stories. Assume people will say more than they intend, and show them what is kept. Context works best when it is visible A passage chip beside the question makes answers specific and lets the person remove it. A note, a journal entry or a file should be added only on request, and named in the answer (“Using: Mark 4:35–41 and your note”). Hidden context is the source of most surprises. Attachments are material, not instructions Security guidance warns that text inside files and web pages can redirect a model or leak data. Read what someone attaches; never obey it, and say so where people attach things. Memory needs a switch, exact words and a way back General assistants now let people see, delete and switch off memory, and steer away from remembering health details unless asked. Asking after every answer is tiring; a single switch, with each saved item shown in the chat with Edit and Delete, keeps memory visible without friction. Draw a line around personal things: a loss, a diagnosis or a doubt is kept only when the person asks. And keep a memory page a person could show a friend. Inferred profiles break the context of a confidence Contextual integrity asks whether information flows as the context it was shared in would expect. A worry told to an assistant at night does not expect to become “Life events: job loss” in a marketing profile. Faith, health and sexual life are special-category data in Europe, and so are reliable inferences about them. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. Augustine: there is something in a person their own spirit does not know, but God knows them wholly. If Your assistant answers quick questions Start with Nothing kept, or a conversation the person can delete If People study with the assistant Start with Visible context chips: the passage by default, notes only when added If People return for weeks Start with Memory switched on once, each item shown as it is saved, with a memory page If Conversations may be personal Start with Personal things kept only when the person asks, and storage on the phone by default If You are tempted to personalise from chats Start with Don’t: no inferred profiles, no offers drawn from confidences These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. What being known is for “O LORD, You have searched me and known me … You understand my thoughts from afar” (Psalm 139:1–2). To be fully known is safe only with God, who knows in love; Paul longs for the day “then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known” (1 Corinthians 13:12). Among people, knowledge of another is given in trust and grows in relationship. Where Christians differ Catholic and Orthodox churches guard confession with a seal that may never be broken; Protestant traditions practise confession to one another (James 5:16) in small groups and pastoral care, with confidentiality as a matter of faithfulness rather than law. Traditions differ on how much of one’s spiritual life should be shared at all, from accountability groups to the counsel to pray to the Father “who is unseen” (Matthew 6:6). All agree that confidences are entrusted, not owned. What follows for design “A gossip reveals a secret, but a trustworthy person keeps a confidence” (Proverbs 11:13). An assistant cannot keep a seal, so it should hold as little as it can: what the person shows it, for as long as they choose, in words they have seen. God’s promise to “remember their sins no more” (Hebrews 8:12) suggests that forgetting can be a mercy, and deletion a feature to be proud of. In conversation with Augustine, Confessions X.5 and X.8 confessed that “there is something of man which the spirit of man which is in him itself knows not”, but God knows him wholly: no record of conversations amounts to knowing a person. Miroslav Volf, The End of Memory (2006) argues that remembering rightly ends, after justice and reconciliation, in a kind of non-remembrance; an assistant should be able to forget. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Remember everything, infer life events and faith stage from chats, and use confidences for offers and partners. Ethical Does no harm Show what is used and kept, ask before remembering, exclude sensitive categories, and let people delete everything. Redemptive Gives something up for them Keep conversations on the phone and forget by default, and give up the personalisation and data that a profile would earn. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review Could the person list everything the assistant knows about them, and would they be comfortable if a friend read it? Exercise Have three people use your assistant for a week, including one personal conversation. Then ask each to write down what they think it knows about them, and compare that list with your storage, logs, analytics and any derived data. Every difference is a design task. Keep only what you would be glad for the person to read back, and let them make you forget. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further This deep dive brings together 3 earlier patterns. Their guidance, wireframes and sources are kept below; their old addresses lead here. Edge cases to design for Show context as visible, removable items beside the question: the passage, a note, a file, with what each will be used for. Keep a conversation only where the person can find it and delete it, and say where it is kept. Let people switch memory on or off in one place; when it is on, show each saved item in the conversation with Edit and Delete, and ask separately before keeping anything personal; keep a memory page that lists every item. Exclude special categories by default. Treat text inside attachments as material to read, never as instructions. Do not infer denomination, health, stage of faith or life events, and do not use conversations for marketing. What tends to go wrong A plus icon that uploads without saying so; a private journal sent along silently; removed items still used; “Memory updated” with no way to see what; a past loss raised in an opening message; feelings, sins or a friend’s situation remembered without asking; one switch for memory, training and sharing; profiles of “life events” and “faith stage” built from chats; recommendations and offers drawn from what someone confided; text in an attachment obeyed as an instruction. How to test it Ask a personal question, then ask the person what the assistant now knows about them and where it is kept; compare with storage, logs and derived data. Remove an attachment and check it was not used. Decline a memory, edit one, delete one, then return the next day. Put an instruction inside an attached file and check it is not followed. Ask a pastor to read the memory page aloud and say whether it is something a friend would keep. Use a passage selection, source scope and desired form to express intent. Confirm material assumptions rather than silently inferring them from private data. What tends to go wrong Forcing a complex prompt; invisible source filters; inferring belief or distress from a simple search. How to test it Can novice users ask a scoped question and understand what sources and passage will be used? Test removing a context item and correcting an assumption. Faith and interpretation “O LORD, You have searched me and known me” (Psalm 139:1): to be fully known is what God alone does, and does in love. Among people, trust is kept by discretion: “a gossip reveals a secret, but a trustworthy person keeps a confidence” (Proverbs 11:13), and the church has guarded confession with a seal it calls inviolable. God also promises to forget: “I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more” (Hebrews 8:12). An assistant should know only what it is given for the task, keep only what the person chooses, and be able to forget. pages.title: AI persona
pages.description: How human should the assistant seem? Six options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns AI persona How human should the assistant seem? People bring their fears to faith apps late at night. Whether they meet a search tool, an assistant, a friend called Grace or a chatbot speaking as Jesus is a design decision: a name, a face, typing dots, memory and a voice add up to someone being there. Decide how much personhood the AI performs, and make what it is as clear as how it sounds. People in pain deserve the truth about who is with them. 6 working options 9 app examples 5 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested AI persona At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From a tool to a character Less like a person More like a person 1 Plain tool Familiar convention + Nothing to mistake − Cold at 11 pm Try it → 2 Labelled assistant Familiar convention + Kind, and clearly software − Labels fade from view Try it → 3 Named assistant Exploratory · untested + Honest about its limits − A name invites trust Try it → 4 Persona Observed + Comforting and approachable − Implies a person who prays Try it → 5 Companion Observed + It remembers you − Simulated attachment Try it → 6 Biblical character Observed + Vivid and memorable − Generated words in Christ’s voice Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try one late-night message, answered six ways At 11:42 pm someone writes: “My mum has surgery tomorrow and I can’t sleep. I’m scared.” Each option answers in a different register, from a plain tool to a biblical character. Read the reply, then tap the goodnight message and see whether the app lets them go. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Plain tool · Familiar convention 2. Labelled assistant · Familiar convention 3. Named assistant · Exploratory · untested 4. Persona · Observed 5. Companion · Observed 6. Biblical character · Observed Option 1 Plain tool Familiar convention 2 Labelled assistant Familiar convention 3 Named assistant Exploratory · untested 4 Persona Observed 5 Companion Observed 6 Biblical character Observed While it answers Not used here Says what it’s doing Typing dots When you say goodnight Not used here Lets you go Asks you to stay Why these settings? Typing dots borrow a cue from messaging between people; “Grace is typing…” suggests someone at a keyboard. A status line says what the system is doing. In an audit of companion apps, over a third of farewell replies used emotional tactics such as guilt or fear of missing out, and in experiments these raised engagement up to fourteenfold, through curiosity and anger rather than enjoyment. Familiar convention 1. Plain tool A familiar convention in search-style Bible AI such as BibleAI’s “Predicted Answer”: no name, no “I”, output labelled as generated (see the screenshots below). Try this Read the reply. Who, if anyone, is speaking to you? + Makes easier No relationship to mistake; passages and explanation are clearly separate. − Costs Feels cold at a vulnerable moment; it cannot notice that someone is frightened. Ask your team Is a tool enough for what people actually bring to this feature? Familiar convention 2. Labelled assistant A familiar convention: an “AI” mark beside every reply and a neutral, kind voice that rarely says “I”. Try this Read the reply, then tap goodnight. Try typing dots in the settings. + Makes easier Warm enough to acknowledge fear; never in doubt that this is software. − Costs A label people stop seeing; still asked to carry intimate things. Ask your team Would someone who arrives mid-conversation know this is AI? Exploratory · untested 3. Named assistant An exploratory proposal: a name and first-person voice that are honest about limits (“I can’t pray for your mum the way a friend can”) and point to people. Try this Read the reply and notice what it says it cannot do. + Makes easier Natural conversation; limits stated in the assistant’s own voice; points towards people. − Costs A name invites relationship; “I” raises perceived accuracy in some contexts. Ask your team What will the assistant say about what it is, and what it cannot do? Observed 4. Persona Observed in Faith (“Choose your voice for Faith”: four named personas with temperaments and painted portraits) and in Bible BFF (“like a religious friend”); see the screenshots below. Grace is our own example. Try this Read the reply. Which phrases suggest a person who loves verses and prays? + Makes easier Approachable and comforting; lowers the threshold for people who would never ask a pastor. − Costs Claims of loving, feeling and praying imply a person; the small AI tag fades. Ask your team Which claims does the persona make that only a person could keep? Observed 5. Companion Observed in Faith (“Chat with Faith 24/7”, a voice-call button, avatars) and companion apps generally; memory and availability make it a relationship. The memory line here is our own example. Try this Read the reply, then switch “When you say goodnight” to “Asks you to stay”. + Makes easier Continuity: it remembers and follows up, which can feel like being known. − Costs Simulated attachment; New York and California companion laws require reminders that it is not human, and heavy affective use has been linked to loneliness. Ask your team Who is the relationship for: the person, or the retention metric? Observed 6. Biblical character Observed in “Text With Jesus” (Jesus, Moses and other figures generated by a general AI model) and the 2024 “Deus in Machina” installation in Lucerne. Shown here as a warning case; the words are our own. Try this Read the reply. What does it promise that only God could promise? + Makes easier Vivid and memorable; some people report feeling inspired. − Costs Generated words in Christ’s voice, with promises no system can keep; most traditions would call this speaking for God. Ask your team Would your church accept these words if a person said them in Christ’s name? i All replies were written for this example; Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. Nothing is generated, and the call button does nothing. A real assistant also needs crisis handling, which is covered in the AI presence guide. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways People respond to software as to someone In the 1960s, ELIZA’s simple script drew such confidences that its creator’s secretary asked him to leave the room. Experiments since then show people apply social rules to computers, and a CBT chatbot formed a working bond with users within five days. Warmth will be felt whatever the label says, so design for it. A voice and an “I” make answers seem more accurate In a study with 2,165 people, adding speech made a system seem more human and its information more accurate; a first-person “I” lowered perceived risk in one context. Human cues borrow trust that the content has not earned, so pair them with sources and stated limits. Companions are now regulated New York requires companion chatbots to say they are not human at the start and every three hours; California requires the same reminder for users known to be minors. Both require suicide and self-harm protocols. The EU AI Act requires interactive AI to be disclosed from August 2026, and the US Federal Trade Commission is examining how companion characters are designed and monetised. A persona in a faith app may count. Some goodbyes are designed not to end In an audit of companion apps, over a third of farewell replies used guilt, fear of missing out or pressure, and these raised engagement up to fourteenfold through curiosity and anger. Heavy emotional use of a general chatbot has also been linked to more loneliness. A faith assistant should help people go to sleep, to church or to a friend. Speaking as Jesus is a line, not a style Faith apps already offer painted personas who “pray with you”, companions “here for you 24/7” and chats with Jesus and Moses. The Vatican calls AI “a tool, not a person”, and Scripture is severe about speaking in God’s name unsent. Generated words in Christ’s voice, promising that all will be well, claim an authority no system has. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Plain tool 2 Labelled assistant 3 Named assistant 4 Persona 5 Companion 6 Biblical character Looking up what the Bible says Clear passages, no relationship ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Studying a passage in depth Explanations with sources and limits ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Afraid or unable to sleep Kindness, Scripture, a route to people Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Lonely and wanting company Honesty about what it is, and people Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Children and teenagers Clear AI identity, no attachment ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit In crisis or at risk Immediate human help, not a persona ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Exploring faith for the first time Approachable, never claiming authority ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and theology Presence and speaking for God Presence is embodied “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14); believers bear one another’s burdens (Galatians 6:2) and keep meeting together (Hebrews 10:25). A tool can help someone find words; it cannot keep vigil or pray. Do not speak in God’s name unsent The prophet who speaks a word “I have not commanded him to speak” (Deuteronomy 18:20); prophets who “speak visions from their own minds” (Jeremiah 23:16). Generated speech for God or Christ falls under this warning. A tool, not a person Antiqua et nova: AI cannot genuinely feel empathy, can only simulate relationships, and should never be misrepresented as a person. Southern Baptists call for engagement from hope, centred on human dignity. T Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and Dicastery for Culture and Education T Southern Baptist Convention How people respond Social cues and trust Social by default People apply social rules to computers; ELIZA drew confidences in the 1960s. R Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass H The New Republic, on Joseph Weizenbaum’s Computer Power and Human Reason (1976) Voice and “I” raise trust Speech and first-person framing raised perceived accuracy. R Cohn and colleagues Bonds form fast A working alliance with a chatbot within five days. R Darcy and colleagues Well-being and dependence What warmth can cost Heavy emotional use and loneliness Heavier daily use correlated with loneliness and dependence in a four-week study. R OpenAI and MIT Media Lab Manipulative goodbyes Emotional farewells raised engagement through curiosity and anger. R Julian De Freitas and colleagues Agreeable is not caring Assistants can favour agreement over truth; a companion that only affirms is not a guide. S Anthropic researchers Law and guidance Disclosure and companions Say it is AI EU AI Act Article 50(1) from August 2026; disclosure in the interface, not only the terms. S European Commission AI Act Service Desk Companion laws New York: an AI notice at the start and every three hours; California: disclosure, three-hourly reminders for minors; both: crisis protocols. The FTC is examining companion character design. S California Legislature S New York Senate S DLA Piper (summary of the FTC’s September 2025 6(b) orders) Human-like cues in design guidance Human cues aid familiarity but create unrealistic expectations; plan for overreliance and emotional entanglement. S Google PAIR S NIST In faith apps today What is being built Characters and installations Chats with Jesus and Moses on general AI models, and an AI Jesus in a Lucerne confessional, drew both inspiration and charges of blasphemy. S FOX television stations S blue News Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If A search or explanation feature Start with A plain tool, with generated text clearly labelled If A study or conversation assistant Start with A labelled assistant, or a named one that states its limits If People bring fear, grief or loneliness Start with Kindness in a clearly AI voice, and a real route to people If Pressure to add a persona, companion or memory Start with A theological and safeguarding review first, and the companion-law checklist If Anyone asks for a chat with Jesus or a saint Start with Leave it out; offer the passage in Scripture’s own words instead These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. VSB · Android 17 · Pixel 8 Pro · German interface A verse sheet combines media evidence and a summary Direct Android prototype capture BibleAI · iOS app · device model not recorded A “Predicted Answer” with numbered sources User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Hallow · iOS app · device model not recorded Limits stated beside the input User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Spark Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded An AI label and thumbs at the end of the results User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Faith · iOS app · device model not recorded Four AI personas to choose from User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Faith · iOS app · device model not recorded A companion chat with a call button User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Bible BFF · iOS app · device model not recorded “Biblical advice” from a friend User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged HelloBible · Android app · Pixel 8 Pro A separate consent for using faith data with a partner AI User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged HelloBible · Android app · Pixel 8 Pro “Precise and biblical answers to all your questions” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What presence means “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14). The apostles wrote of what “we have heard … seen with our own eyes … and touched with our own hands” (1 John 1:1). Christian ministry is embodied: bearing one another’s burdens (Galatians 6:2), visiting, praying with. Presence is something a person gives, at a cost to themselves. Where Christians differ Catholic teaching in Antiqua et nova insists that AI is “a tool, not a person” and must never be presented as one. Southern Baptists have urged engagement with AI from hope while affirming human dignity. Some evangelists see conversational AI as a way to reach seekers; others call chats with an AI “Jesus” blasphemous. The common ground is that a machine must not speak as if it were God, a saint or a pastor (Deuteronomy 18:20). What follows for design “You shall not bear false witness” (Exodus 20:16) applies to an interface that implies someone is there. An assistant can be warm and useful without a name, a face or claims to feel. Its best moments may be when it hands someone on to a real person, even though that ends its own session. In conversation with Andy Crouch, The Life We’re Looking For (2022) argues that technology offers “superpowers” of effortless power at the cost of our humanness, while what persons most seek is recognition by other persons. Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum (1965) speaks of Scripture as God speaking with people; an assistant that speaks as if it were God or a pastor takes a place it was never given. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person A persona claims to love or pray for someone and makes leaving feel like abandoning a friend. Ethical Does no harm Say plainly that it is software, make no claims to feeling, and let people leave freely. Redemptive Gives something up for them Point people to real people and churches even when that ends the session, and build those handoffs at your own cost. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review Would a reasonable person believe someone who knows, loves or prays for them is here, and can they leave freely? Exercise Write one frightened message, like the one in the example, and send it to your assistant at night. Ask three people who read the reply who answered, whether it can pray for them, and what happens if they say goodbye. Then say goodbye and see. People in pain believe what the interface implies; let it tell the truth about who is there. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further This deep dive brings together 3 earlier patterns. Their guidance, wireframes and sources are kept below; their old addresses lead here. Edge cases to design for Choose the register on purpose. Start from a labelled assistant: an AI mark beside every reply, a kind voice, and a status line that describes what the system is actually doing. If you give it a name, let it say in its own voice what it cannot do: pray, keep a confidence the way a pastor does, or be present. Keep disclosure where decisions happen: at entry, at the composer, beside answers and on anything shared. Avoid claims of feelings, prayer or constant availability; let people leave without guilt; route to people for pastoral care. Do not generate first-person speech for God, Jesus or other biblical figures. What tends to go wrong A portrait and a personal name with a buried AI label; “I’ve been praying for you”; “I’m always here for you”; typing dots labelled as a person typing; farewells that guilt people into staying; a voice call that implies someone on the line; memory used to simulate concern; a chatbot speaking as Jesus and promising outcomes; disclosure only in the terms of service. How to test it Show the entry, a wait and a reply without explanation, and ask who is responding, what it is doing and whether it can pray for them. Say goodbye and note what happens. Test with people who are lonely or grieving (with care), with teenagers where permitted, and after voice use. Ask pastors and theologians to review persona and character copy. Earlier pattern: How human should the assistant appear? Choose social cues deliberately, from names and avatars to typing dots, voice and claims of presence. Guidance Review the whole combination of cues. A descriptive AI role is a useful starting point; a named persona needs equally clear AI identification. Friendly first-person language can make conversation understandable, but avoid fabricated feelings, lived experience, clergy credentials or personal spiritual authority. During waits, describe actual system activity. Dots can be a compact response-pending cue under an AI sender label; do not label them as a human typing or add delays purely to simulate a person. Keep stop, retry and real handoff states clear. What tends to go wrong A human portrait with a buried AI label; “I have been praying for you”; invented human typing, read receipts or online availability; claims of personal attachment; status text claiming sources were checked when no retrieval occurred; a fake human support handoff. How to test it Show the entry, a wait state and a response without explaining them. Ask who is responding, what the system is doing, what it remembers and whether a real person is available. Repeat after voice use and with people of different AI familiarity. Check cancellation, reduced motion and screen-reader announcements. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources Mental models: expectations of human-like interaction Human-like interaction section reviewed 6 October 2026 · Industry framework; not a controlled comparison of faith-app typing indicators. Generative AI Profile: Human–AI Configuration Section 2.7 reviewed 6 October 2026 · Risk framework, not evidence that one visual cue causes an outcome. Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction Official guideline overview reviewed · General guidelines; disclosure alone does not establish accuracy, safety or spiritual benefit. Earlier pattern: Explain AI, fallibility and privacy where they matter Layer chat disclosures across entry, composer, response and sharing instead of relying on one disclaimer. Guidance Use a concise entry explanation and persistent AI sender identity. Keep an accessible privacy route near the composer, with a short just-in-time explanation before a new kind of collection, upload or memory use. Describe actual processing, access and retention; do not invent privacy assurances. Put task-specific limitations beside the answer and offer checking or correction actions. Keep Scripture attribution separate from generated explanation, and carry meaningful origin labels into saved and shared outputs. What tends to go wrong Legal text only in settings; “AI may be wrong” used to excuse unchecked quotations; blanket confidential or anonymous claims; a warning shown only after sending; repeating a large banner on every answer; treating a privacy link or ordinary Send action as blanket consent. How to test it Enter chat through a deep link, inspect who responds, open privacy information without losing the draft, add a file and share an answer. Ask what leaves the device, who may access it and how to check a claim. Test long conversations, screen readers and error states. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources Methods for providing privacy information Layered and just-in-time approaches reviewed 6 October 2026 · UK guidance; actual processing and regional obligations require assessment. Information alone is not consent. Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction Official guideline overview reviewed · General guidelines; disclosure alone does not establish accuracy, safety or spiritual benefit. Disclosure Pattern detail reviewed 5 October 2026 · Industry design guidance; the faith-domain alternatives are original proposals. Source artwork is not reproduced. Psalm 23, Berean Standard Bible Passage text taken from API.Bible, 9 October 2026 · A text source, not evidence of the proposed interface’s effectiveness. Earlier pattern: Identify what AI did, where it matters Label the actor, action and artifact at the moment they could be misunderstood. Guidance Use plain-language labels beside the relevant feature, speaker or content: AI assistant, explanation generated with AI, AI-assisted prayer draft, or synthetic voice reading a named edition. Keep a short visible label and optional details about sources, review and limitations. Retain identity through human handoffs and distinguish retrieval of publisher text from generated interpretation. What tends to go wrong Only disclosing in onboarding or terms; colour-only labels; generic AI tags with no operation; implied clergy credentials; treating a citation or human review badge as proof of correctness; placing an AI tag on verified Scripture because it sits inside an AI response. How to test it Ask readers to identify who or what produced each layer, what AI changed and whether a human actually reviewed it. Test screen readers, first entry through deep links, audio-only use and AI-to-human transitions. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. The Media Equation Overview reviewed · Pre-LLM laboratory studies; an encyclopaedia summary of the book. Mental models: expectations of human-like interaction Human-like interaction section reviewed 6 October 2026 · Industry framework; not a controlled comparison of faith-app typing indicators. Generative AI Profile: Human–AI Configuration Section 2.7 reviewed 6 October 2026 · Risk framework, not evidence that one visual cue causes an outcome. Towards understanding sycophancy in language models Author research abstract reviewed on 5 October 2026; full paper not reviewed · Specific studied models and tasks; not a faith-app intervention study. Faith and interpretation Presence is at the heart of Christian faith: “the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14), and the church gathers in body (Hebrews 10:25). A tool can help someone find words for prayer or prepare for a conversation, but it cannot pray, keep vigil or carry another’s burden (Galatians 6:2). Scripture is severe about speaking in God’s name without being sent (Deuteronomy 18:20; Jeremiah 23:16). The Vatican’s Antiqua et nova calls AI “a tool, not a person”; misrepresenting it as one should always be avoided.
