pages.title: Bible audio
pages.description: How should Scripture be heard: as text, voice or read-along? Five options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Bible audio How should Scripture be heard: as text, voice or read-along? Scripture was heard long before it was read silently, and for many people today listening is the main way in: on the way to work, before sleep, or because reading is hard. Apps decide how much the voice leads, whose voice it is, and what happens when the reading ends. Giving Scripture a voice is an old ministry, and a serious one: whoever shapes the voice shapes how people hear the word. 5 working options 7 app examples 5 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Bible audio At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From the page to the ear The text leads The voice leads 1 Text only Leave it out + Nothing to produce − Leaves listeners out Try it → 2 Listen button Familiar convention + Audio wherever the text is − Voice and text drift apart Try it → 3 Read-along Observed + Text follows the voice − Moving text needs control Try it → 4 Audio first Observed + Works with the screen dark − Autoplay runs on Try it → 5 Produced devotional Observed + A whole practice in minutes − Editors’ voices beside Scripture Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try five ways of hearing Psalm 23 Psalm 23 in the Berean Standard Bible, from text alone to a produced daily prayer. Press play in each option and watch what the text does; then try a synthetic voice and music. Playback is simulated: nothing sounds. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Text only · Leave it out 2. Listen button · Familiar convention 3. Read-along · Observed 4. Audio first · Observed 5. Produced devotional · Observed Option 1 Text only Leave it out 2 Listen button Familiar convention 3 Read-along Observed 4 Audio first Observed 5 Produced devotional Observed Voice Not used here Narrator Synthetic Music Not used here Off On Why these settings? Synthetic voices are now hard to tell from people; listeners trust voices less when told they are AI, and from August 2026 the EU AI Act requires generated audio to be marked. The example labels the voice in every player. Music is optional because background music mildly disturbs reading, while many listeners value it. Leave it out 1. Text only Leaving audio out, as many study-focused apps do. Try this Read the psalm. Then imagine reading it while driving, or with low vision. + Makes easier Nothing to produce, license or moderate; the text is the whole experience. − Costs Leaves out commuters, people with low vision or dyslexia, and anyone who receives Scripture by ear. Ask your team Who cannot use your product without audio? Familiar convention 2. Listen button A familiar convention: most Bible apps offer narration with a play button above or below the text. Try this Press play and follow along by yourself. + Makes easier Audio is available wherever the text is, with no change to reading. − Costs Voice and text drift apart; the listener has to keep their own place. Ask your team Is the audio for listening alone, or for reading along? Observed 3. Read-along Observed in Dwell and Soultime, where the verse being read is highlighted or isolated (see the screenshots in the related deep dives). Try this Press play and watch the highlight move. Then pause it mid-verse. + Makes easier Text and voice stay together; helpful for learning to read, for dyslexia and for following closely. − Costs A moving highlight needs a pause, and timing must be accurate to the verse or sentence. Ask your team At what level should the text follow the voice: verse, sentence or word? Observed 4. Audio first Observed in Dwell, the Joseph Prince app and Abide: full players with skip, speed and a sleep timer (see the screenshots below). Try this Press play, skip back 15 seconds, then switch the sleep timer off and see what plays next. + Makes easier Works with the screen dark: walking, driving, falling asleep. − Costs The text is out of sight; autoplay can run on into the next chapter, or into something else entirely. Ask your team What happens when the passage ends? Observed 5. Produced devotional Observed in Pray As You Go, whose sessions combine music, Scripture read twice and reflection questions, with a timestamped script (see the screenshots below). The reflection here is our own. Try this Play the session and jump between segments. Then switch music off and see what changes. + Makes easier A whole practice in a few minutes: Scripture, silence and prayer held together. − Costs Editors’ reflections sit beside Scripture; music can comfort or distract. Ask your team Who wrote the words around the Scripture, and how will listeners know? i Psalm 23, Berean Standard Bible. Playback is simulated at four times speed and nothing sounds; reflection and prayer texts in the produced devotional were written for this example. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Hearing is the older way of receiving Scripture Letters were written to be read aloud to whole churches, and Revelation blesses “they that hear”. Faith Comes By Hearing began as a tape library in 1972 and now records Scripture in over 1,580 languages; a Bible-in-a-year podcast reached No. 1 in the US. Audio is not an accessory to reading. Listening can be understood as well as reading In one study, comprehension was the same whether people read, listened, or did both. Read-along highlighting helped children with dyslexia follow, and karaoke-style subtitles have built literacy at scale. Let the text follow the voice when the screen is on. The ending is a design decision Audio-first players work with the screen dark, which makes the ending matter: autoplay can run on into the next chapter, or something else entirely. A sleep timer that stops at the end of the passage, or a moment of silence, keeps the listener in charge. Pray As You Go ends every session without a next track. Whose voice it is matters Listeners told a voice is AI trust it less, and from August 2026 the EU AI Act requires generated audio to be marked. Label synthetic voices plainly, name human narrators, and never imitate a known pastor’s voice without consent. A voice interprets, as a reader in church does. Music and reflections add other voices Background music mildly disturbs reading but many people value it emotionally, so make it optional. In produced devotionals, say who wrote the reflections and keep them audibly distinct from Scripture. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Text only 2 Listen button 3 Read-along 4 Audio first 5 Produced devotional Commuting or walking Screen off, skip and pause Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit Falling asleep A gentle end, no autoplay Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Learning to read, or dyslexia Text that follows the voice Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Close study The text, at your own pace ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Daily prayer Scripture, silence and prayer together Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit Low vision Audio with large controls Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible Oral cultures and low literacy Audio as the main way in Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition Heard before read Written to be read aloud “Faith comes by hearing” (Romans 10:17). “Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear” (Revelation 1:3). Paul’s letters were read to whole congregations, and Israel heard the law read publicly (Nehemiah 8:8). A voice interprets A reader’s pace and emphasis shape meaning, which is why churches train readers. In an app, the narrator, the music and any reflection are all part of how the passage is received. Listening today What people actually do Audio as a first language Faith Comes By Hearing reports recordings in over 1,580 languages and launched Bible.is in 2010. Advocacy networks estimate most of the world are oral learners; the figures are contested, but the need is real. S Faith Comes By Hearing S Scripture Engagement (Taylor University) Mass listening and daily practice Bible in a Year reached No. 1 among US podcasts, with 170 million downloads reported in 2021. Pray As You Go has offered a daily ten-minute prayer since 2006. S University of St Thomas news S Jesuits in Britain Listening science What helps, what distracts Listening matches reading No significant comprehension difference between reading, listening and both in one study. R Rogowsky, Calhoun and Tallal Text that follows the voice Synchronised highlighting helped children with dyslexia read along; same-language subtitles have supported literacy. R International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning R World Bank blog on Brij Kothari’s work Music is a trade-off Background music slightly disturbs reading but supports emotional response. R Kämpfe, Sedlmeier and Renkewitz Voices, law and access Best practice Label synthetic voices Listeners trust voices less when told they are AI; the EU AI Act requires generated audio to be marked from August 2026. R NSF public access repository S Potter Clarkson (law firm summary) Pause, stop and end Anything that moves for more than five seconds needs a pause; for audio, also skip back, speed and a sleep timer that stops at the end. A W3C Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If People listen on the move or before sleep Start with Audio first, with a sleep timer that stops at the end of the passage If People read and listen together, or are learning to read Start with Read-along at verse or sentence level, with pause If Your product is a daily prayer practice Start with A produced devotional with named authors and optional music If You use synthetic narration Start with A visible label wherever the voice plays, and a human-recorded option if you can These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. Dwell · iOS · publisher release article Separate narration and background music choices Publisher comparison image · historical Dwell · iOS app · device model not recorded The current verse bright, the rest dimmed User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Pray As You Go · iOS app · device model not recorded A session script with timestamps User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Abide · iOS app · device model not recorded The author and narrator, named User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged BeBlessed · iOS app · device model not recorded A choice of background sound User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Joseph Prince · iOS app · device model not recorded A chapter player with a sleep timer User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Spark Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded A timestamped transcript, with recognition errors User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What hearing is for For most of Christian history, Scripture reached people through the ear. Jesus “stood up to read” in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:16), Paul told Timothy, “devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture” (1 Timothy 4:13), and “faith comes by hearing” (Romans 10:17). Public reading is not a delivery format but an act of the community: one voice reads, and everyone hears the same words at the same time. Where Christians differ Liturgical churches treat the reading of Scripture as worship in its own right: the Gospel is often read by a deacon or priest, with the people standing. Many Protestant churches centre the sermon, with the reading as its text. Traditions also differ on who may read publicly. All agree that a reader interprets by tone and pace; that is why churches choose and train readers. What follows for design An app chooses a reader for millions of people. Name that voice, and say whether it is a person. Let the passage end as a reading ends, in silence, rather than rolling into whatever comes next. Treat listening together, in a family or a church, as a first-class case, not an afterthought to solitary listening. In conversation with Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum (1965) asks that prayer accompany reading “so that God and man may talk together”, quoting Ambrose: “we hear Him when we read the divine saying.” Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Life Together (1939) describes a community beginning the day by reading Scripture aloud together, as something received in common before anyone reads alone. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Autoplay rolls into the next episode or an upsell; a synthetic voice is presented as a person. Ethical Does no harm Name the reader and edition, stop when the passage ends, offer text alongside. Redemptive Gives something up for them Pay for human readers in the languages and dialects a market overlooks, and give audio free and offline to people who cannot read. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review Whose voice reads Scripture here, and what happens when it ends? Exercise Listen to your own audio on a commute with the screen off. Note every moment you have to look at the phone, and what plays when the passage ends. Then ask three listeners whether the voice is a person, and how they know. Someone will hear Scripture for the first time in the voice you choose. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further This deep dive brings together 3 earlier patterns. Their guidance, wireframes and sources are kept below; their old addresses lead here. Edge cases to design for Offer audio wherever the text is, and say whose voice it is: a named narrator, or a clearly labelled synthetic voice. When the screen is on, let the text follow the voice at verse or sentence level, with pause and rewind. Build a full player that works with the screen off, with skip, speed and a sleep timer that stops at the end of a passage. In produced devotionals, name who wrote the reflections, keep Scripture distinct from commentary, make music optional, and end with silence or a choice rather than the next track. What tends to go wrong Unlabelled synthetic voices; voices that imitate a known pastor without consent; autoplay that runs into the next chapter or an advert; read-along that cannot be paused; music that cannot be turned off; reflections that sound like Scripture; audio that stops when the screen locks. How to test it Ask listeners whether a voice is human or synthetic and how they know. Listen on a commute with the screen off and check skip, pause and sleep. Compare recall of a passage heard with and without music. Test read-along with screen readers and people with dyslexia. Earlier pattern: The player works without the screen Support listening as a complete mode of use. Guidance Make current passage, playback, interruption and resumption available through suitable device and accessibility controls. Offer speed and sleep options where supported. Preserve the last listening position and a route into reading. What tends to go wrong Voice-only stopping; a hidden player; resuming at the wrong chapter; treating listening as microphone consent. How to test it Test lock-screen use, interruptions, headphones, connectivity loss and switching to text. Confirm what the selected edition actually supports. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources Android Audio Bible Official help article reviewed · Documented behaviour; no direct product usability audit performed. Designing Audio AI People Actually Trust Article reviewed · The author scopes this to responsible audio AI, not a complete conversational-agent guideline. 8 voice AI UX patterns Article reviewed · A design analysis rather than a clinical or Bible-app validation study. The original short link leads through another Friedman post. Digital Spiritual Formation: The Aperto Vision · selected Draft 4 review Selected sections on reading, engagement, multimodal and communal formation, incentives and honest assessment reviewed 5 October 2026 · Not an effectiveness study. Full bibliography and manuscript are not published or comprehensively reviewed here. Towards Full Presence Sections 30–38 on attention and listening reviewed 5 October 2026 · Catholic pastoral reflection on social media; application to app interfaces is an editorial adaptation. Earlier pattern: Playback and reading positions can differ Follow the narration without forcing the reader to follow every movement. Guidance Show the current playback anchor separately from the viewport. Let users follow or explore freely, then deliberately return to the spoken passage. Use continuous text where the task is sustained reading. What tends to go wrong Automatic recentering after manual scroll; stopping playback whenever someone explores; treating the visible paragraph as the actual playback position. How to test it Scroll away during playback, change text size and return to the spoken verse. Does each position remain understandable? Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources Dwell Read Along Publisher feature description reviewed · Publisher claims about comprehension are not independent study results. Return to the playing verse Publisher release description reviewed · Behaviour reference, not a fresh hands-on audit. Android Audio Bible Official help article reviewed · Documented behaviour; no direct product usability audit performed. Psalm 23, Berean Standard Bible Passage text taken from API.Bible, 9 October 2026 · A text source, not evidence of the proposed interface’s effectiveness. Earlier pattern: Choose a devotional format Compare a continuous reading, a sequence of cards and a chaptered audio session. Guidance Separate the content model from its presentation: Scripture, reflection, video, prayer and silence retain their identity in each format. A continuous page supports scanning; multi-page steps offer explicit pacing; story-style cards can combine short media segments. Offer visible Previous, Next and an outline rather than relying on swipes. Avoid timed advance for text by default. Audio needs pause, chapter navigation, transcript and an explicit end. Switching formats should preserve a semantic section where correspondence exists; do not invent word-level synchronisation. What tends to go wrong A story that advances before the reader finishes; tiny text fitted to one card; essential teaching available only in uncaptioned video; media playback counted as prayer; a disabled Next button until personal disclosure; automatic playback of another devotional. How to test it Move through a mixed-media session with sound off, large text, keyboard or screen reader navigation, and an unavailable video. Leave during a section and return. Verify the selected content version and section are restored, and ask what is required versus optional. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources Android: Guided Scripture Sections and navigation reviewed 5 October 2026 · Documentation, not a captured UI or outcome study. Bible.com: Plans Plan contents and completion reviewed 5 October 2026 · Web documentation; platform behaviour differs. Daily Prayer app and podcast Official search-index excerpts reviewed 5 October 2026; full-page fetch blocked · Documented overview only; no live app capture or exhaustive liturgical rules review. Psalm 23, Berean Standard Bible Passage text taken from API.Bible, 9 October 2026 · A text source, not evidence of the proposed interface’s effectiveness. Sources and their limits Research-informed design proposal. Editorial review, not user validation. Does modality matter? The effects of reading, listening, and dual modality on comprehension Report reviewed · One nonfiction text with adult readers; other studies find differences for harder texts. Effects of highlighting text on the reading ability of children with developmental dyslexia: a pilot study Abstract reviewed · Small pilot study. Same language subtitling Article reviewed · Reported programme results; a literacy setting, not Scripture reading. Faith Comes By Hearing: our story Organisation history reviewed · Figures are the ministry’s own. St Thomas alumnus hosts No. 1 podcast in US News report reviewed · Download figures from the publisher. Pray As You Go: about us Organisation page reviewed · Usage figures from the organisation. The impact of background music on adult listeners: a meta-analysis Paper reviewed · Mixed study designs; reading rather than listening tasks. Human vs synthetic voices and listener trust Abstract reviewed · Lab studies with short clips; not Scripture. EU AI Act Article 50: transparency obligations Summary reviewed · Secondary legal summary; applicability depends on role and use. International Orality Network Overview reviewed · An advocacy estimate; definitions and figures vary and are contested. Understanding SC 2.2.2: Pause, Stop, Hide Specification guidance reviewed · A Level A criterion for web content; apply the same intent in native apps. Faith and interpretation “Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17). Scripture was written to be read aloud: “Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear” (Revelation 1:3). A voice is not neutral: tone, pace and emphasis interpret, as a reader in church does. Whose voice reads Scripture, and whether it is a person at all, is a question of trust as well as design. pages.title: Check-ins and assessments
pages.description: What may an app ask about someone, and what may it conclude? Five options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Check-ins and assessments What may an app ask about someone, and what may it conclude? Christians have asked themselves questions for centuries, in the evening Examen, in Wesley’s band meetings and in church gift inventories. Apps now ask too: setup quizzes, daily mood check-ins, long personality tests. Asking can serve personalisation, self-knowledge or a church listening to its members. Decide what each question is for, what is kept, who sees the result, and how much the result claims to know. Being asked about one’s soul is an act of trust, and the answers deserve the care of a pastor, not the appetite of a funnel. 5 working options 11 app examples 5 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Check-ins and assessments At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From a hint for the app to a verdict on a person Shapes what the app offers Claims to know the person 1 A few setup questions Observed + A sensible first suggestion − Can turn into a sales funnel Try it → 2 A daily check-in Observed + Naming a feeling in a minute − A mood record is health data Try it → 3 A gifts inventory Familiar convention + Words for how someone serves − A result can feel like a label Try it → 4 A church survey Familiar convention + A church hears its members − Numbers can become targets Try it → 5 A spiritual score Leave it out + A clear number − Faith becomes a grade and a rank Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try five ways an app can ask about someone It is a Wednesday in October. Each option asks something about a person or a church, and each concludes something different from the answers. Answer as far as you like, then change whether answers are kept and whether a mentor may see a result, and notice what each one claims to know about you. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. A few setup questions · Observed 2. A daily check-in · Observed 3. A gifts inventory · Familiar convention 4. A church survey · Familiar convention 5. A spiritual score · Leave it out Option 1 A few setup questions Observed 2 A daily check-in Observed 3 A gifts inventory Familiar convention 4 A church survey Familiar convention 5 A spiritual score Leave it out Answers Not used here Kept on this phone Not kept Who else sees a result Not used here Only me A mentor I choose Why these settings? Kept answers stay on the phone with a way to delete them; not kept, they shape only the current screen. With a mentor, the check-in offers to send one line, and only when the person taps it; the inventory shares the two areas, never the answers. The church survey is anonymous by design, and the score shows what many apps do. Observed 1. A few setup questions Observed in onboarding quizzes: Abide’s “What brings you here today?” photo grid and Bible BFF’s “How much of the Bible have you read?”; HelloBible asks “What is your gender?” with “I prefer not to answer”, then asks for a name, before a separate consent for using faith data with a partner AI. See the screenshots below. Try this Answer or skip the three questions, then change one on the summary. + Makes easier A sensible first suggestion without browsing a catalogue. − Costs Easily becomes a sales funnel, or asks more than it needs. Ask your team Does each question say what it changes, and can it be skipped? Observed 2. A daily check-in Observed in Soultime’s mood check-in, which asks how you are “With Myself”, “With Others” and “With God” and charts the answers over weeks; see the screenshots below. Try this Name a feeling, optionally how you are with God, then look at what is kept. + Makes easier Naming a feeling, an old practice of self-examination, takes a minute. − Costs A record of moods is health data; a chart invites self-monitoring. Ask your team What happens to the word someone chose, and who could ever see it? Familiar convention 3. A gifts inventory A familiar church practice since the 1970s: spiritual gifts inventories, Willow Creek’s Network course (1994) and similar tools ask people to rate statements and then suggest where to serve. Statements here are written for this example. Try this Rate the six statements and read the places to explore. Then switch on the mentor. + Makes easier A way into serving, and words for what someone already enjoys. − Costs A result can feel like a verdict; scores overlap with personality. Ask your team Does the result point to trying and to other people, or hand out a label? Familiar convention 4. A church survey A familiar tool in congregations: Natural Church Development asks 30 members to rate statements and reports eight “quality characteristics”; Willow Creek’s Reveal survey (2007) measured spiritual growth across churches. Statements here are written for this example. Try this Read the invitation, answer three statements and preview the shared results. + Makes easier A church hears how its members see it, anonymously. − Costs Numbers can become targets; the lowest area can feel like blame. Ask your team Can anyone see a single person’s answers, and does the result start a conversation? Leave it out 5. A spiritual score A composite of patterns observed in assessment and mood apps: a score out of 100, a stage, a ranking against others and a prompt to retake. Soultime’s “Emotional and Spiritual Health Report” sits nearby; see the screenshots below. Try this Read the score, then retake the test. + Makes easier A clear number that motivates some people for a while. − Costs Turns a life with God into a grade, a rank and a trend. Ask your team What would it mean to be 4 points closer to God? i Questions, statements, names and results were written for this example; Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. Nothing is saved or sent. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Say what each answer changes Abide asks “What brings you here today?” with twelve goals, and Bible BFF asks “How much of the Bible have you read?”, with testimonials and a paywall between the steps. A setup question earns its place when it changes what the app offers, says so, and can be skipped. Naming a feeling is enough Soultime’s check-in asks how you are “With Myself”, “With Others” and “With God”, an echo of the Examen’s attention to feelings. Labelling an emotion can itself ease it. Respond with a passage or a next step, not a chart to keep improving. Moods and faith are protected data Answers about anxiety, shame or God are health and religious data under GDPR Article 9, and inferences count too. Keep them on the device by default, let people delete them, and never send anything to friends or leaders automatically, even on a hard day. A result is a starting point, not a verdict Gift inventories overlap heavily with personality, and generic reports feel accurate to almost everyone. Willow Creek’s Network paired the inventory with a consultant and a place to serve. Say how a result was made, and point to trying things and to people who know the person. Churches have measured for decades Natural Church Development surveys 30 members and reports eight areas; Reveal surveyed whole congregations about spiritual growth, and taught its own church something uncomfortable. Anonymous, aggregated surveys can help a church listen. Scores, stages and ranks for individuals measure what only God sees. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 A few setup questions 2 A daily check-in 3 A gifts inventory 4 A church survey 5 A spiritual score Opening the app for the first time A sensible first step ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit A hard week Words for how they are Poor fit ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Looking for a place to serve Where to start Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Leading a church Hearing the members Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit Meeting a mentor Something to talk about Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Wary of being measured Nothing kept, nothing scored ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition Self-examination among people who pray for each other Notice your feelings The Examen’s third step is to pay attention to your emotions. S IgnatianSpirituality.com Questions asked every week Wesley’s bands asked four questions, among friends who prayed together. H John Wesley, 25 December 1738 Gifts are found in serving Network paired the inventory with consultation and a place to serve. S Bruce L. Bugbee and Don Cousins Church assessment What congregations have learned Thirty members, eight areas NCD’s anonymous survey, used to choose a focus and track trends. S Free Methodist Church in Canada Be modest about the research Reviewers questioned the science behind NCD’s claims. R John Ellas and Flavil Yeakley Measuring growth raises questions Reveal’s findings, and whether self-monitoring serves discipleship. T Mark Galli Psychology What questions and results can do Naming eases Labelling an emotion reduced the brain’s response to negative images. R Matthew D. Lieberman et al. Daily sampling is a method Momentary assessment reduces recall bias in research and care. R Saul Shiffman, Arthur A. Stone and Michael R. Hufford Generic reports feel personal People rate the same sketch as accurate about themselves. R Bertram R. Forer Gifts overlap with personality About half the shared variance in one study. R Kenneth J. Stone Measuring makes it work Counting an activity lowered enjoyment of it. R Jordan Etkin Privacy and law Moods and faith are special-category data Health and belief are protected Processing needs an Article 9 condition; inferences count too. S European Data Protection Board S UK Information Commissioner’s Office Such apps have shared data Mozilla’s 2022 review of mental health and prayer apps. S Mozilla Foundation Aggregate, not individual Soultime described trends without tracking people individually. S Hope 103.2 Personalised by life situation HelloBible’s listing and privacy label. S HelloBox Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If You want a sensible first suggestion Start with A few optional setup questions, each saying what it changes If People want to notice how they are Start with A check-in that ends with a passage, kept on the phone If People look for a place to serve Start with An inventory whose result points to trying and to a mentor If A church wants to listen Start with An anonymous survey with results shared by area If You are tempted to score faith Start with Don’t: no scores, stages, ranks or retakes for a better number These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. Abide · iOS app · device model not recorded “What brings you here today?” as a photo grid User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Faith · iOS app · device model not recorded “How old are you?” during setup User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Bible BFF · iOS app · device model not recorded “How much of the Bible have you read?” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Soultime · iOS app · device model not recorded “With God I’m feeling” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Soultime · iOS app · device model not recorded Moods over a week, by dimension User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Soultime · iOS app · device model not recorded A 61-statement personality test User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Soultime · iOS app · device model not recorded An “Emotional and Spiritual Health Report” User-contributed screenshot · resized; name blurred HelloBible · Android app · Pixel 8 Pro A profile of series, time in the app and conversations Screenshot captured for this reference · resized; account name and avatar blurred HelloBible · Android app · Pixel 8 Pro “What is your gender?” with a reason and an opt-out User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged HelloBible · Android app · Pixel 8 Pro A separate consent for using faith data with a partner AI User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Soultime · iOS app · device model not recorded Friends notified automatically “when we think you might need a call” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What self-examination is for “Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith” (2 Corinthians 13:5); “Search me, O God, and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23). Self-examination in Scripture is done before God, often with others, and it leads to confession and change, not to a profile. The Examen and Wesley’s band questions kept that shape. Where Christians differ Evangelical churches have embraced gifts inventories and church health surveys as tools for service and mission. Others are wary of importing management measurement into the church, as Mark Galli asked of Willow Creek’s Reveal. Traditions also differ on the gifts themselves: some expect every gift listed in the New Testament today, others hold that some have ceased. What follows for design Paul wrote, “I do not even judge myself … It is the Lord who judges me” (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). Asking can serve discernment, but only God knows a heart. Make results starting points for conversation and service, keep answers private, and never turn a life with God into a score. In conversation with Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Life Together (1939) placed confession within a community of real people who bear one another’s burdens, not in self-assessment alone. Mark Galli, “Am I Growing Yet?” (2007) asked whether constant monitoring of one’s own growth serves discipleship or turns the disciple inward. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Quizzes that feed a paywall, mood records sent to others, spiritual scores and ranks. Ethical Does no harm Say what each answer changes, let it be skipped, and protect health and belief data. Redemptive Gives something up for them Keep answers on the phone and point results toward serving and toward people who know the person, though the app learns less. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review For each question: what does the answer change, who could ever see it, and what does the result claim to know? Exercise Take your own app’s questions and, beside each, write what it changes and where the answer is stored. Then show five people their results and ask what the app now thinks of them, and whether they agree. Every answer is entrusted to you. Ask only what you are ready to carry with care. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further Edge cases to design for Name the purpose of each question set. For personalisation, ask few questions, say what each changes, allow skipping and editing, and ask nothing about health or belief that the app does not need. For a check-in, let naming be enough, respond with Scripture or a next step rather than a score, and keep the record on the device with a delete option. For gifts, frame results as places to try and people to talk with. For a church survey, keep answers anonymous and aggregated, and share results as a conversation starter. Never send anything automatically, and never rank people. What tends to go wrong Quizzes that cannot be skipped and end in a paywall; questions about anxiety, sins or shame without saying why; mood records sent to servers or friends automatically; charts of feelings that invite self-monitoring; results that hand out a label (“You are a Teacher”); spiritual scores, stages and rankings against others; prompts to retake a test to raise a score; leaders seeing individual answers. How to test it For every question, ask what it changes and who could ever see the answer, and check that it can be skipped. Ask people to read their result aloud and say what it claims about them, and whether that is fair. Check what is stored and sent with a network inspector. Ask a pastor or spiritual director how they would respond to the same answers. Sources and their limits Research-informed design proposal. Editorial review, not user validation. How can I pray? The Daily Examen Page reviewed · A modern adaptation; Ignatius’s own five points in the Spiritual Exercises differ in wording. Rules of the Band-Societies Text reviewed · A small-group discipline for committed members, not a public survey. Natural Church Development Survey Page reviewed · A denomination’s description of the tool, not an evaluation of it. Book review: Natural Church Development by Christian Schwarz Abstract reviewed · A review, from within the church-growth movement. Network: discover your spiritual gifts, personal style and passion Product page reviewed · A publisher’s description. Relationships between personality and spiritual gifts Abstract reviewed · One inventory and one sample. Am I growing yet? Article reviewed · Commentary on a church’s survey, not a study of apps. Putting feelings into words: affect labeling disrupts amygdala activity in response to affective stimuli Abstract reviewed · Laboratory study with images, not mood apps. Ecological momentary assessment Abstract reviewed · A method review for researchers and clinicians. The fallacy of personal validation: a classroom demonstration of gullibility Citation reviewed · A classroom demonstration; later studies refined it. The hidden cost of personal quantification Abstract reviewed · Leisure activities in experiments, not prayer. Process personal data lawfully Official guidance reviewed · Specific lawful basis, retention and DPIA decisions require the actual data flows. What is special category data? Categories and inference guidance reviewed · Context and processing intent matter; not every Bible-page visit automatically establishes a belief. Top mental health and prayer apps fail spectacularly at privacy, security Report summary reviewed · A 2022 review; apps’ practices may have changed since. What the Christian app Soultime has discovered with its mood tracker Article reviewed · A news interview; data practices were not independently verified. HelloBible: interactive Bible (App Store listing) Listing and privacy label reviewed 8 October 2026 · A store listing; the onboarding itself was not tested here. Faith and interpretation Self-examination is old Christian practice. “Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith” (2 Corinthians 13:5); “Search me, O God, and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23). The Examen asks people to notice their feelings each evening, and Wesley’s band meetings asked the same questions every week, among friends. Paul wrote that “to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good” (1 Corinthians 12:7), and told readers, “Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought” (Romans 12:3). He also wrote “I do not even judge myself … It is the Lord who judges me” (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). Asking can serve discernment; only God knows a heart, and no app should pretend to score one. pages.title: Children and families
pages.description: When children meet Scripture through an app, who is with them, and what does the app ask of them?
pages.text: Patterns Children and families When children meet Scripture through an app, who is with them, and what does the app ask of them? When people brought children to Jesus and the disciples turned them away, he “was indignant” and said, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these” (Mark 10:14). Children now meet Bible stories, prayers and songs through apps: some made for them, some made for adults, some built to hold their attention, some run by their church, and AI chat apps rated for all ages. Each decides who is with the child, what it collects, how it keeps them watching, and what happens when a child says something worrying. Most of the time, children’s apps help families share the faith. Design also for the frightening story and the worried child. Draft · waiting for review What needs review: The answer to a child who writes something worrying, the leader’s notes for a youth group, the notes for telling the Flood, and the decision not to tell parents automatically. This touches the safety of people who may already be hurting, and it has not yet been reviewed by people whose work this is: safeguarding; survivor advocacy (ideally survivor-led); pastoral care; data protection; and theology across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions. Please read it as a draft until they have. Is this your field, or do you know someone whose field it is? I would be grateful for your eyes on it, or for an introduction. Offer a review or an introduction 6 working options 9 app examples 7 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Children and families At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From a grown-up beside the child to a child alone A grown-up is with the child The child is alone 1 Read together Familiar convention + A grown-up for the hard parts − Needs time together Try it → 2 Family time in a general app Observed + Families use what they have − The adult app is a tap away Try it → 3 A children’s Bible app Observed + Safe to use alone − Hard stories met alone Try it → 4 Games and episodes Observed + Stories children return to − Attention held for its own sake Try it → 5 A youth group with a leader Observed + Leaders responsible − Leaders see what is posted Try it → 6 A child alone with an AI Leave it out + Answers at any hour − No one is with the child Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try six ways a child meets Scripture A child opens a faith app. Choose their age: four to seven, eight to twelve, or thirteen to sixteen. On an ordinary day the story is Jesus welcoming the children (Mark 10:13–16). Then try a frightening story, the Flood, and then a worrying message: the child writes that they are scared at home. Notice who is with the child, what the app asks and collects, how it holds attention, and who answers the child. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Read together · Familiar convention 2. Family time in a general app · Observed 3. A children’s Bible app · Observed 4. Games and episodes · Observed 5. A youth group with a leader · Observed 6. A child alone with an AI · Leave it out Option 1 Read together Familiar convention 2 Family time in a general app Observed 3 A children’s Bible app Observed 4 Games and episodes Observed 5 A youth group with a leader Observed 6 A child alone with an AI Leave it out Age Not used here 4 to 7 8 to 12 13 to 16 Situation Not used here An ordinary day A frightening story A worry Why these settings? On an ordinary day the story is Jesus welcoming the children (Mark 10:13–16). The frightening story is the Flood (Genesis 6–9). In the worrying message the child writes that they are scared when someone at home shouts; nothing in this example is sent anywhere. Nummer gegen Kummer’s number and hours are from its own website, checked 11 October 2026. Familiar convention 1. Read together Familiar from reading a children’s Bible aloud at home, and from Godly Play, where stories are followed by “I wonder” questions; the WHO encourages “reading and storytelling with a caregiver” for young children. Not observed in this form in an app. The notes for grown-ups are written for this example. Try this Read the story aloud with the questions. Then try the Flood, and then the worrying message. + Makes easier A grown-up is there for the hard parts and the questions. − Costs Needs a grown-up with time; older children may want to read alone. Ask your team What does the grown-up need to say and ask, and what do they do if the child tells them something worrying? Observed 2. Family time in a general app Observed in Pray as You Go’s Kids Prayer and “A Family Examen”, Glorify’s Kids rail, YouVersion’s plans for parents and kids and its Kids Bible Experience card, and Faith’s KIDS-labelled series; see the screenshots below. The app and its content here are written for this example. Try this Play the family prayer. Then try the Flood, and then the worrying message typed into the prayer box. + Makes easier Families use what they already have, together. − Costs The adult app is a tap away, and it cannot tell when a child is typing. Ask your team What can a child reach from the kids’ corner, and what happens to what they type? Observed 3. A children’s Bible app Documented in the Bible App for Kids listing (free, rated 4+, with an email address listed for the developer’s marketing in its privacy label) and Apple’s Kids Category rules: no links out or purchases “unless reserved for a designated area behind a parental gate”, and no third-party analytics or advertising. Screens are on the shot list. The stories, gate and wording here are written for this example. Try this Tap through the story, then try the grown-ups’ area. Then the Flood, and the worrying message. + Makes easier A child can use it alone without being sold to or tracked. − Costs The child may meet a hard story with no one to ask. Ask your team What does the app say to a child alone with a frightening story, or a worry? Observed 4. Games and episodes Documented in the Superbook Kids Bible listing (“Videos, games, audio & more”, free with purchases) and in roundups of Minno’s subscription videos; screens are on the shot list. The EU’s guidelines ask platforms to disable streaks, autoplay and push notifications for minors by default. The episode, stars and countdown here are written for this example. Try this Watch the episode and let the next one start. Then try the Flood, and then look for somewhere to say what worries you. + Makes easier Stories children want to come back to. − Costs Stars, streaks and autoplay hold attention for its own sake. Ask your team Would the child stop on their own, and does anything here help them? Observed 5. A youth group with a leader Documented in KonApp, the Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft’s app for confirmation groups: no personal details needed, consent collected by the parish, and the group deleted six weeks after confirmation; see its store listing and data protection agreement. Church guidance keeps contact with young people in groups with two adults. The group, leaders, replies and safeguarding contact are written for this example. Try this Read the group feed and write in your diary. Then post the worrying message in the group. + Makes easier Young people stay in touch between meetings, with leaders responsible. − Costs Leaders see what is posted, and must know what to do with it. Ask your team What does a leader do, and not do, when a young person writes something worrying? Leave it out 6. A child alone with an AI A warning case. Many AI Bible chat apps are rated 4+ in the App Store without being designed for children, and the EU asks for safeguards around AI chatbots that minors can reach. The replies here are written for this example to show the risk; they were not observed in an app. Try this Ask a question, then ask about the Flood, then type the worrying message. + Makes easier Answers at any hour, on any question. − Costs No one is with the child, and a reply can do harm. Ask your team Should a child be here at all, and what would the app have to do if one is? i The apps, stories, names, replies and contact address were written for this example. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. Nothing is saved or sent. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Design for the grown-up beside the child For young children, the best screen is one a grown-up shares. Give the grown-up the story, a few “I wonder” questions, and notes for the hard parts. Collect nothing a child need not give A children’s app needs no account, no name and no age to tell a story. Keep purchases, links and settings behind a parental gate, and say in plain words what, if anything, is collected and for whom. Switch off what holds attention for its own sake Stars, streaks, autoplay and “next episode in 5” keep a child watching. The EU asks for them to be off by default for minors; leave them out. Progress and streaks → Tell hard stories with care The Flood, the plagues and the cross are part of the story children are told. Mark the hard parts, give the grown-up something honest to say, and suggest that a child alone talks it over with someone. Answer a worried child first When a child writes that they are scared at home, thank them, give a children’s helpline such as Nummer gegen Kummer (116 111) and suggest a trusted adult. Do not send it automatically to a parent: the person a child fears may be the parent. Young people: two leaders, consent, a named contact A church youth app can ask for no personal details, collect parents’ consent, keep leaders in pairs and out of one-to-one messages, delete the group when the course ends, and name a safeguarding contact outside the leadership. Reading together → A child should not be alone with an AI A general AI chat, rated 4+, can answer a frightened child with a verse about obedience. If children can reach it, it needs an age-appropriate mode, a helpline, and no Scripture pressed on a child in distress. Sensitive conversations → Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Read together 2 Family time in a general app 3 A children’s Bible app 4 Games and episodes 5 A youth group with a leader 6 A child alone with an AI A four-year-old on a parent’s lap A story to read aloud, and questions to wonder about ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit A ten-year-old alone with a tablet Nothing to buy, nobody to meet, a way to ask for help ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit A family praying together in the evening Something short to do together ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit A confirmation group between meetings Two leaders, consent, a named contact Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit Poor fit A child meets a frightening story A grown-up, or at least a nudge to find one ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit A child writes something worrying An answer to the child, and help that is not automatically their parent ● Good fit Poor fit ● Good fit Poor fit ● Good fit Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition Welcomed, taught at home, protected Let the children come When the disciples rebuked those who brought children, Jesus “was indignant”; he “took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them” (Mark 10:14, 16). Taught at home Israel was told to teach God’s words to their children “when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Timothy’s faith “first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice” (2 Timothy 1:5). Wondering together In Godly Play, a story is followed by “I wonder” questions and time to respond. There is no right answer to find, and children can bring what troubles them. S Wikipedia, on the method developed by Jerome Berryman Safeguarding and law Protecting children The weight of harm Jesus said that whoever causes “one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble” would be better off with “a large millstone hung around his neck” (Matthew 18:6). Churches have failed children badly, and the inquiries into those failures are why safeguarding rules exist. When Scripture is used to harm A children’s app on a phone Apple’s Kids Category requires that links out and purchases be “reserved for a designated area behind a parental gate”, and that apps “should not include third-party analytics or third-party advertising”. The UK Children’s Code begins with the “Best interests of the child”. S Apple S Information Commissioner’s Office (UK) Private by default, no streaks The European Commission’s 2025 guidelines ask platforms to set minors’ accounts to private by default, to disable streaks, autoplay and push notifications by default, and to put “safeguards around AI chatbots”. The amended US children’s privacy rule requires separate parental consent before children’s data is shared with third parties. S European Commission S Latham & Watkins Young people: in a group, with two adults Church of England guidance recommends group calls rather than one-to-one calls with young people, and one parish allows conversations with young people only where at least two DBS-checked adults are present. KonApp’s data protection agreement has the parish collect consent and deletes a group six weeks after confirmation. S Church of England National Safeguarding Team S All Saints Boyne Hill, Church of England parish S Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft and each parish or institution Products and research What children’s apps do Reading with a grown-up The WHO does not recommend sedentary screen time for one-year-olds and suggests no more than an hour at two, and encourages “reading and storytelling with a caregiver”. At a Cooney Center panel on families watching together, a producer warned that “children may be viewing by themselves” and urged “caution regarding the introduction of material that might be scary or isolating for a child”. R World Health Organization R Joan Ganz Cooney Center at Sesame Workshop The leading children’s Bible apps Bible App for Kids is free and rated 4+, with 9.4K ratings in the US App Store; its privacy label lists an email address for the developer’s marketing. Superbook Kids Bible offers “Videos, games, audio & more”, with 18K ratings. Screens of both are on our shot list. S Life.Church with OneHope S The Christian Broadcasting Network A church-run youth app KonApp, the Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft’s app for confirmation groups, was used by “50.000 jungen Leuten” in 2021, with about 4,500 parishes and institutions running groups; it asks for no personal details to take part. S epd S Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft AI chat apps rated for all ages AI Bible chat apps such as AI Jesus – Bible Chat offer “Unlimited chat” and are rated 4+. A rating says the content is not objectionable, not that anything was designed for a child. S Apple App Store (US) Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If Young children at home Start with Read together: a story and questions for the grown-up If A child using an app alone Start with A children’s app with no account, no ads and a parental gate If Families in an adult app Start with A kids’ corner with nothing else one tap away, and help beside every text box If A confirmation or youth group Start with A church-run group: consent, two leaders, a named contact, deleted when the course ends If You are tempted to add stars, streaks and autoplay Start with Don’t: let the story end, and let the child go These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. Pray As You Go · iOS app · device model not recorded “Kids Prayer”: a prayer adventure every day User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Pray As You Go · iOS app · device model not recorded “A Family Examen” beside children’s prayers User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Glorify · iOS app · device model not recorded A Kids rail among Sleep and Anxiety User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded A Kids Bible Experience card in the Today feed User-contributed screenshot · resized; names and photos of the account holder blurred YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded “A plan for parents & kids” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Faith · iOS app · device model not recorded A “KIDS” label on a story of Lucifer’s fall User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Disney+ · iOS app · device model not recorded Profiles with locks, and a way to add one User-contributed screenshot · resized; names and photos of the account holder blurred WOW · iOS app · device model not recorded A “Kinderprofil” with a Kids badge User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Faith · iOS app · device model not recorded “How old are you?” during setup User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What children are for, in the church Jesus did not treat children as the church’s future but as its present: “the kingdom of God belongs to such as these” (Mark 10:14), and “anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it” (Mark 10:15). Faith is passed on at home, “when you sit at home and when you walk along the road” (Deuteronomy 6:7), as it was from Lois and Eunice to Timothy (2 Timothy 1:5). Where Christians differ Churches that baptise infants receive children into the church before they can speak; others dedicate them and wait for their own confession of faith. Catechism, Sunday school, children’s church, Godly Play and confirmation classes teach in different ways. All take seriously that adults answer to God for how they treat children: “if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble” (Matthew 18:6), a warning the church has had to hear about its own failures. What follows for design Put the app in the hands of the grown-up beside the child where you can. Ask nothing of a child that a story does not need, and sell them nothing. Let stories end. Tell hard stories honestly, with room to wonder. Answer a frightened child with help, never with a verse that tells them to be quiet. In conversation with Martin Luther, Small Catechism wrote each part “As the head of the family should teach them in a simple way to his household”: faith taught at home, by a parent, in plain words. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Collect children’s details for marketing, sell to them, keep them watching with stars, streaks and autoplay, and leave them alone with chat and comments. Ethical Does no harm Ask for no account, no ads and no third-party analytics, put purchases and settings behind a parental gate, switch off streaks and autoplay, and keep youth groups to two leaders. Redemptive Gives something up for them Design for the grown-up beside the child, tell hard stories honestly with room to wonder, answer a frightened child with help instead of an automatic message to a parent, and give up the engagement that games and rewards would bring. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review Who is with the child, what does the app ask of them, and who answers when a child is afraid? Exercise Hand your app to a child of the age you design for, with a grown-up watching. Write down every place the child could buy something, leave the app, meet a stranger or be asked for a detail. Then read the Flood with a five-year-old and note what the app gave the grown-up to say. Finally, type “I’m scared when my dad shouts” where a child could type it, and follow it: who sees it, what the child is told, and who could help. Let the children come, and do not hinder them: design for the grown-up beside them, collect nothing they need not give, and answer a child who is afraid. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further Edge cases to design for Where you can, design for a grown-up beside the child: a story to read aloud with questions to wonder about together. For a child using the app alone, ask for no account and no personal details, show no ads, keep purchases, links and settings behind a parental gate, and leave out streaks, autoplay and notifications. Tell hard stories with care, and suggest talking them over. For young people in a church group, keep conversations in the group with two leaders, get parents’ consent, and name a safeguarding contact. When a child writes something worrying, answer the child: say it was right to tell, offer a helpline for children and a trusted adult, and, in a church-run app, route it to the trained safeguarding contact, not automatically to a parent. What tends to go wrong Accounts, ages and names asked of children; third-party analytics and advertising; purchases and links a child can reach; streaks, badges and autoplay that keep a child watching; frightening scenes labelled “KIDS” with no grown-up in view; one-to-one messages between a leader and a young person; a child left alone with an AI chat or a public comment thread; a worrying message sent automatically to a parent who may be the danger, or answered with nothing. How to test it Hand the app to a child of the target age with a grown-up watching, and note every place the child could buy, leave the app, meet a stranger or be asked for a detail. List every piece of data collected and who receives it. Read the Flood or the crucifixion with a five-year-old and see what the app gives the grown-up to say. Type a worrying message as a child would, and walk through who sees it and what the child is told. Sources and their limits Research-informed design proposal · draft for review. Editorial review, not user validation.
