Faith and interpretation When people brought little children to Jesus and the disciples rebuked them, he “was indignant and told them, ‘Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these’” (Mark 10:14). Israel was told to teach God’s words “to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Jesus also said that whoever causes “one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble” would be better off with “a large millstone hung around his neck” (Matthew 18:6). Children are welcomed, taught at home, and protected. Keep exploring Related patterns Reading together → Sharing with a group → First use → Progress and streaks → Devotional audio →

pages.title: Devotional audio
pages.description: Guided prayer, a podcast, a talk or a sleep story? Five options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Devotional audio Guided prayer, a podcast, a talk or a sleep story? Devotional audio comes in many shapes: guided prayer, teaching podcasts, morning talks, sleep stories, and now generated daily episodes. Each decides how much Scripture is heard, who speaks around it, whether there is silence, and whether the session ever ends. Choose the shape for the listener’s moment, not for listening time. Done well, it gives people Scripture and stillness in the middle of ordinary days. 5 working options 5 app examples 5 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Devotional audio At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further At a glance Four ways to hear a passage, and one that never ends 1 Guided prayer Observed + Scripture whole, with silence − Silence is easy to cut Try it → 2 Teaching conversation Familiar convention + Background and echoes − Hosts can sound like the text Try it → 3 Devotional talk Observed + A word for today − The story can take over Try it → 4 Sleep story Observed + Rest with Scripture in mind − Plays to someone asleep Try it → 5 Endless stream Leave it out + Always something new − Never ends, no author Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try five shapes of devotional audio It is a Wednesday. Each format is built around the same passage, Mark 4:35–41, where Jesus calms the storm. Play each one (playback is simulated and speeded up), jump between segments, and notice what you hear of Scripture, who speaks, and what happens at the end. Then put the script on screen, and let the silence wait for you. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Guided prayer · Observed 2. Teaching conversation · Familiar convention 3. Devotional talk · Observed 4. Sleep story · Observed 5. Endless stream · Leave it out Option 1 Guided prayer Observed 2 Teaching conversation Familiar convention 3 Devotional talk Observed 4 Sleep story Observed 5 Endless stream Leave it out Script Not used here Screen off Script on screen Silence Not used here 30 seconds Waits for you Why these settings? With the script on, each segment shows the line being heard, with Scripture set apart. With the screen off, the screen says it can stay off. In guided prayer, silence can last thirty seconds or wait until the listener continues. The sleep story always fades out and plays nothing after it; the stream shows what many apps do. Observed 1. Guided prayer Observed in Pray As You Go, whose daily sessions move from music to a reading, reflection questions, a second reading and a closing prayer, with the script and music credits in the player; see the screenshots below. Try this Play the session through. Switch the silence to “waits for you” and play again. + Makes easier A way of praying with Scripture, read whole and twice, with room for silence. − Costs Needs a steady pace and careful writing; silence is easy to cut. Ask your team Is the reading heard whole, and does the silence belong to the listener? Familiar convention 2. Teaching conversation A familiar podcast format: two hosts discuss a passage and its background, as in Bible-teaching podcasts across languages. Try this Play it with the script on, and notice where the text ends and the hosts begin. + Makes easier Understanding: background, echoes in other Scripture, the questions a text leaves open. − Costs Hosts can overshadow the text, and confident talk can sound like Scripture. Ask your team Can the listener tell the passage from the hosts’ interpretation, and find the sources? Observed 3. Devotional talk Observed in morning devotionals and in apps such as Abide, which offer sessions by length, from “2 min · Pause & Pray” to “15 min · Meditate & Deepen”; see the screenshots below. Try this Play it and ask afterwards whether you remember the story or the passage. + Makes easier A short word for the day, in a voice people come to trust. − Costs The host’s story can take over the passage. Ask your team Is the passage at the centre, and is the host named as a person with a view? Observed 4. Sleep story Observed in Dwell’s “Sleep to Scripture” and Abide’s sleep shelf with named narrators; see the screenshots below. Try this Play it to the end and see what comes next. + Makes easier Rest at night with Scripture in mind. − Costs The listener may not hear the end; anything that plays next plays to a sleeping person. Ask your team Does it fade to silence, with nothing queued after it? Leave it out 5. Endless stream A composite of patterns from podcast and video apps (“Next from:” auto-queues, autoplay countdowns) and from generated daily devotionals. Try this Watch the countdown, and look for who wrote this. + Makes easier There is always something new to hear. − Costs Listening never ends; no one is accountable for the words. Ask your team Who wrote this, and when does it stop? i Mark 4:35–41 is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. Scripts, hosts, stories and music descriptions were written for this example; playback is simulated. Nothing is saved or sent. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Let Scripture be heard whole, and distinctly Pray As You Go reads the passage in full, often twice, in a different voice from the reflection. Ezra’s Levites read “distinctly, and gave the sense”. Keep reading and commentary audibly apart, and set Scripture apart on screen when a script is shown. Silence belongs to the listener Guided prayer needs silence, and silence is the first thing cut to hold attention. Dwell offers a “Reflect” pause setting. In prayer, let silence wait until the listener continues. Hosts become trusted voices Listeners form friend-like bonds with podcast hosts and feel it when hosts change. Name hosts as people with a perspective and a tradition, and never let a familiar voice stand in for Scripture or for a pastor. Every session should end Autoplay and recommendations undermine people’s sense of agency; search and playlists support it. A devotional that rolls into the next episode, or a sleep story followed by more content, plays to someone who did not choose it. Credit every voice and every note Pray As You Go’s Music Info names the monks of Pluscarden Abbey; Abide names author and narrator. Generated episodes often name no one. Credit authors, readers and musicians, and label synthetic voices. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Guided prayer 2 Teaching conversation 3 Devotional talk 4 Sleep story 5 Endless stream Praying each morning A way into prayer with Scripture ● Good fit Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Studying a book Background and connections Poor fit ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Commuting A short word, eyes free ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Not sleeping Rest with Scripture in mind Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit Poor fit Unable to read Scripture heard whole ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Leading a group Something to listen to together ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition Reading, praying and resting with the word A daily shape for prayer Pray As You Go’s sessions: music, Scripture, reflection, prayer. S Jesuits in Britain Slow, repeated reading Lectio divina reads a short passage more than once. T University of St Andrews, School of Divinity Attention to the day The Examen’s steps behind many guided sessions. S IgnatianSpirituality.com Psychology Hosts, sleep and agency Hosts as trusted friends Listeners’ bonds with podcast hosts, and their loss when hosts change. R M. Olguta Vilceanu Sound can help sleep Relaxing music may improve sleep quality. R Jespersen et al. Autoplay takes agency Autoplay and recommendations undermine sense of agency. R Kai Lukoff et al. Voices and disclosure Who is speaking Synthetic voices How synthetic voices affect trust, and EU disclosure duties for generated audio. R NSF public access repository S Potter Clarkson (law firm summary) Audio for people who cannot read Scripture recordings for oral cultures. S Faith Comes By Hearing Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If People want to pray with Scripture Start with Guided prayer: the passage whole, read twice, with silence that waits If People want to understand a passage Start with A teaching conversation with named hosts and sources If People listen on the way to work Start with A short talk with the passage at its centre If People listen to fall asleep Start with A sleep story that fades out, with nothing after it If You are tempted to fill every minute Start with Don’t: no autoplay, no endless generated episodes, no listening streaks These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. Pray As You Go · iOS app · device model not recorded Music Info names the monks and the composer User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Abide · iOS app · device model not recorded “Pick an audio length” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Abide · iOS app · device model not recorded A sleep shelf with narrators named User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Dwell · iOS app · device model not recorded “Sleep to Scripture”: Psalms for the night User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Wondery+ · iOS app · device model not recorded “Next from”: a podcast player’s auto-queue User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What hearing devotionally is for The Levites read the Law, “explaining it and giving insight” (Nehemiah 8:8): the reading and the explanation were both heard, and heard as different things. Christians have prayed with Scripture aloud in the office, in lectio and in song, and “about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them” (Acts 16:25). The voice that carries Scripture serves it. Where Christians differ Liturgical traditions pray set words and readings, often sung; evangelical traditions value teaching and testimony from a trusted voice; contemplative traditions give silence the central place. Christians also differ on music in worship, from unaccompanied psalm singing to full bands. Each shapes what devotional audio should sound like. What follows for design “I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (Psalm 4:8). Rest is a gift, not a gap to fill. Read Scripture whole, keep commentary audibly distinct, let silence wait, and end every session. “Why spend … your labor on that which does not satisfy?” (Isaiah 55:2). In conversation with Henri Nouwen, The Way of the Heart (1981) commends silence as a discipline that tends the inner life; a devotional that leaves no silence leaves no room for it. Albert Borgmann, Technology and the Character of Contemporary Life (1984) warned that devices deliver experiences effortlessly while focal practices ask for attention; an endless stream is the device paradigm applied to prayer. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Autoplay into the next episode, generated sessions without end, silence cut to hold attention, listening streaks. Ethical Does no harm Name authors, readers and musicians, label synthetic voices, and end the session. Redemptive Gives something up for them Pay for real readers and musicians, keep the silences even when listeners skip them, and let sleep audio fade to nothing. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review After the session, could the listener say what Scripture said, who spoke, and why it ended? Exercise Listen to your own devotional audio with a stopwatch: how many seconds of Scripture, of commentary, of music and of silence? Then ask three listeners to retell the passage and the host’s point separately, and check what plays when the session ends. Judge a session by what the listener carries into the day, not by how long they stayed. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further Edge cases to design for Name the format and its purpose before playback. For prayer, read Scripture whole, often twice, separate reflection from reading, and leave silence that can wait. For teaching, name sources and distinguish the text from the hosts’ interpretation. For a talk, keep the passage at the centre and the host’s story in service of it. For sleep, fade to silence and play nothing after. Credit voices, authors and music, label synthetic voices, and end every session. What tends to go wrong Scripture read in fragments beneath music; commentary that sounds like the text; silence cut to keep attention; hosts presented as friends who know the listener; autoplay into the next episode; sleep content followed by more content; generated episodes without an author; “never run out” offers; streaks for listening. How to test it Ask listeners after a session what the passage said and what the host said, and whether they could tell them apart. Time the silences. Check what plays after the session ends. Ask who wrote and who read each part, and whether any voice was synthetic. Sources and their limits Research-informed design proposal. Editorial review, not user validation. Pray As You Go: about us Organisation page reviewed · Usage figures from the organisation. Introduction to lectio divina Article reviewed · A description of practice, not a study. How can I pray? The Daily Examen Page reviewed · A modern adaptation; Ignatius’s own five points in the Spiritual Exercises differ in wording. Parasocial intimacy, change, and nostalgia in podcast listener reviews Abstract reviewed · Reviews of general podcasts, not faith audio. Listening to music for insomnia in adults Summary reviewed · Music, not spoken or Scripture content. How the design of YouTube influences user sense of agency Abstract reviewed · Video, not devotional audio. Human vs synthetic voices and listener trust Abstract reviewed · Lab studies with short clips; not Scripture. EU AI Act Article 50: transparency obligations Summary reviewed · Secondary legal summary; applicability depends on role and use. Faith Comes By Hearing: our story Organisation history reviewed · Figures are the ministry’s own. Faith and interpretation “Faith comes by hearing” (Romans 10:17), and the church has always shaped how Scripture is heard: read, sung, preached, prayed. Ezra’s Levites read the Law, “explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read” (Nehemiah 8:8), keeping the reading and the explanation distinct. “I will lie down and sleep in peace” (Psalm 4:8). And the prophet asks, “Why spend … your labor on that which does not satisfy?” (Isaiah 55:2). Devotional audio can serve all of these, or replace them with endless listening. Keep exploring Related patterns Bible audio → Prayer → Reading plans → AI persona →

pages.title: Finding a passage
pages.description: Browse, type a reference, or start from a need? Five options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Finding a passage Browse, type a reference, or start from a need? Someone hears “John 3” in a sermon. Someone else wants Isaiah but isn’t sure where it sits. A third person only wants today’s reading. One picker rarely serves all three, and sometimes the best picker is none at all. Opening the right page for someone is a small hospitality, and the first step of every reading. 5 working options 9 app examples 5 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Finding a passage At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further At a glance Five routes to a passage, side by side 1 Step by step Familiar convention + One question per screen − Many taps for a known reference Try it → 2 Expandable book list Observed + Book context stays in view − Long books push the list down Try it → 3 Type a reference Borrowed + Fastest for a known reference − Needs the reference and spelling Try it → 4 Start from a feeling Observed + A way in without a reference − Someone else chose the verses Try it → 5 No passage picker Leave it out + Nothing to decide before reading − Other passages are out of reach Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try five ways to reach a passage Someone is reading Mark 3. A friend mentions John 3 and they want to look it up. Every example starts at Mark 3 in the Berean Standard Bible. Try reaching John 3, then change your mind and cancel. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Step by step · Familiar convention 2. Expandable book list · Observed 3. Type a reference · Borrowed 4. Start from a feeling · Observed 5. No passage picker · Leave it out Option 1 Step by step Familiar convention 2 Expandable book list Observed 3 Type a reference Borrowed 4 Start from a feeling Observed 5 No passage picker Leave it out Opening Not used here Open on tap Review, then open Book list Not used here List Grid Go as far as Not used here Chapter Verse Why these settings? These switches are separate decisions from the options. Opening on tap is faster; reviewing first helps when a mis-tap is costly or the destination is unfamiliar. A book grid fits all 66 books in one view, with no scrolling, at the cost of recognisability: it shows three-character codes (here the USFM identifiers), which suit people who already know the books. A contributed Olive Tree screenshot (undated, captured before May 2026) shows the same idea as a nine-column grid of three-letter codes. A verse step suits study and sermon follow-along, but adds a screen for anyone reading a whole chapter. Familiar convention 1. Step by step A widely used structure, generalized here. Not a copy of a particular app. Try this Tap “Mark 3”, choose John, then chapter 3. Then switch on the book grid and the verse step and try again. + Makes easier Each screen asks one question, with large targets. Readers who recognise a book name but do not remember a reference can always get there. − Costs Several screens for a destination the person already knows. Sixty-six books make a long list; a grid is shorter but relies on abbreviations. Ask your team Do most of your readers know where they are going, or are they finding out? Observed 2. Expandable book list Observed in Mere Bible and YouVersion: chapters open inside the book list (see the screenshots below). Stills do not show gesture or commit timing, so opening follows the switches below, as in option 1. Try this Open the picker. The list opens at Mark with chapter 3 marked. Scroll to John, expand it and choose 3. + Makes easier Book context stays visible while choosing a chapter, and the reader’s current book opens ready. − Costs Long books push the rest of the list down. Psalms puts 150 cells inside the list, and the scroll position has to survive a book collapsing. Ask your team Will your longest books still be manageable inside a list? Borrowed 3. Type a reference Borrowed from address bars and command palettes, where people type a known destination. In a Bible app, the parser decides what counts as a reference. Try this Type “jo”, then “jo 3”, then “jn 3:16”. Press Enter to open. + Makes easier The quickest route to a known reference, such as a sermon slide or a citation in a book. − Costs It assumes the person knows the reference and can spell it. Ambiguous abbreviations and mistakes need clear help. It looks up references only; it does not search words or use AI. Ask your team What should happen when someone types something that is not a reference? Observed 4. Start from a feeling Observed in ESV (“When I’m Feeling” audio playlists) and Glorify (search for “chapters, verses or emotions” with chips such as Anxiety and Doubt); see the screenshots below. The passages in this example are our own illustrative choice. Try this Choose “Weary”, then open Matthew 11:28–30. Then go back and look at what the lists leave out. + Makes easier Someone who does not know where to look can still find a way in, starting from where they are rather than from a reference. − Costs Someone else has decided which verses answer which feeling. Short lists can turn Scripture into remedies, lift verses out of their context and imply how the reader ought to feel. Acute distress needs more than a verse. Ask your team Who chooses the passages for each feeling, and how will readers know? Leave it out 5. No passage picker An exploratory proposal for plan- or session-focused readers. Not attributed to a specific app and untested. Try this Try to reach John 3. Then use the back arrow to see what the plan offers. + Makes easier Nothing to decide before reading. The plan supplies the passage and the back arrow returns to the plan, which can suit a guided session, a devotional or a group reading. − Costs John 3 is out of reach. Someone who wants to follow a reference, check context or wander has to leave for another app or mode. Ask your team Is open-ended lookup part of this product’s job, or does it belong somewhere else? i Options 1 to 3 differ in how the destination is expressed; option 4 replaces the destination with a felt need; option 5 removes the choice. The example uses the Protestant book order and English chapter and verse counts for all 66 books. It contains Mark 3:1–6 only; other destinations show where the reader would arrive. Verse ranges and translation choice are separate decisions not shown here. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways It depends on what the reader already knows Typing is fastest when the reference is in front of someone, and a wall when it isn’t. Browsing takes more taps but never asks anyone to remember. The expandable list sits between the two: the shape of the book stays in view while you choose. Leaving it out is a real option If your product guides people through a plan, a full picker is an exit as much as a feature. Leaving it out keeps the session calm and the scope honest. It also sends someone following a sermon to another app. A feeling asks a different question Not “where is it?” but “where should I begin?”. ESV and Glorify both offer it. It welcomes someone with no reference in mind, and hands quiet authority to whoever wrote the lists. Name the curators, open passages in their chapter, and keep acute distress out of a verse menu. Open on tap; review only when it costs something Opening on tap is what most people expect. A review step earns its place when a wrong destination is costly, such as changing a group’s shared reading. Going down to the verse helps someone following a sermon and slows down someone reading whole chapters. Offer both routes, and keep each one plain Most general Bible readers end up with browsing and typed entry. That works while each route says what it does. A reference field that quietly becomes text search or an AI answer box changes what people expect from it. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Step by step 2 Expandable book list 3 Type a reference 4 Start from a feeling 5 No passage picker Following a sermon or talk A spoken reference, found before the speaker moves on ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit New to the Bible Seeing which books exist and where, without typing ● Good fit ● Good fit Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Studying across books Jumping between references quickly Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Carrying on with a book The saved place, then the next chapter ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit ● Good fit Looking for comfort, with no reference in mind A place to begin, with its chapter around it Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit Poor fit A guided plan or group session Today’s passage without detours Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit Screen readers, large text or limited dexterity Few, large targets and one decision at a time ● Good fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition Finding the place Finding the place is an old practice In Nazareth, “the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to Him. Unrolling it, He found the place where it was written” (Luke 4:17). Before chapters and verses, passages were named by what happened in them: “have you not read about the burning bush in the Book of Moses?” (Mark 12:26). Chapters date from the thirteenth century and verse numbers from 1551. Easy access is a stated commitment The Second Vatican Council asked that “easy access to Sacred Scripture should be provided for all the Christian faithful”. Protestant Bible societies have pursued the same goal through translation and distribution. A picker is where that access succeeds or fails on a phone. T Second Vatican Council How people arrive Lookup, suggestion and habit People reach Scripture in several ways Lifeway’s 2024 survey finds looking up passages, reading ones suggested by others, rereading favourites and reading systematically overlap in the same people. One route will not serve all of them. S Lifeway Research Apps teach a way of reading Hutchings shows Bible apps are designed as persuasive technologies that train reading habits. By the same logic, a picker that always opens at a verse teaches verse reading, and one that opens at a chapter teaches passages. R Tim Hutchings Reading on needs no picker YouVersion documents continuous chapter scrolling and an optional verse picker: for people reading on, the next chapter matters more than a destination. S YouVersion Support Interface research What helps people find Recognition is easier than recall Interfaces that show the options ask less of memory than fields that need someone to remember and type. Browsing books and chapters asks people to recognise; a reference field asks them to recall. Offer both. D Raluca Budiu Forgive the way people type When input is wrong and a correction is known, suggest it. Accept abbreviations, other languages’ book names and “Psalm” for “Psalms”, and say “Did you mean John 3?” instead of “Not found”. A W3C D USFM documentation Many small targets A grid of 150 Psalms or 176 verses packs many targets into a phone screen. Keep each at least 24 pixels with space between, and let the grid reflow when text is enlarged. A W3C D W3C WAI Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If People follow references from a speaker, a book or a study guide Start with A typed reference, with browsing as the fallback If People are new to the Bible, or think in books rather than references Start with Step by step, or the expandable list If People arrive with a need rather than a reference Start with Start from a feeling, with named curators and the whole chapter one step away If Your product is a guided plan, devotional or group session Start with Consider no picker, with a clear route to a full Bible elsewhere These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. YouVersion · Desktop web Continuous prose with reader controls Direct web capture · cropped Mere Bible (formerly NeuBible) · Mobile interface · device and OS not independently verified Chapter navigation beside the reading text User-contributed screenshot · unedited Mere Bible (formerly NeuBible) · Mobile interface · device and OS not independently verified Book list with an inline chapter grid User-contributed screenshot · unedited NeuBible (now Mere Bible) · iOS app · device model not recorded Chapters as a strip inside the book list User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded Book list with history, audio markers and two orders User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded A chapter grid that opens inside the book list User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Olive Tree Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded All 66 books in one view, as three-letter codes User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged ESV Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded Audio playlists by feeling User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Glorify · iOS app · device model not recorded Search for chapters, verses or emotions User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What finding the place is for In Nazareth, Jesus unrolled the scroll and “found the place where it was written” (Luke 4:17). Knowing where a passage sits, in which book and among which neighbours, is part of understanding it. Finding the place is a small act of attention before reading. Where Christians differ The Bible itself is not the same book everywhere. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include books that most Protestant Bibles omit or place in a separate Apocrypha, and the Hebrew Bible orders its books differently from Christian Old Testaments. Many readers know no references at all and come with a feeling or a story. What follows for design Use the canon and book order of the edition being read, and do not impose one tradition’s list on everyone. Serve the reader who knows no references as carefully as the expert, without steering either toward what the publisher wants them to read. In conversation with Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum (1965) “Easy access to Sacred Scripture should be provided for all the Christian faithful”: finding the passage is the first step of access. Martin Luther, Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen (1530) designed his Bible for ordinary people; a picker should serve the reader who knows no references as well as the scholar. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Promoted content stands between the reader and the passage they asked for. Ethical Does no harm Make lookup fast and accessible for people who know a reference. Redemptive Gives something up for them Invest as much in people who know no references, without steering them to what you want them to read. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review Do most of the people you serve know where they are going, or are they finding out? Exercise Watch three people find a chapter you name aloud, then one they choose themselves. Note where each one hesitates, and whether they ever needed a route you didn’t offer. Getting someone to the right page is the first hospitality of every reading. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further This deep dive brings together 4 earlier patterns. Their guidance, wireframes and sources are kept below; their old addresses lead here. Edge cases to design for Offer book browsing and direct reference entry as complementary routes. Preserve the current location, make back and cancel predictable, and show the full destination before opening a parsed reference. What tends to go wrong Unexplained abbreviations; assuming every edition has the same book list; resetting book selection on back; accepting an ambiguous reference without clarification. How to test it Locate an unfamiliar book, enter an abbreviated range, cancel after choosing a chapter and return to the original verse. Test long book names, different canons, large text and one-chapter books. How the example is built, and what it leaves out Built with React, Tailwind and an adapted shadcn/ui Button, styled with the paper visual vocabulary used across these examples. Input stays in browser memory. The examples do not request an AI response, load more than a few verses of Bible text or save reading history. Escape cancels. Opening or cancelling returns focus to the reader’s passage button, and each new screen moves focus to its heading. Chapter cells are ordinary toggle buttons, not an ARIA grid. The comparison selector follows the ARIA tabs pattern. A production implementation still needs a licensed content catalogue, edition-specific book and chapter availability, loading and error states, and testing with assistive technology. The visual style is illustrative, not a required brand treatment. Other approaches are not shown here: separate or combined translation, book and chapter controls; a two-pane browser on wider screens; verse and range selection; Mere Bible’s chapter rail beside the text; a single field that combines book filtering, references and AI suggestions; and different canons or book orders. Earlier pattern: A reference opens at a deliberate destination Choose the content scope, landing position and temporary cue separately. Guidance For contextual reading, open the containing chapter and place the first requested verse in view. For a focused preview, show only the verse or requested passage with a Read in context action. A chapter overview may open at the top, but retain the requested reference and provide Jump to verse. Scrolling and highlighting are independent: landing at a verse can use a temporary outline, a labelled margin cue, or no highlight. Mark a requested range rather than only its first verse when helpful. Temporary navigation cues never become saved annotations. Account for headers, players and delayed layout; retain back navigation to the search or chat. What tends to go wrong Opening at the chapter top without acknowledging the requested verse; permanently marking a deep-link target; hiding a focused excerpt’s boundaries; losing the origin. How to test it Enter one verse, a range and a cross-chapter passage from search, chat and an external link. Check large text, cold loading, missing content and return navigation. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources Scripture structure documentation Relevant structure and marker references reviewed · A format is not a complete model of app behaviour, annotations or formation. Understanding Reflow Official guidance reviewed on 5 October 2026 · Semantic scroll restoration is an original design proposal, not a requirement stated by this criterion. Earlier pattern: Book and chapter pickers: list, grid or drill-down? Choose the browsing shape independently from the search field. Guidance Start with full book names and a clear selected state. Compare a list, a compact grid and progressive book-to-chapter selection for the intended readers. Keep search available, preserve the current location on cancel, and use the selected edition’s actual book and chapter availability. What tends to go wrong Unexplained abbreviations; tiny grid targets; assuming one canon or ordering; losing the list position when returning from a chapter; an unavailable book silently opening elsewhere. How to test it Find an unfamiliar book, select a chapter, go back and cancel. Repeat with long translated names, enlarged text, a one-chapter book and missing edition coverage. Mere Bible: publisher listing and rename Reviewed 6 October 2026 · Does not identify the build shown in the contributed screenshots. Earlier pattern: How do readers move to the next chapter? Compare continuous reading, explicit buttons and a persistent navigation bar. Guidance Match navigation to the current task, not a permanent reader category. Continuous reading can cross a visible chapter boundary without permanent arrows. Discrete chapters benefit from explicit previous and next destinations. A compact bar suits frequent movement, while study may additionally need a back trail, saved place and direct reference entry. A bounded passage can end without a prominent Next action; retain optional wider context where useful. Keep controls clear of the final lines, audio controls and selection tools. What tends to go wrong Swipe-only navigation; wrapping from the last book to the first without warning; hiding the last verse behind a bar; changing chapter during text selection; a missing download leaving a blank page. How to test it Give participants different tasks: continue a narrative, compare distant references, follow a spoken reference, resume a note and finish one shared passage. Observe misnavigation, return to place and unwanted interruptions. Ask whether they wanted a next step; do not infer usefulness from the number of chapters opened. Include large text, assistive technology and unavailable chapters. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Earlier pattern: One field for browsing, references and AI discovery Let one input filter books, recognise a reference and suggest passages, while making each result’s origin clear. Guidance Keep one field above the book browser. As the person types, filter book names immediately and recognise complete references locally. Other queries can request AI-assisted passage suggestions after a pause, with book matches and suggestions visible together. Prioritise a resolved reference, preserve the query and make opening a deliberate action. Clearly label AI suggestions and any exact text matches as different kinds of result. A separate full-text search service or sourced answer preview is an additional capability, not implied by a unified field. What tends to go wrong Presenting type-ahead filtering, direct references and AI suggestions as separate mandatory modes; sending unfinished references without a clear policy; allowing late suggestions to replace current results; describing AI suggestions as exact wording matches; jumping before the person finishes a range. How to test it Start empty, type a partial book name, extend it into a reference and then a range, and replace it with a topic. pages.title: First use
pages.description: What does someone have to give before they reach what they came for? Six options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns First use What does someone have to give before they reach what they came for? When two disciples began to follow Jesus, he asked, “What do you want?”, and when they asked where he was staying, he said, “Come and see” (John 1:38–39). The first minutes in a faith app ask the same question from the other side. Many apps put a tour, an account, questions, a rating, permission prompts and a subscription offer in front of the first verse, prayer or answer. Some people arrive curious, some in a hard night, some coming back after years away or after being hurt in a church. Apps also cost money to build and run, and every AI answer has a price, so how and when to ask for support is a real question, not a trick. Welcome people first, and ask honestly. Draft · waiting for review What needs review: Help for someone arriving in a hard night, the wording for someone coming back after being hurt in a church, and the reflection on paying for Scripture, teaching and AI. This touches the safety of people who may already be hurting, and it has not yet been reviewed by people whose work this is: crisis support and suicide prevention; pastoral care; survivor advocacy (ideally survivor-led); and theology across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions. Please read it as a draft until they have. Is this your field, or do you know someone whose field it is? I would be grateful for your eyes on it, or for an introduction. Offer a review or an introduction 6 working options 19 app examples 7 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested First use At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From nothing asked to everything asked Less is asked first More is asked first 1 Open on what they came for Familiar convention + What they came for, at once − Nothing saved yet Try it → 2 A first page of places to start Familiar convention + A way in without a reference − Someone chose the passages Try it → 3 Guest first, an account when there is something to keep Observed + Use first, decide later − The later ask can feel like a wall Try it → 4 A short tour first Observed + Expectations set − Often skipped, soon forgotten Try it → 5 Questions first Observed + A first suggestion that fits − Questions before content Try it → 6 Asking for payment Observed + Pays for the work − Up front, it asks before giving Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try six ways to begin Someone has just installed a faith app. Choose what kind of app it is: a Bible reader, a prayer app or an AI companion. Then choose who is arriving: someone curious, someone in a hard night, or someone coming back after years away or after being hurt in a church. Count what each option asks before they reach what they came for, and see where help is. For the last option, compare asking for payment up front with asking after a first use. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Open on what they came for · Familiar convention 2. A first page of places to start · Familiar convention 3. Guest first, an account when there is something to keep · Observed 4. A short tour first · Observed 5. Questions first · Observed 6. Asking for payment · Observed Option 1 Open on what they came for Familiar convention 2 A first page of places to start Familiar convention 3 Guest first, an account when there is something to keep Observed 4 A short tour first Observed 5 Questions first Observed 6 Asking for payment Observed App Not used here Bible reader Prayer app AI companion Arriving Not used here Curious A hard night Coming back Asking Not used here Before first use After first use Why these settings? The Bible reader opens on John 1:38–39, the prayer app on an evening prayer with Psalm 4:8, and the AI companion on a question box. Someone in a hard night types or chooses that they are not coping; someone coming back has been away from church for years, or was hurt in one, and answers “no church right now”. Asking after a first use says what is free, what costs money and roughly how much; the figure for an AI answer is our estimate from Anthropic’s published prices. Familiar convention 1. Open on what they came for Familiar from church practice: the Diocese of York tells someone who has picked up a Bible to start with Mark, “Start with chapter 1 and read as much as feels manageable”; a pew Bible or a prayer book asks nothing first. The app, its passage, prayer and question box are written for this example. Try this Read, play or ask straight away. Then arrive in a hard night, and then come back after years away. + Makes easier Nothing stands between the person and what they came for. − Costs Nothing is saved until they choose to save it. Ask your team What is the one thing a new person should be able to do in the first ten seconds? Familiar convention 2. A first page of places to start Familiar from the Gideon Bible, whose front pages carry “topical indexes to point the reader to what the Bible says about various topics, problems and life situations”. Not observed in this form in an app. The situations, passages and help line are chosen for this example; the TelefonSeelsorge numbers are from its own website, checked 11 October 2026. Try this Choose a place to start. Then arrive in a hard night and see what comes first. + Makes easier A way in for someone without a reference, with help at the top. − Costs Someone chose the passages, and the list can feel like a diagnosis. Ask your team Who chose these situations and passages, and what comes first for someone in danger? Observed 3. Guest first, an account when there is something to keep Observed in Startblock (“Ohne Anmeldung fortfahren”, continue without signing in), Bible.is (“Create account later”) and Joseph Prince, where a guest can read and copy but is asked to sign up “to begin highlighting”; see the screenshots below. Apple’s review guidelines ask apps without significant account-based features to “let people use it without a login”. The wording here is written for this example. Try this Use the app, then try to keep something. Then arrive in a hard night. + Makes easier People use the app first and decide later whether to stay. − Costs The later ask can still feel like a wall, if it comes at the wrong moment. Ask your team What is the first thing worth keeping, and is that the right moment to ask? Observed 4. A short tour first Observed in Startblock’s five skippable intro slides, whose fourth reads “Das brauchst du: Eine Bibel aus Papier, ein Notizheft, einen Stift und etwas Zeit” (you need a paper Bible, a notebook, a pen and some time), in ESV’s welcome carousel, which ends in an offer to create a free account, and in Joseph Prince’s intro video and feature tour; see the screenshots below. The slides here are written for this example. Try this Step through the tour, or skip it. Then arrive in a hard night. + Makes easier Sets expectations, as Startblock’s paper Bible and pen do. − Costs Often skipped and soon forgotten; it delays the first use. Ask your team What would a person miss if they skipped every slide? Observed 5. Questions first Observed in Abide’s “What brings you here today?” photo grid, Bible BFF’s “How much of the Bible have you read?” and Faith’s questions for a name, an age range and a profile picture; see the screenshots below and the check-ins deep dive. The questions here are written for this example. Try this Answer, or skip, each question. Then come back after years away and answer “no church right now”. + Makes easier A first suggestion that fits. − Costs Every question delays the first use, and some ask what is not needed. Ask your team What does each answer change, and can someone skip it? Observed 6. Asking for payment Observed in Bible BFF, which asks people to rate the app before using it and then offers a weekly plan; Spark Bible, which asks for notifications before the first verse and later says “You just used your last free study”; Abide, whose trial screen gives the reminder day and charge date; and Pray.com, which asks for a mobile number at sign-up; see the screenshots below. The second setting, asking after a first use and saying what things cost, is a proposal; its costs are our estimate from published AI prices. Try this Count what is asked before the first verse. Then switch to asking after a first use, and try the AI companion. + Makes easier Asked after a first use, honestly, it keeps the work going. − Costs Asked before anything is given, it turns people away and puts help behind a wall. Ask your team What is free, what costs you money, and does the person know before they pay? i The app, its wording, passages and prices were written for this example; the TelefonSeelsorge numbers are from its own website, checked 11 October 2026. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. Nothing is saved or sent. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Let people reach what they came for first Startblock offers “Ohne Anmeldung fortfahren” (continue without signing in), and Bible.is “Create account later”. Open on today’s passage, a prayer to play or a question box, and count everything asked before it. Ask for an account when there is something to keep Joseph Prince lets a guest read and copy, and asks for an account “to begin highlighting”. A highlight, a plan or a conversation worth keeping is the honest moment to ask; say what the account holds, and how to delete it. Ask for permissions when a feature needs them Spark Bible asks for notifications before the first verse; Android’s guidance is to ask “in context, when the user starts to interact with the feature that requires it”. Ask when someone sets a reminder. Help in a crisis comes before everything Someone may open a faith app in a hard night. Keep a way to a person on the first screen, and never put it behind an account, a question, a free-answer limit or a paywall. Offer help, not verses, unless the person asks for Scripture. Sensitive conversations → “No church right now” is an ordinary answer Someone coming back after years away, or after being hurt in a church, may meet questions about their church on the first screen. Ask only if the answer changes something, let it be skipped, and don’t praise or correct any answer. When Scripture is used to harm → Ask for payment after a first use, and say what costs money Abide’s trial screen gives the reminder day and the charge date; Spark Bible tells people when they have used their “last free study”. Say what is free, what costs money and roughly why: licensed notes, recordings, AI answers. A free allowance that explains itself is fairer than a wall. Neither free nor paid is the only faithful way The church has long supported those who serve the word, and has long distrusted those who sell it. A subscription can be honest and a free app can be manipulative. The test is what is asked before anything is given, and whether the person knows what they are paying for. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Open on what they came for 2 A first page of places to start 3 Guest first, an account when there is something to keep 4 A short tour first 5 Questions first 6 Asking for payment Someone curious, with no reference A way in without a quiz ● Good fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Someone in a hard night A person to talk to, before anything else ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Someone coming back after years away, or after harm Nothing that asks where they have been ● Good fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit A church member sent a link Today’s reading, and their church’s plan ● Good fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit An AI companion that costs money per answer A free allowance that says why ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit Licensed study notes or recordings A fair price, after a first use ◐ Possible Poor fit ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition Welcome first, commitment later Come and see Jesus asked two would-be followers, “What do you want?”, and answered their question with an invitation: “Come and see” (John 1:38–39). They spent the rest of the day with him. Guests received like Christ The Rule of Benedict asks that “all guests who arrive be received like Christ”, and, for someone asking to join the community, that they “not be granted an easy entrance”. Welcome is free; commitment is asked for later, of those who want to stay. S Benedict of Nursia, sixth century A place to start, and permission to read a little The Diocese of York tells someone who has picked up a Bible to try Mark: “Start with chapter 1 and read as much as feels manageable. You could also listen to it.” The Gideons put “topical indexes” for “topics, problems and life situations” at the front of their Bibles. S Diocese of York (Church of England) S The Gideons International in Australia Scripture and church practice Paying those who serve the word The worker is worthy of his wages The Levites received the tithes of Israel “in return for the work they do” (Numbers 18:21). Paul wrote that “those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14) and that “the one who receives instruction in the word must share in all good things with his instructor” (Galatians 6:6). He also chose, for himself, to “offer it free of charge” (1 Corinthians 9:18). Offerings, and a line against trading Catholic church law permits a priest “to receive an offering to apply the Mass for a specific intention”, by which the faithful “support its ministers and works”, and requires that “Any appearance of … trading is to be excluded entirely”. Protestant churches pay their ministers through offerings, tithes or, in Germany, church tax. S Holy See Support, and suspicion of those who ask The Didache, an early church manual, says a true teacher “is himself worthy, as the workman, of his support”, and that a travelling apostle who asks for money “is a false prophet”. Peter told Simon, who offered money for the Spirit, “you thought you could buy the gift of God with money!” (Acts 8:20), and Paul refused to “peddle the word of God for profit” (2 Corinthians 2:17). S Early Christian text, late first or early second century Products and research What a first use asks, and what it costs Use first, then decide Apple’s review guidelines say that an app without significant account-based features should “let people use it without a login”, and that an app with accounts must let people delete them. Its design guidance asks for onboarding that is “fast, fun, and optional”, and for letting people experience an app “before prompting them for ratings or purchases”. S Apple S Apple Tutorials are skipped Nielsen Norman Group found that deck-of-cards tutorials “didn’t improve task performance”, and that users “frequently skip them”. D Alita Kendrick D Nielsen Norman Group A required account turns people away In Baymard’s survey of US online shoppers, 18% of those who abandoned a checkout for reasons other than browsing said “The site wanted me to create an account”. That is shopping, not faith apps, but the moment is the same: someone ready to begin is asked for something first. R Baymard Institute Asking again and again European data protection authorities name “continuous prompting” a deceptive design pattern: users “repeatedly asked” for more data or consent tend to give in. S European Data Protection Board What it costs to serve someone An AI answer that reads about 6,000 tokens (instructions, passages and the conversation so far) and writes about 600 costs about 1.8 cents on Claude Sonnet 5.5 and about a tenth of a cent on Claude Haiku 5.5, at published prices. At 20 answers a day, that is about $10.80 or $0.54 a person each month, before hosting and staff. Translations cost too: Crossway’s free ESV terms exclude apps that sell, take donations or carry advertising, while the Berean Standard Bible is in the public domain. And free apps are paid for by someone: in 2018 YouVersion’s $8.3 million budget came from a church’s tithes and donations. S Anthropic S Crossway S Berean Bible S Religion News Service Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If A Bible reader Start with Open on today’s passage; ask for an account when someone wants to keep something If A prayer or audio app Start with Play first; ask for notifications when someone sets a reminder If An AI companion Start with A free allowance that says why, with crisis help never counted If Licensed notes or recordings Start with A price after a first use, with the trial’s reminder and charge dates If You are tempted to put the paywall first Start with Don’t: let people meet what you made, then ask, honestly These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. Hallow · iOS app · device model not recorded “Pray for others, be prayed for” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Abide · iOS app · device model not recorded “What brings you here today?” as a photo grid User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Startblock · iOS app · device model not recorded A way to continue without signing in, on the first screen User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Startblock · iOS app · device model not recorded “What you need”: a paper Bible, a notebook, a pen and some time User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Bible.is · iOS app · device model not recorded “Create account later” beneath the mission User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Joseph Prince · iOS app · device model not recorded A second ask when continuing as a guest User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Joseph Prince · iOS app · device model not recorded An account asked for at the moment of highlighting User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Bible BFF · iOS app · device model not recorded “Rate the app” before the app has been used User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Bible BFF · iOS app · device model not recorded A weekly plan as the first offer User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Abide · iOS app · device model not recorded A trial screen with the reminder and charge dates User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Abide · iOS app · device model not recorded “Your subscription fuels a greater purpose” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Spark Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded “You just used your last free study” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Pray.com · iOS app · device model not recorded A mobile number at sign-up User-contributed screenshot · resized; the entered phone number blurred Faith · iOS app · device model not recorded “How old are you?” during setup User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Spark Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded A notification prompt before the first verse User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Hallow · iOS app · device model not recorded A tracking request that says what it is for User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Bible BFF · iOS app · device model not recorded “How much of the Bible have you read?” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Joseph Prince · iOS app · device model not recorded A notification request over “Set a schedule” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Pray.com · iOS app · device model not recorded A ministry donation that brings an ad-free subscription User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What a welcome is for Jesus asked two would-be followers, “What do you want?”, and answered with an invitation: “Come and see” (John 1:38–39). Isaiah’s call is to “come, buy wine and milk without money and without cost!” (Isaiah 55:1), and the last page of the Bible invites “the one who desires the water of life” to “drink freely” (Revelation 22:17). Grace is not for sale, and a first welcome should feel like it. Where Christians differ, and agree The same Scriptures pay those who serve: the Levites lived from the tithe (Numbers 18:21), and “the worker is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7). Catholics give an offering for a Mass, under canon law that excludes “any appearance of … trading”; Protestant churches pay ministers from offerings, tithes or church tax; Paul took support from some churches and chose to preach to others “free of charge” (1 Corinthians 9:18). Both traditions warn against those who “peddle the word of God for profit” (2 Corinthians 2:17). An app that charges is in a long line of honest support, and of temptation. What follows for design Let people come and see before anything is asked of them. Keep help within reach from the first screen. Then ask for support as the church at its best has done: openly, for real costs, never for access to grace, and never from someone in a crisis. Say what is free, what costs money and why, and let people pay what they can. In conversation with John Wesley, “The Use of Money” (sermon 50) told Methodists to “gain all you can” by honest work, but called gain made “by hurting our neighbour in his soul” “dear-bought”; then to save all you can and “give all you can”. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Put a quiz, a rating, permission prompts and a weekly trial before the first verse; make the free tier feel like a punishment; keep crisis help behind the paywall. Ethical Does no harm Open on what people came for, ask for an account when there is something to keep, ask for payment after a first use, and give the trial’s reminder and charge dates. Redemptive Gives something up for them Keep Scripture and crisis help free, say plainly what things cost you, let people pay what they can, and give up the conversions that a gate before the first use would bring. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review What must someone give before they reach what they came for, and what does it honestly cost you to serve them? Exercise Install your app on a fresh phone and write down every screen, field, prompt and offer before the first verse, prayer or answer. Do it again as someone who types, in the first box they see, that they don’t want to be here anymore. Then write one paragraph, in plain words, telling a new user what is free, what costs money, roughly what it costs you, and why. Would you be glad for them to read it on the first day? Welcome people as guests: let them reach what they came for first, keep help within reach, and ask for support honestly. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further Edge cases to design for Open on what the person came for: today’s passage, a prayer to play, a question box. Offer a short page of places to start, with help in a crisis at the top. Let people use the app as a guest, and ask for an account when there is something to keep, such as a highlight or a plan. Keep any tour short and skippable. Ask questions only when the answer changes something, and let each be skipped. Ask for permissions when a feature needs them. Ask for payment after a first use: say what is free, what costs money and roughly how much, and give the charge date before a trial begins. What tends to go wrong An account, a phone number or a quiz before the first verse; a request to rate the app before it has been used; notification and tracking prompts at launch; a weekly subscription as the default; testimonials and social proof between questions; crisis help behind a sign-up or a quota; questions about church attendance or Bible knowledge that cannot be skipped and that praise every answer; payment framed as the only way to be faithful, or free use framed as the only way to be faithful. How to test it Install the app on a fresh phone and count the taps, fields and prompts before the first verse, prayer or answer. Do it again as someone who says, in the first box they see, that they don’t want to be here anymore, and time how long it takes to reach a person. Do it as someone who answers “no church right now”. Write down, for a year of use, what the person pays, what it costs you to serve them, and whether the app says so. Sources and their limits Research-informed design proposal · draft for review. Faith and interpretation When two disciples began to follow Jesus, he asked them, “What do you want?”, and when they asked where he was staying, he said, “Come and see” (John 1:38–39). They spent the day with him before anything was asked of them. The same Scriptures say both “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew 10:8) and “the worker is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7): welcome freely, and pay honestly those who serve.
