pages.title: Giving and offerings
pages.description: How should a faith app ask for gifts, and what should it never promise? Seven options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Giving and offerings How should a faith app ask for gifts, and what should it never promise? “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Giving is worship, and it pays for churches, missions and the apps people pray with. More of it now happens on a phone: in a church’s app, through a QR code during the service, or with a Give button in a Bible app. The design decides what is chosen for the giver, where the ask appears and what a gift is said to do. Most people who give through an app want it to be simple and safe. Design also for the person who is short of money this month, and for the one who has just told the app about their grief. Draft · waiting for review What needs review: What is shown to someone short of money or who has just shared a prayer request, the description of seed-faith appeals, the treatment of tithing and church tax, and the use of YouVersion screens from the owner’s own account. This touches the safety of people who may already be hurting, and it has not yet been reviewed by people whose work this is: pastoral care; theology across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions; and charity and consumer law. Please read it as a draft until they have. Is this your field, or do you know someone whose field it is? I would be grateful for your eyes on it, or for an introduction. Offer a review or an introduction 7 working options 12 app examples 7 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Giving At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From the giver’s choice to the app’s The giver decides The app decides 1 Giving stays with the church Familiar convention + Nothing asked in the app − Nothing pays for the app Try it → 2 A quiet way to give Observed + There when wanted − Easy to miss Try it → 3 The church’s offering Observed + To their own church, by fund − Fees and records Try it → 4 A regular gift Observed + Steady, chosen support − Easy to forget Try it → 5 What a gift does Observed + Shows where it goes − Figures age and overpromise Try it → 6 A gift tied to a benefit Observed + Supports others too − A price dressed as a gift Try it → 7 Pressure and promises Leave it out + Raises money fast − Trades on faith and fear Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try seven ways a faith app can ask for gifts The same faith app, made by a small ministry and used by members of St Luke’s church, handles giving in seven ways. Choose who is giving: someone who gives every month, someone who installed the app this week, someone short of money this month, or someone who has just shared a prayer request. Then look at where the ask appears, the screen where they give, and what happens afterwards. Nothing is paid. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Giving stays with the church · Familiar convention 2. A quiet way to give · Observed 3. The church’s offering · Observed 4. A regular gift · Observed 5. What a gift does · Observed 6. A gift tied to a benefit · Observed 7. Pressure and promises · Leave it out Option 1 Giving stays with the church Familiar convention 2 A quiet way to give Observed 3 The church’s offering Observed 4 A regular gift Observed 5 What a gift does Observed 6 A gift tied to a benefit Observed 7 Pressure and promises Leave it out Giver Not used here Gives monthly New this week Money is tight Just shared a prayer request Why these settings? Someone who has just shared a prayer request is shown no ask in the better options; the warning case shows what happens when an app asks then. Help for someone in a hard moment is TelefonSeelsorge, whose numbers are from its own website, checked 11 October 2026. Familiar convention 1. Giving stays with the church Familiar from churches where the offering, a bank transfer or church tax carries giving, and from Startblock’s support page, which asks first for prayer and help, then gives a bank account and a receipt on request; see the screenshot below. The church and wording here are written for this example. Try this Look for the ask as each person, then follow the link to the church. + Makes easier Nothing in the app asks for money. − Costs Nothing pays for the app, and some people want to give there. Ask your team Who pays for this app, and do its users know? Observed 2. A quiet way to give Observed in YouVersion, captured 11 October 2026: Give from the profile, an amount that starts at zero, a regular gift switched off, and a choice between YouVersion and Bible translation; see the screenshots below. The ministry, funds and wording here are written for this example. Try this Find Give in the menu as someone new, then as someone short of money. + Makes easier Easy to find when someone wants it, and silent otherwise. − Costs Easy to miss, and it raises less than an ask. Ask your team Where would someone look for this, and is it there? Observed 3. The church’s offering Observed in Churchome, captured 11 October 2026: Give in the menu, named funds, Pushpay, Apple Pay or PayPal, and a recurring gift changed in the person’s Pushpay account; see the screenshots below. Church giving apps such as Givelify (101K ratings), Church Center and Tithe.ly work the same way. In Germany congregations show a QR code during the service that leads to their own donation form. The church, funds and fee here are written for this example. Try this Try someone who gives every month, then someone new at the service. + Makes easier The gift goes to the person’s own church, by fund, with a receipt. − Costs Card fees, and the church’s giving records held by a platform. Ask your team Does the giver see the fee, and who keeps their giving history? Observed 4. A regular gift Observed in YouVersion’s “Become a Sower”, a monthly gift switched off until the person turns it on, and in Abide’s donate sheet with “Make it a monthly donation” unticked; see the screenshots below. Recurring giving is 35% of digital church giving in one vendor’s data. The reminder before a change is a proposal. Try this Set a monthly gift as someone who gives, then stop it. + Makes easier Steady support the person chose, on a day they chose. − Costs Easy to forget that it is running. Ask your team Is stopping as easy as starting, and when does the giver hear about it? Observed 5. What a gift does Observed in YouVersion’s Sowers page, a slider from $10 to $100 a month with Bibles per year beside it, and Pray as you go’s “80%” of a donation going to content; see the screenshots below. The figures here are written for this example. Try this Move the amount as someone who gives, then read the source line. + Makes easier People see where the money goes and what it makes possible. − Costs Figures age, and a number per dollar can promise too much. Ask your team Could you show the source and the date of every figure? Observed 6. A gift tied to a benefit Observed in Pray.com’s “Support & Go Ad Free”, where a ministry donation brings “an Ad Free Subscription”, and Glorify’s “Pay it Forward” tiers with “Most popular” ticked; see the screenshots below. Apple treats a gift tied to content as a purchase. The tiers here are written for this example. Try this Open the ad-free offer as someone new, then as someone who just shared a prayer request. + Makes easier People who would pay anyway support others too. − Costs A purchase dressed as a gift, with a tier chosen for the giver. Ask your team Is this a gift or a price, and would the receipt say which? Leave it out 7. Pressure and promises A warning case. Evangelical theologians at Lausanne described prosperity teaching that promises health and wealth through the “sowing of seeds” in tithes and offerings; regulators objected to a default “tip” added to gifts. The seed, the countdown, the tip and the ask after a prayer request here are written for this example to show the pattern; no app is named. Try this Try someone short of money, then someone who has just shared a prayer request. + Makes easier It raises money quickly. − Costs Trades on faith, fear and need, and promises what God has not. Ask your team Would you say this to the person’s face, in your own name? i The ministry, St Luke’s church, the funds, amounts, fees and every sentence were written for this example. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. Nothing is paid, saved or sent. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Start with no amount, and a one-off gift YouVersion’s give screen starts at zero with its monthly gift switched off; Churchome’s opens with $100.00 already filled in, and Abide’s donate sheet offers six amounts with $50 already chosen and a monthly box left unticked. An empty amount leaves the decision to the giver; if you suggest amounts, choose none in advance. Name who receives the gift, and what it pays for YouVersion asks whether a gift goes to the app or to Bible translation; Bible.is asks people to “Donate online” for recordings in oral cultures. Say which organisation receives the money, what it pays for, and whether a receipt follows. Keep the ask out of prayer, grief and crisis Giving belongs in a menu, after a service or on its own page, not between a prayer request and the next screen. Someone who has just written about their grief, or is in danger, should see help and nothing else. Sharing with a group → Keep gifts and purchases apart Pray.com’s “Support & Go Ad Free” gives donors “an Ad Free Subscription”, and Glorify’s “Pay it Forward” ticks “Most popular” in advance. If a payment unlocks something, call it a price; if it is a gift, let it unlock nothing. First use → Stopping is as easy as starting Keep every regular gift in one place, with its next date, and let it be changed or stopped there in one step. Churchome sends people to “your Pushpay account” to change one: say where, and link to it. Remind the giver before a yearly gift or a change in amount. Say what a gift does, truly, and when enough is enough YouVersion’s Sowers page sets Bibles per year beside a monthly amount; Pray as you go says 80% of a donation goes to its content. Give each figure a source and a date, and when a need is met, say so, as Moses did. Never promise a return A gift is not a seed that obliges God to send a harvest. Leave out anything that ties a gift to healing, prosperity, answered prayer or a blessing, and anything that ranks givers or shows who gave what. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Giving stays with the church 2 A quiet way to give 3 The church’s offering 4 A regular gift 5 What a gift does 6 A gift tied to a benefit 7 Pressure and promises A church that wants its offering in its own app Funds, a receipt, a QR code at the service ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit A Bible app run by a ministry A quiet way to give, and honest figures ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit A mission or translation project What a gift does, with source and date Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit An app that also sells a subscription Keep gifts and purchases apart ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Someone short of money this month Nothing chosen for them, no ask they didn’t look for ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Someone who has just shared a prayer request No ask at all in that moment ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition Given freely, in secret, as one is able Decided in the heart “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7); “the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what he does not have” (2 Corinthians 8:12). The poor widow’s two coins were “more than all the others” (Mark 12:43). In secret, and set aside “When you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret” (Matthew 6:3–4). Paul asked each to “set aside a portion of his income” “on the first day of every week” (1 Corinthians 16:2): a regular gift, planned, not pressed out at the moment of asking. Handled openly, and enough is enough Paul took “great care to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord but also in the eyes of men” in handling a gift (2 Corinthians 8:21). When the people brought more than was needed for the tabernacle, which Bezalel built, Moses “sent a proclamation throughout the camp” and “the people were restrained from bringing more” (Exodus 36:6). Tithe, offering and church tax Christians give in different ways: a tenth, as Israel brought “the full tithe into the storehouse” (Malachi 3:10); a proportion “as he is able” (Deuteronomy 16:17); weekly offerings; or, in Germany, church tax collected with income tax. Jesus did not set the tithe aside but named “justice, mercy and faithfulness” as weightier (Matthew 23:23). Platforms and rules What the stores, regulators and tax offices ask A gift, or a purchase On iPhone, “Approved nonprofits may fundraise directly within their own apps”, with Apple Pay, and “must disclose how the funds will be used”; others “may only collect funds outside of the app”. A gift “connected to or associated at any point in time with receiving digital content or services must use in-app purchase”. Google Play exempts “tax exempt donations” from its billing. S Apple S Google Play Console Help Pressure has a name The UK Code of Fundraising Practice requires “not putting undue pressure on a person to donate, not using unreasonably persistent approaches and accepting a request to end an interaction”. In 2026 US state regulators objected to “the application of a default “tip” that went directly to GoFundMe”. S Fundraising Regulator (UK) S Crowell & Moring client alert, March 2026 Receipts belong to the gift In the US, organisations give a written acknowledgment for “contributions of $250 or more”, which may say that “the organization only provided intangible religious benefits”. A UK Gift Aid declaration must explain that “the donor is responsible to pay any difference”. S Internal Revenue Service (US) S HM Revenue & Customs (UK) Current, complete and accurate Christian ministries in the ECFA agreed that what they tell donors “must be current, complete and accurate”, that past events “must be appropriately dated”, and that appeals “must not create unrealistic donor expectations of what a donor’s gift will actually accomplish”. S Evangelical Council for Financial Accountability Research and practice What defaults, recognition and promises do A suggested amount moves people Goswami and Urminsky found “a scale-back effect, in which low defaults reduce average donation amounts”, and “a lower-bar effect, in which defaulting a low amount increases donation rate”. Any default also weakened “other cues such as positive charity information”. R Indranil Goswami and Oleg Urminsky Being seen raises gifts In a field experiment, “charitable gifts increase in response to the promise of public recognition primarily because of individuals’ desire to improve their social image”: the motive Jesus warned against in Matthew 6. R Dean Karlan and Margaret A. McConnell Much church giving is now digital Churches that offer digital giving “reported that 41% of their giving came from digital methods”, and “Recurring giving accounted for 35% of the digital giving in 2025”, in one vendor’s US data. Givelify, the giving app with the most ratings (101K), says it “has processed $6 billion in donations”. In Württemberg almost 400 congregations take the collection through a QR code and a web form. S Ministry Brands, 2026 S Givelify S David Seeley S Wochenblatt-Reporter Seeds and harvests Evangelical theologians at Lausanne described prosperity teaching that promises health and wealth through “the “sowing of seeds” through the faithful payments of tithes and offerings”, and warned against “Replacing the traditional call to repentance and faith with a call to give money”. T Lausanne Theology Working Group, Africa chapter Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If A church app Start with The church’s offering: funds, a receipt, a QR code at the service, fees shown If A Bible or prayer app run by a ministry Start with A quiet way to give, a regular gift if chosen, honest figures If A mission or translation project Start with What a gift does, with every figure sourced and dated If An app that also sells a subscription Start with Keep the price and the gift apart; let a gift unlock nothing If You are tempted to add a seed, a countdown or an ask after a prayer request Start with Don’t: let people give what they decided in their heart These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. Abide · iOS app · device model not recorded “Your subscription fuels a greater purpose” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Pray.com · iOS app · device model not recorded A ministry donation that brings an ad-free subscription User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Glorify · iOS app · device model not recorded “Pay it Forward”: tiers with “Most popular” ticked User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Abide · iOS app · device model not recorded A donate sheet with $50 chosen and monthly left unticked User-contributed screenshot · resized; email address blurred Startblock · iOS app · device model not recorded Prayer first, then help, then a bank account User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Pray As You Go · Website on iPad · device model not recorded “The fruit of your gratitude”, with 80% to content User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Bible.is · iOS app · device model not recorded A donation appeal for oral cultures User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded A give screen that starts at zero, with monthly switched off Editor’s screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded “Give to”: the app, or Bible translation Editor’s screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded Monthly gifts as Bibles per year Editor’s screenshot · resized; account holder’s name blurred Churchome · iOS app · device model not recorded A church’s give screen with $100.00 filled in Editor’s screenshot · resized, content unchanged Churchome · iOS app · device model not recorded A recurring gift changed in another service Editor’s screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What giving is for “Who am I, and who are my people, that we should be able to give as generously as this? For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You” (1 Chronicles 29:14). Giving returns to God what was already his, supports those who serve the word, and cares for those in need. Jesus said that “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35), and looked not at the size of a gift but at what it cost the giver. Where Christians differ Some churches teach the tithe as the measure of faithful giving; others teach proportional giving “as he is able” (Deuteronomy 16:17) and see the tithe as a starting point or as Israel’s law. Catholics give through the offertory, Mass offerings and parish appeals; in Germany church tax carries most church income and the collection is for a named cause. Pentecostal and charismatic churches range from careful teaching on stewardship to the prosperity teaching that the Lausanne statement rejected. All agree that a gift is free, and that those who receive it must handle it honestly. What follows for design Let people give what they decided in their heart: nothing chosen for them, nothing asked in a moment of need. Say who receives the gift and what it truly does, keep it in secret unless the giver chooses otherwise, and make a regular gift easy to stop. Never promise a return, and when the need is met, say so. In conversation with Henri Nouwen, A Spirituality of Fundraising (2010) wrote that “Fundraising is first and foremost a ministry”, “a way of announcing our vision and inviting other people into our mission”, and “precisely the opposite of begging”. John Wesley, “The Use of Money” (sermon 50) told Methodists to “gain all you can”, “save all you can” and “give all you can”: giving is the end that earning and saving serve. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Choose the amount and the tier for the giver, switch on monthly by default, add a tip unless it is removed, ask after a prayer request, and promise a harvest for a seed. Ethical Does no harm Start with no amount and a one-off gift, name who receives it and what it pays for, show fees, send receipts, and let a regular gift be stopped in one step. Redemptive Gives something up for them Ask only where people look for it, never in prayer, grief or need; give every figure a source and a date, say when enough has been given, and give up the gifts that pressure would bring. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review What is chosen for the giver, where does the ask appear, and what does the app say a gift will do? Exercise Give the smallest gift your app allows, three times: as someone new, as someone who has just lost their job, and as someone who has just shared a prayer request. Write down every amount, tick and toggle chosen for you, and every place the ask appeared. Set up a regular gift and time how long it takes to stop it. Then read every sentence about what a gift will do aloud to a member of your church who gives faithfully and has little, and ask whether you would say it to their face. Make room for cheerful giving: let people give what they decided in their heart, tell them truly what it does, and say when it is enough. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further Edge cases to design for Put giving where someone looks for it, in a menu or after a service, not in the middle of reading or prayer. Start with an empty amount and a one-off gift; let the person switch on a regular gift and choose its day. Name who receives the gift and what it pays for, show fees as fees, send a receipt, and keep a history the person can stop or change in one place. Speak of what a gift does with current, complete and accurate figures, and say when enough has been given. What tends to go wrong A “Most popular” tier ticked in advance; a tip of a sixth of the gift added unless someone slides it to zero; a monthly gift switched on by default; a gift box on the screen after someone shares a prayer request; “Sow a seed of faith today and expect a harvest” beside a countdown; givers ranked by amount; a figure from five years ago presented as today’s; a recurring gift that can only be stopped by email. How to test it Give the smallest possible gift in your app as someone new, then as someone who has just lost their job, then as someone who has just shared a prayer request. Write down every amount, tick and toggle that was chosen for you, every place the ask appeared, and how many steps it takes to stop a regular gift. Then read every sentence about what a gift will do, and ask whether you could show the figure’s source and date. Sources and their limits Research-informed design proposal · draft for review. Faith and interpretation “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Jesus said that the poor widow who put in two small coins “has put more than all the others into the treasury” (Mark 12:43), and told those who give, “do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matthew 6:3). When the people brought more than enough for the tabernacle, Moses “sent a proclamation throughout the camp” to stop (Exodus 36:6). pages.title: Highlights and notes
pages.description: How should readers mark a passage? Five options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Highlights and notes How should readers mark a passage? Readers mark Scripture to come back, to remember, to ask a question or to talk with others. Every mark says something and is kept somewhere: a ribbon says only “return here”, a highlight says “this”, a note says what the reader thinks, and a shared note says it to others. Decide how much a mark asks, how it looks, and who can see it. A mark is a small act of attention, sometimes of prayer. Treat what people mark as theirs. 5 working options 7 app examples 5 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Highlights and notes At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From a silent mark to a shared note Just for me, little said More said, to others 1 Bookmark Familiar convention + A place to return to − Records no thought Try it → 2 Highlight Observed + One tap, the exact words − Stays with one translation Try it → 3 Labelled marks Familiar convention + Readable without colour − A scheme to maintain Try it → 4 Private note Familiar convention + Your own words, remembered − Sensitive, so must stay private Try it → 5 Shared note Observed + Reading with others − Others’ words inside Scripture Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try five ways to mark “Be still!” Mark 4:35–41 in the Berean Standard Bible, with the words “Be still!” in verse 39 already selected. Each option offers a different kind of mark, from a silent bookmark to a note others can read. Make a mark, then switch the translation to the BSB and see what happens to it. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Bookmark · Familiar convention 2. Highlight · Observed 3. Labelled marks · Familiar convention 4. Private note · Familiar convention 5. Shared note · Observed Option 1 Bookmark Familiar convention 2 Highlight Observed 3 Labelled marks Familiar convention 4 Private note Familiar convention 5 Shared note Observed Translation Not used here BSB KJV Audio Not used here Off Playing Why these settings? Highlights on exact words belong to the translation they were made in: “Be still!” has no exact match in the KJV’s “Peace, be still.” Bookmarks and notes attach to the verse, so they follow any translation. With audio playing, the playing verse is underlined so it cannot be mistaken for a saved highlight. Familiar convention 1. Bookmark A familiar convention: a ribbon that means only “return here”, as in NeuBible’s three-item menu (Highlight, Copy, Bookmark); see the screenshot below. Try this Bookmark the verse, then switch the translation. + Makes easier Says nothing and asks nothing: a place to come back to. − Costs Records no thought; many bookmarks become a list nobody returns to. Ask your team Is a place to return to enough for what readers are trying to keep? Observed 2. Highlight Observed in the Joseph Prince app (“Highlight added · Add Note”) and most Bible apps; see the screenshot below. Try this Highlight the words, then undo. Turn audio on and compare the two cues. Switch to the BSB. + Makes easier One tap, with undo; marks the exact words that stood out. − Costs Highlighting alone does little for learning; a mark on exact words cannot follow a different translation. Ask your team What happens to a highlight on exact words when the reader switches translation? Familiar convention 3. Labelled marks A familiar convention in study tools, which offer named highlighter styles. Here each label has its own shape, not only a colour. Try this Mark the words as a Question, then a Promise. Notice how each looks. + Makes easier A personal shorthand that is readable without colour and easy to find later. − Costs Asks for a decision before saving; labels can drift into a scheme to maintain. Ask your team Are labels optional, readable without colour, and owned by the reader? Familiar convention 4. Private note A familiar convention: a note attached to the verse, private by default. Here it follows the verse into any translation. Try this Add a note, save it, then switch to the BSB. + Makes easier The reader’s own words, which are remembered better than words they only read. − Costs Takes effort; notes on Scripture reveal faith and struggles, so privacy is not optional. Ask your team Where are notes stored, who can see them, and do people know? Observed 5. Shared note Observed in Glorify, where a “Public Notes” toggle shows other readers’ notes in the text (353 on Genesis 1); see the screenshot below. Community notes here were written for this example. Try this Open the community notes on verse 39. Then write a note and choose Everyone. + Makes easier Reading with others: their questions and comfort beside the text. − Costs Others’ words sit inside Scripture; private struggles can be shared too widely; moderation is needed. Ask your team Before someone shares a note, do they know exactly who will see it? i Mark 4:35–41 in the BSB and KJV, both public domain. Nothing is saved; marks are kept only until you switch option. Community notes, names and the group were written for this example. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Reading with a pen is old Readers have marked Bibles for centuries; Jonathan Edwards filled an interleaved Bible with over five thousand notes. A study of used textbooks found placemarks, signals, interpretation and problem working, and students sought out well-annotated copies. Support several kinds of mark, not one palette. Highlighting is for returning, notes are for remembering A review of study techniques rated highlighting low for learning, and decades of studies show people remember what they put in their own words. That does not make highlights pointless: they say “come back here”. Offer a note one tap away, never as a requirement. Colour cannot carry the meaning alone Marks, selection, search and read-along highlighting often share the same tint. Give each label a shape (underline, outline, wavy line) and show playback with a different cue, so the reader can tell a saved mark from a moving one without relying on colour. A mark belongs to a translation, a note to the verse A highlight on the BSB’s “Be still!” has no exact match in the KJV’s “Peace, be still.” Keep exact-word marks with their translation and say so when the reader is elsewhere; let bookmarks and notes follow the verse. Notes on Scripture are sensitive Notes record faith, doubt, grief and sin. Under European data law, religious belief is special-category data. Keep notes private by default, make sharing a separate step that names the audience, and label other readers’ notes as theirs, as Glorify’s Public Notes switch begins to do. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Bookmark 2 Highlight 3 Labelled marks 4 Private note 5 Shared note Keeping a place Come back later ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Marking what stood out Quick, the exact words Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Study and teaching Find marks by kind Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Prayer and reflection Private, in my own words ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit Small group Share with known people Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit Reading in greyscale or with a screen reader Marks that are not only colour ● Good fit Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and practice Keeping the word Write it, hide it, ponder it Deuteronomy 6:9; Psalm 119:11; Luke 2:19. Marking and noting are ways of keeping Scripture, not only of studying it. Reading with a pen Edwards’s Blank Bible; annotated textbooks valued by later readers. H Yale University Press R Catherine C. Marshall Learning science What marks do for memory Highlighting is low utility for learning Rated low in a review of ten study techniques. R Dunlosky and colleagues Own words are remembered Information people generate is remembered better than information they read. R Bertsch, Pesta, Wiscott and McDaniel Privacy and access Best practice Religious belief is special-category data Processing needs an Article 9 condition; inferences about belief from behaviour count too. S European Data Protection Board S UK Information Commissioner’s Office How Bible apps handle it Current annotation and plan privacy settings in Olive Tree and YouVersion. S Olive Tree Support S YouVersion Support Not colour alone Colour must not be the only way to tell marks apart. A W3C WAI Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If People mainly want to keep their place Start with A bookmark, one tap, following the verse If People mark what stands out as they read Start with One-tap highlight with undo, attached to the translation If People study and want to find marks again Start with A few labelled marks, each with its own shape If People pray and reflect Start with Private notes on the verse, stored and exported carefully If Groups read together Start with Sharing as a separate step that names the group; others’ notes switchable These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. VSB · Android 17 · Pixel 8 Pro · German interface A selection survives returning from its study sheet Direct Android prototype capture Glorify · iOS app · device model not recorded Other readers’ notes inside the text User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Joseph Prince · iOS app · device model not recorded “Highlight added”, with a route to a note User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged NeuBible (now Mere Bible) · iOS app · device model not recorded Three actions over a selected verse User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded Other readers’ notes related to a verse User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Glorify · iOS app · device model not recorded A public thread under a verse User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Joseph Prince · iOS app · device model not recorded An account asked for at the moment of highlighting User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What keeping the word is for Scripture asks to be kept: written “on the doorposts of your houses” (Deuteronomy 6:9), hidden in the heart (Psalm 119:11), pondered as Mary “treasured up all these things” (Luke 2:19). The blessed person meditates on the law “day and night” (Psalm 1:2). A mark is often a prayer, a question or a promise held onto in a hard week. Where Christians differ Some traditions treat the physical book with great reverence: the Gospel book is carried in procession and kissed, and some believers would not write in a Bible. Others have read with a pen for centuries: Jonathan Edwards filled an interleaved Bible with thousands of notes. Traditions also differ on how personal interpretation relates to the church’s reading (2 Peter 1:20). What follows for design A mark belongs to the reader. Keep it private unless they choose otherwise, let it travel with them if they leave, and never mine it for advertising. Make marks distinguishable from the text itself, so a reader’s note is never mistaken for Scripture. In conversation with Eugene Peterson, Eat This Book (2006) commends lectio divina, dwelling on a short passage until it is taken in; a mark is often the trace of that dwelling. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Life Together (1939) pairs life together with time alone with Scripture: what a reader keeps privately belongs to that time alone. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Notes are public by default to grow a feed, and locked into the app. Ethical Does no harm Keep notes private by default, allow undo, and make every mark readable without colour. Redemptive Gives something up for them Let people export all their notes in an open format and take them elsewhere, giving up lock-in. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review Can someone mark in one tap and undo, tell every mark apart without colour, and say exactly who can see each note? Exercise Ask three readers to mark Mark 4:39 as they would at home, then switch translation and explain where their mark went. Turn the screen to greyscale and repeat. Finally, ask who can see the note they wrote, and check. A mark is a reader’s answer to the text; keep it as carefully as they made it. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further This deep dive brings together 4 earlier patterns. Their guidance, wireframes and sources are kept below; their old addresses lead here. Edge cases to design for Offer a small menu over the selection with one-tap marking and undo; leave labels and organisation for later. Give each kind of mark its own shape, and keep selection, search and playback cues visibly different from saved marks. Attach highlights to the exact words in their translation and say so elsewhere; attach bookmarks and notes to the verse so they follow any translation. Keep notes private by default and treat them as sensitive data. Make sharing a separate step that names the audience and previews what they will see; label other readers’ notes as theirs and let people turn them off. What tends to go wrong A colour picker before every highlight; colour as the only difference between marks; read-along highlighting that looks like a saved mark; highlights silently lost or moved onto different words after switching translation; notes public by default; a “share” that publishes to everyone; others’ notes styled like study notes; inferring mood or belief from marks for analytics. How to test it Mark, undo and re-mark a phrase; repeat with a screen reader and in greyscale. Switch translation and ask where each mark went and why. Play audio over marked verses. Ask people who can see a note they just shared, and compare with the truth. Earlier pattern: The annotation anchor is explicit Make exact wording and reference-based notes different personal objects. Guidance Allow quick marking without forced organisation. Explain whether the annotation targets an exact edition-specific selection or a passage reference. Colours and labels are optional personal conventions. What tends to go wrong Assuming a colour reveals theology or mood; requiring tags before saving; promising exact word transfer across translations. How to test it Can users understand where their note will appear after switching editions? Test unlabelled highlights and annotations across verse ranges. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources Record your insights using Notes Official documentation reviewed · Documentation does not validate all proposed sync or overlap behaviour. Android Annotation Overview Help updated July 2026; reviewed 5 October 2026 · Provider documentation; edition mapping and actual accessibility need separate testing. Earlier pattern: Overlaps remain legible Distinguish playback, selection, search and saved highlights. Guidance Use different visual and accessible cues for transient and saved states. Carry reference-based notes through reliable reference mappings. Keep exact selections attached to their original edition when no word alignment exists. What tends to go wrong Everything represented by background colour; inventing a new selection in another edition; hiding the original annotation when mapping fails. How to test it Combine playback, search and a personal mark on one verse. Switch editions and check that every annotation remains explainable and recoverable. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources Record your insights using Notes Official documentation reviewed · Documentation does not validate all proposed sync or overlap behaviour. EPUB Media Overlays Relevant specification section reviewed · Not proof of a particular Bible app implementation. Understanding Reflow Guidance reviewed · Some content has defined exceptions; test the actual experience. Android Annotation Overview Help updated July 2026; reviewed 5 October 2026 · Provider documentation; edition mapping and actual accessibility need separate testing. Earlier pattern: Mark a passage without interrupting the thought Quick highlighting and deeper organisation can happen at different moments. Guidance Offer a small selection menu with Highlight, Note and More. Apply a sensible last-used or default style with undo. Make style labels and organisation optional, preserve the selection anchor, and provide an accessible selection path beyond long press. What tends to go wrong Marking the wrong range; gesture-only selection; requiring a colour taxonomy; confusing an audio cue with a saved mark; losing marks on edition changes. How to test it Select a range crossing paragraphs, apply and undo a mark, add a note, then switch editions. Check narrow screens, handles near screen edges, keyboard access and save feedback. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources Android Annotation Overview Help updated July 2026; reviewed 5 October 2026 · Provider documentation; edition mapping and actual accessibility need separate testing. Understanding Reflow Official guidance reviewed on 5 October 2026 · Semantic scroll restoration is an original design proposal, not a requirement stated by this criterion. Earlier pattern: Keep my note distinct from a shared comment Origin, audience and anchor belong to the note—not just its screen. Guidance Start personal notes as private. Show the passage or exact-text anchor and save state. Make sharing a separate previewed action with an explicit audience. Keep publisher commentary and AI suggestions visibly separate from the person’s own words. What tends to go wrong A public composer styled like a private journal; changing visibility without confirmation; silent sync failure; quoting someone else’s disclosure into a shared thread. How to test it Create a private note offline, inspect its anchor and preview sharing with a group. Cancel sharing, change edition and find the original note. Check what deletion can and cannot remove from recipients’ copies. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources Android Annotation Overview Help updated July 2026; reviewed 5 October 2026 · Provider documentation; edition mapping and actual accessibility need separate testing. Android: Plan Privacy Official help article reviewed 5 October 2026 · Documented Android behaviour, not a captured or tested flow. Help text may change. Sources and their limits Research-informed design proposal. Editorial review, not user validation. Annotation: from paper books to the digital library Paper reviewed · Textbooks in one university setting; paper, not apps. The Works of Jonathan Edwards, vol. 24: The “Blank Bible” Publisher description reviewed · One exceptional reader. Improving students’ learning with effective learning techniques Summary reviewed · Educational learning outcomes, not devotional reading. The generation effect: a meta-analytic review Abstract reviewed · Laboratory memory tasks, mostly word lists. Process personal data lawfully Official guidance reviewed · Specific lawful basis, retention and DPIA decisions require the actual data flows. What is special category data? Categories and inference guidance reviewed · Context and processing intent matter; not every Bible-page visit automatically establishes a belief. Android Annotation Overview Help updated July 2026; reviewed 5 October 2026 · Provider documentation; edition mapping and actual accessibility need separate testing. Android: Plan Privacy Official help article reviewed 5 October 2026 · Documented Android behaviour, not a captured or tested flow. Help text may change. Understanding Use of Color Guidance reviewed · Accessibility guidance. Faith and interpretation Scripture asks to be kept, not only read: “Write them on the doorposts of your houses” (Deuteronomy 6:9); “I have hidden Your word in my heart” (Psalm 119:11); Mary “treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart” (Luke 2:19). Christians have long read with a pen: Jonathan Edwards filled an interleaved Bible with over five thousand notes across three decades. A mark is often a prayer or a question, and belongs to the reader. Keep exploring Related patterns Translations → Numbers, headings and notes → Bible audio → Progress and streaks →

pages.title: How much text at once
pages.description: One word, a verse, a passage or a whole chapter? Five options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns How much text at once One word, a verse, a passage or a whole chapter? People increasingly read Scripture on phones, in short and frequent sessions. Apps answer with verse cards, focus modes, read-along highlighting and even speed readers. Each decides how much of the Bible someone holds in mind at once, from a single word to a whole chapter. The church has read in many measures. An app should help people hear the word, not just get through it. 5 working options 6 app examples 5 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested How much text at once At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From one word to a whole chapter Less text at once More text at once 1 One word at a time Borrowed + Total focus, no lost place − No looking back Try it → 2 One verse at a time Observed + Slow, meditative, memorable − Context out of sight Try it → 3 One verse in focus Observed + Attention with context − Moving text needs control Try it → 4 One passage Observed + A natural beginning and end − Boundaries are editorial Try it → 5 Whole chapter Familiar convention + The story stays whole − Long on a phone Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try five amounts of text Someone has a few minutes before work and opens Mark 4 at the storm on the sea (4:35–41). Every option starts there, in the Berean Standard Bible. Read to the end of the passage, then try to find what Jesus was doing just before. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. One word at a time · Borrowed 2. One verse at a time · Observed 3. One verse in focus · Observed 4. One passage · Observed 5. Whole chapter · Familiar convention Option 1 One word at a time Borrowed 2 One verse at a time Observed 3 One verse in focus Observed 4 One passage Observed 5 Whole chapter Familiar convention Verse numbers Not used here Show Hide Read aloud Not used here Off On (simulated) Why these settings? Verse numbers are a sixteenth-century addition: helpful for finding and citing, and a reason people read sentences apart from their argument. Hiding them gives a reader’s-edition feel. Read-aloud is simulated: nothing plays, but the focus or highlight moves at about 180 words a minute, as it would with narration. One word at a time has its own speed control and ignores both settings. Borrowed 1. One word at a time Borrowed from speed-reading tools such as Spritz and Kindle Word Runner, which flash one word at a time at a chosen speed. Try this Press Start at 250 words a minute. Halfway through, try to look back at what the disciples said. + Makes easier No eye movement and no lost place; it can feel fast and very focused for short, familiar text. − Costs You cannot glance back, and readers reread 10–15% of the time; comprehension tends to drop. It also turns Scripture into a speed. Ask your team Is there any reading in your product that should be faster rather than slower? Observed 2. One verse at a time Observed in Glorify, which steps through a short passage one verse per screen with a segmented bar (see the screenshots below). Try this Step through to the end of the passage. Then switch on Context and see the verses either side. + Makes easier An easy start and a slow pace that suits meditation and memory. Each verse gets the whole screen. − Costs The chapter is out of sight, and a lone verse is easy to read or share apart from its setting. Ask your team How far is every verse from its context, and how does someone get there? Observed 3. One verse in focus Observed in Dwell and Soultime during listening (current verse bright, the rest dimmed or hidden); borrowed from iA Writer’s focus mode and karaoke captions. Try this Move through with Next verse, then tap a verse further up. Switch on read-aloud and press play. + Makes easier Attention on one verse with the passage still in view; with audio it keeps reader and narrator together. − Costs Dimmed text must stay readable and reachable for screen readers, and moving text needs a pause. Ask your team Will the focus follow the reader, the narrator, or both? Observed 4. One passage Observed in Glorify’s passage readings (Judges 6:11–16 with its own audio); lectionaries, plans and sermons also assign passages. Titles here are our own. Try this Read the passage, then open “Before this” to see the parable that comes first. + Makes easier A clear beginning and end, the unit sermons and study guides use, and the neighbouring passages one tap away. − Costs Where a passage begins and ends, and what it is called, are editorial decisions. Some readers will want the whole chapter. Ask your team Who sets the passage boundaries and titles, and how will readers know? Familiar convention 5. Whole chapter A familiar convention in Bible apps and e-books; reader’s editions such as the ESV Reader’s Bible remove numbers and headings for longer reading. Try this Scroll up from where you stopped to the sower, then switch verse numbers off for a reader’s edition. + Makes easier The argument and story stay whole; the best fit for reading a book through. − Costs Long on a phone, and one verse is harder to hold in mind. Headings and numbers shape the reading as much as they help. Ask your team Do your readers mostly read through, or dip in? i The example contains Mark 4 only, in the Berean Standard Bible. Passage titles are our own editorial labels. Timing is simulated. Real implementations also need text size, contrast, screen-reader and reduced-motion testing. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Phones invite shorter, more selective reading Screen reading involves more scanning, keyword spotting and selective reading, and less sustained reading (Liu). Comprehension on screens falls behind paper mainly under time pressure, not when people read at their own pace (Delgado et al.). Dyer found app readers completed more days of a plan, while men understood less than in print. Smaller units fit the sessions; they do not guarantee understanding. One word at a time removes looking back Readers look back at earlier words 10–15% of the time, and taking that away tends to reduce comprehension (Rayner et al.). For Scripture, which rewards rereading, it is the weakest fit; it also invites reading as a speed. If you offer it, keep it for short, familiar text, with a rewind. A smaller unit has a long devotional history Lectio divina reads a few verses slowly and repeatedly. A verse at a time, or a verse in focus, can support that kind of attention and memorisation, as long as the passage is one tap away. Verse numbers date from 1551; a verse was never meant to stand alone. Focus with context is the middle path A highlighted verse with the passage dimmed around it keeps attention and context together, and works best with audio: read-along highlighting helped children with dyslexia follow, and karaoke-style subtitles have supported literacy at scale. Let readers choose the window, as Immersive Reader does with one, three or five lines. Passage and chapter carry the argument A passage gives a reading its natural shape, the unit preachers and plans use, but its boundaries and titles are editorial. Reader’s editions such as the ESV Reader’s Bible remove numbers and headings so people read longer and follow the story. Make the longer mode calm and easy to enter, and keep the reader’s place across modes. Use cases Which reading, which unit? People read Scripture for different reasons, sometimes in the same week. Each reason fits some points on the spectrum better than others. How well each option fits each reading Reading Needs 1 One word at a time 2 One verse at a time 3 One verse in focus 4 One passage 5 Whole chapter Finding or checking a verse The verse, in its passage Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit Skimming for a theme Headings and boundaries to jump between Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit A daily reading or devotional A clear beginning and end Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible Meditation and lectio divina Slowness, repetition, room to pause Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Memorising a verse Recall, not rereading ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Listening along Text that follows the voice, with pause Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Study or preparing to teach Context, cross-reference, notes Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit Reading a book through Continuity and a kept place Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition How the church has read Read aloud, together, and whole Israel heard the law read publicly: “they read from the Book of the Law of God, explaining it and giving insight” (Nehemiah 8:8). Paul’s letters were read aloud to whole congregations, “after this letter has been read among you” (Colossians 4:16), and Timothy is told, “devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture” (1 Timothy 4:13). For most of Christian history, Scripture was heard in continuous portions. Silent, private reading came later Augustine was struck that Ambrose read with his eyes on the page and his voice silent. Personal reading spread with literacy, printing and vernacular Bibles. A phone continues that private line, and can also reconnect people with reading aloud and together. H Translation and commentary at Sententiae Antiquae Small units for prayer and memory “I have hidden Your word in my heart” (Psalm 119:11). Lectio divina dwells on a few verses read slowly and repeatedly; memorisation works verse by verse. Small units are not a modern shortcut; they have their own devotional history. T University of St Andrews, School of Divinity Context guards meaning Chapter divisions date from the thirteenth century and verse numbers from 1551. Fee and Stuart’s principle, that a text cannot mean what it could never have meant for its first readers, depends on reading a verse within its passage, book and genre. T Zondervan, 4th edition 2014 (quotations listing) Digital reading today What people actually do Most Bible reading is now on screens Two-thirds of US Bible users access the Bible digitally. YouVersion reports over a billion installs and named Isaiah 41:10 its most engaged-with verse of 2025, the fourth time in six years: much digital engagement happens one verse at a time. R American Bible Society D ChurchLeaders, reporting YouVersion Screen reading is more selective People report more browsing, scanning, keyword spotting and one-time reading on screens, and less concentrated reading (Liu). Hutchings shows Bible apps are designed to train particular reading habits. R Ziming Liu R Tim Hutchings Completion is not comprehension In Dyer’s church study, app readers finished about two more days of a ten-day plan than print readers, while men understood less on screen. A unit that is easy to finish may not be the one that is understood. R John Dyer Reading science Different readings, different needs Normal reading is about 240 words a minute Adults read non-fiction at about 238 words a minute, most between 175 and 300. The storm on the sea takes about a minute to read: short enough for any morning. R Marc Brysbaert Skimming finds, deep reading understands Skimmers jump ahead once a section stops paying off; they catch the main points but understand less. Speed-reading displays remove the looking back that comprehension relies on. R Duggan and Payne R Rayner, Schotter, Masson, Potter and Treiman Listening is reading too One study found no difference in comprehension between reading, listening, and doing both. Read-along modes serve people who listen as much as people who read. R Rogowsky, Calhoun and Tallal R International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning Memory grows by recall Students who practised recalling a passage remembered 61% a week later; those who reread it remembered 40%. A verse-at-a-time mode for memorisation should ask, not just show. R Roediger and Karpicke Pace matters more than medium Screens fall behind paper mainly when people read under time pressure. Let readers set the pace. R Delgado, Vargas, Ackerman and Salmerón Accessible reading Best practice Anything that moves needs a pause Content that moves or updates for more than five seconds needs a way to pause, stop or hide it: auto-advancing verses, read-along and word-by-word display all qualify. A W3C Measure, spacing and size Aim for lines under 80 characters, line spacing of at least 1.5, unjustified text and resizing to 200% without sideways scrolling. A W3C Let readers choose the window Immersive Reader lets people focus on one, three or five lines. Offer the size of the focus as a setting, and respect reduced motion. D Microsoft Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If Meditation, prayer or memorising a short passage Start with One verse at a time, or a verse in focus, with the passage one tap away If Listening while reading, or readers who lose their place Start with A verse in focus that follows the audio, with pause and rewind If A daily reading, devotional or group study Start with One passage with its reference, neighbours and a way into the chapter If Reading a book through, narrative or argument Start with The whole chapter, with an option to hide numbers and headings If Speed, skimming or “getting through it” Start with Leave single-word display out for Scripture study These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. Lumen Bible · Desktop web · English interface Phrase-grouped text inside a chapter reader Direct signed-out web capture Glorify · iOS app · device model not recorded One verse per screen, with a step bar User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Soultime · iOS app · device model not recorded A single verse isolated during playback User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Dwell · iOS app · device model not recorded The current verse bright, the rest dimmed User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Glorify · iOS app · device model not recorded One passage with its own audio User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded A chapter with section headings and verse ranges User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What attention is for Mary “sat at the Lord’s feet listening to His message” (Luke 10:39), and Jesus said she had chosen the good part. Lectio divina dwells on a few verses slowly; reading a whole letter at once shows its argument. Both are forms of attention, and attention is a form of love. Where Christians differ Devotional traditions favour short passages for meditation and memory. Biblical scholars and many teachers urge reading whole books, warning that verse numbers invite reading sentences apart from their context. Silent private reading, which Augustine found remarkable in Ambrose, is itself a later development beside public reading aloud. What follows for design The question is not which unit is more spiritual, but whether the screen keeps a verse connected to its passage and leaves the reader’s attention free. Design for the reader to finish, put the phone down and live what they read (James 1:22). In conversation with Albert Borgmann, Technology and the Character of Contemporary Life (1984) contrasted “focal practices” that ask for attention and skill with devices that deliver commodities effortlessly; reading Scripture is a focal practice a device can support or displace. Eugene Peterson, Eat This Book (2006) calls for slow, attentive reading in which the text is taken in, not skimmed. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person A feed, badges and notifications compete with the passage for attention. Ethical Does no harm Offer focus settings and respect the system’s accessibility preferences. Redemptive Gives something up for them Design for the reader to finish and close the app, and measure success by that. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review What unit of Scripture does this screen ask someone to hold in mind, and how do they reach the rest? Exercise Ask two people to read Mark 4:35–41 in different modes, then retell it and say what Jesus was doing just before. Time how long it takes each to find the verse before 4:35. Repeat with a screen reader and with reduced motion switched on. Choose the unit that helps someone hear the word, not the one that helps them finish. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further This deep dive brings together 1 earlier patterns. Their guidance, wireframes and sources are kept below; their old addresses lead here. Edge cases to design for Decide which reading this screen serves. For meditation or memory, show a verse at a time or a verse in focus with the passage dimmed around it. For listening, move the focus with the audio. For a daily reading, show one passage with its reference, what comes before and after, and a way into the chapter. For a book read through, offer calm long-form text. Keep the same place when someone changes mode, and never strand a verse without a route to its context. What tends to go wrong A verse shown alone with no way to its chapter; editorial headings presented as Scripture; word-by-word display used for study; auto-advancing text with no pause or rewind; focus modes that hide the text from screen readers; losing the reader’s place when switching modes. How to test it Ask people to read the same passage in two modes, then retell it and answer a question that depends on the verse before. Time how long it takes to find the context of a single verse. Test focus and read-along with screen readers, reduced motion and people with dyslexia or attention difficulties. Earlier pattern: A bounded passage with a route to wider context Choose the reading unit by the task while keeping its boundaries and context visible. Guidance Present the full chosen passage, its reference and edition. Explain editorial headings and passage boundaries. Offer preceding and following context and continuous reading without losing the original selection. What tends to go wrong Clipping a passage without notice; treating one boundary as universal across editions; replacing source text with an AI summary; making context available only through chat. How to test it Compare focused and continuous layouts for orientation, comprehension, voluntary rereading and context access. Include poetry and passages crossing chapter boundaries. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources The Habits and Hermeneutics of Digital Bible Readers Published abstract reviewed; author discussion reviewed separately · Population and study context limit transfer. Abstract-level review does not establish causal effects or a preferred passage length. How Digital Apps Are Changing How We Read the Bible Author’s public account reviewed · An author summary of research, not an independent replication; it does not test pericope pages. Aperto passage-centred design direction Local passage model reviewed; design rationale documented as a hypothesis · Neither this architecture nor the product direction establishes a measured improvement in comprehension or formation. AI podcast behaviour was not independently exercised. Scripture structure documentation Relevant structure and marker references reviewed · A format is not a complete model of app behaviour, annotations or formation. Digital Spiritual Formation: The Aperto Vision · selected Draft 4 review Selected sections on reading, engagement, multimodal and communal formation, incentives and honest assessment reviewed 5 October 2026 · Not an effectiveness study. Full bibliography and manuscript are not published or comprehensively reviewed here. Sources and their limits Research-informed design proposal. Editorial review, not user validation. Reading behavior in the digital environment Abstract reviewed · A 2005 survey of readers about their own habits; describes reported behaviour, not comprehension. Don’t throw away your printed books: a meta-analysis on the effects of reading media on reading comprehension Meta-analysis abstract and summary reviewed · Studies of general texts, mostly before current phone reading apps; not Scripture. So much to read, so little time: how do we read, and can speed reading help? Review summary reviewed · Review of reading research; not specific to devotional reading. The habits and hermeneutics of digital Bible readers News summary reviewed; article not reviewed in full · Small sample from three Dallas churches; reported through a news summary. How many words do we read per minute? A review and meta-analysis of reading rate Summary reviewed · English readers; slower for children, older adults and second-language readers. Does modality matter? The effects of reading, listening, and dual modality on comprehension Report reviewed · One nonfiction text with adult readers; other studies find differences for harder texts. Skim reading by satisficing: evidence from eye tracking Abstract reviewed · Expository texts in a lab under time pressure. Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention Review reviewed · Prose passages with students; not Scripture memorisation specifically. State of the Bible USA 2025 Report summary reviewed · US survey by a Bible society; self-reported. YouVersion announces 2025 Verse of the Year News report reviewed · Company-reported figures; “engaged with” is YouVersion’s own measure. Augustine, Confessions 6.3, on Ambrose reading silently Passage reviewed in translation · How unusual silent reading was in antiquity is debated by historians. Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth Book quotations reviewed · A widely used evangelical introduction to interpretation; one approach among several. ESV Reader’s Bible Publisher description reviewed · Publisher’s rationale, not a study of its effects. Introduction to lectio divina Article reviewed · A description of practice, not a study. Understanding SC 2.2.2: Pause, Stop, Hide Specification guidance reviewed · A Level A criterion for web content; apply the same intent in native apps. Understanding SC 1.4.8: Visual Presentation Specification guidance reviewed · Level AAA; a strong target rather than a minimum. Focus Mode Support documentation reviewed · A writing tool; the reader’s situation differs. Use Line focus in Immersive Reader Support documentation reviewed · Vendor documentation, not an outcome study. Effects of highlighting text on the reading ability of children with developmental dyslexia: a pilot study Abstract reviewed · Small pilot study. Same language subtitling Article reviewed · Reported programme results; a literacy setting, not Scripture reading. Amazon’s tool for reading, one word at a time News report reviewed · Feature report from 2015; availability may have changed. Maryanne Wolf: building deep reading skills in a digital world Article reviewed · An argument drawing on neuroscience, not a controlled trial of interfaces. Design and the digital Bible: persuasive technology and religious reading Abstract reviewed · Design analysis of two apps; not a study of readers. Faith and interpretation Verse numbers date from the sixteenth century and chapter divisions from the thirteenth; neither is part of the inspired text, and both make it easy to read a sentence apart from its argument. Smaller units also have a long devotional history: lectio divina dwells on a few verses read slowly and repeatedly. The question is not which unit is more spiritual, but whether the screen keeps the verse connected to the passage it belongs to.
