pages.title: Notifications and reminders
pages.description: When may a faith app interrupt someone, in whose voice, and who decides? Seven options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Notifications and reminders When may a faith app interrupt someone, in whose voice, and who decides? “Morning, noon, and night, I cry out in distress, and He hears my voice” (Psalm 55:17). For centuries a bell has called Christians to prayer at shared hours. Now a phone beside the bed can call them at any hour, about anything, in any voice: a reminder they set, a verse of the day, a friend who prayed for them, a countdown on a streak, or an AI companion that says it has been thinking about them. Notifications are the strongest tool an app has to bring people back, and the most intimate. Most of the time a reminder helps someone keep a practice they want to keep. Design also for the person who has been away for weeks, and for the one who is awake at 2 am. Draft · waiting for review What needs review: What reaches someone awake at night, the help offered when they open the app, the warning case of an AI persona and an app that tells friends, and the use of the church’s hours. This touches the safety of people who may already be hurting, and it has not yet been reviewed by people whose work this is: crisis support and suicide prevention; pastoral care; and theology across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions. Please read it as a draft until they have. Is this your field, or do you know someone whose field it is? I would be grateful for your eyes on it, or for an introduction. Offer a review or an introduction 7 working options 7 app examples 7 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Notifications At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From the person’s choice to the app’s The person decides The app decides 1 The app waits Familiar convention + Nothing interrupts − Nothing calls them back Try it → 2 Their own bell Observed + Their days, time and words − Needs setting up Try it → 3 The church’s hours Familiar convention + A rhythm shared with others − A fixed time may not fit Try it → 4 A daily word Observed + A small daily start − Piles up when unwanted Try it → 5 People, not the app Observed + Carries what someone did − Quiet without friends Try it → 6 Engagement-driven Observed + More people come back − Urgency as a tool Try it → 7 Messages about the person Leave it out + Feels personal − A persona pleads and guesses Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try seven ways a faith app can call someone The same faith app, seven ways of sending notifications. Choose who is holding the phone: someone who installed it yesterday, someone who opens it most days, someone who has been away for three weeks, or someone awake at 2 am. Then choose what their phone does: show everything on the lock screen, collect it in a Scheduled Summary at 8:00, or keep Sleep Focus until 7:45. Look at the lock screen now, what the app sent this week, and the settings it offers. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. The app waits · Familiar convention 2. Their own bell · Observed 3. The church’s hours · Familiar convention 4. A daily word · Observed 5. People, not the app · Observed 6. Engagement-driven · Observed 7. Messages about the person · Leave it out Option 1 The app waits Familiar convention 2 Their own bell Observed 3 The church’s hours Familiar convention 4 A daily word Observed 5 People, not the app Observed 6 Engagement-driven Observed 7 Messages about the person Leave it out Person Not used here Most days Just installed Away three weeks Awake at 2 am Phone Not used here Lock screen Scheduled Summary Sleep Focus Why these settings? The Scheduled Summary arrives at 8:00 and Sleep Focus lasts until 7:45, so at 7:30 and at 2:07 both hold back ordinary notifications; anything marked Time Sensitive breaks through. Someone awake at 2 am sees what the app sent overnight, and opening the app at night offers TelefonSeelsorge, whose numbers are from its own website, checked 11 October 2026. Familiar convention 1. The app waits Familiar from Bibles on the web and from widgets: Bible Widgets (118K ratings) puts verses on the lock and home screens, “turning every phone unlock into a moment of connection with God”, and Bible Chat and Universalis offer widgets too; see their store listings. The widget here is written for this example. Try this Look at the lock screen as each person. Then check what was sent this week. + Makes easier Nothing interrupts; Scripture is there when someone looks. − Costs Nothing calls anyone back, and some people want to be called. Ask your team Who would miss a reminder, and could they set one themselves? Observed 2. Their own bell Observed in ESV’s “Remind me on these days.”, Glorify’s wake-up and wind-down times and Joseph Prince’s “Set a schedule”, each asking for permission when the reminder is set; see the screenshots below. The question after seven unopened reminders is a proposal. Try this Try someone new, then someone away for three weeks. + Makes easier The person chooses the days, the time and the words. − Costs It needs setting up, and a reminder still interrupts. Ask your team What happens when the reminders stop being opened? Familiar convention 3. The church’s hours Familiar from church bells and the Angelus, prayed “three times each day, morning, noon, and evening, at the sound of the bell”, and from the Liturgy of the Hours; documented in Hallow’s Angelus and Universalis’s “reminders and alarms”. Sending the hours as shared notifications is a proposal; the wording here is written for this example. Try this Try each person, and then Sleep Focus. + Makes easier A shared rhythm, kept by others at the same hour. − Costs A fixed time may not fit someone’s day. Ask your team Which hours would your community actually keep together? Observed 4. A daily word Observed in daily verse notifications such as YouVersion’s Verse of the Day, and documented in Blessed’s “evening Scripture and prayer prompt … even in the dark”; see the store listing. The verse and times here are written for this example. Try this Try someone who opens it most days, then someone away for three weeks. + Makes easier A small, predictable start to the day. − Costs It arrives whether or not it is wanted, and piles up. Ask your team Is it still a gift on the twenty-first unopened day? Observed 5. People, not the app Observed in YouVersion’s notifications list and documented in Echo Prayer, which lets someone “send out a notification to let them know you’ve prayed”; see the screenshot and store listing below. Holding messages at night is a proposal; the names and messages are written for this example. Try this Try someone new, then someone awake at night. + Makes easier Every notification carries something a person did. − Costs Quiet for someone with no friends in the app. Ask your team Does the person sharing know their prayer becomes someone’s notification? Observed 6. Engagement-driven Observed in Pray.com’s Community Board, which lists “Active Streakers” to praise and friends to “Remind”; see the screenshot below. Duolingo tuned the wording of “millions of daily reminders” for return. The streak warnings, offers and Time Sensitive marking here are written for this example to show the pattern. Try this Try someone away for three weeks, then turn on Sleep Focus. + Makes easier More people come back, at least for a while. − Costs Prayer becomes a habit to sell, and urgency a tool. Ask your team Who is this notification for: the person, or the app’s numbers? Leave it out 7. Messages about the person A warning case. Soultime with Friends “discreetly nudges your friends automatically when we think you might need a call”; see the screenshot below. Companion apps answer goodbyes with guilt and fear-of-missing-out hooks in 37% of farewells, researchers found. The AI messages here are written for this example; they were not observed in a faith app. Try this Try someone away for three weeks, then someone awake at 2 am. + Makes easier It feels personal, and it brings people back. − Costs A persona pleads and guesses, and friends are told without asking. Ask your team Would you send this in your own name, as a person, to someone you know? i The app, the persona “Grace”, the names and every message were written for this example. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. Nothing is saved or sent. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Ask when someone sets a reminder Spark Bible asks for notifications before the first verse; ESV and Joseph Prince ask when someone sets a reminder. The second gives people a reason to say yes. First use → Let the person choose the days, the time and the words A reminder in someone’s own words, on their days, is their bell, not the app’s. Offer the church’s hours Morning, midday and night prayer, shared with others who pray at those hours, are an old answer to the question of when to call people. Three predictable moments are also what the research on batching found easiest to live with. Mark nothing urgent that is not A reading, a verse or an offer is never Time Sensitive. Let Scheduled Summary and Focus do their work; a streak warning that breaks through Sleep Focus at 23:50 breaks trust. Progress and streaks → After silence, ask once, then stop When reminders go unopened, ask whether to keep them, change the time or pause them, and then be quiet. Never count what was missed, and never write “we miss you”. Reading plans → Keep quiet hours Send nothing from late evening to morning unless the person chose it, and when someone opens the app at night, put help within reach. No persona writes first An AI that says it has been thinking about someone, asks “Did I say something wrong?” or tells their friends they might need a call is using a voice that is not a person’s to bring them back. Leave it out. AI persona → Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 The app waits 2 Their own bell 3 The church’s hours 4 A daily word 5 People, not the app 6 Engagement-driven 7 Messages about the person Someone who wants to read each morning A reminder at their time, in their words Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit A parish that prays the hours The same bell for everyone who chose it Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Someone who comes when they choose Nothing that interrupts ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit A small group praying for each other Word when someone prayed for them Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Someone away for three weeks One question, then quiet; nothing about what they missed ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Someone awake at 2 am Silence at night, and help when they open the app ● Good fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition Called at the hours, and left alone at night Morning, noon and night “Morning, noon, and night, I cry out in distress, and He hears my voice” (Psalm 55:17); Daniel prayed “three times a day” (Daniel 6:10). The Angelus is prayed “three times each day, morning, noon, and evening, at the sound of the bell”, and began with the evening bell. S Herbert Thurston The signal is a responsibility In Benedict’s Rule, “as soon as the signal is heard, let them abandon whatever they may have in hand”; so the signal “by day and by night shall devolve upon the Abbot”. Whoever rings the bell answers for it. The same Rule asks for silence “especially during the hours of the night”. S Benedict of Nursia, sixth century A still, small voice God was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in “a still, small voice” (1 Kings 19:12). When the disciples found Jesus praying alone and said, “Everyone is looking for You!”, he went on instead of going back (Mark 1:37–38). Not every call needs answering. Platforms and research What the phone allows, and what notifications do Urgency is a promise Apple’s guidelines define four interruption levels and ask apps to “Build trust by accurately representing the urgency of each notification”: “Never use the Time Sensitive interruption level to send a marketing notification.” Apple’s review rules allow marketing by push only if “customers have explicitly opted in to receive them via consent language displayed in your app’s UI”. S Apple S Apple Ask when they set a reminder Android’s guidance: “Before you ask users to grant any permissions, let them familiarize themselves with your app”; a good moment is when “The user taps an "alert bell" button.” S Android Developers Three times a day In a field experiment with 237 people, those whose notifications were “batched three-times-a-day felt more attentive, productive, in a better mood, and in greater control of their phones”. Those with no notifications at all “experienced higher levels of anxiety and “fear of missing out” (FoMO)”. R Nicholas Fitz, Kostadin Kushlev, Ranjan Jagannathan, Terrel Lewis, Devang Paliwal and Dan Ariely Tuned for return Duolingo used an algorithm to “optimize millions of daily reminders”, which led “to a 0.5 % increase in total daily active users (DAUs) and a 2 % increase in new user retention”. The measure is use. R Kevin P. Yancey and Burr Settles, Duolingo A persona that will not let go Companion apps answered goodbyes with guilt, fear-of-missing-out hooks and similar tactics in 37% of 1,200 real farewells; in experiments, such replies raised engagement “by up to 14×”, driven by “reactance-based anger and curiosity—rather than enjoyment”. The EU asks platforms to switch off push notifications for minors by default. R Julian De Freitas, Zeliha Oğuz-Uğuralp and Ahmet Kaan-Uğuralp S European Commission Products What faith apps send Widgets instead of interruptions Bible Widgets (118K ratings, #8 in Reference) puts verses on the lock screen, “turning every phone unlock into a moment of connection with God”; Bible Chat, #1 in Reference, offers a verse widget and a “Send a Blessing Widget”. S Monkey Taps S Book Vitals Reminders shaped by a practice Intercede sends “timely, gentle reminders that ensure you never miss a day of your novena prayers”; Universalis offers “reminders and alarms” for the hours; Hallow includes the “Angelus” and the “Ability to set prayer reminders”. S Devoted Coders S Universalis Publishing S Hallow A word in the evening Blessed sends “a fresh evening Scripture and prayer prompt to quiet your mind, restore your heart, and remind you of God’s presence — even in the dark”, and also offers to “track your prayer streak”. S Everblessed Technology What people did Echo Prayer lets someone “send out a notification to let them know you’ve prayed for their shared prayer”. S The Parable Group Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If A reading or prayer habit Start with Their own bell: a reminder they set, asked for when they set it If A parish or a liturgical app Start with The church’s hours, chosen at setup, with silence at night If A group praying for each other Start with People, not the app: word when someone prayed or invited If A Bible reader with no reminders Start with The app waits, with a widget for those who want one If You are tempted to add streak warnings, “we miss you” or AI messages Start with Don’t: ask once whether to keep reminding, then stop These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded A friend’s new prayer among badges and friendships User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Spark Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded A notification prompt before the first verse User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Pray.com · iOS app · device model not recorded “Active Streakers” to praise, and friends to “Remind” User-contributed screenshot · resized; names and photos of other users blurred Soultime · iOS app · device model not recorded Friends notified automatically “when we think you might need a call” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged ESV Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded Permission asked when a reminder is set User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Glorify · iOS app · device model not recorded “Wake up” and “Wind down” reminders User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Joseph Prince · iOS app · device model not recorded A notification request over “Set a schedule” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What a call to prayer is for “Morning, noon, and night, I cry out in distress, and He hears my voice” (Psalm 55:17). Daniel kept his hours “three times a day”, “just as he had done before” (Daniel 6:10), and the church has rung bells for morning, noon and evening prayer for centuries. A call to prayer is an invitation into something others are doing too; it is answered freely, and whoever rings the bell answers for it. Where Christians differ Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican Christians keep set hours, the Angelus and the Daily Office; many evangelicals keep a personal quiet time at an hour they choose; Reformed and Pietist traditions warn against mistaking regular habits for faith. Some find a daily reminder a help to a practice they love; others find that any reminder turns prayer into a task. Scripture holds both: Daniel’s fixed hours, and Jesus going out “while it was still dark” (Mark 1:35) and not going back when he was told, “Everyone is looking for You!” What follows for design Let the person, or the church’s shared hours, decide when the phone calls. Speak in “a still, small voice” (1 Kings 19:12): no urgency that is not real, no counting of what was missed, no persona writing first. Keep the night quiet, and when someone stops answering, ask once and let them go. In conversation with James K. A. Smith, You Are What You Love (2016) argues that habits are “liturgies” that train what we love; a daily notification is a small liturgy, and it teaches whether prayer is a gift or a task. Albert Borgmann, Technology and the Character of Contemporary Life (1984) urged that technology support focal practices rather than replace them with commodities; a reminder should lead into the practice and then get out of the way. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Ask for notifications before the first verse, count down streaks marked Time Sensitive, send more the longer someone is away, put offers in the reminder’s place, and let an AI persona write first. Ethical Does no harm Ask when someone sets a reminder, let them choose days, time and words, keep marketing out unless they opted in, mark nothing urgent that is not, and keep quiet hours. Redemptive Gives something up for them Call people at the church’s hours or their own, in a still, small voice; after silence ask once and then stop; and give up the returning users that urgency, guilt and a persona’s voice would bring. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review Who chose this interruption, how urgent does it claim to be, and what does it say to someone who has stopped coming? Exercise Install your app on a test phone, allow notifications, use it once and leave it for two weeks. Log every notification: time, words, interruption level and who chose it. Turn on Sleep Focus and a Scheduled Summary and see what breaks through. Then read every notification aloud as someone who is grieving, depressed or awake at 2 am, and ask whether you would send it in your own name to a friend. Call people as the church’s bell does, at hours they chose, in a still, small voice; never with urgency, guilt or a voice that is not a person’s. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further Edge cases to design for Start with the person’s own choice. Ask for permission when someone sets a reminder, not before the first verse, and let them choose the days, the time and the words. Offer the church’s hours, morning, midday and evening, as a rhythm others keep too. Notify for what people did, a prayer said for them, an invitation, not for what the app wants. Mark nothing Time Sensitive that is not, keep quiet hours, and let the phone’s summary and Focus do their work. When someone stops opening the app, ask once whether to keep reminding them, then stop. What tends to go wrong A permission prompt before the first verse; “Your 12-day streak ends at midnight!” marked Time Sensitive to break through Sleep Focus; reminders that multiply after silence; “We miss you” and “Did I say something wrong?” in the voice of an app or an AI; reminders to friends who stopped; telling someone’s friends that the app thinks they need a call; marketing offers in the prayer reminder’s place. How to test it Install the app on a test phone, allow notifications, use it once and leave it for two weeks. Log every notification: time, words, urgency and who chose it. Then turn on Sleep Focus and a Scheduled Summary and see what breaks through. Finally, read every notification as someone who is grieving, depressed or awake at 2 am would read it. Faith and interpretation “Morning, noon, and night, I cry out in distress, and He hears my voice” (Psalm 55:17). Daniel prayed “three times a day” (Daniel 6:10), and the Psalmist “Seven times a day” (Psalm 119:164); the church has rung bells for its hours ever since. But when the disciples found Jesus praying alone and said, “Everyone is looking for You!”, he did not go back (Mark 1:37–38). God spoke to Elijah not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in “a still, small voice” (1 Kings 19:12). pages.title: Numbers, headings and notes
pages.description: How much should surround the text? Seven options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Numbers, headings and notes How much should surround the text? Almost nothing around the words of the Bible is part of them. Verse numbers, chapter breaks, section titles, red letters, footnotes, study notes and now teaching videos were added by printers, translators and editors over centuries. Each helps someone find, follow or understand, and each quietly teaches them how to read. Whoever adds to the page today joins a long line of printers and editors, and shares their responsibility. 7 working options 7 app examples 6 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Numbers, headings and notes At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From the bare text to inline media Less around the text More around the text 1 Reader’s edition Familiar convention + Reads as continuous writing − Hard to find or cite Try it → 2 Verse numbers Familiar convention + Easy to find and follow − Small breaks everywhere Try it → 3 Section titles Observed + Orientation at a glance − Titles interpret Try it → 4 Note markers Observed + Help one tap away − Invites detours Try it → 5 Study layout Familiar convention + Context where questions arise − Borrowed authority Try it → 6 Inline media Observed + Teaching at the verse − Extras crowd the text Try it → 7 Reader decides Observed + Each reader sets it − Defaults still decide Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try seven reading layouts The same passage, Mark 4:30–41 in the Berean Standard Bible, with more or less around it. Read the storm on the sea in each option, open a note and come back, then try the reading settings in the last option. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Reader’s edition · Familiar convention 2. Verse numbers · Familiar convention 3. Section titles · Observed 4. Note markers · Observed 5. Study layout · Familiar convention 6. Inline media · Observed 7. Reader decides · Observed Option 1 Reader’s edition Familiar convention 2 Verse numbers Familiar convention 3 Section titles Observed 4 Note markers Observed 5 Study layout Familiar convention 6 Inline media Observed 7 Reader decides Observed Layout Not used here Paragraphs Verse per line Words of Jesus Not used here Plain In red Why these settings? Verse per line was the norm in printed Bibles for centuries and is still common in apps; paragraphs follow the sense of the text. Red letters were introduced in 1899 by Louis Klopsch. Both are editorial choices that sit alongside the six options, and in “Reader decides” they can also be changed in the drawer. Familiar convention 1. Reader’s edition Familiar from print reader’s editions such as the ESV Reader’s Bible and Biblica’s The Books of the Bible, which remove numbers, headings and notes. Try this Read from the mustard seed to the end of the storm. Then try to tell someone where “Be still!” is. + Makes easier The text reads as continuous writing; nothing interrupts, and nothing suggests reading sentence by sentence. − Costs Harder to find or cite a verse, or to follow a preacher who says “verse 39”. Ask your team Is reading through, or finding and citing, the main job here? Familiar convention 2. Verse numbers The default in almost every Bible app; verse numbers date from Estienne’s 1551 Greek New Testament. Try this Find verse 39. Then switch to one verse per line in the settings. + Makes easier Easy to find, cite and follow along in church or a group. − Costs Each number is a small break; text can start to read as a list of separate sayings. Ask your team How light can the numbers be while still easy to find? Observed 3. Section titles Observed in YouVersion and Bible.is, where translation editors’ titles and verse ranges head each section (see the screenshots below). Titles here are our own. Try this Skim for the storm. Then read the title and ask whether it says anything the text does not. + Makes easier Orientation at a glance, and better memory for how a chapter is organised. − Costs Titles interpret. “The storm on the sea” or “Jesus calms the storm” steer attention differently, and can be mistaken for Scripture. Ask your team Who writes the titles, and does the styling make clear they are added? Observed 4. Note markers Observed as a “Note Indicators” switch in Mere Bible’s reading settings (see the screenshots below). Notes here are examples written for this demo. Try this Open note e on “Be still!”, read it, and go back. Are you on the same verse? + Makes easier Translation choices and cross-references are one tap away, without leaving the passage. − Costs Every marker invites a detour; more markers mean more decisions while reading. Ask your team Which notes earn a marker in the main reading view? Familiar convention 5. Study layout Familiar from study Bibles in print and in apps, where notes sit alongside the text. Notes here are examples written for this demo. Try this Read the study note after the storm. Then ask what it told you to look for. + Makes easier Context and background right where questions arise; useful for study and preparing to teach. − Costs Notes speak with borrowed authority. The Scofield notes shaped how millions read prophecy for a century. Ask your team Whose interpretation do the notes carry, and does the reader know? Observed 6. Inline media Observed in the Joseph Prince app’s study Bible: a swipeable row of video, image, audio and book-excerpt cards pinned to exact verses, some locked for subscribers (see the screenshots below). Cards here are examples written for this demo. Try this Read up to “Be still!”, swipe through the cards and open one. Then ask what you remember of the verse. + Makes easier Teaching arrives exactly where the question arises, in the format someone prefers to learn in. − Costs Interesting extras can crowd out the text: in learning research, vivid but non-essential media reduced recall and understanding. It also puts a ministry’s voice, and sometimes a paywall, inside Scripture. Ask your team Whose voice is pinned to the verse, and does it serve the reading or compete with it? Observed 7. Reader decides Observed in Mere Bible’s reading-settings drawer, with switches for red letters, verse numbers, note indicators and section headings. Try this Open Aa, switch on red letters and the larger text, then close it. Did your place stay put? + Makes easier Each reader sets what they need, and can change it for a different kind of reading. − Costs Most people never change defaults, so the default still decides what most people see. Ask your team What should the default be, and how will people find the switches? i The example contains Mark 4:30–41 only, in the Berean Standard Bible. Section titles, translation notes, cross-references, study notes and media cards are examples written for this demo, not from a published edition. Real implementations also need text size, contrast, screen-reader and poetry-layout testing. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Everything around the text is someone’s addition Chapters date from the thirteenth century, verse numbers from 1551, red letters from 1899. Section titles and notes come from translators and editors. Genette calls this a threshold of interpretation: it shapes how the text is received before anyone reads a word. Notes have always carried theology The Geneva Bible’s marginal notes were partisan enough that the 1604 rules for the King James Version banned notes except for Hebrew and Greek words. Three centuries later, the Scofield notes carried dispensationalism to millions. A study layout is a voice beside the text, and readers should know whose. Headings help structure, and steer meaning Headings improve memory for how a text is organised, and titles bias comprehension towards what they name. “The storm on the sea” and “Jesus calms the storm” point a reader at different things. Style titles so they cannot be mistaken for Scripture, and say who wrote them. Every marker is a decision In hypertext research, links add decisions and visual processing that can impair reading, most for less experienced readers. Keep markers few and typed, open notes in a sheet over the passage, and return to the same verse. Media inside the text is a voice and a cost The Joseph Prince app pins video, image, audio and book-excerpt cards to exact verses, some locked for subscribers, and hides the layer in paragraph mode. Teaching at the verse can help, but learning research finds vivid, non-essential extras reduce recall and understanding. Say whose teaching it is, keep it switchable, and think hard before putting a paywall inside Scripture. Defaults decide for most people Mere Bible lets readers switch numbers, headings, note markers and red letters. That serves people who look for it; most never change a default. Choose the default for your main reading, and make the switches easy to find. Use cases Which reading, which unit? People read Scripture for different reasons, sometimes in the same week. Each reason fits some points on the spectrum better than others. How well each option fits each reading Reading Needs 1 Reader’s edition 2 Verse numbers 3 Section titles 4 Note markers 5 Study layout 6 Inline media 7 Reader decides Reading a book through Nothing between sentences ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible Following a sermon or group Numbers to find the verse Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible A first read of a passage Orientation without interruptions ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible Careful study Translation notes and cross-references Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Preparing to teach Context, background, other views Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Reading aloud in church Clean text, clear sense breaks ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible Readers with dyslexia or low vision Size, spacing, fewer marks ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science History and tradition How the apparatus arrived Numbers and chapters are late arrivals Stephen Langton’s chapters date from the thirteenth century; Robert Estienne numbered New Testament verses in 1551, and the Geneva Bible of 1560 was the first English Bible to use them. H Brewminate Notes were contested from the start The 1604 rules for the King James translators allowed no marginal notes except for Hebrew or Greek words, partly in reaction to the Geneva notes. The Scofield Reference Bible of 1909 shows the opposite: notes that taught a framework to millions. H Christian History Institute H Museum of the Bible Red letters and reader’s editions Red letters began with Louis Klopsch in 1899. Reader’s editions, such as Biblica’s The Books of the Bible and the ESV Reader’s Bible, remove numbers, titles and notes so the books can be read whole, and churches have read them together. H Crossway S Scripture Engagement (Taylor University) D Crossway Interpretation Why apparatus is never neutral A threshold, not a border Genette describes titles and notes as a threshold that influences how a text is received. For Scripture, that means headings and notes are interpretation, however modest. S Gérard Genette Context guards meaning Reading a verse within its passage and genre is the first rule of interpretation in widely used evangelical guides. Numbers make it easy to lift a verse out; headings and paragraphs keep the passage visible. T Zondervan, 4th edition 2014 (quotations listing) Reading science What helps and what costs Headings help memory for structure Signals such as headings improve memory for a text’s organisation, and titles bias comprehension towards their topic. R Lorch and colleagues Extras can crowd out the essential In a meta-analysis of learning studies, interesting but non-essential details, especially visual ones, reduced both recall and transfer. R The eLearning Coach, summarising Rey (2012) and Mayer’s coherence principle Markers cost attention Links and markers add decisions that can impair reading, especially for readers with less prior knowledge or working memory; clearly typed and restricted links help. R DeStefano and LeFevre Accessible reading Best practice Size, spacing and emphasis Aim for 16–19 px text, 1.5 line spacing and left alignment, and mark additions with weight or colour rather than italics. A British Dyslexia Association, 2023 A W3C Notes that return to the place Open notes over the passage, move focus into the note and back to the marker when it closes, and keep markers large enough to tap without crowding the line. Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If People read whole books or long passages Start with A reader’s edition, with numbers available on request If People follow sermons, groups or plans Start with Light verse numbers and clearly styled section titles If People study or prepare to teach Start with Note markers with typed notes; study notes clearly attributed If Your ministry’s teaching is the point of the app Start with Inline media that names its teacher, can be switched off and keeps the text first If Your audience is mixed Start with A sensible default with a settings drawer that keeps the place These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. YouVersion · Desktop web Continuous prose with reader controls Direct web capture · cropped Bible Gateway · Desktop web A footnote preview inside the passage Direct web capture Lumen Bible · Desktop web · English interface Phrase-grouped text inside a chapter reader Direct signed-out web capture Mere Bible (formerly NeuBible) · Mobile interface · device and OS not independently verified Reading settings in a bottom drawer User-contributed screenshot · unedited YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded A chapter with section headings and verse ranges User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Joseph Prince · iOS app · device model not recorded Teaching cards pinned to a verse User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Joseph Prince · iOS app · device model not recorded A study layer you can switch off User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What the page around Scripture is for “Do not add to His words, lest He rebuke you and prove you a liar” (Proverbs 30:6). Chapter and verse numbers, headings and notes are all additions, made over centuries to help readers find and follow the text. They serve the words; they are not the words. Where Christians differ The King James translators banned interpretive notes; the Scofield Reference Bible carried a whole interpretive system in its notes; reader’s editions remove almost everything. Red letters for the words of Jesus are loved by some and questioned by others, since all Scripture is “God-breathed” (2 Timothy 3:16). No choice is neutral. What follows for design Make every addition look like an addition and name who added it. Default to the least apparatus your readers need, and let them add more. Never place promotion inside the text, where it borrows Scripture’s authority. In conversation with Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum (1965) asks for “suitable footnotes”: apparatus is welcomed, and judged by whether it suits the reader. Augustine, On Christian Doctrine I.36.40 gives the test for any note: does it build up love of God and neighbour? Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Promotions and media placed inside the text, where they borrow its authority. Ethical Does no harm Label every addition and name who wrote it. Redemptive Gives something up for them Default to the clean text even where study content would earn more. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review What surrounds the text by default, who wrote it, and can a reader tell it apart and turn it off? Exercise Show three people your reading screen and ask them to point to everything that is not Scripture. Then open a note and close it, and switch a setting mid-chapter: does each person land on the same verse? Everything you add is a voice beside God’s word; let readers always tell which is which. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further This deep dive brings together 5 earlier patterns. Their guidance, wireframes and sources are kept below; their old addresses lead here. Edge cases to design for Choose a default by the main reading the product serves: a reader’s edition for reading through, numbers and titles for finding and following, notes and study material for study. Make every addition look like an addition: lighter type for numbers, a different style for titles, markers that open notes in a sheet and return to the same verse. Say who wrote headings and notes. Offer a settings drawer that changes the apparatus without moving the reader’s place, and keep poetry lineation and paragraphing from the edition. What tends to go wrong Headings styled like Scripture; study notes that read as the text’s own voice; note markers too small to tap or that jump away from the passage; settings that reflow and lose the reader’s place; red letters or headings that cannot be switched off; verse-per-line layouts that break poetry and paragraphs. How to test it Ask readers which parts of the screen are Scripture and which were added. Open a note and return: does the reader land on the same verse? Switch settings mid-chapter and check the place is kept. Compare retelling after reading the same passage as a reader’s edition and as a study layout. Earlier pattern: Verse numbers that help without taking over Separate locating a verse from the precision needed to select it. Guidance Use modest inline numbers for a general reading default. Compare margin numbers for reference-heavy tasks and an optional quiet view. Preserve an accessible way to reveal references and select a verse without tapping a tiny superscript. What tends to go wrong Colour-only selection; hiding numbers with no way to recover a reference; a long-press-only action; copying text without its edition and reference. How to test it Find and select a verse with enlarged text, keyboard and screen reader. Check that hiding visual numbers does not remove reference access. Cognitive load in hypertext reading: a review Abstract reviewed · Hypertext research, not Bible apps. Dyslexia Friendly Style Guide Guide reviewed · Guidance for general documents. Understanding SC 1.4.8: Visual Presentation Specification guidance reviewed · Level AAA; a strong target rather than a minimum. Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth Book quotations reviewed · A widely used evangelical introduction to interpretation; one approach among several. Faith and interpretation Traditions disagree about apparatus. King James forbade marginal notes because the Geneva notes argued politics and theology; the Scofield notes later carried a whole system of interpretation to millions of readers. Reader’s editions remove everything so the books can be read whole. None of these is neutral: what surrounds the text quietly teaches people how to read it. pages.title: Prayer
pages.description: How can an app make room for prayer? Five options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Prayer How can an app make room for prayer? Every control on a prayer screen says what counts as prayer. A church’s office gives words to say, a guided outline gives steps, a list holds the people someone carries, and a quiet space asks for nothing at all. A counter asks for more. Decide which practice the surface serves, and what it asks someone to read, type, share or count. Prayer belongs to God and the one praying. The screen is only a room. 5 working options 7 app examples 5 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Prayer At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From words received to no words at all Words given by the church Silence or one’s own words 1 Order of prayer Observed + Words shared with a church − Needs a named calendar Try it → 2 Guided steps Observed + A way in for beginners − Prompts are someone’s words Try it → 3 People I pray for Observed + Holds the people one carries − The most sensitive data Try it → 4 Quiet prayer Familiar convention + Nothing to fill in − Little guidance Try it → 5 Counted prayer Observed + Motivates while it lasts − Prayer becomes a number Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try five ways an app can make room for prayer It is Tuesday evening, 20 October. Each option makes room for prayer differently, from the words of a church’s evening office to silence. Pray through each one as far as you like, then switch to praying with a group and see what changes, and what each option asks you to type, share or count. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Order of prayer · Observed 2. Guided steps · Observed 3. People I pray for · Observed 4. Quiet prayer · Familiar convention 5. Counted prayer · Observed Option 1 Order of prayer Observed 2 Guided steps Observed 3 People I pray for Observed 4 Quiet prayer Familiar convention 5 Counted prayer Observed Praying Not used here Alone With a group Timer Not used here No timer 10 minutes Why these settings? Alone, the order of prayer asks the reader to say every part; with a group it labels Officiant and People, and nothing advances by itself. Guided steps give the leader a note about silence instead of collecting answers. The prayer list is private on the phone; with a group, every request names who shared it and until when. Quiet prayer with a group lets the leader end the silence. Counted prayer shows what many apps do. Observed 1. Order of prayer Observed in daily-office apps and sites: Hallow’s Daily Readings name the day (“Friday of the Twenty-fourth Week in Ordinary Time · Lectionary: 447”), and Lebens Liturgien opens on “Es ist Freitag Mittag”; see the screenshots below. The text here is Compline from the 1979 Book of Common Prayer. Try this Pray Compline, then open Calendar and look ahead to Sunday. Switch to a group and look at the labels. + Makes easier Received words, shared with a church across a day and a year. − Costs Needs a named tradition and accurate calendar data; unfamiliar to many. Ask your team Whose calendar is this, and can someone tell responses, instructions and silence apart? Observed 2. Guided steps Observed in guided-prayer sessions such as Pray As You Go and Hallow, which move through set stages; here the five steps of the Ignatian Examen, with prompts written for this example. Try this Move through the steps at your own pace. Try writing a private note, then discard it. + Makes easier An invitation to pray, for people who do not know where to begin. − Costs A method can feel like a form to complete; prompts are someone’s words. Ask your team Can someone pause, skip or finish without answering anything? Observed 3. People I pray for Observed in Hallow’s “Pray for an Intention” sheet and in community prayer-request feeds such as Glorify’s; see the screenshots below. Try this Pray through the list and mark one answered. Then switch to a group and add a request. + Makes easier Holds the people someone carries, in their own words. − Costs The most sensitive data an app can hold: health, family, faith. Ask your team Who will see this request, for how long, and did the person it is about agree? Familiar convention 4. Quiet prayer A familiar pattern in meditation and prayer apps: begin, put the phone down, end with a bell or by choice. Try this Begin without a timer, then switch to ten minutes and begin again. + Makes easier Room for silence or one’s own words, with nothing to fill in. − Costs Little guidance; a timer can feel like a test. Ask your team Does the screen recede, and does it end without a score? Observed 5. Counted prayer Observed in Pray.com’s prayer streak and its Community Board with Praise and Remind buttons, and in Hallow’s “1,111,432,374 Prayers Prayed” counter; see the screenshots below. Try this Start today’s prayer. Then switch to a group and look at the board. + Makes easier A visible habit that motivates some people while it lasts. − Costs Prayer becomes minutes, streaks and totals, shown to others. Ask your team What does this count teach people about prayer? i Compline is quoted from the 1979 Book of Common Prayer (Episcopal Church). The Examen prompts, names, requests and counts were written for this example. Nothing is saved or sent. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Name whose words and whose calendar A daily office belongs to a tradition. Hallow names the day (“Friday of the Twenty-fourth Week in Ordinary Time · Lectionary: 447”); a generic “today’s prayer” hides it. Name the book, church and calendar, and let people look ahead without changing today. Three kinds of text in one order An office mixes instructions, the leader’s lines and everyone’s responses. The Book of Common Prayer sets rubrics in italics and marks Officiant and People, and leaves room: “Silence may be kept.” Keep all three visibly different, and never advance by itself. Prayer requests are the most sensitive data They name illnesses, families and doubts, often about people who never agreed to be mentioned. Mozilla gave 28 of 32 mental health and prayer apps its privacy warning. Keep requests on the device by default; for a group, name the audience and an end date first. Not heard for many words Jesus warned against praying “to be seen of men” and against “much speaking”; Benedict asked that prayer be “short and pure”. Measuring an activity tends to make it feel like work. Streaks, minutes and global totals measure exactly what prayer is not. Let silence be complete A quiet space needs no words, no timer and no score. Offer an optional end bell, let the screen recede, and finish with nothing recorded. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Order of prayer 2 Guided steps 3 People I pray for 4 Quiet prayer 5 Counted prayer Praying the daily office Received words for the hour ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Not knowing where to begin A way in ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Carrying a sick parent Someone to pray for ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Praying without words Silence Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit ● Good fit Poor fit Leading a group Prayer together, nobody exposed ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit Preparing Sunday’s service Looking ahead in the calendar ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition Words given, words of one’s own, and silence Not for many words Prayer is heard for purity of heart, not length; in community, keep it short. H Saint Benedict, 6th century An order for the night Compline: rubrics, Officiant and People, and room for silence. S Book of Common Prayer (1979) A calendar ties days to texts Each Sunday has its collect; daily offices follow a named calendar. S Book of Common Prayer (1979) S Church of England S USCCB An outline for the end of the day The Examen’s five steps, after Ignatius of Loyola. S IgnatianSpirituality.com Psychology Ways of praying, and counting People pray in different ways Colloquial, meditative, petitionary and ritual prayer relate differently to wellbeing, and differ across faiths. R Black, Pössel, Jeppsen, Tariq and Rosmarin Measuring makes it work Counting an activity raised how much people did and lowered their enjoyment. R Jordan Etkin S Deci, Koestner and Ryan Privacy and law Prayer is special-category data Religious belief is protected Processing needs an Article 9 condition; inferences about belief count too. S European Data Protection Board S UK Information Commissioner’s Office Prayer apps have shared data Mozilla’s 2022 review of mental health and prayer apps. S Mozilla Foundation “Prayer is between you and God” A prayer app that collects no personal data. S Jesuits in Britain Accessibility Pace belongs to the person Nothing advances by itself Anything that moves for more than five seconds needs a way to pause or stop it. A W3C Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If People pray with a church’s words Start with An order of prayer, with its book and calendar named If People want help to begin Start with Guided steps with an outline, at their own pace If People pray for others Start with A private list; for groups, a named audience and an end date If People want silence Start with A quiet space with an optional bell, and nothing recorded If You are tempted to count prayer Start with Don’t: no minutes, streaks, totals or reminders to friends These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. Hallow · iOS app · device model not recorded The day named before its readings User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Lebens Liturgien · Mobile web · device model not recorded “Es ist Freitag Mittag” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Hallow · iOS app · device model not recorded A typed intention before a session User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Pray.com · iOS app · device model not recorded A prayer streak with missed days crossed out User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Glorify · iOS app · device model not recorded One prayer thread for the whole community User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Pray.com · iOS app · device model not recorded Praise and Remind buttons for other people’s streaks User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Hallow · iOS app · device model not recorded A running total of prayers prayed User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What prayer is for When the disciples asked, “Lord, teach us to pray” (Luke 11:1), Jesus gave them words. He also told them to pray to the Father “who is unseen” and warned against thinking “that by their many words they will be heard” (Matthew 6:6–7). Paul urges prayer “without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17), and the Spirit prays for us “with groans too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). Prayer is relationship with God, not output. Where Christians differ Some traditions pray mainly with set words, such as the daily office or the rosary; others prize extemporary prayer, and Puritans objected to prescribed prayer books. Contemplative traditions and Quaker meeting give silence the central place. Churches also differ on praying with saints and on the shape of the liturgical year. Each of these is a long and serious practice. What follows for design “Man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). An app cannot see prayer and should not count it. Name the tradition behind any words it offers, keep requests private, make silence possible, and finish with nothing recorded that the person did not choose to keep. In conversation with Henri Nouwen, The Way of the Heart (1981) drew on the desert fathers to commend solitude, silence and prayer as the way of the heart, the things a busy screen most easily crowds out. Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum (1965) describes prayer with Scripture as conversation: “we speak to Him when we pray; we hear Him when we read.” Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Minutes, streaks and public totals; prayer requests shared with advertisers. Ethical Does no harm Keep requests private by default and treat prayer as special-category data. Redemptive Gives something up for them Collect nothing about prayer, as Pray As You Go does, and give up the analytics; let silence end without a score. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review Could someone pray here meaningfully and leave nothing for your dashboard to count? Exercise Ask five people how they prayed this week. Then let each pray with every option and ask what the screen expected of them, and what they would not want anyone else to see. Build a room, not a scoreboard. What happens there is between them and God. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further This deep dive brings together 2 earlier patterns. Their guidance, wireframes and sources are kept below; their old addresses lead here. Edge cases to design for Decide which practice the surface serves. For set prayer, show the order with its source and calendar, keep rubrics, the leader’s lines and the people’s responses visibly different, and let people look ahead without changing today. For guided prayer, show the outline, let people move at their own pace and keep any note optional and private. For people someone prays for, store requests on the device by default; for groups, name the audience and an end date before anything is shared, and ask before sharing someone else’s story. For silence, offer a complete untimed route and an optional end bell. Record nothing about prayer that the person did not choose to keep. What tends to go wrong A generic “today’s prayer” with no tradition named; a confession and its rubric in the same type; steps that advance by themselves; a required text field before continuing; prayer requests public by default or shown on the lock screen; marking a request “answered” automatically; minutes prayed, streaks and global totals; “Remind” buttons for friends who missed a day; sharing “I prayed 14 minutes” to social media; selling prayer data to advertisers. How to test it Pray each surface without typing, recording or sharing anything, and ask what the app expected of you. Ask people to tell a response from an instruction in the office, and to name the calendar. Add a request for a group and ask who will see it and until when. Sit in silence with and without a timer. Check what is stored and sent with a network inspector. Earlier pattern: Make room for prayer Compare a prayer text, a guided sequence and a quiet space without requiring personal input. Guidance Identify the prayer’s source, author or tradition and any adaptation. For set forms, keep instructions and responses distinguishable, with adjustable text and optional audio. For guidance, show an outline and let people pause without requiring written answers. For silence, offer an optional timer or end cue with a complete untimed route. Request lists and journals are separate, optional functions with explicit storage, deletion and sharing rules. Playback should not activate a microphone; generated wording requires clear provenance and review before saving or sharing. What tends to go wrong Requiring a typed prayer to continue; claiming an AI response speaks for God; marking a request answered automatically; treating minutes or taps as prayer quality; uploading dictated prayer without clear choice; exposing a request on a lock screen. How to test it Pray from a set text at large type, pause a guided sequence, and finish a silent session with no timer. Confirm that no recording or entry is required. If journalling is offered, test save, discard, deletion and audience understanding with synthetic content. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources Daily Prayer app and podcast Official search-index excerpts reviewed 5 October 2026; full-page fetch blocked · Documented overview only; no live app capture or exhaustive liturgical rules review. Android: Guided Prayer Official help page reviewed 5 October 2026 · Product precedent, not validation of the proposed interfaces. Earlier pattern: Orient within a liturgical calendar Make the tradition, date and observance clear before offering readings or prayer. Guidance Name the calendar and jurisdiction, service or office, civil date and source. Persist an explicitly chosen calendar without inferring belief from location. Separate browsing another date from changing today. Use authoritative calendar data and review tradition-specific rules for transfers, precedence, optional observances and evening boundaries. If a source offers alternatives, name them rather than silently choosing. Cache a versioned date range and disclose unavailable or stale data. What tends to go wrong Treating one tradition’s calendar as universal; silently switching calendars on travel; substituting ordinary readings for an unavailable observance; using liturgical colour as the only identifier; showing missed feasts as overdue tasks. How to test it Check representative movable and fixed observances, competing observances and year boundaries against the named authority. Test a date link while travelling, offline access outside the cached range, large text and return to today. Have a knowledgeable reviewer verify the supported tradition and locale. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Sources Liturgical Calendar for the Dioceses of the United States Official search-index excerpts reviewed 5 October 2026; full-page fetch blocked · US Catholic scope; not a universal calendar or implementation specification. Daily Prayer app and podcast Official search-index excerpts reviewed 5 October 2026; full-page fetch blocked · Documented overview only; no live app capture or exhaustive liturgical rules review. Sources and their limits Research-informed design proposal. Editorial review, not user validation. The Rule of Benedict, chapter 20: reverence at prayer Chapter reviewed · A monastic rule for a community. An Order for Compline Text reviewed · One tradition’s office; other churches order night prayer differently. Collects: Season after Pentecost (contemporary) Text reviewed · One church’s calendar. How can I pray? The Daily Examen Page reviewed · A modern adaptation; Ignatius’s own five points in the Spiritual Exercises differ in wording. Daily Prayer app and podcast Official search-index excerpts reviewed 5 October 2026; full-page fetch blocked · Documented overview only; no live app capture or exhaustive liturgical rules review. Liturgical Calendar for the Dioceses of the United States Official search-index excerpts reviewed 5 October 2026; full-page fetch blocked · US Catholic scope; not a universal calendar or implementation specification. Poloma and Pendleton’s (1989) Prayer Types Scale in Christian, Jewish, and Muslim praying adults Abstract reviewed · Self-report survey; correlations, not effects of apps. The hidden cost of personal quantification Abstract reviewed · Leisure activities in experiments, not prayer. A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation Abstract and reward distinctions reviewed 5 October 2026 · Not a blanket effect of gamification, a Bible-app trial or a one-month threshold. Top mental health and prayer apps fail spectacularly at privacy, security Report summary reviewed · A 2022 review; apps’ practices may have changed since. Pray As You Go privacy policy Page reviewed · The same policy says anonymous navigation and error data may be stored by Google Firebase. Process personal data lawfully Official guidance reviewed · Specific lawful basis, retention and DPIA decisions require the actual data flows. What is special category data? Categories and inference guidance reviewed · Context and processing intent matter; not every Bible-page visit automatically establishes a belief. Android: Guided Prayer Official help page reviewed 5 October 2026 · Product precedent, not validation of the proposed interfaces. Understanding SC 2.2.2: Pause, Stop, Hide Specification guidance reviewed · A Level A criterion for web content; apply the same intent in native apps. Faith and interpretation Jesus told his disciples to pray to the Father “who is unseen”, not “to be seen by men”, and warned against thinking “that by their many words they will be heard” (Matthew 6:5–7); when they asked, “Lord, teach us to pray”, he gave them words (Luke 11:1–4). The early church “devoted themselves … to prayer” together (Acts 2:42), and the Spirit helps “with groans too deep for words” when we do not know what to pray (Romans 8:26). Received words, one’s own words and silence all belong to Christian prayer. Benedict wrote that “we are heard not for our many words but for our purity of heart”, and asked that prayer be “short and pure”. An app cannot tell whether someone prayed, and should not pretend to count it.
