pages.title: Progress and streaks
pages.description: What should a reading history show? Nine options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Progress and streaks What should a reading history show? Twelve chapters into a plan, someone misses nine days. When they open the app again, the progress screen speaks first. It can tell them they broke a streak, that they have read most of Mark, what they noticed along the way, or nothing at all. What it says can encourage a weary reader back to God, or send them away ashamed. 9 working options 9 app examples 4 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Progress and streaks At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further At a glance Nine ways to reflect reading back, side by side 1 Activity chart Borrowed + Starts when the reader started − A chart to keep filled Try it → 2 Levels and badges Familiar convention + Quick early rewards − The app’s idea of progress Try it → 3 Book map Borrowed + A finite plan you can finish − The whole Bible looks unreachable Try it → 4 No progress view Leave it out + No score to protect − No sense of a journey Try it → 5 Today’s step Observed + Only the next step − Little sense of the whole Try it → 6 Month calendar with a streak Familiar convention + A clear daily rhythm − Gaps become the headline Try it → 7 Time with Scripture Borrowed + No finish line − Minutes are not attention Try it → 8 Where you keep returning Borrowed + Shows what someone loves − Counts opens, not reading Try it → 9 Reflection notes Exploratory · untested + The reader’s own words − Asks for effort and trust Try it → Stills from the working example below. Scroll sideways to see all of them. Choose one to try it. Try it Try nine progress views The same synthetic reader appears in three situations: in their first week with the app, reading steadily since July, and back after nine days away. Switch between them and watch which views celebrate, which stay the same, and which make the gap the headline. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Activity chart · Borrowed 2. Levels and badges · Familiar convention 3. Book map · Borrowed 4. No progress view · Leave it out 5. Today’s step · Observed 6. Month calendar with a streak · Familiar convention 7. Time with Scripture · Borrowed 8. Where you keep returning · Borrowed 9. Reflection notes · Exploratory · untested Option 1 Activity chart Borrowed 2 Levels and badges Familiar convention 3 Book map Borrowed 4 No progress view Leave it out 5 Today’s step Observed 6 Month calendar with a streak Familiar convention 7 Time with Scripture Borrowed 8 Where you keep returning Borrowed 9 Reflection notes Exploratory · untested Situation Not used here First week Reading since July Back after nine days Borrowed 1. Activity chart Borrowed from GitHub’s contribution graph. This version starts at the reader’s first week rather than showing an empty year. Try this Compare the first week with the reader since July. Notice that the chart never shows weeks before they started. + Makes easier Accumulation is visible at a glance, and a single missed week barely registers against a summer of reading. − Costs Gaps are still visible, and a dense chart can become something to keep filled. It counts days in the app, not attention. Ask your team Should the chart begin when the person began, or on a calendar you chose? Familiar convention 2. Levels and badges Popularised by language-learning apps such as Duolingo. Related mechanics appear in faith apps: Abide’s switchable streak, BeBlessed’s seventh-day gift and Glorify’s growing tree (see the screenshots below). Generalized here. Try this Open the first week: level 2 arrives quickly. Then return after nine days and look at the streak. + Makes easier Early levels come fast, so a beginner sees movement on day three. Badges can name milestones that matter, such as finishing a first book. − Costs Points turn reading into a score, and losing a streak is built in. The incentive is the app’s, not the reader’s, unless they chose it. Ask your team Would this reader still open the Bible if the points disappeared tomorrow? Borrowed 3. Book map Borrowed from completion views such as maps of visited places; Olive Tree’s “1 of 3 Complete · Next” bar is a plan-scoped relative (see below). Switch inside the example between this plan and the whole Bible. Try this Switch from “This plan” to “Whole Bible”. + Makes easier Measured against a chosen plan, twelve of sixteen chapters feels like real progress, and a break changes nothing. − Costs Measured against all 1,189 chapters, the same reading becomes a scatter of dots, about 2%. The denominator decides whether progress feels meaningful. Ask your team What scope is this person measuring themselves against, and who chose it? Leave it out 4. No progress view The app opens on the next passage and counts nothing. Dwell’s “Resume Genesis 1:3” works this way: a way back in, with no score (see below). Try this Compare this view across all three situations. + Makes easier Nothing to fall behind on. Day three and a return after nine days look the same. − Costs No overview of what has been read, no help finishing a chosen plan, and no encouragement for someone who wanted to see it. Ask your team What would a reader lose if this screen never existed, and who would miss it? Observed 5. Today’s step Observed in Olive Tree’s in-text “1 of 3 Complete · Next” bar (see below); also borrowed from meditation apps whose home card advances to the next day. Generalized here. Try this Compare the first week with the return after nine days. Look for any mention of the days away. + Makes easier The home screen is the progress indicator: one next step, sized to the plan, with nothing to catch up on. A break simply waits. − Costs It shows little of the bigger picture, and someone who wants to see their history or skip ahead needs another route. The plan still sets the pace. Ask your team Is “what’s next” all this person needs to see? Familiar convention 6. Month calendar with a streak Common in habit and reading apps. Generalized here, not copied from one product. Try this Compare the streak before and after the break. + Makes easier Makes consistency visible for someone who has chosen a daily habit and wants feedback on it. − Costs After a break the streak drops to zero and the gap becomes the most visible thing on the screen. Ask your team Is consistency what this person asked you to track? Borrowed 7. Time with Scripture Borrowed from meditation and fitness apps that total minutes. Try this Compare the totals in the first week and since July. + Makes easier Minutes add up from the first session and have no finish line, so there is nothing to feel small against. − Costs Time in the app is not attention, and a bigger number is not a better reader. It can reward leaving the app open. Ask your team Does more time mean anything good for the person you are designing for? Borrowed 8. Where you keep returning Borrowed from “most played” lists in music apps: frequency and recency without a total to complete. Try this Look for the passages read more than once. + Makes easier Shows a person their own habits of attention: the Psalms they come back to and the book they are in now. No denominator at all. − Costs Repeated reading can look like a lack of progress to someone who expects coverage. Recency labels can still imply neglect. Ask your team Is returning to a familiar passage something your app treats as progress? Exploratory · untested 9. Reflection notes A proposal: progress made of the reader’s own words. Not observed in a specific app. Try this Read the earlier notes, then open today’s optional prompt. + Makes easier Puts what stayed with someone ahead of how often they opened the app. A break leaves no mark. − Costs Writing takes effort and many people will not do it; an empty journal can feel like failure too. Private reflections need deliberate decisions about storage, sync and sharing. Ask your team Would people write here, and who could ever read it? i Synthetic data for one hypothetical reader. These views record different things: days, points, chapters, minutes, returns, the reader’s words, or nothing. They are not interchangeable charts of one number, and none of them measures spiritual growth. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Against the whole Bible, any start looks tiny The Bible has 1,189 chapters. Open “Whole Bible” in the book map: the reader since July has read about 2%. Someone who has just started can easily conclude they have barely begun and never will finish. Smaller frames encourage, and bring their own pressure Today’s step shows only the next reading. The activity chart starts when the person did. Levels come quickly at first. Minutes and returns have no finish line, and a chosen plan is small enough to complete. Each adds its own pull: a chart to fill, a streak to protect, a score that is the app’s idea of progress rather than the reader’s. The return after a gap tells them apart After nine days away, the calendar and levels make the gap the headline; the chart, map, minutes and returns barely move; notes and the plain reader say nothing. None of them knows about the chapter read aloud at church. Say what each view counts, let people choose the frame, and let them hide it. Support the practice; don’t keep score of the person Daily Scripture and prayer are long-valued disciplines, and helping someone keep a rhythm they chose is worth building. Habit research adds that missing a day doesn’t undo a habit, while seeing a broken streak makes people likelier to stop. Let people choose what is counted, who sees it and whether it is shown at all. Theology, habit research and consent → Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Activity chart 2 Levels and badges 3 Book map 4 No progress view 5 Today’s step 6 Month calendar with a streak 7 Time with Scripture 8 Where you keep returning 9 Reflection notes Just starting out Encouragement that starts with them ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Keeping a chosen daily rhythm Gentle feedback on the habit ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Reading a book through Where they are in it Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Coming back after weeks away No headline about the gap ◐ Possible Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Looking back on a season What changed, not how much Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit Perfectionism or a competitive streak Nothing to win or lose ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Reading together as a group A shared place, a private record Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition Rhythm without a scoreboard Small beginnings count “Who has despised the day of small things?” (Zechariah 4:10). Against 1,189 chapters, every start looks small; a view that makes it look like failure works against the one reading. The plan’s author warned against his plan M’Cheyne, whose calendar still shapes reading plans, named its dangers: formality, self-righteousness, careless reading and “a yoke too heavy to bear”, and told readers to “throw aside the fetter” when it became one. H Robert Murray M’Cheyne, 1842 Rules served the rhythm Benedict set out the weekly psalter in detail, then told anyone who found it unsatisfactory to arrange it better, as long as the whole psalter was prayed each week. H Saint Benedict, 6th century Report truthfully The Cape Town Commitment calls for truthful reporting and questions demands for visible results. A progress screen is a report; it should not inflate or shame. S Lausanne Movement Motivation research What counting does Expected rewards can undermine interest Across 128 experiments, expected tangible rewards tied to doing a task reduced intrinsic interest; informational positive feedback did not. S Deci, Koestner and Ryan Measuring can drain enjoyment In six experiments, measuring walking or reading made people do more but enjoy it less. R Jordan Etkin Gamification depends on design A meta-analysis of educational gamification finds effects that vary with design and context; points and badges are not a reliable lever on their own. S Michael Sailer and Lisa Homner Autonomy matters Self-determination theory distinguishes doing something because one values it from doing it under pressure; support for autonomy, competence and relatedness sustains the first. S Ryan and Deci S Center for Self-Determination Theory Habits and returning Missing a day, starting again Habits form at different speeds In a study of everyday habits, the time to automaticity varied widely between people, and missing a single opportunity did not materially set it back. S Lally et al. A broken streak makes stopping likelier Across seven studies, highlighting a broken streak reduced later engagement, most when people blamed themselves, and less when the streak could be repaired. R Jackie Silverman and Alixandra Barasch New beginnings help Goal-directed behaviour rises after temporal landmarks such as a new week or month: a natural moment to invite someone back. R Hengchen Dai, Katherine L. Milkman and Jason Riis Shame drives people away Shame focuses on the self and tends to prompt hiding and withdrawal; guilt about a specific act tends to prompt repair. A return screen should never be a verdict on the person. R June Price Tangney, Jeff Stuewig and Debra J. Mashek Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If Someone is new to the app or to the Bible Start with A frame that starts with them: an activity chart from their first week, a short plan, or returns If Someone chose a daily habit and wants feedback on it Start with A calendar or activity chart, with any streak optional and easy to hide If Someone is working through a book or a finite plan Start with Coverage of that plan, not of the whole Bible If Your product leans on points and badges Start with Make them opt-in, and test what happens when someone loses a streak If You don’t know yet Start with Start with no progress view and a saved place. Add a record when people ask for one These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. HelloBible · Mobile-format marketing image A daily verse card alongside practice entry points Publisher promotional mockup Olive Tree Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded “1 of 3 Complete” and the next reading, inside the text User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Abide · iOS app · device model not recorded A streak you can switch off, with history behind Premium User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged BeBlessed · iOS app · device model not recorded A seventh-day gift for daily listening User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Glorify · iOS app · device model not recorded Progress as a growing tree User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Dwell · iOS app · device model not recorded A saved place, with no personal progress User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded A profile that lists badges and verse images as activity User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged HelloBible · Android app · Pixel 8 Pro A profile of series, time in the app and conversations Screenshot captured for this reference · resized; account name and avatar blurred Pray.com · iOS app · device model not recorded “Active Streakers” to praise, and friends to “Remind” User-contributed screenshot · resized; names and photos of other users blurred Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What growth is “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow” (1 Corinthians 3:6). The seed grows, “though he knows not how” (Mark 4:27), and “the kingdom of God will not come with observable signs” (Luke 17:20). Paul pressed on, “forgetting what is behind” (Philippians 3:13–14). Spiritual growth is real, but it is mostly hidden, even from the person growing. Where Christians differ Some traditions value keeping a record: spiritual journals, Puritan diaries, Wesley’s accountability. Others warn that measuring piety breeds pride or despair. Willard argued that grace is opposed to earning, not to effort, and many readers find a simple record helpful for a chosen discipline. What follows for design A record of reading is not a measure of faith. Show what was read, not a score, let people turn tracking off, and never compare them with others. Leave room for the seasons when the best thing a person did was not open the app. In conversation with James K. A. Smith, You Are What You Love (2016) warns that “secular liturgies” carry a story about who we are; badges and leaderboards tell a story of competition. Dallas Willard, “Spiritual Disciplines and Means of Grace” (2002) distinguished effort from earning: a record of reading must never become a record of merit. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Levels, leaderboards and badges turn reading into a contest. Ethical Does no harm Make any tracking optional and describe it honestly. Redemptive Gives something up for them Show what was read rather than how much, and give up the engagement numbers a contest produces. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review What will this screen say to someone on the day they come back? Exercise Complete this sentence as a team: when someone returns, we will show ___ because they are trying to ___. Then ask two people who use your app what they would want to see after a week away. Decide what this screen says to someone in the worst week of their year. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further What the views leave out Each view counts something an app can see. None can see a passage remembered on a hard day or a week spent caring for someone instead of opening the app. When would putting the phone down be the good outcome? Expected, contingent rewards can weaken intrinsic interest under some conditions, while cues and habit support that someone chose can genuinely help. The research does not support a single rule such as “streaks help for a month and then backfire”. Read the research note on gamification Edge cases to design for Define each state before designing the indicator. Store the saved passage separately from sessions the person marks complete and the dates assigned by a plan. Allow completion to be corrected. Rescheduling changes dates without filling gaps or erasing notes. Explain whether recorded activity is private or shared before enabling group visibility. Offer a clear next action; do not require a progress dashboard to reach the reading. What tends to go wrong Silently counting an opened passage as read; resetting completion when changing dates; presenting calendar delay as spiritual failure; using colour alone for status; turning a private activity record into a group ranking; claiming app activity captures reading elsewhere. How to test it Ask readers to find their next session, correct an accidental completion and join today’s group reading without completing earlier sessions. Repeat with a screen reader, large text and an offline update. Ask what the display implies about them and who can see it. Compare usefulness and pressure with a saved-place-only version. Sources and their limits Research-informed design proposal. Editorial review, not user validation. Android: Catch Me Up Scheduling and availability guidance reviewed 5 October 2026 · Documented behaviour; exact interface and discovery were not tested. A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation Abstract and reward distinctions reviewed 5 October 2026 · Not a blanket effect of gamification, a Bible-app trial or a one-month threshold. Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation from a self-determination theory perspective Definitions and autonomous motivation discussion reviewed 5 October 2026 · Theoretical research review; application to faith-app features remains a design judgment. The Cape Town Commitment: integrity and success Part II E.4 reviewed 5 October 2026 · Evangelical missional commitment, not a comparison of interface or funding-model effectiveness. Daily Bread: M’Cheyne’s calendar for daily readings, with his preface Preface text reviewed · A pastor’s preface, not a study. The Rule of Benedict, chapter 18: the order for reciting the psalms Chapter reviewed · A monastic rule for a community, not individual readers. The hidden cost of personal quantification Abstract reviewed · Leisure activities in experiments, not prayer. The Gamification of Learning: a Meta-analysis Publisher abstract and article metadata reviewed on 5 October 2026 · Education evidence does not establish spiritual growth or effects for every faith-app population. Self-Determination Theory: the theory Official theory overview reviewed on 5 October 2026 · A broad framework, not a validation of specific Bible-app interventions. How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world Abstract reviewed 5 October 2026 · Not a gamification study or a test of intrinsic motivation replacing incentives. On or off track: how (broken) streaks affect consumer decisions Abstract reviewed · Consumer and lab studies; not Scripture reading. The fresh start effect: temporal landmarks motivate aspirational behavior Paper reviewed · Archival field data on health and goals. Moral emotions and moral behavior Review and abstract reviewed · General moral-emotion research, not app design. Faith and interpretation A record can serve a chosen discipline without becoming a verdict on the person. Daily reading may matter deeply to someone; a period of absence tells the app little about their faithfulness. Describe what is known and leave space for the person’s own account of its meaning. pages.title: Reading plans
pages.description: What happens when someone misses days? Five options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Reading plans What happens when someone misses days? A reading plan decides what time means: a date to keep, a next step whenever the reader is ready, a number for the week, or the readings that belong to today. Life always interrupts, and the plan then decides whether coming back feels like a welcome or a bill. Decide what the plan asks of time, and what it says after days away. A plan is a gift to someone who wants to keep a rhythm; it should never become a debt. 5 working options 9 app examples 5 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Reading plans At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From shared dates to a day of its own Time set by the plan Time set by the reader 1 Dated plan Observed + Reading together on one day − Days away become visible Try it → 2 Sequence Observed + Nothing is ever late − No shared day Try it → 3 Weekly rhythm Familiar convention + A fresh start every week − Needs a sense of the week Try it → 4 Daily readings Familiar convention + Nothing piles up − No book to finish Try it → 5 Streak Observed + Motivates while it lasts − A missed day becomes a loss Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try five ways a plan can hold time A plan through Exodus in 40 days, a chapter at a time. It is Tuesday 20 October, day 20. Each option holds time differently, from a dated plan to readings that belong to each day. Read today’s chapter, then switch the situation to “Back after nine days” and see what each plan says. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Dated plan · Observed 2. Sequence · Observed 3. Weekly rhythm · Familiar convention 4. Daily readings · Familiar convention 5. Streak · Observed Option 1 Dated plan Observed 2 Sequence Observed 3 Weekly rhythm Familiar convention 4 Daily readings Familiar convention 5 Streak Observed Situation Not used here On day 20 Back after nine days Reading Not used here Alone With a group Why these settings? The reader last read Exodus 11 on Sunday 11 October. A dated plan offers three places to start and never says “behind”; open days stay unmarked. A sequence and a weekly rhythm simply continue. Daily readings have nothing to catch up. The streak shows what many apps do. With a group, each option shows how the reader relates to the group’s day, without showing anyone’s progress to others. Observed 1. Dated plan Observed in most Bible apps, where each plan day has a date. Bible.is offers “Change Start Date” and ESV “Read at My Own Pace”, and YouVersion documents “Catch Me Up”; see the screenshots below. Try this Come back after nine days and try each way to start. Then open Plan settings. + Makes easier A shared day, so a church or group can read together. − Costs Days away become visible, and a plan can turn into a debt. Ask your team When someone returns, does the plan offer a place to start, or a list of what they missed? Observed 2. Sequence Observed in Olive Tree’s “1 of 3 Complete | Next” bar, which moves to the next reading whenever the reader is ready; see the screenshot below. Try this Come back after nine days. Then turn the group on. + Makes easier The plan waits; nothing is ever late. − Costs No shared day: a group may be several chapters ahead. Ask your team If people read together, how will they stay close without dates? Familiar convention 3. Weekly rhythm A familiar convention in five-day plans, which leave weekends for catching up. Here the week starts fresh each Monday. Try this Read today, then come back after nine days and look at the week. + Makes easier Fits irregular lives; every Monday is a fresh start. − Costs Readers need a sense of the week; a group still needs a meeting point. Ask your team Does a new week truly start fresh, or does last week follow it? Familiar convention 4. Daily readings A familiar practice in daily offices, lectionaries and the Moravian daily texts, where each date has its own readings. The readings here were chosen for this example. Try this Come back after nine days. Look for anything you owe. + Makes easier Nothing piles up; everyone reading today reads the same passages. − Costs No book to finish; passages arrive out of their context. Ask your team Is today’s reading enough on its own, and can someone find their way into the whole book? Observed 5. Streak Observed in Abide, which shows a streak but lets people switch it off, and in many learning apps that sell streak repairs; see the screenshot below. Try this Come back after nine days and read the message. + Makes easier A visible record that motivates some people while it lasts. − Costs A missed day becomes a loss; people who feel they have failed often stop. Ask your team What does this count teach people about reading Scripture? i The plan, the daily readings, the group and the streak repair offer were written for this example. Nothing is saved or sent. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways The plan’s author wanted readers free Robert Murray M’Cheyne warned that his own calendar could become “a yoke too heavy to bear”, and told readers to “throw aside the fetter”. Benedict told anyone who found his weekly psalter unsatisfactory to arrange it better. Build that freedom in: pause, own pace and moving dates. A missed day does not undo a habit In a study of people forming new daily habits, missing one opportunity did not materially affect how automatic the habit became. A plan that treats a missed day as failure misreads how habits work. Broken streaks drive people away Across seven studies, showing people a broken streak reduced their later engagement, most when they blamed themselves. Shame tends to make people hide and withdraw, guilt to repair. Avoid counts and copy that make a reader feel they have failed. Dates are for reading together Shared dates let a church or group read the same passage on the same day. That is worth keeping for group plans, with open days left unmarked and a choice on return. For personal reading, a sequence or a weekly number that starts fresh each Monday removes the debt altogether, as ESV’s “Read at My Own Pace” begins to do. Begin again on a landmark People start goals after temporal landmarks: a new week, a new month. A plan can offer a fresh start on Monday, or simply today’s reading, without first listing what was missed. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Dated plan 2 Sequence 3 Weekly rhythm 4 Daily readings 5 Streak A group reading together Same passage, same day ● Good fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit Personal reading at any pace Never late Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Shift work, small children, illness Irregular days Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Coming back after weeks away A good place to start ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit ● Good fit Poor fit Finishing a book or the Bible A whole to complete ● Good fit ● Good fit ● Good fit Poor fit ◐ Possible Daily prayer with the church Today’s readings ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Tradition Rules that served the reader “Throw aside the fetter” M’Cheyne’s four dangers of his own reading calendar. H Robert Murray M’Cheyne, 1842 Arrange whatever is better Benedict’s weekly psalter, with freedom to rearrange it. H Saint Benedict, 6th century Readings that belong to the day Daily texts and the daily office. S Herrnhuter Brüdergemeine in der Schweiz S Church of England Discipline and grace A chosen rhythm is not spiritual merit. S Dallas Willard / Modern Reformation Psychology Habits, streaks and shame A missed day is not fatal Habit automaticity grew despite a missed opportunity, on very different timelines for different people. S Lally et al. Broken streaks reduce engagement Most when people blame themselves; less when the streak can be repaired. R Jackie Silverman and Alixandra Barasch S Duolingo Shame withdraws, guilt repairs Moral emotions and what they lead people to do. R June Price Tangney, Jeff Stuewig and Debra J. Mashek Fresh starts Temporal landmarks prompt new beginnings. R Hengchen Dai, Katherine L. Milkman and Jason Riis Practice How Bible apps handle it Catch up without pretending YouVersion’s “Catch Me Up” reschedules without marking readings complete, and is not available for plans with friends. S YouVersion Support Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If A church or group reads together Start with A dated plan with open days unmarked and a choice on return If People read on their own, at their own pace Start with A sequence that waits If Lives are irregular Start with A weekly number that starts fresh each Monday If The practice is daily prayer Start with Readings that belong to each day, with nothing to catch up If You are tempted to add a streak Start with Ask what it teaches; if you keep it, let people switch it off and never sell repairs These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. Olive Tree Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded “1 of 3 Complete” and the next reading, inside the text User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Abide · iOS app · device model not recorded A streak you can switch off, with history behind Premium User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged ESV Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded Plan settings with “Read at My Own Pace” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Bible.is · iOS app · device model not recorded Change the start date of a plan User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded Progress and participants on each plan User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded “A plan for parents & kids” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Spark Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded A notification prompt before the first verse User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged ESV Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded Permission asked when a reminder is set User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Glorify · iOS app · device model not recorded “Wake up” and “Wind down” reminders User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What a rhythm is for “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27). Daily offices, lectionaries and the Moravian daily texts give each day its words so that no one has to choose alone. God’s mercies are “new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23): a rule of reading exists to bring people back to that newness, not to measure them. Where Christians differ Liturgical churches read by a shared calendar, so a congregation hears the same texts on the same day. Many evangelicals favour personal plans, often reading through the whole Bible in a year. Some value discipline as a means of grace; others warn that a plan can become a law. Dallas Willard distinguished effort from earning: a chosen discipline is not merit. What follows for design M’Cheyne warned that his own calendar could become “a yoke too heavy to bear”. Design the plan so that coming back is grace, not debt: no streaks to lose, no reminders that escalate, and a welcome that offers today’s reading without a bill for the days missed. In conversation with James K. A. Smith, You Are What You Love (2016) argues that habits are “liturgies” that train what we love; a streak is a small liturgy, and it teaches something about God and ourselves. Dallas Willard, “Spiritual Disciplines and Means of Grace” (2002) insisted that “grace is not opposed to effort, but to earning”: a plan is effort, never merit. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Streaks, paid streak repair and reminders that escalate after silence. Ethical Does no harm No shame in the copy; let people pause, move dates and change pace. Redemptive Gives something up for them Let the plan wait and welcome people back owing nothing, giving up the retention a streak buys. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review After nine days away, does the plan offer a good place to start, or a bill? Exercise Ask three people who abandoned a reading plan what the app said when they last opened it. Then show them each option after nine days away, and ask which one they would open tomorrow. A plan should welcome someone back after a hard week, never send them a bill. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further This deep dive brings together 2 earlier patterns. Their guidance, wireframes and sources are kept below; their old addresses lead here. Edge cases to design for Decide what the plan is for. For reading together, keep shared dates but treat open days as available, not overdue, and on return offer today’s reading, where they stopped, or moving their own dates. For personal reading, use a sequence that waits, or a weekly number that starts fresh. For daily texts, let each day stand on its own. Explain what each change will do before it happens, keep completed readings and notes, let people pause without reminders, and say nothing about absence beyond what helps them choose. What tends to go wrong “You are 9 days behind”; a catch-up list of every missed reading; streak counters on the home screen; streak repair for money or gems; reminders that escalate after silence; resetting the plan and erasing history; group dashboards that show who is behind; asking why someone was away. How to test it Ask people returning after a week, a month and a year what they would do next and how the screen makes them feel. Try each change (pause, move dates, own pace) and ask what will happen before confirming. Test with a group plan: can someone fall back without the group seeing it? Earlier pattern: A flexible reading rhythm Help someone choose a reading rhythm—and adjust it when life changes. Guidance Let the person choose between a dated plan and a sequence that waits for them. Offer reminders separately. Before pausing or moving dates, explain what will change and preserve completed sessions, notes and the saved place. For a group plan, distinguish a personal adjustment from a change to the shared calendar. What tends to go wrong Forced daily goals; erasing progress after rescheduling; presenting missed days as moral failures. How to test it Study real reading rhythms, including irregular and shared practice. Can users change pace without losing their place or feeling penalised? Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. In a dated plan, distinguish resuming from opening today’s reading. Make a different starting point available without erasing earlier work. Keep paused reminders paused unless the person chooses to restart them. A return should not require an explanation or a new commitment. What tends to go wrong A guilt message; demanding reasons for absence; “save your streak” payments; escalating reminder frequency after silence. How to test it Compare returning-user experiences through interviews and longitudinal observation. Does the welcome respect choice rather than merely increase opens? Faith and interpretation Christians have long read Scripture by rule and by calendar: the daily office, lectionaries and the Moravian watchwords give each day its texts. Rules served the reader. Benedict asked that the whole psalter be prayed each week, yet told anyone who found his arrangement unsatisfactory to arrange whatever he judged better. Robert Murray M’Cheyne, whose 1842 calendar is still widely used, warned that it might become “a yoke too heavy to bear”: “throw aside the fetter, and feed at liberty in the sweet garden of God.” His mercies are “new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23); a plan should be too. pages.title: Reading together
pages.description: When people read Scripture together through an app, what do the others see, and who looks after the conversation?
pages.text: Patterns Reading together When people read Scripture together through an app, what do the others see, and who looks after the conversation? Reading Scripture with others is one of the oldest ways of reading it. Two disciples on the road to Emmaus asked each other afterwards, “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32). Apps now offer the same passage on the same day, guides for a group, plans with friends, comments on every verse and feeds of what friends have read. Each decides what the others see of your reading, and who looks after the conversation. Most days, reading together is a gift. Some days someone falls behind, or a verse is turned against the person who has just shared. Design for both. Draft · waiting for review What needs review: The verse turned against someone who shared, the leader’s notes and replies, the youth-group rules and the safeguarding contact in the working example. This touches the safety of people who may already be hurting, and it has not yet been reviewed by people whose work this is: safeguarding; pastoral care; survivor advocacy (ideally survivor-led); and data protection. Please read it as a draft until they have. Is this your field, or do you know someone whose field it is? I would be grateful for your eyes on it, or for an introduction. Offer a review or an introduction 6 working options 6 app examples 7 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Reading together At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From the same passage to everything shown Less of your reading is seen More of your reading is seen 1 The same passage, nothing shown Familiar convention + Nothing to compare or answer − No one to talk it over with Try it → 2 A guide for meeting in person Borrowed + Words stay in the room − Needs people in one place Try it → 3 A group with a leader Observed + Someone looks after the talk − The leader sees who answers Try it → 4 A plan with friends Observed + Friends reading the same day − Everyone sees who is behind Try it → 5 A feed of friends’ activity Observed + Friends’ reading in view − Every completion is a signal Try it → 6 A public thread on the verse Observed + Many voices on a verse − Strangers interpret for you Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try six ways to read a passage together A small group is reading Matthew 18:21–22, where Peter asks how many times he must forgive. First try an ordinary day. Then fall four days behind and see what you, and the others, can see. Then read on as Lena shares that she is finding it hard to forgive someone who hurt her badly, and another member answers her with a verse. Notice what each person sees of the others, and who looks after the conversation. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. The same passage, nothing shown · Familiar convention 2. A guide for meeting in person · Borrowed 3. A group with a leader · Observed 4. A plan with friends · Observed 5. A feed of friends’ activity · Observed 6. A public thread on the verse · Observed Option 1 The same passage, nothing shown Familiar convention 2 A guide for meeting in person Borrowed 3 A group with a leader Observed 4 A plan with friends Observed 5 A feed of friends’ activity Observed 6 A public thread on the verse Observed Situation Not used here An ordinary day You fell behind A verse misused Group Not used here Adults A youth group Why these settings? On an ordinary day the group reads Matthew 18:21–22. When you fall behind, you are four days behind the others. In the hard situation Lena shares that she is finding it hard to forgive someone who hurt her badly, and another member answers with “seventy-seven times” and Matthew 6:15, as these passages have been used to press people to forgive quickly. A youth group adds two leaders to every conversation, no one-to-one messages, and a named safeguarding contact. Familiar convention 1. The same passage, nothing shown Familiar from shared daily texts: the Moravian Daily Texts, printed since 1731, lectionaries and a church’s own reading plan. Everyone reads the same words on the same day; nothing in the app shows who read. The church and its Thursday group are written for this example. Try this Read today’s passage. Then fall behind, and then try the hard situation. + Makes easier Nobody is compared, and nobody can answer badly. − Costs No one to talk it over with, unless the group meets. Ask your team Where will people talk about what they read, if not here? Borrowed 2. A guide for meeting in person Borrowed from group practice outside apps: the seven steps of Bible sharing (the Lumko method), whose rule for sharing is “Keine Diskussion, kein Vortrag” (no discussion, no lecture), and the Västerås method’s marks for questions, insights and experiences. Not observed in an app. The steps are shortened, and the leader’s notes are written for this example. Try this Step through the evening. Switch to the hard situation at the Share step, then to a youth group. + Makes easier What is said stays in the room, and the steps start with listening. − Costs Needs people in one place, and a leader who follows the guide. Ask your team What does the guide tell a leader to do when a share goes wrong? Observed 3. A group with a leader Observed in Startblock, where people join a group with a code from their leader and work through units with a question banner; see the screenshots below. The leader’s replies, the group’s agreement and the safeguarding contact are proposals. Try this Answer the question, then fall behind and see where the group starts you. Try the hard situation, then a youth group. + Makes easier Someone looks after the conversation, and the group is closed. − Costs The leader sees who answers, and may be close to a concern. Ask your team Who looks after the group when the leader is part of the problem? Observed 4. A plan with friends Observed in YouVersion’s Plans with Friends: participants “see each other’s progress as you finish days” and talk in a “private discussion area”; only the host can invite people, and anyone who leaves cannot rejoin. See the screenshots below and YouVersion’s help centre. Names and comments are written for this example. Try this Open Talk It Over. Then fall behind and look at the ticks. Then try the hard situation. + Makes easier Friends far apart reading the same day, with somewhere to talk. − Costs Everyone sees who is behind, and no one is asked to look after the talk. Ask your team What does the friend who fell behind see when they open the plan? Observed 5. A feed of friends’ activity Observed in YouVersion, where a plan set to Friends Only puts each completed day in friends’ Community Feed and “Plan activities on the Community Feed or your timeline cannot be deleted”, and in YouVersion’s profile, where badges and verse images are listed as activity; see the screenshots below. Names and entries are written for this example. Try this Scroll the feed. Then fall behind, and then try the hard situation. + Makes easier Friends’ reading in view, as encouragement. − Costs Every completed day becomes a signal, and absence shows too. Ask your team Would each friend choose to have this entry shown, today? Observed 6. A public thread on the verse Observed in Glorify, where a thread on a verse fills with comments from people across the app, and in YouVersion’s public notes from other readers on the same passage; see the screenshots below. Names and comments here are written for this example. Try this Read the comments, post your own, and try the hard situation. + Makes easier Many voices on a verse, at any hour. − Costs Strangers interpret the text, and answer people they don’t know. Ask your team Who reads these comments, and what happens when one is turned on someone? i The church, group, names, comments and contact address were written for this example. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. Nothing is saved or sent. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Share the passage, not the record A church can read the same words on the same day without anyone seeing who read; the Moravian Daily Texts have done it since 1731. Share the passage and the day, and keep each person’s completed days to themselves unless they choose to show them. Say what others will see before the plan starts In YouVersion, people in a plan with friends see each other’s completed days, and with Friends Only each day appears in friends’ feeds, where it “cannot be deleted”. Before anyone joins, show what participants and friends will see, and where. Let people delete it. Falling behind should be a way back, not a signal Ticks show the group who is behind, and YouVersion’s Catch Me Up isn’t available for plans with friends. Let someone rejoin where the group is today, mark nothing as missed, and remember that comparison motivates some people and discourages others. Give the conversation a shape Bible sharing asks each person to speak about themselves: “Keine Diskussion, kein Vortrag”. A prompt such as “Which word spoke to you?” invites a share; “What should we all learn from this?” invites a lecture. Carry the shapes groups already trust into the app, and let people answer only if they want. A verse can be turned on the person who shared When someone says they are struggling to forgive, a reply of “seventy-seven times” and Matthew 6:15 can press them to forgive quickly, keep quiet or go back. Groups can agree how they answer, and someone responsible needs to see the reply, step in and reach the person who shared. When Scripture is used to harm → Young people: two leaders, no one-to-one, a named contact Church safeguarding guidance keeps conversations with young people in the group, with two adults present. A youth group in an app can make that the rule, and name a safeguarding contact outside the group’s leadership, as the prayer request deep dive does. Sharing with a group → Strangers’ notes are interpretation Glorify’s thread on Jeremiah 17:6 and YouVersion’s related notes put other readers’ interpretations beside the verse. Label them as other people’s words, say who moderates them, and keep them a deliberate step away from the text. Highlights and notes → Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 The same passage, nothing shown 2 A guide for meeting in person 3 A group with a leader 4 A plan with friends 5 A feed of friends’ activity 6 A public thread on the verse A house group that meets each week Something to read before, and a shape for the evening ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Friends who live far apart The same day, and somewhere to talk ◐ Possible Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit A youth or confirmation group Two leaders, no one-to-one messages, a named contact ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Someone who has fallen behind A way back without being watched ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible A hard passage, or a hard week People who listen before they answer Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Reading alone, with questions Other voices, clearly not the text Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition Reading in company Hearts burning on the road As two disciples “talked and deliberated, Jesus Himself came up and walked along with them” (Luke 24:15); afterwards they asked, “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32). The conversation was part of the reading. Teaching and fellowship together The first church “devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer” (Acts 2:42). The same words on the same day The Moravian Daily Texts were first printed in Herrnhut in 1731; since 1788 each day’s watchword has been drawn by lot from around 2,000 Old Testament texts. Christians across the world read the same words each day, and nobody counts who read them. S Moravian Church in North America Church practice Giving the conversation a shape Share, don’t discuss In the seven steps of Bible sharing, each person speaks about themselves in the first person: “Keine Diskussion, kein Vortrag”, no discussion and no lecture. S Erzbistum Köln Questions, insights and experiences The Västerås method invites everyone to mark verses with a question, an insight or an experience, and to share experiences without pressure. Its guide names the risks: some verses stay unclear, and some people talk too much. S Diözese Linz Young people: in the group, not one to one Church of England guidance recommends group calls rather than one-to-one calls with young people; one parish’s policy allows conversations with young people only in groups where at least two DBS-checked adults are present. S Church of England National Safeguarding Team S All Saints Boyne Hill, Church of England parish Products and research What reading together shows Plans with friends show progress In YouVersion’s Plans with Friends, participants see each other’s completed days and talk in a private discussion area; up to 300 friends can be invited, only the host can invite, and anyone who leaves cannot rejoin. S YouVersion Support S YouVersion Support Feeds keep what they show With a plan set to Friends Only, each completed day appears in friends’ Community Feed, and YouVersion says these activities “cannot be deleted”. S YouVersion Support Comparison helps some, not all A review of physical activity apps found that comparison features give inconsistent results: they “may motivate PA for some people under some circumstances”. No figure we found shows that reading with friends helps people finish plans. R Danielle Arigo, Megan M. Brown, Kristen Pasko and Jerry Suls S YouVersion blog Groups matter to many people In Lifeway Research’s survey of US Protestant churchgoers, those in a small group five or more times a month scored higher on a discipleship assessment than those in none. A correlation, not proof that groups cause growth. R Aaron Earls Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If A church or house group Start with The same passage, and a guide for meeting in person If Friends far apart Start with A plan with friends: progress private by default, and a way to rejoin If A youth group Start with Two leaders, no one-to-one messages and a named safeguarding contact If Comments on verses Start with Others’ words labelled, a step away from the text, with someone moderating If You are tempted to show everyone’s progress Start with Don’t: show the passage and the conversation, not the record These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. Startblock · iOS app · German interface · device model not recorded Joining a group with a code from the leader User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded Progress and participants on each plan User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded A profile that lists badges and verse images as activity User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded Other readers’ notes related to a verse User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Glorify · iOS app · device model not recorded A public thread under a verse User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Startblock · iOS app · German interface · device model not recorded A question for the group at the end of a unit User-contributed screenshot · resized; other users’ names blurred Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What reading together is for The disciples on the road to Emmaus “talked and deliberated” until Jesus walked with them and “opened the Scriptures” (Luke 24:15, 32). The first church devoted itself “to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship” (Acts 2:42). Others help us hear what we would miss, and a passage read together becomes something a community shares. Where Christians differ Liturgical churches read appointed texts on the same day, and Moravians have shared daily texts since 1731. Bible sharing, which began at the Lumko Pastoral Institute in South Africa and is used in German dioceses today, asks members not to discuss or correct each other; many evangelical small groups study a passage with a leader and questions. Traditions differ on who may interpret for others, and on how much a group should hear of each person’s life. What follows for design Share the passage and the conversation, not the record. Give the conversation a shape that starts with listening, name who looks after it, and prepare for a verse turned against someone. A completed day is between the reader and God unless they choose to show it. In conversation with Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Life Together (1939) balanced “The Day with Others” and “The Day Alone”: “Only in the fellowship do we learn to be rightly alone and only in aloneness do we learn to live rightly in the fellowship.” Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Show every friend’s ticks and streaks, fill feeds with each completed day, and nudge whoever falls behind. Ethical Does no harm Say what others will see before a plan starts, let people delete their activity, and give a way back to anyone who fell behind. Redemptive Gives something up for them Keep each person’s record private and give up the engagement that visible progress brings; pay for someone to look after the conversation, and give groups shapes for listening instead of feeds. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review What will each person see of the others’ reading, and who looks after the conversation when it goes wrong? Exercise Take one week of a group plan. For each person, list what the others will see: that they started, which days they finished, what they wrote, and what appears in anyone’s feed. Then write a reply that turns a verse against someone who shared something hard, and walk through your design: who sees it, who can step in, and how the person who shared is looked after. Share the passage and the conversation, not the record, and make sure someone looks after what is said. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further Edge cases to design for Share the passage and the day, and keep each person’s record private unless they choose to show it. Say before a plan starts what participants and friends will see, and let people delete it. Let someone rejoin where the group is today. Give groups prompts that ask what touched each person, not what others should do. When a church or leader runs the group, name who looks after it, keep conversations with young people in the group, and name a safeguarding contact. Label others’ notes as theirs, say who moderates them, and keep them a step away from the text. What tends to go wrong Completion ticks for everyone in a group by default; friends’ feeds filled with each completed day that cannot be deleted; no way back for someone who fell behind except by catching up in view of everyone; strangers’ readings shown inside the verse; a verse quoted at someone who shared a hurt, with no one able to step in; leaders messaging young people one to one; badges and streaks in the same stream as the group’s conversation. How to test it Run a week of a group plan with five people. Ask each to list what the others can see of them, and where. Have one fall behind and watch what they see when they return. Post a reply that turns a verse against someone who shared, and time how long it takes for someone responsible to notice and reach the person. Check what a young person in the group can receive, and from whom. Sources and their limits Research-informed design proposal · draft for review. Editorial review, not user validation. iOS: Plan with Friends Article and FAQ reviewed 10 October 2026 · Publisher documentation for iOS; the interface was not tested end to end. iOS: Plan Privacy Article reviewed 10 October 2026; the Android article says the same · Publisher documentation; the default setting is not stated. iOS: Plan with Friends – Comments Article reviewed 10 October 2026 · The article does not describe reporting or moderation; it may exist elsewhere in the app. Announcing Plans with Friends Post reviewed 10 October 2026 · A launch announcement; it gives reasons, not completion figures. Android: Catch Me Up Scheduling and availability guidance reviewed 5 October 2026 · Documented behaviour; exact interface and discovery were not tested. A brief history of the Moravian Daily Texts Article reviewed 10 October 2026 · A church’s own history of its publication. Anleitung Bibelteilen Leaflet reviewed 10 October 2026 · One diocese’s leaflet; other versions have six steps or name them differently. Methoden praktischer Bibelarbeit Section on the Västerås method reviewed 10 October 2026 · A practical guide, not a study of outcomes. Video calling: safeguarding questions Guidance reviewed 10 October 2026 · Written for video calls during the pandemic; the principle comes from wider guidance. Guidance on use of social media and private messaging with young and vulnerable people Guidance reviewed 10 October 2026 · One parish’s policy applying diocesan guidance; German churches set their own rules. Social comparison features in physical activity promotion apps: scoping meta-review Abstract reviewed 10 October 2026 · A review of reviews about physical activity apps, not Bible reading. Small group participation linked to higher discipleship scores Article reviewed 10 October 2026 · A correlation from self-report; it does not show that groups cause growth. US Protestants only. Section 4.2: Spiritual Abuse Official indexed excerpts reviewed on 5 October 2026; direct page access returned 403 · Institutional safeguarding guidance, not universal law or an automated abuse classifier; full-page review remains outstanding. Process personal data lawfully Official guidance reviewed · Specific lawful basis, retention and DPIA decisions require the actual data flows. Faith and interpretation Two disciples on the road to Emmaus “talked and deliberated” until Jesus “came up and walked along with them” (Luke 24:15), and afterwards asked each other, “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32). The first church “devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship” (Acts 2:42). Reading together is a gift, and the conversation needs tending: a verse can open the Scriptures to someone, or be turned against them.
