pages.title: Sharing with a group
pages.description: When someone shares a prayer request, who hears it, and who looks after it? Seven options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Sharing with a group When someone shares a prayer request, who hears it, and who looks after it? Someone asks others to pray: for a mother’s surgery, for a new job, for something they have never said aloud. A prayer app decides who hears it, from one friend to everyone in the app, and what comes back: a heart, a verse, a stranger’s reply, or a person who knows what to do. Most requests are ordinary, and being prayed for by people who know you is a gift. Some are not, and the people closest to a worry are not always the right ones to hear it first. Paul asks the church to “rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). Design for both. Draft · waiting for review What needs review: Who hears a prayer request, the duty-to-report and safeguarding-contact wording, the independent routes, and the hard situation in the working example. This touches the safety of people who may already be hurting, and it has not yet been reviewed by people whose work this is: safeguarding; survivor advocacy (ideally survivor-led); pastoral care; and data protection. Please read it as a draft until they have. Is this your field, or do you know someone whose field it is? I would be grateful for your eyes on it, or for an introduction. Offer a review or an introduction 7 working options 9 app examples 7 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Sharing with a group At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From between you and God to everyone in the app Fewer people hear it More people hear it 1 Between you and God Leave it out + Nothing to leak or misread − No one prays with them Try it → 2 Through a person you choose Borrowed + The listener is chosen and named − A church must name someone Try it → 3 A few people you choose Observed + People who know them − Replies are unguided Try it → 4 A group with a leader Observed + Someone looks after it − Leaders may be too close Try it → 5 The whole church Observed + A parish prays together − Hundreds see a name and a need Try it → 6 A public wall Observed + Someone prays at any hour − Strangers answer Try it → 7 Ranked by prayer streaks Leave it out + Motivates while it lasts − Prayer becomes a ranking Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try seven ways to share a prayer request Someone wants others to pray with them. First share an ordinary request: their mother’s surgery on Thursday. Then switch to something hard: a worry about how a youth helper messages their daughter, from someone who doesn’t know who to tell. Notice who hears it, what each listener can or must do with it, and what comes back. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Between you and God · Leave it out 2. Through a person you choose · Borrowed 3. A few people you choose · Observed 4. A group with a leader · Observed 5. The whole church · Observed 6. A public wall · Observed 7. Ranked by prayer streaks · Leave it out Option 1 Between you and God Leave it out 2 Through a person you choose Borrowed 3 A few people you choose Observed 4 A group with a leader Observed 5 The whole church Observed 6 A public wall Observed 7 Ranked by prayer streaks Leave it out Situation Not used here An ordinary request Something hard Set up by Not used here A church, contact named No church Why these settings? The ordinary request is about a mother’s surgery. In the hard situation a parent is worried about how a youth helper messages their daughter and doesn’t know who to tell; in several options a reply quotes Matthew 18:15 back, as that passage has been used to send people to confront someone privately first. When a church sets the app up, it names its safeguarding contact, someone outside the youth team, and says before anyone shares that church workers may have to pass a concern on. The independent route stays available either way. Leave it out 1. Between you and God Leaving sharing out. Hallow’s help centre describes the private setting: an intention “will only be saved to your journal and not shared with others”. Here the whole app works that way and points people to those they know and to their own church. Try this Write the request and keep it. Switch to the hard situation and open “Who can I talk to?”. + Makes easier Nothing to leak, misread or answer badly. − Costs No one prays with them, and no one hears what is hard. Ask your team Where does this app send someone who needs a person, not a journal? Borrowed 2. Through a person you choose Borrowed from careful church practice outside apps: one person receives a request, agrees what is passed on and names no one without consent; and from safeguarding roles that sit apart from leadership, such as a Church of England parish’s lay safeguarding officer. Not observed in an app. Names, replies and the church are written for this example. Try this Choose each person and read “What happens next” before sending. Switch the church set-up off and on. + Makes easier The listener is chosen, and what they must do is said before anything is shared. − Costs Asks the church to name and train someone, and keep the details current. Ask your team Who is named here, and are they outside the leadership a concern might be about? Observed 3. A few people you choose Observed in Soultime with Friends (up to 10 supporters, with automatic notifications switched on) and in YouVersion Prayer (“Keep your prayers private, or invite friends to pray with you”); see the screenshots below. Try this Share with your circle and read the replies. Then switch to the hard situation. + Makes easier Prayer with people who know them, at a size they chose. − Costs Friends reply as they like, and may quote a verse back. Ask your team What do friends see before they reply, and who decided when they are notified? Observed 4. A group with a leader Observed in Startblock, where people join with a code from their group leader, and in Planning Center’s confidential member groups, where only leaders see who is in the group; see the screenshots below. The group’s ways of praying together and the note before sharing are proposals. Try this Share with the group. Switch to the hard situation, then turn the church set-up off. + Makes easier A known circle with someone looking after it. − Costs Leaders may be close to the person a concern is about. Ask your team Does the group know who to tell if the leader is part of the problem? Observed 5. The whole church Observed in Hallow’s Church tab: requests go to friends, a church or a group, are limited to 240 characters, can’t be anonymous or edited, stay active for 7 days, and are answered with a heart; see the screenshots below. Try this Write a request within 240 characters and post it. Tap the heart. + Makes easier A whole parish praying, in a few taps. − Costs Hundreds of people see a name and a need; hearts become a count. Ask your team Would the person still share this if they could see every member’s face? Observed 6. A public wall Observed in Glorify’s community prayer requests, a single thread with hundreds of thousands of responses under first names; see the screenshots below. Names and requests here are written for this example. Try this Post to the wall, then read the replies and the requests around yours. + Makes easier Someone, somewhere, prays, at any hour. − Costs Strangers answer; requests from people in crisis sit beside exam worries. Ask your team Who reads this wall, and what happens when someone posts that they are not safe? Leave it out 7. Ranked by prayer streaks Observed in Pray.com’s Community Board, which lists “Active Streakers” with Praise and Remind buttons; see the screenshots below and the prayer deep dive. Shown here as something to leave out. Try this Post a request to the board and look at what sits above it. + Makes easier Visible habit that motivates some people while it lasts. − Costs Prayer becomes a ranking, and requests become content for it. Ask your team What does this board teach people about prayer, and about each other? i The church, names, requests, replies and contact address were written for this example; Anlaufstelle.help’s number and hours are from its own website, checked 10 October 2026. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. Nothing is saved or sent. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Say who will hear it, before it is written Hallow’s requests go to friends, a church or a group, can’t be anonymous or edited, and stay active for 7 days; its help centre suggests writing “For a special intention” to keep details private. Show the audience, how long a request stays and whether it can be changed before someone starts typing, and ask before naming anyone else. Some listeners have to pass things on In Germany’s Protestant churches, church workers, volunteers included, must report a justified suspicion of sexualised violence to the church’s reporting office; pastoral confidentiality and the seal of confession are left untouched. A group leader may not be able to keep a secret, and shouldn’t promise to. Say so before someone shares, and say what happens next. Name the safeguarding contact When a church sets an app up, show its safeguarding contact with a way to reach them from inside the app, as a parish shows it on the noticeboard. Choose someone outside the leadership a concern might be about. German Catholic institutions must have a person trained in prevention; a Church of England parish must appoint a safeguarding officer, who should be a lay person. Keep an independent route beside the church’s Some people will not tell anyone at their church first, and sometimes they are right. Offer an independent service next to the church’s contact and say what each does with what it hears. The church route is often the right one; it should never be the only one. A verse quoted back can wound A reply such as “go and confront him privately” (Matthew 18:15) can send someone alone to the person they are afraid of. Groups can agree how they answer: listen first, pray, and offer verses only when asked. When Scripture is used to harm → Friends are not always the safest listeners A circle of friends is a gift for ordinary requests. For something hard, reactions from people close to us can be the most negative, so offer a trained listener beside them. Soultime nudges friends automatically “when we think you might need a call”, switched on; ask each time instead. Leave out what ranks prayer Hearts, counts and streak boards turn requests into content. A board with Praise and Remind buttons ranks people by how often they pray, and puts someone’s need underneath. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Between you and God 2 Through a person you choose 3 A few people you choose 4 A group with a leader 5 The whole church 6 A public wall 7 Ranked by prayer streaks A parent’s surgery this week People who know them, praying ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Something never said aloud One trusted listener ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit A worry about someone’s safety A person who knows what to do Poor fit ● Good fit Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit A grief or recovery group Privacy from other members Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit A request about someone else Their agreement first ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Poor fit A joy to share A community rejoicing Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Late at night, no one to call Someone, somewhere ◐ Possible ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit ◐ Possible Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and tradition Being with someone Weep with those who weep “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). Being with someone comes before fixing them, and a reply box can make room for that. Silence before answers Job’s friends “sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights, but no one spoke a word to him because they saw how intense his suffering was” (Job 2:13). Their trouble began when they started to explain. In secret and together Jesus taught his disciples to pray behind a shut door (Matthew 6:6), and the first church prayed together (Acts 2:42). Both are prayer, so neither should be the only setting an app offers. Church practice and church law Who hears, and who must act Ask before naming someone A United Methodist church suspended printed prayer requests after complaints about what they disclosed, then asked for written approval before praying for someone other than the person asking. S Amy Green Some listeners must report The EKD’s guideline against sexualised violence (2019) obliges church workers, volunteers included, to report a justified suspicion to a reporting office, protecting their identity; pastoral confidentiality and the seal of confession stay untouched. S Evangelische Kirche in Deutschland A trained person, and routes made known The German Catholic bishops’ framework for prevention, in force since January 2020, requires a person trained in prevention for every institution, and that advice and reporting routes be made known. S Deutsche Bischofskonferenz A safeguarding officer apart from leadership In the Church of England, a parish must appoint at least one safeguarding officer, who should be a lay person, with contact details displayed in all church premises. S Diocese of Durham, Church of England Members hidden from each other Planning Center’s confidential groups let support groups protect their members: “only group leaders will have access to the complete member list”. S Jon Aleixo Research and law What sharing costs Requests are special-category data A request names faith and often health, about the person and others. Under European data law both need an Article 9 condition, and inferences count too. S European Data Protection Board S UK Information Commissioner’s Office How a listener reacts matters In a study of 228 women disclosing sexual assault, reactions from friends and family were more negative than those from police or service providers, and gave less practical help. R National Institute of Justice Groups help many people In Lifeway Research’s survey of US Protestant churchgoers, those in a small group five or more times a month scored 74.1 on a discipleship assessment, against 60.4 for those in none. A correlation, not proof that groups cause growth. R Aaron Earls Independent help has limits too thirtyone:eight shares information without consent only in exceptional cases, such as serious and immediate risk; Anlaufstelle.help is anonymous and passes people on to church offices only if they want. S thirtyone:eight S Run for the EKD and Diakonie by the independent specialist service of Pfiffigunde Heilbronn e.V. Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If Most requests are ordinary Start with A few people or a group they chose, with audience and end date shown first If A church sets the app up Start with Name its safeguarding contact, and say before sharing who may have to pass things on If Someone may not be safe Start with One person they choose, a trained contact or an independent service, not the group If Support and recovery groups Start with Confidential members, a named leader, and a route around the leader If You are tempted to rank or count Start with Don’t: no streaks, boards or public totals These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. Soultime · iOS app · device model not recorded Up to ten friends who support you User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Soultime · iOS app · device model not recorded Friends nudged automatically, switched on User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Startblock · iOS app · German interface · device model not recorded Joining a group with a code from the leader User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Hallow · iOS app · device model not recorded “Pray for others, be prayed for” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Glorify · iOS app · device model not recorded One prayer thread for the whole community User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged YouVersion · iOS app · device model not recorded A friend’s new prayer among badges and friendships User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Pray.com · iOS app · device model not recorded Praise and Remind buttons for other people’s streaks User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Pray.com · iOS app · device model not recorded “Active Streakers” to praise, and friends to “Remind” User-contributed screenshot · resized; names and photos of other users blurred Soultime · iOS app · device model not recorded Friends notified automatically “when we think you might need a call” User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What sharing a burden is for Paul asks the church to “carry one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2) and to “weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15); James to “pray for each other so that you may be healed” (James 5:16). Sharing a need is an act of trust, and hearing it is a charge: whoever listens becomes responsible for what they heard. Where Christians differ Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess sins to a priest, under a seal; many Protestant churches share requests openly in a prayer chain or a small group; Methodist class meetings and accountability groups ask members to tell each other how they are really doing. The same passages that call for bearing burdens have also been used to press people to disclose more than they chose, or to keep concerns about a leader inside the church. What follows for design Let people choose who hears them, and tell them before they share what each listener can and must do. Name a trained contact apart from the leadership, and keep an independent route beside it. Help groups listen before they answer, offer verses only when asked, and count nothing. In conversation with Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Life Together (1939) held that because a fellow Christian is Christ to me, I must listen to them as patiently as I listen to Christ, and bear their burdens as I share in his cross. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Make every request public and countable, notify friends automatically, and rank who prays most. Ethical Does no harm Show the audience before sharing, ask before naming others, let requests expire, and let people delete them. Redemptive Gives something up for them Send something hard to one trained person instead of the feed, keep an independent route even when it takes people away from your community, and give up the engagement a public wall would bring. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review When someone shares something hard here, who hears it first, and what are they able, and obliged, to do? Exercise Write three requests: an ordinary one, one about someone else, and a worry about someone’s safety. For each option you plan to build, list everyone who will see each request, for how long, and what each of them can or must do with it. Find your church’s safeguarding contact and an independent service, and ask both to read your wording before launch. Let people choose who hears them, and make sure whoever hears something hard knows what to do with it. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further Edge cases to design for Let the person choose the audience before writing, and show who will see the request, for how long and whether it can be edited or deleted. Ask before naming someone else. Offer a route to one chosen person, with what each listener can and must do shown before sending. When a church sets the app up, name its safeguarding contact and keep an independent service beside it. Give groups ways to respond that start with listening, keep support groups’ members confidential, and send no automatic notifications about someone without asking them each time. What tends to go wrong A public feed as the default; first names and requests visible to strangers; a request about someone else posted without their consent; friends notified automatically when the app infers a low mood; a leader as the only route for a concern about the leader’s team; verses quoted back at someone who disclosed harm; hearts and counts on requests; streak boards with Praise and Remind buttons; promising confidentiality a listener cannot keep. How to test it Ask people to share an ordinary request and something hard, then to name everyone who will see each, for how long, and what each listener must do with it. Read the replies a group gives to a hard request. Find the safeguarding contact and an independent service from inside the app in under a minute. Check what notifications say, and to whom. Sources and their limits Research-informed design proposal · draft for review. Editorial review, not user validation. Richtlinie der EKD zum Schutz vor sexualisierter Gewalt (Gewaltschutzrichtlinie) Sections 2, 7 and 8 reviewed 10 October 2026 · Each Landeskirche implements the guideline in its own law, with different numbering; the EKD planned a revision in 2024. Not a statement of state law. Rahmenordnung Prävention gegen sexualisierte Gewalt Sections 3.4, 3.5 and 4 reviewed 10 October 2026 · A framework; dioceses set the details in their own Präventionsordnungen, and names for the role differ. Process personal data lawfully Official guidance reviewed · Specific lawful basis, retention and DPIA decisions require the actual data flows. What is special category data? Categories and inference guidance reviewed · Context and processing intent matter; not every Bible-page visit automatically establishes a belief. Top mental health and prayer apps fail spectacularly at privacy, security Report summary reviewed · A 2022 review; apps’ practices may have changed since. Faith and interpretation Paul asks the church to “rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15), and to “carry one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2). Job’s friends did best when they “sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights, but no one spoke a word to him because they saw how intense his suffering was” (Job 2:13). Hearing a request is a charge as well as a gift. The same passages have been used to press people to share more than they chose, or to keep concerns inside a church, so the listener’s care matters as much as the sharer’s trust. pages.description: Where should commentary and notes open? Five options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Study helps Where should commentary and notes open? Commentaries, cross-references, study notes and sermon clips can answer a question at the verse where it arises, or pull the reader away from the text for good. Where the help opens decides which. Decide how readers find help, where it opens, whose voice it carries, and how they get back to the verse. Help should serve the reader’s encounter with the text, never replace it. 5 working options 10 app examples 5 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Study helps At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From a glance to a page of its own The passage stays in view The help takes over 1 Preview card Observed + A glance without leaving − Room for a sentence Try it → 2 Sheet over the text Observed + The whole resource, verse in sight − Covers half the passage Try it → 3 Study panel Observed + Reading and study together − Half a screen each Try it → 4 Full page Familiar convention + Full attention − The passage disappears Try it → 5 On request Observed + An undisturbed text − Help may go unfound Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try five ways to open help on Psalm 23:4 Psalm 23 in the BSB. Verse 4, “the valley of the shadow of death”, has two public-domain commentaries that read it differently, a sermon clip and a cross-reference. Each option opens the same help in a different place, from a small card under the verse to a page of its own. Open it, read, then go back to the psalm and notice whether you are still on verse 4. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. Preview card · Observed 2. Sheet over the text · Observed 3. Study panel · Observed 4. Full page · Familiar convention 5. On request · Observed Option 1 Preview card Observed 2 Sheet over the text Observed 3 Study panel Observed 4 Full page Familiar convention 5 On request Observed Opens first Not used here Commentary Sermon clip Panel Not used here Follows reading Pinned Why these settings? Commentary shows who wrote it and when, and two commentaries on verse 4 disagree about what “the shadow of death” means. The sermon clip shows where the excerpt sits in the whole sermon, offers the two minutes before it, and has captions and a timestamped transcript. A following panel changes with the verse you are reading; a pinned panel stays on its verse and offers a way back to it. Observed 1. Preview card Observed in Bible Gateway, where a lettered footnote opens a small card while the passage stays visible, and in Spark Bible’s footnote tooltips; see the screenshots below. Wikipedia’s page previews work the same way. Try this Tap the marker after verse 4. Step through the four resources, then open one in full. + Makes easier A glance without leaving the verse; the reader decides whether to go further. − Costs Room for a sentence or two; a long note or a video needs somewhere else to go. Ask your team Is a short preview enough for most help, with the full resource one tap away? Observed 2. Sheet over the text Observed in Spark Bible, where a video docks over the reader with the verse still showing, and in the VSB prototype’s verse sheet; see the screenshots below. Try this Open the help on verse 4, switch to the sermon clip, then expand the sheet and come back. + Makes easier Room for the whole resource while the verse stays in sight above it. − Costs Covers half the passage; easy to lose track of which verse the sheet belongs to. Ask your team When the sheet is open, can the reader still see the verse it is about? Observed 3. Study panel Observed in Olive Tree’s Study Center, whose Resource Guide follows the passage in a panel below the text; see the screenshot below. Try this Scroll the psalm and watch the panel follow you. Then pin it in the settings and scroll again. + Makes easier Reading and study side by side; resources keep up with the reader. − Costs Half a screen each on a phone; a following panel changes under you, a pinned one goes stale. Ask your team Does the reader always know which verse the panel is showing, and why it changed? Familiar convention 4. Full page A familiar convention: the resource opens on its own page, and Back returns to the verse. Try this Open the help on verse 4, read the commentary, then go back. + Makes easier Full attention and room for long commentary and video. − Costs The passage disappears; the reader must find their way back and pick up the thread. Ask your team Does Back return the reader to the same verse, and show them where they were? Observed 5. On request Observed in Spark Bible’s and Mere Bible’s reading settings, which let readers switch resource markers off. Here nothing marks the text; a Study button lists everything on the psalm. Try this Read the psalm, then open Study from the top bar and choose a resource. + Makes easier An undisturbed text; help is there when someone asks for it. − Costs People may never discover what is available; help is no longer tied to a verse at a glance. Ask your team Can someone who wants help find it, without the help interrupting everyone else? i Psalm 23 in the Berean Standard Bible (public domain). Commentary from Matthew Henry’s Concise Commentary (1706) and A. F. Kirkpatrick’s Cambridge Bible (1891), both public domain, quoted from their published text. The sermon, speaker and church were written for this example; nothing plays. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Keep the verse in sight, or bring the reader back to it People learn more when related material is placed together, and interruptions are paid for in stress and lost threads. A preview under the verse or a sheet that leaves it visible keeps the two together. When help takes the whole screen, Back should land on the same verse and show it. A panel must say what it is following Olive Tree’s Resource Guide follows the passage; a pinned panel stays on its verse. Both are useful, and both confuse when the reader cannot tell which is happening. Say “Following your reading” or “Pinned · Go to verse”. Markers are an invitation, not a menu Every link is a decision, and a review of 38 hypertext experiments found that the extra load falls hardest on readers with less background knowledge. Mark verses with help quietly, as Spark Bible does on Psalm 23:4, and let people switch markers off, as Spark and Mere Bible do. Whose voice is beside the text? Medieval glossed Bibles set the commentary around the text in a smaller hand; the King James translators kept interpretive notes out of the margin altogether. On screen, name the kind of resource, its author and date, and where readings differ, as Matthew Henry and the Cambridge Bible do on verse 4, show more than one. A clip is part of a whole A minute of a sermon can mean something different from the sermon. Show where the clip sits, offer what came before, and caption it. Spark Bible’s timestamped transcripts are useful, but its automatic transcription is visibly wrong in places (“Full Or Theological Seminary”); correct a transcript before anyone quotes it. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. How well each option fits each situation Situation Needs 1 Preview card 2 Sheet over the text 3 Study panel 4 Full page 5 On request Daily devotional reading Help only when wanted ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit ● Good fit A quick question on a verse Glance and carry on ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Poor fit Group or sermon preparation Several voices, read in full Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Study on a tablet or desktop Text and help side by side Poor fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit Poor fit Poor fit Watching teaching on a verse Media with its context Poor fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible ● Good fit ◐ Possible 200% text or a screen reader Clear focus and a way back ◐ Possible ◐ Possible Poor fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ● Good fit ◐ Possible Poor fit Editorial judgments drawing on the research below, not test results. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and history Help beside the text Giving the sense Nehemiah 8:8; Acts 8:30–31. Scripture shows readers helped to understand as they read. Text in the centre, help around it Glossed Bibles separated Scripture and commentary by place and script; the King James translators allowed no interpretive notes in the margin. R DeStefano and LeFevre Together, not apart Related material placed together is learned better. R Noah L. Schroeder and Ada T. Cenkci Interruptions cost People compensate for interruptions with speed, stress and effort. R Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke Practice and access Products and standards Preview before leaving Wikipedia’s page previews let readers check a link without leaving the article. A W3C WAI D W3C WAI Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If Most help is short: footnotes, cross-references, a first look Start with A preview card under the verse, with the full resource one tap away If People read commentary or watch teaching on a phone Start with A sheet that leaves the verse in sight and expands on request If People study for long stretches on larger screens Start with A study panel that says whether it follows the reading or is pinned If Resources are long or need full attention Start with A full page whose Back returns to the same verse and shows it If The app is mainly for devotional reading Start with No markers by default; help on request, from one clear place These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. Olive Tree · macOS A study workspace beside the passage Publisher help screenshot Bible Gateway · Desktop web A footnote preview inside the passage Direct web capture VSB · Android 17 · Pixel 8 Pro · German interface A verse sheet combines media evidence and a summary Direct Android prototype capture VSB · Android 17 · Pixel 8 Pro · German interface A selection survives returning from its study sheet Direct Android prototype capture Mere Bible (formerly NeuBible) · Mobile interface · device and OS not independently verified Reading settings in a bottom drawer User-contributed screenshot · unedited ESV Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded Audio playlists by feeling User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Spark Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded A small media marker on Psalm 23:4 User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Spark Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded A video docked over the passage User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Spark Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded A timestamped transcript, with recognition errors User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Olive Tree Bible · iOS app · device model not recorded A Resource Guide panel below the text User-contributed screenshot · resized, content unchanged Explore the growing app-example collection Theological reflection What is this practice for? What help is for The Levites read the Law, “explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read” (Nehemiah 8:8). The Ethiopian asked, “How can I … unless someone guides me?” (Acts 8:31). The risen Jesus “explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself” (Luke 24:27). Help is part of how Scripture is received, and the Bereans still “examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true” (Acts 17:11). Where Christians differ Catholic canon law allows translations prepared with other Christians to be published “provided with appropriate annotations”. The King James translators allowed no interpretive notes at all, after the Geneva Bible’s notes were judged partisan. Protestant traditions affirm that Scripture is clear enough to read without an interpreter, while valuing teachers; Catholic and Orthodox traditions read Scripture within the church’s teaching. What follows for design Every note carries a voice and a tradition. Name the author, date and tradition, keep the help visibly beside the text and not inside it, and always return the reader to the verse. Offering more than one voice respects readers as Bereans who can weigh what they hear. In conversation with Augustine, On Christian Doctrine I.36.40 held that whoever interprets Scripture in a way that does not “build up this twofold love of God and our neighbor, does not yet understand them as he ought.” Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum (1965) asks for editions “provided with suitable footnotes”, even for readers outside the church: help is part of access. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person Sponsored or in-house commentary appears without an author and crowds out the text. Ethical Does no harm Name author, date and tradition, and always return to the verse. Redemptive Gives something up for them Include trusted voices from other traditions and the global church, not only the publisher’s own. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review Does the reader know who is speaking, which verse the help is about, and how to get back to it? Exercise Give three readers Psalm 23:4 with your app’s help on it. Ask each to open it, say who wrote it and when, and return to reading. Note who lands on the same verse. Then play a sermon clip and the minute before it, and ask whether the meaning changed. Good help sends the reader back to the verse with more than they came with. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further This deep dive brings together 3 earlier patterns. Their guidance, wireframes and sources are kept below; their old addresses lead here. Edge cases to design for Start with a short preview anchored to the verse, with the full resource one tap away. For longer help, use a sheet that leaves the verse visible, or a study panel on larger screens, and say whether the panel follows the reading or is pinned. If help takes the whole screen, make Back return to the same verse and show it. Mark verses with resources quietly, and let readers turn markers off. Show the kind of resource, its author and date, and where several voices disagree, show more than one. For media, show where the clip sits in the whole, offer what came before, and provide captions and a corrected transcript. What tends to go wrong A commentary styled like Scripture; no author or date; markers on every verse; autoplaying video between verses; a panel that changes without saying so; Back that returns to the top of the chapter; a 30-second clip presented as the speaker’s whole view; automatic transcripts quoted uncorrected; locked resources shown as if available. How to test it Ask readers to open help on a verse, read it and return; note whether they are on the same verse. Ask who wrote the help and when. Scroll with a following panel and ask why it changed. Watch a clip, then the two minutes before, and ask whether the meaning changed. Test with captions, a screen reader and 200% text. Earlier pattern: Preview before deep study Reveal relevant information from a passage without replacing the reader. Guidance Offer a small selection action menu, then preview the relevant resource before deeper study. Let a linked panel either follow the passage or remain pinned, with its current anchor visible. What tends to go wrong A panel silently following a different verse; a resource opened without source context; a crowded selection menu that prevents reading. How to test it Test moving between verses with a linked and pinned panel. Can readers identify the panel’s anchor and recover the main reading task? Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Guidance Choose the visibility of supplementary material by the reading task. Keep it clearly separate from Scripture, with author and type visible. Offer a quiet reading mode. A hidden-on-selection design still needs a discoverable Resources action and keyboard and assistive-technology access. What tends to go wrong A teaching card mistaken for part of the translation; unexplained icons; autoplay between verses; a gesture-only resource menu; locked material presented as already available. How to test it Ask a new reader to find supplementary content, identify its author, hide it and resume at the same verse. Compare continuous reading with an intentional study task; include unavailable and paid resources. Earlier wireframe comparison, kept for reference. Faith and interpretation Scripture itself shows readers helped beside the text: the Levites “read from the Book of the Law of God, explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read” (Nehemiah 8:8), and the Ethiopian asked, “How can I … unless someone guides me?” (Acts 8:31). The medieval Glossa Ordinaria set the text in the centre of the page and the commentary around it, in a smaller hand. The King James translators allowed no interpretive notes in the margin, only notes on words and cross-references, because the Geneva Bible’s notes were thought partisan. Where help sits, and whose voice it carries, has always been a theological question as well as a layout one. pages.title: Translations
pages.description: One at a time, side by side or verse by verse? Five options side by side, from apps in use today to leaving a feature out, with the research and a working example.
pages.text: Patterns Translations One at a time, side by side or verse by verse? In John 1:5 the KJV says the darkness “comprehended it not”; most recent translations say it “has not overcome it”. Both are faithful to one Greek word. Apps decide whether readers ever see that, how they choose a translation, and whether they stay on the same verse while they compare. Bringing God’s word into people’s own language is one of the church’s oldest callings; an interface can honour the translators’ care or hide it. 5 working options 8 app examples 5 takeaways Editorial review, not user-tested Translations At a glance Try it Takeaways Use cases Research Which fits Examples Reflection Three ways Decide Go further The spectrum From one translation to the Greek One translation at a time Closer to the original 1 One translation Observed + One clear text, chosen well − The alternatives stay hidden Try it → 2 Switch in place Familiar convention + Check a verse without leaving − One wording at a time Try it → 3 Verse by verse Observed + Differences at a glance − Reading becomes comparing Try it → 4 Parallel panes Observed + Two continuous texts − Half a screen each Try it → 5 Interlinear Familiar convention + Shows why they differ − Glosses pose as meaning Try it → Stills from the working example below. Choose one to try it. Try it Try five ways to compare John 1:1–5 John 1:5 in the KJV says the darkness “comprehended it not”; most recent translations say it “has not overcome it”. Each option shows John 1:1–5 in public-domain translations, from one translation chosen well to the Greek with a gloss under every word. Find out why verse 5 differs. Prototype controls ↺ Restart Option 1. One translation · Observed 2. Switch in place · Familiar convention 3. Verse by verse · Observed 4. Parallel panes · Observed 5. Interlinear · Familiar convention Option 1 One translation Observed 2 Switch in place Familiar convention 3 Verse by verse Observed 4 Parallel panes Observed 5 Interlinear Familiar convention Compare with Not used here BSB YLT WEB Mark differences Not used here Marked Plain Scrolling Not used here Linked by verse Independent Rows Not used here Greek and gloss Add transliteration and grammar Why these settings? All four English translations here are in the public domain: KJV, the Berean Standard Bible (dedicated in 2023), the World English Bible and Young’s Literal Translation. Most modern translations are licensed; the ESV, for example, allows up to 500 verses to be quoted without permission. Marked words are those that do not appear in the KJV verse at all. Observed 1. One translation Observed in Hallow (suggested Bibles with notes on each) and Mere Bible (a sheet of full names); see the screenshots below. The scale of approaches is our addition. Try this Open the translation menu and read what distinguishes each one. Choose one. + Makes easier One clear text, chosen with enough context to choose well; nothing to compare or reconcile. − Costs Readers never see that verse 5 can be read two ways. Ask your team What does a reader need to know to choose a translation, and when? Familiar convention 2. Switch in place A familiar convention in most Bible apps: a translation switch above the text. Keeping the selected verse in place follows the earlier “change translation without losing the passage” pattern. Try this Verse 5 is selected. Switch to the other translation and watch where verse 5 lands. + Makes easier Quick to check one verse in another wording without leaving the reading. − Costs Only one wording is visible at a time; readers must remember the other. Ask your team When someone switches, which verse is the anchor: the one they selected, or the one at the top? Observed 3. Verse by verse Observed in Lumen Bible, which groups translations under each verse (see the screenshot below). Try this Scroll to verse 5. Then switch “Mark differences” off and on. + Makes easier Both wordings side by side, verse by verse; differences are easy to spot. − Costs Breaks the flow of the passage; reading becomes comparing. Ask your team Is the reader comparing wording, or trying to follow the passage? Observed 4. Parallel panes Observed in YouVersion’s web parallel view and Olive Tree’s split screen (an ASV pane synced under a German text); see the screenshots below. On a phone, panes stack so lines stay readable. Try this Scroll the top pane, then switch scrolling to “Independent” and scroll again. + Makes easier Each translation reads as continuous text; linked panes keep them on the same verse. − Costs Half the screen for each; panes drift apart unless linked by verse, not by pixels. Ask your team Do the panes follow each other, and how does a reader get them back together? Familiar convention 5. Interlinear A familiar convention in study tools such as Bible Hub, STEP Bible and Logos. The Greek here is Scrivener’s Textus Receptus; the glosses are our own. Try this Tap the highlighted word in verse 5. Then add transliteration and grammar. + Makes easier Shows why translations differ: one Greek word, κατέλαβεν, can mean grasp or overcome. − Costs Glosses look like a translation and invite word-by-word meanings that the language does not support. Ask your team Who is this for, and what stops a gloss from being read as the meaning? i John 1:1–5 only. The approach scale and all glosses were written for this example; a real interlinear needs a licensed or open lexical dataset and specialist review. Hebrew, which reads right to left, needs its own testing. Switching options restarts the example from the same starting point. What we noticed Takeaways Comparing translations is an old discipline The 1611 KJV translators, quoting Augustine, held that variety of translations helps find the sense of Scripture, and printed alternatives in the margin. Lamin Sanneh argued that translatability is at the heart of Christian mission. Showing that translations differ is not a threat to trust. Choosing needs more than abbreviations Readers choose between approaches without knowing it: Nida’s formal and dynamic equivalence still describe the range. Show full name, date and approach when people choose, as Hallow does with short notes. The full Bible exists in 776 languages, so pickers must handle many languages and partial Bibles. Keep the verse, not the scroll position Different wording changes text height, so switching or scrolling by pixels lands on a different verse. Anchor on the selected or visible verse; in parallel panes, link by verse and offer a way to realign, as Olive Tree’s linked split screen does. Two columns on a phone are too narrow Very short lines are read more slowly. On a phone, stack panes so each keeps a readable line, and group translations under each verse when the task is comparing wording. A gloss is not the meaning Barr and Carson warn against reading meaning from a single gloss or a word’s root. Label interlinear rows, call glosses word aids, and show how translations actually render a word, as κατέλαβεν shows in John 1:5. Use cases Which situation, which option? People come with different needs, sometimes in the same week. Each need fits some options better than others. The research behind it Theology, practice and science Scripture and history Read in translation from the start Translation is the Christian norm Pentecost was heard in every hearer’s own language (Acts 2:6); the KJV preface defends variety of translations; Sanneh calls translatability intrinsic to mission. H Miles Smith for the KJV translators, 1611 T Lamin Sanneh How translations are made Formal and dynamic equivalence describe a range most translations sit within. S Eugene Nida, 1964 Many languages, partial Bibles The full Bible in 776 languages, the New Testament in 1,798 more. S Wycliffe Global Alliance Reading and comparing What the research says Comparing is demanding Building one understanding from several texts is a distinct skill; help readers connect them. R Liron Primor and Tami Katzir Line length Very short lines slow reading; avoid narrow columns on phones. R Mary Dyson and Gary Kipping Words mean in context Root and gloss fallacies: meaning comes from usage, not etymology. S Wisconsin Lutheran Seminary, reviewing Carson (1984) and James Barr’s The Semantics of Biblical Language (1961) Licensing and access Best practice Licences limit comparison The BSB is public domain; the ESV allows up to 500 verses without a licence. S Berean Bible S Crossway Language and layout Tag Greek and Hebrew with their language; content must reflow at 200%; keep versification mappings. A W3C WAI D W3C WAI D USFM documentation Every source, with what it can and cannot show, is listed under Go further → Sources and their limits. Where to start Which fits your product? If Most reading products Start with One translation, chosen with name, approach and date in view If Readers check a verse in another wording Start with Switch in place, keeping the selected verse as the anchor If Groups and preachers compare wording Start with Verse by verse, with differences marked If People read two translations through Start with Stacked panes linked by verse, with realign If Study and teaching preparation Start with Interlinear with named rows and word detail; glosses labelled as aids These are editorial judgments from design review, not results of user testing. In real apps Examples in use Attributed screenshots with dates and review limits. A screenshot shows an implementation; it does not show that it works for every audience. What translation is for At Pentecost the crowd asked, “How is it then that each of us hears them in his own native language?” (Acts 2:8). The vision of Revelation includes “every nation and tribe and people and tongue” (Revelation 7:9). Christianity has no sacred original language for worship: the New Testament itself quotes the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures. Lamin Sanneh argued that this translatability is part of the gospel’s character. Where Christians differ Churches differ on which translations may be used in worship: Catholic canon law requires that editions of Scripture be approved by the Apostolic See or the bishops’ conference, while most Protestant churches leave the choice to congregations. Some hold to a single historic translation; the Orthodox read the Old Testament from the Septuagint. Translators differ on how closely to follow the form of the original. The 1611 translators defended variety as a help to understanding. What follows for design Comparing translations is an old discipline, not a sign of doubt. Show what kind of translation each is and who approved it, keep the reader on the same verse, and show where translations disagree rather than hiding it. Treat languages that do not pay for themselves as part of the mission, not a market decision. In conversation with Martin Luther, Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen (1530) told translators to ask “die Mutter im Hause, die Kinder auf der Gasse, den gemeinen Mann auf dem Markt” and listen to how they speak: translation serves the hearer. Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum (1965) opens its chapter on Scripture in the life of the church: “Easy access to Sacred Scripture should be provided for all the Christian faithful.” Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. This reflection is the editor’s, written from within the Christian tradition and open to correction. How we approach theology here → Three ways to build What would each way do here? Exploitative Takes from the person One translation is sold as “the real meaning”; others sit behind a paywall to upsell. Ethical Does no harm Name each translation and its approach, and keep the verse in place while comparing. Redemptive Gives something up for them License heart-language translations that will never pay for themselves, and show readers where translations disagree even when it complicates the product. The three ways are Praxis’s frame for redemptive entrepreneurship; their application here is ours. Why we use it, and its limits → Take into your next review Does the reader know what kind of translation this is, and stay on the same verse while comparing? Exercise Pick a verse your translations disagree on. Ask three people to find out why, using your app. Note where they lose the verse, and whether anyone reads a gloss as the real meaning. Behind every translation are people who gave years so others could hear God in their own language. Let readers see that care. Record the decision with the worksheet → Something missing or wrong here? Send a correction or suggest a topic . Details Go further This deep dive brings together 6 earlier patterns. Their guidance, wireframes and sources are kept below; their old addresses lead here. Edge cases to design for Show full names, approach and date when people choose, and say which translations are available offline or with audio. When switching, keep the selected or visible verse in place. For checking wording, group translations under each verse and mark what differs. For reading two texts, use full-width panes stacked on a phone, linked by verse with a clear way to unlink and realign. Offer interlinear for study, with each row named, glosses labelled as word aids, and word detail that shows how translations render a word. Respect licensing and versification. What tends to go wrong Abbreviation-only lists; switching that jumps to the chapter start; side-by-side columns of 20 characters on a phone; panes linked by scroll position; marking every reordered word as different; glosses presented as the meaning; Greek or Hebrew without a language tag or right-to-left support; quoting licensed translations beyond their limits. How to test it Ask readers to explain the difference between two translations they chose. Switch with a verse selected, while reading and while listening, and check the place is kept. Compare a verse in each layout at 200% text size. Ask readers what a gloss means, and whether it is “the real meaning”. Test Hebrew with right-to-left reading and a screen reader. Earlier pattern: Choose a translation with enough context Make language, edition and availability understandable before switching. Guidance Search by full name and abbreviation, group by language when useful, and show the active edition. Use a short favourites list for frequent switching with a clear route to all editions. Separate choosing an edition from downloading or starting audio. A short catalogue may need only a popover list, without search. A large multilingual collection may use language → edition drill-down, with optional favourites or downloaded filters. Confirm an unavailable passage before switching editions. What tends to go wrong Replacing an unavailable edition silently; presenting a popularity ranking as theological authority; losing the current passage; unclear download size or licence constraints. How to test it Choose an unfamiliar edition, find a known abbreviation, cancel a download and change editions offline. Confirm the chosen text and retained reference. Faith and interpretation Christianity has always been read in translation: the New Testament quotes the Greek Septuagint, and at Pentecost “each one heard them speaking his own language” (Acts 2:6). The 1611 translators, quoting Augustine, held that variety of translations helps readers find the sense of Scripture. Lamin Sanneh argued that translatability is at the heart of Christian mission: no language is too common for the word of God. Comparing translations is an old discipline, not a sign of doubt. pages.title: A passage and a song
pages.description: A morning devotional format from Aperto: one bounded passage and one song written from the same exegesis, with Mary’s song (Luke 1:46–56) as the worked example.
pages.text: Prototypes Experiment · Aperto A passage and a song A morning devotional format from Aperto: about five minutes that open the day with one bounded passage and one song written from the same exegetical work. Not a verse of the day with music behind it — the reading and the song come from one study of the text. One passage One song About 5 minutes Audio-first, screen optional Reviewed 8 October 2026 Format study, not a recommendation What the format is On the page for Mary’s song (Luke 1:46–56), the Morning Devotional is labelled “A passage and a song to begin your day”, about five minutes long. It sits beside a three-minute podcast, the song itself, an eight-minute Evening Reflection and a ten-minute Spiritual Practice — five ways into the same passage, each with its own duration and its own address. What makes this a format rather than a playlist is the shared origin. Aperto builds a deep exegesis for each passage — the Greek text, commentaries across traditions, cultural and historical background — and produces translation, context and multimedia from that one base. The morning devotional is the day-opening member of that family: small enough for a real morning, bounded enough to finish. Most devotional apps pair a short verse with reflective text and a music bed chosen by mood. Here the music is not a mood bed. The song is a second reading of the same passage, written from its exegesis — which is precisely what makes the format worth studying. The example: Mary’s song The worked example is the strongest possible case: a passage that is already a song. Luke puts the reversal at its centre — He acted in strength. He scattered the proud, caught in their own plans. He brought the powerful down from their thrones. He raised up the forgotten ones. He filled the hungry with good things. He sent the rich away empty. Luke 1:51–53 · Aperto translation, quoted unchanged · CC BY-ND 4.0 · aperto.bible Two of the family members make the morning format concrete. The devotional pairs the passage with the day-opening frame; the song “The Nobody” is where the exegesis becomes music. Its title answers to the passage’s own note on verse 48, where ταπείνωσιν names Mary’s social location — “the girl from nowhere” — rather than the virtue of humility. Whether the lyrics actually make that connection is checkable: Aperto publishes a transcript with the song. Recorded example · served from aperto.bible Morning Devotional “A passage and a song to begin your day” · 5 min as labelled · Mary’s Song, Luke 1:46–56 As offered on the passage page . If playback fails here, listen there. Recorded example · served from aperto.bible The Nobody Neo-Soul Hip-Hop · 3:48 · “The overlooked become the voice of revolution” · with lyrics and a published transcript As offered on the passage page . If playback fails here, listen there. The direction of travel is what distinguishes this from background music: the song is meant to send you back to the text with a sharper question — does the song’s energy match the verbs of reversal, or does it smooth them? Questions the format raises Sequence. Does the listener know when the passage ends and the song begins — and can they replay one without the other? Authority. A song is interpretation in a form that disarms scrutiny. Whose reading is it, and is that labelled where the listening happens? Length. Five minutes is a decision about mornings, not a neutral default. Some mornings have four minutes; some have forty. The ending. What follows the last second — silence, a replay, or the next item in the family? Dependence. If the song is the hook, does the text ever get read on its own? Take into your next review If you borrow the format, borrow its grounding: one bounded passage, its exegesis, and a song that could not exist without both. Try it Open Mary’s song and listen to the morning devotional with the screen off. Then read Luke 1:46–56 and open the song’s transcript. Check one lyrical claim against the passage and the notes. Notice what the song made you hear — and what only the text settled. Record the decision with the worksheet → Details Go further Provenance, rights and limits Observed on the public page at aperto.bible on 8 October 2026. The audio and cover art are served directly from aperto.bible, and the live page may change at any time. Aperto describes its workflow as AI-assisted and human-accountable. The translation text is licensed CC BY-ND 4.0 and is quoted here unchanged and attributed; the song, audio and artwork remain Aperto content, embedded as review material. Aperto is an author-associated project, as disclosed on the about page . This experiment studies the author’s own product; it does not establish that the format improves engagement, comprehension or formation, and it does not recommend shipping it in every app. Keep exploring Related Listening grounded in the text: the wider experiment → Mary’s Song — the live passage page on aperto.bible → The hearing Scripture pattern family → AI podcasts and source-grounded audio → Observed on the public page at aperto.bible on 8 October 2026; descriptions of the audio items come from Aperto’s own labels, not from transcribing or evaluating their content. pages.text: Prototypes Some ideas are easier to judge once you can touch them. This page holds creative interface experiments: unfinished, sometimes playful, and always labelled as exploration rather than recommendation. Experiments Rocks that cry out A logo study: a silicon rock, wider at the base, that slowly turns and throws a cross-shaped glint when a facet catches the light. After Luke 19:40, the Berlin TV tower’s “Pope’s revenge” and the star filters of photographers. pages.title: Listening grounded in the text
pages.description: Experiments from Aperto, where generated devotional audio stays tied to the passage and the commentary behind it. Mary’s song, Luke 1:46–56, as the worked example.
pages.text: Prototypes Experiment · Aperto Listening grounded in the text Experiments from Aperto, where generated devotional audio stays tied to the passage and the commentary behind it. One page — Mary’s song, Luke 1:46–56 — carries a whole family of listening: read it, hear it discussed, hear it sung, pray with it in the morning and at night. One passage 5 audio formats Study notes in five categories Live example · reviewed 8 October 2026 Editorial observation, not user-tested The example One passage, a whole family of listening On the page for Mary’s song (Luke 1:46–56), Aperto anchors everything to one bounded passage. Reading, study and listening share that spine: a literary translation with visibly woven context, footnotes in five labelled categories, and a set of generated audio formats — each with its own address, so a single item can be shared without losing the passage it belongs to. The listening family on one Aperto passage page Item As labelled on the page Podcast · 3 min A short generated discussion of the passage. The Nobody · 3:48 An original song (Neo-Soul Hip-Hop), “The overlooked become the voice of revolution”, with lyrics and a published transcript. Morning Devotional · 5 min “A passage and a song to begin your day.” Evening Reflection · 8 min “A quiet moment to close your day.” Spiritual Practice · 10 min A longer guided practice on the same passage. The podcast is the purest case of the experiment: generated talk, grounded in the same exegetical work as the translation, and living under the passage it explains rather than in a feed that moves on. Recorded example · served from aperto.bible Podcast Mary’s Song, Luke 1:46–56 · 3 min as labelled As offered on the passage page . If playback fails here, listen there. The grounding The text underneath Everything above rests on a page that keeps its layers distinguishable — the same rule this reference asks of any app. Woven context is visually marked so you know what is Scripture and what is enrichment; the footnotes name their category (Text, Culture, Context, Life, Difficult) and anchor to verses. Verse 47 reads “God is my rescuer”, and the note on σωτήρ explains why the concrete “one who pulls you out” was chosen over the churchly abstraction “savior”. The opening of the song: Everything in me celebrates God. Everything. My whole spirit, awake. God is my rescuer. He saw me. Me. His servant, nobody, from nowhere. And now: every generation will call me happy. The Mighty One did this. For me. His name: holy. Luke 1:46–49 · Aperto translation, quoted unchanged · CC BY-ND 4.0 · aperto.bible The question the page silently answers: can every generated minute be traced back to the text and the sources it came from? Here the route exists by construction — each listening item belongs to the passage, and the study layer is one tap away. Whether a listener ever uses that route is the open question. What this explores Auditable listening. Generated audio as interpretation you can check, not a broadcast you can only accept: every claim has a passage and a note behind it. A shared spine. Reading, discussion, song and prayer anchored to one passage unit — instead of a daily feed that leaves the passage behind. Does the family reinforce the reading, or quietly replace it? A song as exegesis. The title “The Nobody” answers to the passage’s own note on verse 48, where ταπείνωσιν names Mary’s social location — “the girl from nowhere” — rather than the virtue of humility. Can a song carry a scholarly observation better than a paragraph? Rhythm without pressure. Morning and evening shapes are offered on one page, with no streak and no feed; the passage ends, and nothing autoplays on. What it does not establish No user testing: there is no measured effect on comprehension, memory or formation anywhere behind this page. Aperto is an author-associated project — Tobias Treppmann works on both Aperto and this reference. Treat this as a worked prototype under review, not independent evidence. Generation quality varies. A sibling Aperto reflection prototype was recorded returning “Generation failed” on a documented attempt ( observed example ). A generated discussion is interpretation. Keeping it distinguishable from a recording of the text itself is a standing design burden, not a solved problem. Formats and files may change at any time; observations are dated 8 October 2026. Take into your next review Could a listener check every generated sentence against the passage it claims to explain? Try it Read Luke 1:46–56 first. Then listen to one item — the podcast or the morning devotional — with the screen off. Open the study notes afterwards and pick one claim; try to find where it comes from. If the route back is easy, the grounding is real. If you give up, it is decoration. pages.title: Rocks that cry out
pages.description: A logo study: a slowly turning silicon rock that throws a cross-shaped glint when a facet catches the light.
pages.text: Prototypes Rocks that cry out A logo study for Bible & Faith Patterns “If they remain silent, the very stones will cry out” (Luke 19:40). Programmers like to say a microchip is a rock we tricked into thinking. This study turns a faceted silicon rock slowly in the light. When a facet mirrors the light towards you, it shines as a cross, the way sunlight on the Berlin TV tower’s steel sphere does, and the way a photographer’s star filter shapes a sun star. What it is made of An irregular convex rock, generated from fixed points so every visitor sees the same one, wider at the base and flattened at both ends. A metallic, blue-grey material with a faint interference sheen, like a polished silicon wafer, lit by a studio environment. Each frame, the facet that mirrors the light into the camera receives a Latin-cross glint; its brightness follows how exactly it mirrors. It pauses when off screen, and shows one still frame, turned to its brightest cross, for people who prefer reduced motion. A study, not yet the site’s logo. The cross shines best on a dark ground; on white, the beams beyond the rock disappear.

pages.title: Make room for rest, and say when it is enough
pages.description: A faithful product sometimes asks for less: it ends a session, keeps the night quiet, stops asking when the need is met, and lets itself end when its work is done.
pages.text: On this page From the calling Scripture and tradition In and out Test a design In the deep dives Home / Principles Missional by Design · The practice Make room for rest, and say when it is enough A faithful product sometimes asks for less: it ends a session, keeps the night quiet, stops asking when the need is met, and lets itself end when its work is done. From the calling Leave room for rest Keep a sabbath from shipping Scripture and tradition “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27). When the people kept bringing offerings for the tabernacle Bezalel built, Moses “sent a proclamation throughout the camp”, and “the people were restrained from bringing more, since what they already had was more than enough to perform all the work” (Exodus 36:6–7). The Rule of Benedict keeps silence especially at night. FaithTech’s practice of stewardship includes “choosing not to release a product or allowing one to end”. Sources: The Rule of Benedict · The FaithTech Playbook What it rules in, and out In Sessions that end in silence instead of autoplay Quiet hours; after silence, ask once and stop An appeal that says when the need is met A regular gift or subscription as easy to stop as to start Out An endless feed of devotional content Reminders that multiply when someone stops answering Asking again and again What the maker gives up. Time in the app, and the comfort of a product that never has to end. Qualification. Some people want more: a long listen, a full plan. Enough is the person’s to choose; the product’s part is to offer an end and keep it. Test a design Where does our product stop, and does it ever tell someone they have done enough? What would we stop sending if we believed rest is a gift? pages.title: Feed the flock, not on it
pages.description: Attention, time, devotion and money are entrusted, not harvested. Ask for them honestly, never through guilt, fear, urgency or a promise.
pages.text: On this page From the calling Scripture and tradition In and out Test a design In the deep dives Home / Principles Missional by Design · The practice Feed the flock, not on it Attention, time, devotion and money are entrusted, not harvested. Ask for them honestly, never through guilt, fear, urgency or a promise. From the calling The burden: shepherds who feed themselves Attention is entrusted, not harvested Scripture and tradition “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2). “Feed My sheep” (John 21:17). “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Praxis asks builders to make “what people want to want”, instead of products that appeal to “our most self-centered, lonely, addictive tendencies”. FaithTech names the tools of the reckless posture: “Dopamine loops, infinite scrolling, doomscrolling, echo-chamber, and engineered dependencies”. faith.tools asks that any cost be “very clear”. Sources: The Redemptive Business playbook: products · The FaithTech Playbook · faith.tools selection criteria What it rules in, and out In Reminders the person sets; streaks that can be switched off; a return without shame Gifts that start at no amount; prices that say what they pay for An honest free allowance, and a subscription that is easy to end Out Broken-streak warnings marked urgent “We miss you” in a persona’s voice Preselected tiers and added tips; asks after a prayer request Weekly plans, hidden renewals and hard cancellation What the maker gives up. The daily users, conversions and revenue that pressure would bring. Qualification. Asking is not wrong: the church has always supported those who serve the word, and a chosen rhythm can help. The line is crossed when the ask uses guilt, fear, a moment of need or God’s name. Test a design Does this serve growth in faith, or only the usage numbers? Freedom or anxiety? Would someone who was short of money, or grieving, feel pressed by this screen? pages.title: Plant and water; leave the growth to God
pages.description: Measure what serves the person and the task. Never score a soul, and never claim the fruit as yours.
pages.text: On this page From the calling Scripture and tradition In and out Test a design In the deep dives Home / Principles Missional by Design · The people Plant and water; leave the growth to God Measure what serves the person and the task. Never score a soul, and never claim the fruit as yours. From the calling We plant and water; God gives the growth The app is a means, not the destination Scripture and tradition “Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God, who makes things grow” (1 Corinthians 3:7). The seed “sprouts and grows, though he knows not how” (Mark 4:27). “So My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty” (Isaiah 55:11). Dallas Willard distinguished effort from earning. FaithTech warns of the Killer App Trap, “the belief that technology will solve our deepest problems”. Sources: Spiritual Disciplines and Means of Grace: Contrast or Continuum? · The FaithTech Playbook What it rules in, and out In Honest evaluation of usability, understanding, burden and harm Accounts people choose to give Saying what the product does not know Out Faith scores and maturity levels inferred from use Global prayer counters as achievements Usage presented as spiritual fruit “Life-changing” claims without evidence What the maker gives up. The impressive number for the pitch. Qualification. Humility is not a reason to avoid evaluation. Measure usability, safety and understanding carefully; it is spiritual maturity that no telemetry can show. Test a design What would we stop measuring if we believed growth is God’s? Will the person’s motivation survive removing the feature?
