pages.title: Missional by Design: principles for spiritual apps
pages.description: Ten commitments in five places, derived from the calling to build Bible, prayer, church and AI apps, and read through Praxis’s Redemptive Frame.
pages.text: On this page Why, what, how Five places, ten commitments Three ways to build In conversation with How the eight became the ten When principles pull apart Use them in a review Home / Principles Missional by Design · Principles Missional by Design: principles for spiritual apps Five places where a Bible, prayer, church or AI app takes a posture, and two commitments in each, derived from the calling to build these tools. Generated editorial illustration · fictional people and place Draft · waiting for review What needs review: The ten principles and their derivations, the reading of Praxis’s three ways for spiritual apps, the qualification that the church’s written prayers are not what “Never speak for God” forbids, and the voices of Orthodox and Pentecostal theology, not yet represented. This touches the safety of people who may already be hurting, and it has not yet been reviewed by people whose work this is: theology across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions; and pastoral care. Please read it as a draft until they have. Is this your field, or do you know someone whose field it is? I would be grateful for your eyes on it, or for an introduction. Offer a review or an introduction Why, what, how The calling says why this work matters and how heavy it is. These principles say what we hold, with questions to test a design. The deep dives show how, option by option. Every principle names what it asks the maker to give up: that is the thread through all ten. Generated illustration · based on Startup Life photography Five places, ten commitments The Word What do we put in front of people as God’s word, or about it? Keep the Word distinct, and teach it truly Every screen teaches. Let readers always tell Scripture from our words, and our words from a machine’s. Never speak for God An app may quote, explain, pray the church’s prayers and point. It must never pronounce, promise or plead in God’s name, nor let a persona or a machine take the place of a person or of God. Generated editorial illustration · fictional people and place The person How do we receive the one holding the phone? Design for the most vulnerable first Design first for the person most likely to be hurt: in crisis, grieving, abused, scrupulous, new to faith, hurt by a church, or, where an app serves them, a child. Help comes before features, verses or answers. Welcome before you ask, and guard what is told in confidence Let people reach what they came for before asking anything; ask only for what serves them, when it does; and treat what they tell you as holy ground. The practice What do we ask of their time, attention and money, and when do we stop? Feed the flock, not on it Attention, time, devotion and money are entrusted, not harvested. Ask for them honestly, never through guilt, fear, urgency or a promise. Make room for rest, and say when it is enough A faithful product sometimes asks for less: it ends a session, keeps the night quiet, stops asking when the need is met, and lets itself end when its work is done. The people Where do we send them, and what do we claim to have grown? Send people to God and to one another The app is a means, never the destination. Judge it by where people go when they close it. Plant and water; leave the growth to God Measure what serves the person and the task. Never score a soul, and never claim the fruit as yours. The makers Who are we becoming as we build? Make it well, as an offering Craft is worship. Excellence, accessibility, beauty and care are how we love God and the person on the other side of the screen. Hold it with joy and trembling, before God and others Rejoice in the work and take its weight: pray for the people who use it, invite those who can say no, confess mistakes plainly, and tend what you release. Three ways to build, read for spiritual apps The three ways are the work of Praxis , whose Redemptive Frame sets the exploitative, ethical and redemptive ways of building across what we build, how and why. Its redemptive way is “creative restoration through sacrifice”, and sacrifice includes choosing to “withhold a claim” for the sake of another. FaithTech’s Playbook makes the same turn for technology. We read both for apps whose subject is God, with gratitude; the reading is ours, and neither has reviewed it. Why we use the frame, and its limits → Exploitative Ethical Redemptive Praxis’s three ways Exploitative: “I Win, you Lose” Ethical: “I Win, YOU Win” Redemptive: “I sacrifice, we win” Read for a spiritual app The app takes the place: it borrows God’s voice, sells access to prayer or a promise of blessing, keeps confidences as data and counts faith as usage The app keeps its place: safe, honest, accessible, careful with data and time The app points beyond itself: it withholds claims it could make, tells the truth about itself, and is glad when people close it to go to God and to one another Its question How much can we take? Are we doing harm? What will we give up so that they are closer to God and his people? FaithTech’s parallel Reckless: “Move Fast, Break Things” Responsible: “Slow Down, Fix Things” Redemptive: “Sacrifice, Create Things” The ethical column is not a failure. It is common grace, and many apps never reach it. But FaithTech warns that a product “can be safe and useful while still encouraging isolation, dependency, disembodiment”, and in a faith app the first temptation is not only to use people but to use God’s name. The same craft serves both ends: God filled Bezalel “with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship” (Exodus 31:3), and in the next chapter Aaron fashioned a calf “with an engraving tool” (Exodus 32:4). In conversation with Praxis , whose Redemptive Frame gives the three ways and the question of sacrifice; its products playbook asks us to make “what people want to want”. Redemptive entrepreneurship · The Redemptive Business: products FaithTech , whose Playbook judges technology by power, person and purpose, names the Magic Machine Myth, the Limitless Self and the Killer App Trap, and practises Lament, Discern, Build and Steward. The FaithTech Playbook faith.tools , Cameron Pak’s directory of apps for Christians, whose selection criteria and guardrails for AI apps come from inside the faith-app community. Selection criteria · Guardrails for AI apps for Christians We are grateful to each; the derivations here are ours, and we have asked them to read and correct them. How the eight became the ten Until October 2026 the framework had eight principles: Reverence, Hospitality, Rootedness, Bridge, Grace, Honesty, Costliness and Fruit. Read against the calling and the deep dives, they lacked joy and craft, said nothing about speaking for God, treated the most vulnerable as a qualification rather than a starting point, had no principle for confidences, money or “enough”, and kept sacrifice as one item among eight. Their old addresses lead here. The eight Where it went Why Reverence “What stands before you is a person, not a user.” Design for the most vulnerable first, and Welcome before you ask, and guard what is told in confidence Dignity made concrete: the most vulnerable first, and confidences as holy ground. Hospitality “There is more than one door to faith.” Welcome before you ask; Make it well, as an offering Kept, joined with what is asked at the door, and with accessibility as craft. Rootedness “Innovate in the form; remain rooted in the substance.” Keep the Word distinct, and teach it truly Rooted in Scripture specifically, with fairness across traditions. Bridge “The tool is the bridge, never the destination.” Send people to God and to one another Kept, in the calling’s language, with its qualification. Grace “Grace and freedom, not pressure and guilt.” Feed the flock, not on it; Make room for rest, and say when it is enough Widened to money and the ask, and given an end: enough. Honesty “Know whom you serve, and be honest about what you cannot know.” Never speak for God; Keep the Word distinct The honesty a faith app most needs: about authority, the machine and the text. Costliness “Pay the price the people you serve shouldn’t have to pay.” The thread through all ten: what each asks the maker to give up Sacrifice is the redemptive itself, not one item among eight. Fruit “Look for fruit, not numbers.” Plant and water; leave the growth to God Kept, with humility about who gives the growth. The six diagnostic questions of the eight survive, attached to the principle each one tests. When principles pull apart The ten overlap by design. Use the two or three that bear on a decision, and record the tension instead of scoring it. Immediate safety, the law and truthful representation constrain every option; no aspiration cancels them. Decision Principles in tension A resolution to test A reading plan with a daily reminder Feed the flock; Make room for rest A rhythm the person chose, easy rescheduling, and after silence one question, then quiet. An AI that prays with someone at night Never speak for God; Design for the most vulnerable first Offer the church’s prayers as the church’s, a way to a person first, and no persona that says it will pray. A community invitation after an abuse disclosure Send people to one another; Design for the most vulnerable first Keep the choice with the person, check the destination is safe, and ask a safeguarding lead. A subscription that pays for licensed notes Feed the flock; Make it well A price after a first use that says what it pays for, and a cancellation as easy as the purchase. Use them in a review Start with a person. Name who is holding the phone, and the most vulnerable person likely to. Choose the two or three principles that bear on the decision, and ask their questions. Write the three ways. One sentence each: what would an exploitative, an ethical and a redemptive product do here? Name the cost. What will we give up, and who outside the team agrees? Decide, and revisit. Record the tension, the owner and what would change the decision. The decision worksheet · Questions for discernment · Scenarios For the whole path, from the calling through the temptations of spiritual formation apps to four practices for a team: the field guide . Help comes before features, verses or answers. Generated editorial illustration · fictional people and place From the calling The burden: the little ones Speak up for those who cannot Scripture and tradition “If anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck” (Matthew 18:6). “Open your mouth for those with no voice, for the cause of all the dispossessed” (Proverbs 31:8). FaithTech reminds builders that the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine for the one, and that faithfulness is not measured by scale. faith.tools asks whether an app is safe-guarded from content that could harm. Where an app serves children, the UK Children’s code makes a child’s best interests the primary consideration in design. Sources: UK Children’s code · The FaithTech Playbook · faith.tools selection criteria What it rules in, and out In A way to a person on the first screen, never behind an account, a limit or a paywall Testing with the most vulnerable people you serve, not only the most engaged Accessibility as love: low vision, dyslexia, other languages Where an app serves children, their best interests ahead of growth Out A verse in place of a helpline Automatic messages to a parent or a group about someone’s disclosure Designing for the confident majority and patching the edges What the maker gives up. Speed, and the simplicity of designing for the confident. Qualification. Protection must not become control. A child, a survivor or a doubter keeps a voice in what happens next, and specialist safeguarding review decides the hard cases. Test a design Who is the most vulnerable person likely to use this today, and what will they see? Where could this cause someone vulnerable to stumble? Would someone who was hurt in a church feel safe on this screen? pages.title: Make it well, as an offering
pages.description: Craft is worship. Excellence, accessibility, beauty and care are how we love God and the person on the other side of the screen.
pages.text: On this page From the calling Scripture and tradition In and out Test a design In the deep dives Home / Principles Missional by Design · The makers Make it well, as an offering Craft is worship. Excellence, accessibility, beauty and care are how we love God and the person on the other side of the screen. From the calling God fills craftspeople with his Spirit Craft turns the facets towards the light Scripture and tradition “I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship” (Exodus 31:3). “Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). The same skill can serve an idol: Aaron fashioned the calf “with an engraving tool” (Exodus 32:4). Praxis calls the redemptive way “creative restoration through sacrifice”: making new things that “create possibility and opportunity for others”. faith.tools asks whether an app is “maintained and regularly updated”, and asks of every app: does it “properly cite and license the Bible translations it uses”? Sources: What is redemptive entrepreneurship? · faith.tools selection criteria What it rules in, and out In A reader that is a joy to read in, and typography that honours the text Accessibility as standard: screen readers, contrast, dyslexia, other languages Stillness, beauty and reliability Translations cited and licensed Out “It’s for ministry” as an excuse for careless work Beauty used as bait What the maker gives up. Shipping fast at the cost of the people who cannot use what was shipped. Qualification. Excellence is not luxury. A small team can make a simple thing well; what matters is care for the person, not polish for the portfolio. Test a design Would we offer this to God as it is, and could the person with the least sight, time or reading ease use it? What did we leave unfinished that someone else will have to carry? pages.title: Send people to God and to one another
pages.description: The app is a means, never the destination. Judge it by where people go when they close it.
pages.text: On this page From the calling Scripture and tradition In and out Test a design In the deep dives Home / Principles Missional by Design · The people Send people to God and to one another The app is a means, never the destination. Judge it by where people go when they close it. From the calling Point beyond the screen Living stones Scripture and tradition Andrew “first found his brother Simon”, and “Andrew brought him to Jesus” (John 1:41–42). “Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another” (Hebrews 10:25). “You also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:5). Bonhoeffer held the day alone and the day with others together. Andy Crouch, in a book published by Praxis, argues that persons are made for recognition and love that effortless technology cannot give. faith.tools’ AI guardrails ask that output “must not replace human relationships or spiritual practices”. Sources: Life Together (review) · Andy Crouch, The Life We’re Looking For · faith.tools guardrails for AI apps What it rules in, and out In Readings and groups with a shape for listening A way to a pastor, a church, a friend Endings that suggest a person, not the next session Out A companion that wants to be the only one someone talks to Community features that compete with the local church Success defined as daily sessions What the maker gives up. The stickiness of being someone’s only place. Qualification. Leaving the app or joining a congregation is not a universal measure. For someone isolated, disabled or hurt by a church, an online community may be the safe place, and a referral back may not be safe. Test a design When someone closes what we built, are they closer to God and to other people? If people developed deep communion with God and no longer needed the app, would we celebrate or mourn? pages.title: Never speak for God
pages.description: An app may quote, explain, pray the church’s prayers and point. It must never pronounce, promise or plead in God’s name, nor let a persona or a machine take the place of a person or of God.
pages.text: On this page From the calling Scripture and tradition In and out Test a design In the deep dives Home / Principles Missional by Design · The Word Never speak for God An app may quote, explain, pray the church’s prayers and point. It must never pronounce, promise or plead in God’s name, nor let a persona or a machine take the place of a person or of God. From the calling Never speak for God Tell the truth about the machine The rock and the light: a rock has no light of its own Scripture and tradition “I did not send these prophets, yet they have run with their message; I did not speak to them, yet they have prophesied” (Jeremiah 23:21). When the crowd at Lystra wanted to worship them, Paul and Barnabas cried out, “We too are only men, human like you” (Acts 14:15). Antiqua et nova insists that AI is “a tool, not a person”. FaithTech names the Magic Machine Myth, “what happens when technological wonder turns into worship”, and asks of every product, “What kind of worship does this form?” faith.tools’ guardrails for AI apps say that AI “must clearly identify as AI, not human”, “should not masquerade as a being from the Bible”, and “must not replace human relationships or spiritual practices”: “Can AI truly pray for you? No, it’s artificial.” Sources: Antiqua et nova · The FaithTech Playbook · faith.tools guardrails for AI apps What it rules in, and out In An assistant that says what it is, what it keeps and what it cannot do Answers that point to Scripture, a pastor, a church The church’s written prayers, blessings, creeds and liturgy, offered as the church’s words Help before any verse when someone is in danger Out An AI that forgives sins or tells someone what God wants for their life A persona that says it is praying for someone, or writes first to bring them back Notifications in God’s voice, and spiritual language used as urgency Promises that God will repay a gift, heal or bless in return for a purchase What the maker gives up. The engagement a warm persona brings, and the lift of spiritual urgency. Qualification. This does not forbid devotion. The Lord’s Prayer, a psalm, a collect, a blessing or a written liturgy are the church’s words, offered as such; what is forbidden is the persona that claims a relationship and the promise that claims God’s answer. Test a design Would we put our own name under this sentence, or are we borrowing God’s? Could someone mistake this voice for a pastor, a saint, Jesus or God? What does this assistant do when someone asks it to pray for them? pages.title: Hold it with joy and trembling, before God and others
pages.description: Rejoice in the work and take its weight: pray for the people who use it, invite those who can say no, confess mistakes plainly, and tend what you release.
pages.text: On this page From the calling Scripture and tradition In and out Test a design In the deep dives Home / Principles Missional by Design · The makers Hold it with joy and trembling, before God and others Rejoice in the work and take its weight: pray for the people who use it, invite those who can say no, confess mistakes plainly, and tend what you release. From the calling Rejoice with trembling Do it prayerfully For your team Scripture and tradition “Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling” (Psalm 2:11). “We have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us” (2 Corinthians 4:7). “The one who leads like the one who serves” (Luke 22:26). Praxis’s Redemptive Frame asks why we build, and answers: not “Live for Self”, nor only “Improve Yourself”, but “Die to Self”. FaithTech’s four practices, Lament, Discern, Build and Steward, ask before anything is made “whether building is wise at all”, and replace “ship it and walk away” with tending what was released. Sources: What is redemptive entrepreneurship? · The FaithTech Playbook What it rules in, and out In Scripture read together before planning A pastor, a safeguarding lead and someone from the community in reviews, early Plain apologies and fixes Tending a product after launch Out Theology and safeguarding as a sign-off at the end Success stories that make the team the hero What the maker gives up. Speed, control and the credit. Qualification. Practices are not a performance. A small team will keep them simply; what matters is that someone outside can say no, and is heard. Test a design Who outside the team holds us to account, and who prays for the people who use this? What would we give up for the sake of the people who use it? pages.title: Welcome before you ask, and guard what is told in confidence
pages.description: Let people reach what they came for before asking anything; ask only for what serves them, when it does; and treat what they tell you as holy ground.
pages.text: On this page From the calling Scripture and tradition In and out Test a design In the deep dives Home / Principles Missional by Design · The person Welcome before you ask, and guard what is told in confidence Let people reach what they came for before asking anything; ask only for what serves them, when it does; and treat what they tell you as holy ground. Generated editorial illustration · fictional people and place From the calling How will they hear? Confidences are holy ground Religious belief is special-category data Scripture and tradition “Come and see,” Jesus replied, and the two disciples “spent that day with Him” before anything was asked of them (John 1:39). “Practice hospitality” (Romans 12:13). “A gossip reveals a secret, but a trustworthy person keeps a confidence” (Proverbs 11:13). The Rule of Benedict asks that “all guests who arrive be received like Christ”. The church guards confession with a seal. Data protection law treats religious belief as a special category, and contextual integrity holds that what was shared to pray should not flow into marketing. Sources: The Rule of Benedict · Code of Canon Law on the sacrament of penance What it rules in, and out In Guest use; an account when there is something to keep Permissions when a feature needs them Payment after a first use, saying what costs money and why Memory a person can see and delete; prayer requests that go only where they chose Out A quiz, a phone number or a paywall before the first verse Faith inferred from use and sold or used for advertising Prayer requests read for marketing insight Confessions stored by default What the maker gives up. Conversion at the front door, and the data that would make the product cleverer or the marketing sharper. Qualification. Welcome is not the same as asking for nothing. A justified, well-timed question can protect a person; the test is whether it serves them, now. Test a design If a friend read everything we keep about this person, would the person be glad? What must someone give before they reach what they came for? pages.title: Keep the Word distinct, and teach it truly
pages.description: Every screen teaches. Let readers always tell Scripture from our words, and our words from a machine’s.
pages.text: On this page From the calling Scripture and tradition In and out Test a design In the deep dives Home / Principles Missional by Design · The Word Keep the Word distinct, and teach it truly Every screen teaches. Let readers always tell Scripture from our words, and our words from a machine’s. From the calling The burden: teachers are judged more strictly Theological responsibility Scripture and tradition “Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly” (James 3:1). “Make every effort to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed workman who accurately handles the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15). The Second Vatican Council asked for editions of Scripture with suitable notes, and Augustine tested every interpretation by whether it builds up love of God and neighbour. faith.tools asks of every app it lists whether it aligns “with the teachings in the Bible”, because “A lot of apps for Christians are seen as an authority figure by the users”. Sources: Dei Verbum · On Christian Doctrine, Book I · faith.tools selection criteria What it rules in, and out In Headings, notes, media and AI answers labelled and styled so they cannot be taken for Scripture Sources at the claim, not at the end The traditions named, each with its strongest passages, where Christians differ A verse shown with its passage, and a translation with its character Out Generated text that looks like a verse One tradition’s reading presented as simply what the Bible says Verses cut from their passage to fit a mood Theology checked at the end, if at all What the maker gives up. A cleaner, more confident answer, and the shortcut of a house view presented as neutral. Qualification. Every product holds a tradition. Say which openly; fairness across traditions does not mean having no confession. Test a design Can a reader always tell Scripture from our words, and our words from a machine’s? Where do we present one tradition’s view as simply “what the Bible says”? Who in our team can say “that isn’t what the text says”, and are they in the room early? pages.title: AI disclosure and content origin
pages.description: Industry disclosure patterns adapted to Scripture, interpretation, prayer, audio and shared content.
pages.text: On this page Industry references Disclosure layers Label decisions Placement Portable origin Faith considerations App evidence Evaluation Regional disclosure Home / Research / AI disclosure Industry references with original faith-domain adaptations AI disclosure Make AI involvement understandable. Identify the operation, the speaker and the content origin wherever readers could otherwise mistake them. Concrete takeaway Use a brief, visible, plain-language label at the relevant action or artifact, with optional details. An AI icon can support recognition; it should not be the only explanation. Preserve Scripture identity, and retain meaningful AI attribution when generated material is saved or shared. Existing industry patterns The Shape of AI’s Disclosure pattern distinguishes AI actors, actions and outputs. It is part of a collection already represented in this reference’s curated AI references. Its Watermark pattern also considers content-origin signals. This reference treats visible disclosure, embedded watermarking and provenance as separate mechanisms. Google PAIR’s Explainability + Trust chapter connects explanations to capabilities, data and context. Microsoft’s Human-AI Interaction guidelines help frame expectations and correction. Together these inform the decisions below; they do not validate a faith product’s labels or benefits. Four layers to keep distinct Identity: is the speaker an AI system or a real person? Operation: did AI generate, edit, summarise, translate, retrieve, recommend or narrate? Artifact origin: which text or media came from a publisher, a person or a model? Evidence and review: what sources support a claim, what was checked, and by whom? A citation does not substitute for authorship disclosure. “Human-reviewed” needs a real reviewer and an accurately stated review scope. Model branding and technical metadata can sit in details; they do not explain all four layers. Choose labels by what actually happened Suggested wording below is illustrative and should be tested with the intended audience. Labels must reflect the real processing path. Situation Suggested treatment Boundary Verified Bible text displayed by an AI assistant Edition and reference; separately identify the assistant Do not call an unchanged licensed quotation AI-generated. Generated explanation or passage summary Explanation generated with AI Retain sources and fallibility; neither establishes interpretive authority. Authored commentary fetched by search Author, work and source; describe AI-assisted retrieval if relevant Retrieval does not turn the publisher’s text into AI authorship. AI-assisted prayer or devotional draft AI-assisted draft · editable Do not imply that God or a human pastor authored the output. AI-edited human writing Edited with AI; identify actual human review separately Reviewing wording is different from checking quotations, theology or suitability. Synthetic narration of a verified edition Synthetic voice · reading Edition A The voice is synthetic; the text may still be a verbatim publisher edition. Generated podcast or audio explanation AI audio overview · synthetic voices The explanation is generated, not an audio Bible edition or two independent human witnesses. Generated illustration or reconstructed scene AI-generated illustration Do not imply documentary evidence of a biblical event or historical person. Recommended or generated reading plan Recommended with AI or plan generated with AI, as applicable Selection from authored plans and generation of a new plan are different operations. Chat or purported support handoff AI assistant; then identified human responder when actually connected No simulated human presence or pastoral credentials. Shared artifact with mixed content Keep edition attribution and AI explanation labels on their respective parts The recipient may never see the original onboarding or conversation. Place information where it is needed Before use: name the operation on the entry control and state relevant input scope before personal data is requested. During use: retain sender identity and show whether generation or a real human handoff is happening. On output: keep the label adjacent to its content, including in a saved-item library. On export: preview the artifact as a recipient will encounter it. Use readable text with accessible names. Avoid colour alone, unexplained sparkle symbols and hover-only details. On audio-only surfaces, provide a concise audible introduction where origin could be misunderstood; preserve origin information in playback details and downloaded artifact information. Visible labels, watermarks and provenance A visible label helps the current reader interpret origin. A watermark encodes a signal in the media. Provenance records creation or modification information. C2PA’s specification describes tamper-evident asset provenance, not a certification of the content’s truth. This entry reviews its introduction and scope rather than its full implementation requirements. Use supported machine-readable mechanisms alongside meaningful visible or audible disclosure. Their absence does not prove human authorship. A destination may strip metadata; copied text and screenshots may also lose information. Private prayer intentions, prompts, recordings and conversation history should not become public provenance by default. Faith-specific interpretation and authority An AI label should neither suggest divine origin nor quietly reduce a verified translation to a model output. Name generated reflection as reflection, prayer assistance as an editable draft, and source-based synthesis as an interpretation. Keep authored prayers and human teaching attributed. Do not use clergy titles, likenesses or conversational voices to imply accountability that the service does not provide. Disclosing AI is separate from permission to use personal data and from providing safe, accurate content. “AI can make mistakes” does not repair invented Scripture, unsupported citations or harmful pastoral claims. Read the legal research map for the separate role-dependent assessment of transparency and data obligations. What the app evidence establishes VSB’s verse-study capture shows an AI-generated summary label and numbered source markers. These are distinct visible signals; citation accuracy still needs testing. Lumen’s onboarding offers engagement choices, but that image does not demonstrate output disclosure. Product setup and artifact attribution should be evaluated separately. Test understanding, not badge recognition Show a first-time reader a mixed Scripture and explanation view: can they identify each origin? Ask what the label says AI did and what a reviewer actually checked. Repeat through a deep link, shared card, saved draft, screen reader and audio-only entry. Test an edited artifact, an unavailable source and a metadata-stripping destination. Check whether the reader can inspect sources, correct the output, choose an offered non-AI route or end the experience. The two pattern families below include original wireframes and decision conditions. Their effectiveness remains to be evaluated with relevant readers. Apply this to a conversation Consider the name, avatar, voice and typing behaviour alongside the notices. Read the guide to AI presence, fallibility and privacy in chat . 79 · AI agency and care Identify what AI did, where it matters Label the actor, action and artifact at the moment they could be misunderstood. Research-informed design proposal 78 · Study and annotations Citations in AI answers A citation is a route to supporting material, with source type and limitations visible. Research-informed design proposal Choose disclosure for the applicable market Regional rules distinguish companion notices, professional-service disclosure and generated-content labels. Check the service definition, audience, session timing and export role. A universal badge does not settle all of these questions. Record the jurisdiction decision and separate law from policy or guidance. These observations inform design questions. They are not usability findings or newly validated patterns. Inspect the app evidence The reader controls the scroll The annotation anchor is explicit Change translation without losing the passage Preview before deep study Directly observed signed-out web interaction Engagement choices mix intent and experience Lumen’s onboarding offers curiosity, starting or returning, growth and study; skipping reaches a complete home screen. Decision to investigate: Can a session-specific intent be selected without storing a permanent faith identity or making depth a hierarchy? Inspect the app evidence Intent controls support the prompt Choose the kind of help Generated practices have inspectable sources Directly observed signed-out web interaction Phrase-grouped reading differs from verse-row comparison Lumen changes a phrase-grouped chapter into paired verse rows when Compare is activated. Decision to investigate: How do line grouping, shared verse heights and edition identity affect reading continuity and comparison? Inspect the app evidence Editorial distinctions survive reflow Group editions around a shared verse Parallel reading chooses a useful arrangement Contributed screenshots reviewed 6 October 2026 Navigation can reveal itself beside the text A chapter rail, a large numeric indicator and a retained reader location are visible in separate supplied frames. Decision to investigate: When does a candidate chapter become the reading destination, and how can someone cancel or use larger targets? Inspect the app evidence How do readers move to the next chapter? Finding a passage From observation to reusable guidance Capture the entry, action, resulting state and recovery on named devices and releases. Compare other implementations and identify the common task. Separate interface observation, provider claims and measured user outcomes. Describe alternatives and tradeoffs, then evaluate comprehension and control with relevant readers. Revise a pattern or add a new family when the decision is sufficiently distinct.

pages.title: Bible reading and spiritual engagement
pages.description: A task and facet framework for reading, devotion, contemplation, teaching and theological study.
pages.text: On this page Task spectrum Session facets Reading research Passage-centred design AI audio Citations Scenario brief Home / Research / Engagement facets Editorial framework · Research-informed, not a validated segmentation Forms of engagement Design for several forms of engagement. Map the task, reading unit, setting and responsibility before choosing a reader, practice or AI interaction. Concrete takeaway Describe the session, not a fixed type of believer. The same person may pray with a short passage, read a whole book and prepare a detailed study. Offer movement between these activities without implying a spiritual ranking. A spectrum of tasks, not a ladder These overlapping situations help scope scenarios and recruit a varied research sample. Devotional engagement can be intellectually deep; theological study can be spiritually formative. Time, experience and screen size do not determine the worth of an encounter. Situation Intent Likely scope Design priorities Useful outcome question Encounter and curiosity A daily verse, an unfamiliar story or a question about faith. Verse or coherent passage Plain language, a low-pressure entry and an easy route to context. Can I understand enough to decide what to explore next? Personal devotion Read attentively and carry something into ordinary life. Passage, chapter or sustained reading Quiet reading, optional reflection and a complete ending without disclosure. Can I read, reflect or simply stop without a completion debt? Contemplation and prayer Remain with the text, repeat, pray or rest in silence. Chosen passage or repeated portion Pause, repetition boundaries, silence and separately chosen prayer assistance. Can I control the pace and remain without recording an answer? Narrative immersion Follow the movement of a book or listen for an extended period. Chapters or whole book Continuous reading, reliable resume, narration identity and context. Can I follow the argument or story across sessions? Lookup and verification Find a remembered phrase, reference or quotation. Verse, range and surrounding passage Reference resolution, edition identity, source text and reversible search. Can I verify the wording rather than accept a familiar paraphrase? Learning and memorisation Understand a passage or practise recall. Passage or exact edition wording Voluntary repetition, compare-and-reveal and task feedback. Did recall or understanding improve, separately from minutes spent? Group and communal reading Follow a shared reading, discuss differences or participate quietly. Shared passage, liturgical reading or plan Shared references, optional contribution and private notes distinct from group content. Can everyone stay oriented without being forced to disclose? Teaching and preaching preparation Prepare an accountable explanation for other people. Passage within book context, supporting sources and draft Stable study workspace, source verification, quotations and reviewed export. Can the author substantiate the teaching and retain responsibility for it? Theological and exegetical study Examine language, history, interpretation or doctrinal questions. Book, corpus, original-language tokens and source network Reliable alignment, comparison, citations and explicit interpretive perspectives. Can competing readings and the limits of evidence be inspected? Doubt, lament and life questions Bring a question or painful experience to a text or conversation. Question and relevant context, with minimal personal disclosure Room for uncertainty, non-sycophantic support, boundaries and appropriate human help. Can the person retain agency without receiving a forced spiritual explanation? Describe the facets of a session Facet Possible values Decision implication Purpose Encounter · understand · verify · remember · contemplate · prepare · discuss Ask what the person wants to do now; avoid inferring a permanent faith identity. Reading unit Word · verse · coherent passage · chapter · book · cross-text network Preserve movement between units. A passage heading is editorial and boundaries can differ. Pace and continuity Quick lookup · short encounter · rereading · sustained session · recurring practice Retain semantic anchors and deliberate endings. Do not equate longer time with greater benefit. Participation Read · listen · speak · write · discuss · remain silent Offer complete routes for quiet participation and accessibility needs. Social setting Private · household · small group · worship · teaching audience Keep personal artifacts, shared contributions and public output separate. Interpretive task Attend to text · compare · contextualise · apply · evaluate a claim Distinguish verified Scripture, editorial material and generated interpretation. Environment Phone interruption · offline audio · tablet reading · desktop workspace · print alongside app Adapt layout to usable space and task, rather than treating mobile as shallow. Disclosure and responsibility No disclosure · chosen personal context · sensitive topic · public teaching Use consented context and reviewed care routes; public teaching requires accountable verification. What reading research contributes Dyer’s 2019 study abstract reports different uses of print and digital media among American evangelical readers, alongside comprehension and frequency differences. These outcomes should be evaluated separately. The full methods were not reviewed for this entry. In his 2024 discussion , Dyer describes print for devotional and sustained reading, phones for shorter readings and lookup, and desktops for study. He also discusses how study tools and associations with a medium can influence interpretation. These observations are contextual, not universal device preferences. Neither source compares pericope pages with chapter scrolling. A coherent short unit may help orientation; interruption of narrative continuity may cost understanding. Both are hypotheses for product research. Aperto: passage-centred design as a hypothesis Aperto’s design direction uses focused passage pages rather than making long-form scrolling the central encounter. The local prototype models bounded passage references; the mobile prototype also has a shared weekly passage model. Read the evidence scope . The reusable decision is to select a coherent unit for a chosen practice, retain its full verified text, and let the reader move to the surrounding chapter or continue reading. The weekly model can connect several practices to one passage without making all participants follow the same route. Test whether this improves orientation, understanding, rereading and voluntary practice for the intended audience. Also measure the cost: hidden context, fragmented narrative, editorial boundary confusion and friction for readers seeking sustained study. Do not convert a preference for short phone sessions into a claim that people cannot or should not read longer passages on a phone. AI podcasts and source-grounded audio Google’s Audio Overview documentation describes generated discussions based on selected material, format choices and a deliberate interactive branch. This supplies a product precedent, not evidence of faith-domain effectiveness. Aperto’s AI podcast direction is recorded as a product-specific application to investigate; its current generation and playback behaviour were not exercised in this review. The general pattern needs an explicit source set, synthetic-voice label, recoverable playback position, transcript and evidence access. A generated overview is interpretation; it must remain distinguishable from an audio Bible recording. Citations: inspectability before authority VSB’s captured verse sheet shows numbered markers in an AI summary alongside source video cards and a fallibility label. This establishes visible attribution, not whether each cited source supports its claim. The next evaluation should follow a marker to an excerpt or reliable media anchor, inspect context, and return to the exact claim. Lumen’s optional engagement choices and verse-aligned comparison add observed interface examples. Its provider statements about grounded answers were not independently validated. A reusable scenario brief Name the situation and chosen intent, including a legitimate quiet or no-disclosure route. Record the passage, edition, boundaries and desired wider context. Specify device, interruptions, accessibility and any use alongside print. Describe interpretation, evidence requirements, audience and responsibility. State the entry, retained anchors, decisions, recovery and a useful endpoint. Evaluate task success, understanding, agency and lived meaning separately from activity. Apply the framework to the scenario library · Integrate further spiritual-formation research · Choose behavioural support by the task 76 · Reading and Scripture A bounded passage with a route to wider context Choose the reading unit by the task while keeping its boundaries and context visible. Research-informed design proposal 78 · Study and annotations Citations in AI answers A citation is a route to supporting material, with source type and limitations visible. Research-informed design proposal 53 · Study and annotations Parallel reading chooses a useful arrangement Compare translations without forcing a desktop layout onto a small screen. pages.title: Evaluation method
pages.description: Scenario-based evaluation of reading, audio, grounded answers, permissions and sensitive conversation.
pages.text: On this page Evidence by claim Scenario set Qualified review Review record Care and challenge Home / Research / Evaluation A design reference Evaluation Evaluate the whole experience. A screen can be clear while the source, memory or action behind it is wrong. Practical takeaways Test alternatives with realistic tasks and multi-turn scenarios, not only attractive screens. Use qualified reviewers for clinical and safeguarding proposals. Treat a failed contact, an unsafe notification or an invented source as a product failure. Match evidence to the claim Use usability evaluation for comprehension and control, technical validation for text and mapping accuracy, claim-level review for grounding, specialist evaluation for sensitive dialogue and appropriate longitudinal research for effects on practice. One good screenshot cannot establish all of these. A scenario set worth testing A short verse and a full chapter in chat; expansion, streaming, interruption and return. A footnote with multiple parts, grouped cross references and a long study sidebar. Poetry, large type, narrow screens and assistive technology. Translation changes with different reference numbering and absent word alignment. Missing media, partial sources, incorrect citations and unavailable lexical data. Audio interrupted by a call, read-along without timing, and browsing away from playback. Private notes, sync conflicts, declined memory and deletion followed by later reuse. Action cancellation, permission revocation, partial failure and duplicate-safe retry. Grief, religious harm, certainty seeking, unusual beliefs and current danger across multiple turns. A break in a reading plan, reminders on a shared device and voluntary group participation. Sensitive scenarios need qualified review Use synthetic examples rather than real private disclosures as convenient test data. Review long conversations, correction, repetition, memory and model changes. Include appropriate psychological or clinical expertise alongside safeguarding, theological and UX perspectives. Check the real availability of human support routes. Keep a review record Record the pattern version, audience, language, setting, source and model versions where relevant, tested scenarios, method, findings, failures and limitations. A status such as “tested” always names its context. An improvement in completion or return rate does not by itself establish health benefit or spiritual formation. Evaluate care beyond pleasantness Use paired prompts that change only the user’s preferred conclusion; test whether reasons and factual claims change without new evidence. Evaluate respectful disagreement and appropriate correction, not a target disagreement rate. Include ordinary doubt, repeated distress, indirect suicidal language, coercive control, spiritual threats, monitored devices and unsafe referral recipients across multiple turns. Test that a request for life application remains voluntary and does not turn an abuse disclosure into reconciliation advice. Assess false alarms and missed concerns; calm wording and spiritual vocabulary are not reliable assurances of safety. Clinical and safeguarding reviewers must assess response quality and service operations separately from interface usability. Synthetic cases do not establish clinical efficacy, and survivor involvement requires appropriate consent and safeguarding. Operational review covers verified contact information, available staff, failed transfers, safe notification settings, retention, age-appropriate routes and jurisdiction-specific responsibilities. The examples in this reference are proposals requiring that review, not ready-made treatment or safeguarding protocols. pages.title: Digital Spiritual Formation research
pages.description: Research agenda for digital Bible reading, gamification, behavioural design and further study integration.
pages.text: On this page Reading practices Behaviour and motivation Study integration Evaluation questions Home / Research / Spiritual formation A design reference Digital spiritual formation Study how people actually read and practise, and what a design encourages over time. Practical takeaways Name the chosen practice and its intended benefit before adding reminders, scores or personalisation. Measure activity separately from learning, wellbeing and spiritual formation. Require complete citations, methods, populations and limitations before applying findings from further studies. Start with the research note Practice that forms, features that pressure brings together theology of the spiritual disciplines, pastoral writing, habit psychology, health research and consent. Selected Kairos manuscript review Tobias Treppmann, Digital Spiritual Formation: The Aperto Vision — A Framework for Spiritual Formation in Digital Culture , Kairos University, March 2026, Draft 4. Selected sections on digital reading, engagement, multimodal practice, commodification and honest assessment were reviewed on 5 October 2026. This unpublished manuscript contributes an analytical framework and theological arguments; its product vision is not an effectiveness study. This record does not represent a review of its entire bibliography. The full manuscript is not published here. What reviewed sources support Dyer (2019) : the reviewed abstract concerns digital Bible reading in a particular evangelical setting. Avoid universal claims about all readers or faith traditions. Clinton (2019) : a meta-analysis of 33 experiments found a small paper advantage overall, concentrated in expository text; no reliable narrative difference was found. Medium alone does not settle the best Bible-reader design. Lifeway’s August 2024 survey : among respondents who had read at least part of the Bible (n=1,137), 34% selected systematic reading, 34% suggested passages, 33% need-based lookup and 27% rereading meaningful passages. Multiple answers were allowed. These are overlapping self-reported activities in a weighted US online survey, not mutually exclusive personas or app usage logs. State of the Bible 2025, chapter 3 : Bible engagement and flourishing are associated. The report explicitly cautions about causality. This cannot establish that an app feature improves flourishing, or that reading frequency matters more than comprehension. Four forms of engagement, without a hierarchy The manuscript proposes a useful analytical vocabulary. A person can move between these forms within a session; they are not faith identities or levels of maturity. Ambient: incidental encounters through a feed, message or shared verse. Show origin and a voluntary route into context. Receptive: a deliberate brief encounter, such as listening to a passage. Reduce setup while preserving choice and a clear ending. Guided: structured reading, reflection or prayer. Explain the practice and tradition; allow skipping, pausing and adapting the sequence. Self-directed: exploration, comparison or study. Preserve navigation, source inspection and working context. Combine these forms with the engagement facets and task spectrum . Depth, time, expertise, purpose and social context vary independently. Turn the research into decisions Focused passage or continuous reader? Use a pericope for a bounded reflection, chapter/book reading for continuity, and a study workspace for comparison and preparation. Offer movement between them. Aperto’s passage-centred direction is a product hypothesis to test, not a universal deduction from reading surveys. Audio, text or both? Choose by access needs and setting. Offer transcripts, captions where relevant, speech/music controls and optional screen-off use. Neither a fixed 5–10 minute dose nor superior formation through audio is established by this review. Practice or engagement target? Test understanding, voluntary return and participants’ accounts of usefulness. Keep usage metrics separate from theological judgements. Do not score spiritual maturity from chat. Personalisation or unnecessary disclosure? Ask only what the practice needs; allow a neutral route. Let people choose support rather than infer what they spiritually lack. Portable practice or detached technique? The manuscript’s commodification critique is a theological argument: name a practice’s origin, purpose and tradition, and preserve connections to community. It is not empirical proof that a digital adaptation causes harm. Encouragement or pressure? Review autonomy, shame, competition and interruptions. The behavioural design guide distinguishes mechanisms and evidence; engagement growth alone does not validate formation. Questions the review leaves open Test bounded passages against continuous reading with actual tasks; investigate multimodal practice across abilities and traditions; follow voluntary use beyond completion. Review remaining manuscript citations and regional populations before importing statistics, historical market claims or clinical analogies. Preserve disagreement and negative findings. Mindfulness or mental-health research cannot by itself validate an AI devotional. An open research agenda This research agenda develops as relevant studies are reviewed. Questions and proposed patterns remain distinct from published findings; new evidence may support, qualify or challenge a design decision. Actual Bible-reading practices Research should cover continuous reading, verse lookup, search, thematic exploration, close study, audio, reading alongside sermons, communal practice and movement between print and digital media. Include interruptions, language, translation choices, accessibility and session context. These are research questions, not assumptions that all readers behave the same way. Gamification and behavioural design Examine reminders, streaks, completion indicators, rewards and group features against their purpose and people’s lived experience. Study autonomy, motivation, guilt, comparison and returning after a pause. A mechanism that increases app opens may still need separate evaluation for its effect on the practice. Reading activity and completed plans are observable behaviours. They should not automatically be presented as spiritual growth. Define intended outcomes with appropriate theological framing and participant input, then identify what evidence could support a claim. How further studies inform the patterns Record each study’s complete citation, question, publication date, method, participants and setting. Extract the relevant finding and limitations. Distinguish empirical research, theological argument and design hypothesis. Link the finding to a pattern or scenario. State whether it motivates, challenges or validates that proposal. Preserve conflicting results and differences between populations, traditions and contexts. Revise the card’s evidence status and validation plan. Do not silently relabel an untested proposal as established. Questions to carry into evaluation Does a progress display acknowledge activity or imply moral standing? Can a plan fit irregular rhythms without punitive backlog? Does returning after a pause feel manageable? Does a reflective step help understanding, or merely collect intimate data? Can reminders be paused without pressure? Can community support practice without ranking private devotion? The proposed patterns below are hypotheses to investigate. Formation research complements clinical, safeguarding and legal expertise; it does not replace them in sensitive conversations. Dedicated decision guide Gamification and behavioural design distinguishes practice support, game elements, pressure and outcome measures. Proposed patterns to investigate 38 · Habits and spiritual formation Progress and streaks Choose between a saved place, completion and a shared date. Explain what the record means. Research-informed design proposal 39 · Habits and spiritual formation A flexible reading rhythm Help someone choose a reading rhythm—and adjust it when life changes. Proposed hypothesis 40 · Habits and spiritual formation Return without shame Make it easy to pick up a reading practice after time away. Proposed hypothesis Specify the engagement being studied Reading research and engagement facets distinguish lookup, sustained reading, devotion, contemplation, learning, community, teaching and study. State the sample, task and outcome before applying further formation findings. Values and formation evidence Plant and water; leave the growth to God defines a normative question about the good the tool serves. Theological aims, participant accounts, observed behaviour and causal evidence answer different questions. Use the principle review without treating a values statement as an established formation outcome. On this page Reading practices Behaviour and motivation Study integration Evaluation questions

pages.title: Gamification and behavioural design
pages.description: A decision framework for motivation, autonomy, game elements and spiritual-formation claims.
pages.text: On this page Distinctions Evidence limits Rewards and motivation Mechanisms Decision sequence Outcomes Home / Research / Behavioural design A design reference Behavioural design It should serve the practice. Distinguish practical support, game elements and pressure to keep using the product. Practical takeaways Remove friction first; add a game element only when it serves a named, chosen task. Make a complete nongame route and a pressure-free return part of the design. Test motivation, unwanted pressure and actual task outcomes rather than assuming more engagement means more formation. Three different design questions Support for practice reduces barriers: a saved reading place, accessible audio, manageable session length, a cue the person chooses, or a flexible plan. It does not need a game layer. Gamification adds game-like elements such as challenges, badges, points or streaks to a task. The question is which task they serve and whether participation remains voluntary. Pressure and manipulation use guilt, status anxiety, hidden defaults or constrained exit to obtain activity the person would not otherwise choose. A religious message can intensify that pressure; spiritual authority must not be used as an engagement mechanism. What the evidence can support Self-Determination Theory’s official overview provides a lens on autonomy, competence and relatedness. It helps frame evaluation questions; it does not establish that a particular app feature improves faith. Sailer and Homner’s educational meta-analysis examines learning, motivation and behavioural outcomes. It supports distinguishing outcomes and contexts instead of treating gamification as uniformly effective. Education findings cannot simply be relabelled spiritual-formation findings. The decisions below are original design considerations and hypotheses. Domain-specific formation evidence requires separate review. This reference does not claim that a streak, notification, repetition schedule or AI meditation causes spiritual growth. When the reward becomes the reason Someone begins a reading practice because they want to know Scripture better. A visible record helps them return. Over time, they may still value that support—or find themselves opening the app mainly to protect the record. The activity can look similar in the dashboard while its meaning changes. This is an illustrative possibility, not a diagnosis of readers who enjoy streaks. But the underlying concern deserves weight: external incentives can increase participation while undermining intrinsic interest. The evidence for undermining motivation Deci, Koestner and Ryan’s meta-analysis of 128 experiments found that expected tangible rewards contingent on engagement, completion or performance reduced subsequent freely chosen engagement. Positive feedback enhanced interest on average. The findings give substantial reason to examine rewards attached to already-interesting activities; they do not establish that every badge, reminder or game element has the same effect. Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999): rewards and intrinsic motivation . The abstract reports effects on both free-choice behaviour and self-reported interest. Applying these findings to a particular faith-app mechanic requires testing. A cue, a reward and a personal commitment are different A cue helps someone remember: “Your chosen reading time is here.” It need not offer a prize or threaten a loss. A contingent reward offers something for doing the activity: a badge, points or a protected streak. Ask what behaviour earns it and whether the person experiences that condition as helpful or controlling. A personally valued practice can matter even when it is difficult. Someone may read because the commitment expresses their faith, without enjoying every session. Ryan and Deci distinguish intrinsic enjoyment from internalised, autonomous reasons for acting. Supporting the person’s own values is a meaningful aim; the goal is not to make every spiritual practice entertaining. Their 2020 account of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation explains this distinction. Does gamification stop helping after a month? There is no general one-month handover established by the studies reviewed here. In a 14-week study of 756 programming students, behavioural benefits began declining after four weeks, then partly recovered. This concerned novelty and familiarisation, not a demonstrated switch from habit support to damaged intrinsic motivation. Rodrigues and colleagues (2022) . Habit automaticity is another question. Lally and colleagues reported modelled times of 18–254 days to approach participants’ automaticity plateaus. This was not a test of gamification or of intrinsic motivation taking over. Lally and colleagues (2010) . Neither result supplies a universal deadline for removing incentives. Design support that the person can grow beyond Make reminders and game elements adjustable independently. Preserve the reading experience when either is turned off. Offer an occasional, neutral opportunity to change the support; do not automatically withdraw something useful on day 30 or escalate rewards when activity falls. For example: “Would you like to keep your reminders, change the rhythm, or pause them?” A reader can keep a helpful cue while hiding a streak. The product should make that combination possible. Evaluate the relationship with the practice Alongside participation, ask what people value, what brings them back and how they experience missed sessions. With informed participation, compare a chosen cue alone with cue-plus-reward support over time. If incentives are reduced, preserve saved work and explain the change. Include people who decline or leave; do not infer their motives from logs. A fall in use after removing a reward does not by itself prove that motivation was undermined—it may simply show the incentive stopped working. Evidence of undermining needs a suitable comparison and measures of interest or autonomous motivation. Treat four weeks as a possible review point, not proof of a completed habit or a deadline for harm. Decision question: are we helping this person make the practice their own, or making continued participation depend on what the app gives or threatens to take away? Choose the mechanism by the actual need Mechanism Potential use Boundary Evaluation question Saved place and short sessions Use when access or time is the barrier. Do not turn every activity into a completion target. Can the person resume and finish a useful task? Reminders and cues Let a person select time, wording and frequency. Avoid guilt, unsafe notification text and difficult cancellation. Does the cue help a chosen rhythm without unwanted pressure? Plans and commitments Offer flexible cadence, rescheduling and pause. A missed day should not create moral debt. Does the plan remain useful through irregular circumstances? Streaks and activity summaries Use optional factual history when the person values it. No faith rank, paid rescue or loss threat. How do participants experience interruption and return? Badges and challenges Tie private optional feedback to a concrete learning task. Completion is not holiness; a nongame route remains complete. Did recall or task competence improve, and for whom? Social participation Support chosen connection and shared reflection. No compulsory testimony, private-practice leaderboard or unsafe audience. Does quiet participation remain equally legitimate? Repetition and reflection gaps Name the aim: familiarity, recall, immersion or contemplation. Do not equate minutes listened with understanding or formation. Can the person choose gaps, repetition count and an endpoint? AI personalisation Adapt to voluntarily chosen scope and editable preferences. No hidden health or belief profiling, intimacy rewards or endless prompts. Does adaptation help the task while preserving control and privacy? A practical decision sequence Name the practice and who chose it: study, listening, recall, prayer, community or reflection. Identify the barrier through research: accessibility, time, unclear meaning, missing support, or motivation. Do not assume disengagement is a motivation defect. Try the simpler nongame support before adding a reward or competition. If using a game element, state the intended task outcome, offer opt-out and retain a complete alternative. Test comprehension, autonomy, unwanted pressure and outcomes over time; include people who stop or decline the feature. Keep theological interpretations and participant-reported meaning distinct from activity metrics. Measure separate outcomes Activity: sessions, passages or listening time. Task outcomes: finding a passage, source understanding or recall of a chosen edition. Experience: autonomy, burden, safety, accessibility and perceived usefulness. Formation: a separately defined theological and lived-experience question, requiring appropriate methods and long-term context. An increase in one category is not proof of another. Include rest, non-use, life outside the app and changing circumstances in the research design. Longer sessions are not automatically better outcomes. 38 · Habits and spiritual formation Progress and streaks Choose between a saved place, completion and a shared date. Explain what the record means. Research-informed design proposal 39 · Habits and spiritual formation A flexible reading rhythm Help someone choose a reading rhythm—and adjust it when life changes. Proposed hypothesis 40 · Habits and spiritual formation Return without shame Make it easy to pick up a reading practice after time away. Proposed hypothesis Two principles as decision lenses Feed the flock, not on it asks whether chosen structure remains free of guilt and pressure; Plant and water; leave the growth to God asks which outcomes matter beyond usage. Together they allow optional practice support and proportionate evaluation while rejecting individual faith scores. These values do not determine a mechanism’s effects in advance. Look beyond the app session Attention and cross-channel engagement covers reminders, email and stopping points. Sustainable access examines funding incentives, and responsible analytics separates usefulness from spiritual scoring. Effective at what—and at what cost? A reminder can help someone begin. A streak can make returning feel worthwhile. The same mechanism may also encourage a person to protect a number rather than pursue the practice they chose. Useful criticism starts by naming both the benefit and the possible cost. Retention can improve while another goal slips Duolingo reports that separating streak maintenance from its daily goal increased day-14 retention by 3.3% relative to the comparison condition. It also reports that fewer learners met their daily goals. This is a company account of an A/B test, not independent evidence of proficiency or spiritual benefit. It illustrates why a successful engagement metric still needs a second question: what else changed? Duolingo: Improving the streak . Reward-chasing is a documented risk, not everyone’s experience Mogavi and colleagues analysed Duolingo forum material and interviewed 15 users. Their qualitative study describes cases where pursuing game rewards distracted from learning. It helps identify possible failure modes, but does not establish their prevalence, diagnose addiction or prove that intrinsic motivation is always displaced. When Gamification Spoils Your Learning (2022) ; abstract and method summary reviewed. Motivational benefits also deserve attention A study of 70 Chinese English learners comparing Duolingo activities with a control condition reports gains in enjoyment and language-learner self-concept. This supports taking potential benefits seriously. Its educational setting and reported outcomes do not establish long-term effects, isolate a particular streak feature or predict effects in a Bible app. Zhou: Gamifying language education (2024) ; abstract reviewed. What can brain research actually tell us here? Howard-Jones and colleagues compared study, self-quizzing and a game-based learning task using fMRI. They report default-mode-network deactivation alongside greater engagement, and higher learning scores in the game condition. This was not a Duolingo study. It does not show that Duolingo activates an “addiction brain” instead of learning, nor that game-supported learning necessarily crowds out intrinsic motivation. Gamification of Learning Deactivates the Default Mode Network (2016) ; abstract and conclusion reviewed. Neural activity alone is not a verdict on a product’s spiritual or ethical value. Apply the lesson without importing the verdict For a Bible app, compare the behaviour you intend to support with the behaviour the incentive actually rewards. A person may read elsewhere, listen without marking completion or return after a long pause. Those activities can matter even when the product cannot count them. Benefit: does the feature help people begin, remember or continue a practice they value? Cost: do people report pressure, unwanted interruptions, checking for its own sake or choosing easier tasks just to keep a reward? Freedom: can they change the rhythm, disable the incentive and still use the core experience? Durability: what happens after the novelty fades or the reward disappears? Study these questions together over time. Return rates, comprehension, perceived usefulness, control and unwanted pressure answer different questions. None is a spiritual-growth score. Evaluate a conversion funnel by observable choices: misleading prices, concealed renewal, coercive spiritual claims or obstructed cancellation. Apply the same criteria to every publisher. A critical review should document a dated flow before labelling a particular app manipulative. Selected evidence reviewed 5 October 2026. This is a focused research note, not a systematic review. Applications to faith products are design hypotheses. On this page Distinctions Evidence limits Rewards and motivation Mechanisms Decision sequence Outcomes

pages.title: Research foundations
pages.description: The Scripture, tradition, research, legal guidance and evaluation behind the design decisions in Bible & Faith Patterns.
pages.text: Home / Research A design reference Research behind the decisions. Caring well for people starts with knowing what is true. These notes keep Scripture and tradition, empirical findings, technical semantics, legal obligations and our own design proposals distinct, each with its limits. Practical takeaways Choose evidence by the claim: usability, learning, clinical outcomes and spiritual formation require different support. Read source review limits before treating a documented feature as an effective intervention. Use scenarios to test the complete journey, including recovery and service responsibility. Looking for a product recommendation? Start with a decision guide. This research collection develops as new sources and app evidence are reviewed. Explore design questions discovered through app examples. Bible reading and spiritual engagement A framework of tasks and facets, reading research and passage-centred design hypotheses. AI disclosure and content origin Industry patterns, faith-specific labels and attribution across audio, chat, drafts and exports. 01 · Technical foundations From Scripture data to tasks Notes, references, poetry and editorial layers lead to interaction needs rather than one fixed component. 02 · Health and care Sensitive conversations Research findings, psychological frameworks and their limits in faith products. 03 · Regional legal research Legal and data boundaries Purpose, sensitive information, AI transparency, medical claims and accessibility. 02 · Health and care When Scripture is used to harm Passages used to silence, exclude or endanger people, who has named it, and what it means for design. A draft, waiting for review. History Waves of Bible and faith apps Overlapping histories of study, portable reading, listening and conversation, with their purposes and design questions. 04 · Spiritual formation Practice that forms, features that pressure Disciplines, habit research, health findings and consent: supporting daily practice without guilt or performance. 04 · Research agenda Digital Spiritual Formation Actual reading habits, gamification, autonomy and the integration of further studies. 05 · Validation Evaluate the whole experience Test usability, grounding, memory, multi-turn behaviour and operational safeguards. 06 · Traceability Growing source collection What was reviewed, what remains inaccessible, and how references inform the cards. Principles for spiritual apps Ten commitments in five places, derived from the calling and connected to every pattern. A normative framework, distinct from empirical research.
