pages.title: Waves of Bible and faith apps
pages.description: Five overlapping histories of Bible and prayer tools, their documented milestones, purposes and design possibilities.
pages.text: Research Research note · history Waves of Bible and faith apps New technologies have opened different ways to read, investigate, listen and pray. The histories overlap: a pocket Bible, a study library and a shared prayer rhythm can serve different needs today. Trace what a feature was meant to help someone do before deciding what to carry forward. 5 overlapping histories Selected Bible and prayer tools Historical sources reviewed 13 October 2026 Waves Timeline The waves Feature histories Purposes and communities Design possibilities Sources At a glance Five overlapping histories 0 1980s onward Search and study on computers 1 1993 onward Scripture through the web 2 1998 handhelds / 2008 smartphones Portable reading and connected practice 3 2006 podcast / 2010 audio app / 2018 prayer app Listening and guided prayer 4 2023 onward Generative AI conversation These are selected milestones, not first inventions or stages of spiritual maturity. Portable Bible software predates the iPhone; audio ministry predates podcasts. Earlier tools remain useful. Before these consumer-facing milestones, John Dyer’s history identifies an academic computing era in the 1950s–70s. His four-era history of Bible software differs from the five overlapping histories used here to include prayer and listening. The waves Possibilities and design questions Wave 0 1980s onward Search and study on computers A KJV search program in 1986, QuickVerse in 1988 and Logos in 1991 illustrate an expanding field of searchable texts and study libraries. Faithlife history · QuickVerse history by Craig Rairdin What it makes possible Quicker reference work, linked resources and tools for investigating a passage. These possibilities serve teaching, study and personal reading in different ways. Questions for design Which reader and task does the library serve? What requires specialist knowledge, a purchased resource or a licensed translation? Finding a passage → Numbers, headings and notes → Wave 1 1993 onward Scripture through the web Bible Gateway began in 1993. Browser access made Scripture available without installing a complete study library. About Bible Gateway What it makes possible Search and reference through a widely available interface, with translation and resource choices that could grow over time. Questions for design Can someone understand the passage and its context, as well as locate or copy it? Who provides the text, interpretation and ongoing access? Finding a passage → Numbers, headings and notes → Wave 2 1998 handhelds / 2008 smartphones Portable reading and connected practice Laridian introduced PalmBible for Windows CE in 1998. YouVersion followed a web project with its iPhone app in July 2008; plans, sharing and rewards developed on separate timelines. Laridian history · YouVersion early history What it makes possible Reading away from a desk, saved position, chosen plans and ways to read with others. Small screens and offline access also create distinct design tasks. Questions for design Does a reminder, progress record or reward support the chosen practice? Can someone change pace, return after interruption or participate without a public score? YouVersion Olive Tree Bible Progress and streaks → How much text at once → Wave 3 2006 podcast / 2010 audio app / 2018 prayer app Listening and guided prayer Pray As You Go began as a podcast in 2006, Bible.is launched in 2010, Hallow in 2018 and Lectio 365 in 2019. These continue several traditions of listening and prayer. Pray As You Go history · Faith Comes By Hearing history · The Hallow story · Introducing Lectio 365, November 2019 What it makes possible Audio can support language access, listening together and prayer in everyday settings. A guided session can offer music, a passage, reflection and a clear ending. Questions for design What kind of practice is being offered, from which tradition, and in what setting? How do pacing, silence, accessibility and payment affect participation? Dwell Hallow How much text at once → Progress and streaks → Wave 4 2023 onward Generative AI conversation Magisterium AI has a public product record from July 2023. Current faith apps use conversation for questions and explanations; their source handling and roles differ. Magisterium AI changelog, July 18, 2023 What it makes possible A person can phrase a question in ordinary language and explore follow-ups. Connecting an answer to inspectable sources can make interpretation easier to examine. Questions for design What is the system allowed to claim or do? Can the person inspect its sources, recognise uncertainty and reach human help? Does remembering context help enough to justify storing it? BibleAI Joseph Prince Citations in AI answers → Actions on AI answers → Feature histories One platform can carry several intentions YouVersion’s iPhone launch, adjustable reading plans, badges and app-open streaks were separate product decisions. Reading them as one inherited mobile package hides opportunities to keep useful support while reconsidering a particular mechanism. Selected YouVersion announcements Date Documented decision Source 2008 iPhone access following a web and mobile-web project. Provider history 2009 Plans with adjustable duration, completion tracking and synchronized progress. Plans announcement 2010 Sharing, badges and a collective reading-minutes target. Year in review 2017 Streaks based on consecutive app opens, with reminders and celebrations. Streaks announcement These records support examining the relationship between an intended Bible habit and the behaviour counted. They do not establish that every reminder, badge or streak originated in an advertising business, or that such features always help or harm readers. A launch account establishes a stated purpose; evaluating effects requires research with people. Hutchings’s study of YouVersion and GloBible examines how interfaces encourage particular evangelical reading practices. Religious tradition belongs in the design history, alongside platforms, publishing, funding and user circumstances. Practice, motivation and consent → Purposes and communities Formation runs across the histories A technology generation does not determine a product’s purpose. These examples show different relationships between a practice, its community and a delivery medium. Prayer in an ordinary journey Pray As You Go began with Ignatian reflection for commuters. Its later app continues a practice shaped around a short session of music, Scripture and questions. Pray As You Go history → Listening and language access Faith Comes By Hearing’s audio work and Bible.is connect mobile delivery to a longer listening ministry. Audio need not begin with a meditation subscription or assume solitary use. Audio ministry timeline → Learning within a congregation KonApp’s 2019 launch connected Bible texts, journaling, teaching tasks and communication within confirmation groups. The smartphone served an existing educational relationship. EKD launch announcement → A shared rhythm with room to choose Lectio 365 launched in 2019 with a rhythm inspired by lectio divina. Shared content can be a considered choice; variation, adaptation and personal memory are different design decisions. Lectio 365 launch → Personalization can help someone find a suitable response, but remembering more is not proof of knowing or accompanying a person well. Ask what may be adapted, whose judgement shapes it, what remains private and where a human relationship is needed. A finite shared practice and an adaptive interface can each be appropriate. Design possibilities What could this technology help people do better now? Exercise Choose one feature. Describe the person’s situation and intended benefit, then trace the feature’s documented history. Preserve what still helps. Sketch one familiar response and one newly feasible alternative. Compare the whole journey, including interruption, recovery and finishing, with people in the relevant situation. Our editorial proposal is to use history as a source of possibilities and questions. A faster prototype can make a better experiment affordable; neither novelty nor fidelity to tradition settles which design serves someone well. Record the decision with the worksheet → Sources Sources and scope All sources Faithlife history Provider retrospective: KJV search in 1986; Logos released in December 1991; translation licensing shaped its business model. QuickVerse history by Craig Rairdin Creator retrospective: initial release in September 1988; Parsons distribution in January 1989. A participant account, not an independent market history. Laridian history Provider retrospective: PalmBible for Windows CE introduced in October 1998. The product name is not the Palm OS platform. About Bible Gateway Provider history: founded by Nick Hengeveld at Calvin College in 1993. YouVersion early history Provider retrospective from 2023: website in September 2007; mobile website in spring 2008; iPhone app on July 10, 2008. YouVersion plans announcement, December 2009 Contemporaneous announcement: adjustable schedules, completion tracking and synchronized progress. YouVersion 2010 year in review Contemporaneous provider account: sharing, badges and collective reading-time targets; not the origin of every engagement mechanism. YouVersion streaks announcement, August 2017 Contemporaneous announcement: consecutive app opens, reminders and milestone celebrations, presented as support for a Bible habit. Pray As You Go history Organisation retrospective: commuter prayer podcast in 2006; app in 2014; daily music, Scripture and reflection. Faith Comes By Hearing history Organisation timeline: tape-lending library in 1972; Digital Bible Platform and Bible.is in 2010. The Hallow story Founder account: app launched at the end of 2018, drawing on Catholic contemplative prayer. Stated intention does not establish user effects. Introducing Lectio 365, November 2019 Contemporaneous 24-7 Prayer announcement: devotional resource inspired by lectio divina, produced with CWR. KonApp launch, October 2019 EKD announcement: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft app supporting confirmation teaching, Bible access, journals and group communication. Magisterium AI changelog, July 18, 2023 Contemporaneous product record establishes operation by this date and a growing document collection; not the first religious AI service. Tim Hutchings, Design and the digital Bible, 2017 Research on YouVersion and GloBible as persuasive designs supporting evangelical reading practices. A two-product study, not a verdict on all Bible apps. John Dyer, People of the Screen, 2023 Four eras: academic computing in the 1950s–70s, desktop pastoral tools from 1980, popular internet from 1995 and mobile apps from the 2000s. This periodization differs from our five histories. Copyright 2023; online publication November 2022. The starting framework comes from Tobias Treppmann’s Kairos research, section 1.3. These five histories are an editorial interpretation of selected Bible and prayer tools, with a largely European and North American source base. They are not a complete global history of Christian software. Company accounts establish dates and stated intentions; app observations establish visible behaviour; neither alone establishes spiritual outcomes or a universal causal story. Installed-device totals and store rankings are not measures of formation.

pages.title: Follow the calendar into prayer
pages.description: Open a named observance and participate in an appropriate prayer practice.
pages.text: On this page Proposed flow Recovery Completion Patterns Home / Scenarios / Flow A design reference Follow the calendar into prayer Open a named observance and participate in an appropriate prayer practice. Design proposal · User validation required Entry Today’s view or a date shared by a community. Proposed flow Confirm context Identify calendar, date, region and service. Open Show sourced readings or prayer, with alternatives explained. Participate Choose text or supported audio, with instructions and responses clear. Pause Preserve the chosen date and section rather than replacing it at midnight. Finish Allow an ending without recording completion or sharing personal content. Recovery and alternative routes Missing calendar data is disclosed. Offer cached material only with its date and version clear. A return to today is an explicit action. What counts as a complete outcome The person can follow the chosen practice and understand where its material came from. Decisions within this flow 92 · Habits and spiritual formation Orient within a liturgical calendar Make the tradition, date and observance clear before offering readings or prayer. Research-informed design proposal 93 · Habits and spiritual formation Make room for prayer Compare a prayer text, a guided sequence and a quiet space without requiring personal input. Research-informed design proposal 20 · Audio and guided practice Choose a devotional format Compare a continuous reading, a sequence of cards and a chaptered audio session. Research-informed design proposal 17 · Audio and guided practice The player works without the screen Support listening as a complete mode of use. Research-informed design proposal Engagement facets to specify Possible situations: Contemplation and prayer, Group and communal reading. These are overlapping task contexts, not fixed user categories. Specify the chosen purpose, passage unit, pace, participation, social setting, interpretive task, environment and disclosure or teaching responsibility. Use the scenario framework . Reflect Repeat a chosen portion or offer an optional question. Pray Offer authored words, editable assistance or silence. Rest Use an untimed pause or a timer chosen by the person. Proposed flow Read in context Read the coherent passage and wider book context before extracting a claim. Compare Inspect editions, reliable lexical alignment and attributed perspectives. Collect evidence Attach quotations, excerpts and media anchors to specific draft claims. Review the draft Separate verified Scripture, source interpretation, AI suggestions and the teacher’s own conclusions. Export deliberately Check quotation rights, references and audience; retain human ownership and a versioned source trail. pages.text: On this page Proposed flow Recovery Completion Patterns Home / Scenarios / Flow A design reference Respond to a sensitive disclosure with accountable support Keep disclosure, present safety, user choice and service responsibility distinct. Sensitive design proposal · Clinical and safeguarding review required Entry A personal conversation includes distress, possible harm or coercion. Proposed flow Listen Take the account seriously without blame, forced interpretation or an abuse verdict. Clarify present needs Ask only relevant questions; suicide concerns and immediate danger require the specialist-reviewed response. Check safe access Consider whether the device and contact method are safe; quick exit has limited privacy protection. Offer real support Use independent verified destinations; do not route to an implicated person or invent a staffed transfer. Explain data and responsibility Name actual sharing and confidentiality limits; apply reviewed local safeguarding duties. Recovery and alternative routes Unavailable services need real alternatives. Ordinary doubt, historical text analysis and repeated questions must not automatically become diagnoses. This flow is not a clinical scale or an abuse investigation. What counts as a complete outcome Human-help routes remain reachable; the app does not claim rescue, monitoring or clinical efficacy. pages.description: Attributed AI design resources with review scope, application, limits and additional primary sources.
pages.text: Home / Sources An evolving source collection · Updated 6 October 2026 Sources, with their limits. See what was reviewed, what each resource contributes, and where it informs this reference. This growing bibliography brings together interaction design, Scripture data, product documentation, spiritual formation, health research and legal sources. Its AI design references include a collection curated in Vitaly Friedman’s LinkedIn resource post . That collection is credited below alongside an expanding domain bibliography. Their depth of review varies: reading a public syllabus is not the same as taking a course, and reviewing an index is not an audit of every pattern. General principles are adapted into original domain scenarios and wireframes. App examples are presented separately with provenance and attribution. Protected course materials are not reproduced. Read the evidence method before treating a card as a validated recommendation. AI and interaction design references Resource 01 · AI UX Playground AI UX Playground Catalogue and selected detail pages reviewed Contribution: Named patterns for citations, control, streaming, memory and agent actions. Application: Useful foundation for evidence cards, readable conversation and bounded agency. Limit: Selected relevant entries reviewed; the entire catalogue was not audited. Its FAQ currently describes 150 patterns in 11 categories. Intent controls support the prompt Citations in AI answers Curator’s link to this resource Resource 02 · Brandon Harwood · quietloudlab AI Interaction Atlas Official repository and taxonomy reviewed Contribution: Separates human tasks, AI tasks, system tasks, data artifacts, constraints and touchpoints. Application: Use its vocabulary to assign review, execution, state management and recovery responsibilities. Limit: A taxonomy, not a prescriptive UI framework. The official repository is available at https://github.com/quietloudlab/ai-interaction-atlas under Apache 2.0. Used in: Editorial method and further learning . No specific interaction or research claim is derived from unreviewed teaching material. Resource 03 · Sharang Sharma GenAI UX Design Patterns Public framework overview reviewed Contribution: Organises design around needs, trust, control, errors and safety. Application: Use these lenses to assess a family of patterns rather than treating AI as a single chat feature. Limit: A store listing, not a test of the app. Blessed – Daily Verse & Prayer (App Store listing) Blessed – Daily Verse & Prayer (App Store listing) · Everblessed Technology · Apple App Store (US) Listing reviewed 11 October 2026 “a fresh evening Scripture and prayer prompt to quiet your mind, restore your heart, and remind you of God’s presence — even in the dark”, and “Get daily reminders, track your prayer streak”; 104K ratings. A daily word can be gentle, and the same app can count a streak. Limit: A store listing, not a test of the app. Echo Prayer (App Store listing) Echo Prayer (App Store listing) · The Parable Group · Apple App Store (US) Listing reviewed 11 October 2026 “After praying for someone, send out a notification to let them know you’ve prayed for their shared prayer”; reminders by push or email; 22K ratings. A notification can carry something a person did for someone else. Limit: A store listing, not a test of the app. Intercede – Catholic Novenas (App Store listing) Intercede – Catholic Novenas (App Store listing) · Devoted Coders · Apple App Store (US) Listing reviewed 11 October 2026 “timely, gentle reminders that ensure you never miss a day of your novena prayers”; 36K ratings. Reminders can follow the shape of a practice, such as the nine days of a novena, and end with it. Limit: A store listing, not a test of the app. Universalis (App Store listing) Universalis (App Store listing) · Universalis Publishing · Apple App Store (US) Listing reviewed 11 October 2026 The Liturgy of the Hours and the Mass for every day, with “Home Screen widgets; liturgical events for your iOS calendar; daily email service … reminders and alarms”; 9.6K ratings, $9.99. An app for the hours offers reminders and alarms as tools, not as a strategy. Limit: A store listing, not a test of the app. Hallow: Prayer & Meditation (App Store listing) Hallow: Prayer & Meditation (App Store listing) · Hallow · Apple App Store (US) Listing reviewed 11 October 2026 Minute meditations including the “Angelus”, and the “Ability to set prayer reminders”; 379K ratings. The largest Catholic prayer app offers the Angelus as content and reminders as a setting. Limit: A store listing, not a test of the app. Bible Chat: Daily Devotional (App Store listing) Bible Chat: Daily Devotional (App Store listing) · Book Vitals · Apple App Store (US) Listing reviewed 11 October 2026 “spiritual prompts, Christian calendar reminders”, a lock-screen verse widget and a “Send a Blessing Widget”; 365K ratings, chart position #1 in Reference. The leading AI Bible app reaches people through reminders and widgets as well as chat. Limit: A store listing; its notifications are on the diary list. App Store Review Guidelines: 3.2.1 (vi) and (vii), 3.2.2 (iv) App Store Review Guidelines: 3.2.1 (vi) and (vii), 3.2.2 (iv) · Apple Guidelines reviewed 11 October 2026 “Approved nonprofits may fundraise directly within their own apps or third-party apps, provided those fundraising campaigns … offer Apple Pay support”; they “must disclose how the funds will be used” and “ensure appropriate tax receipts are available to donors”. Others “may only collect funds outside of the app, such as via Safari or SMS”. A gift “connected to or associated at any point in time with receiving digital content or services must use in-app purchase”. On iPhone, a gift is either a gift to an approved nonprofit, with Apple Pay, or collected outside the app; a gift that unlocks content is a purchase. Limit: Rules for one platform; they change, and approval as a nonprofit is a separate process. Payments policy (Google Play) Payments policy (Google Play) · Google Play Console Help Policy reviewed 11 October 2026 Google Play’s billing is not required where “payments include peer-to-peer payments, online auctions, and tax exempt donations”. On Android, donations to tax-exempt organisations can use the organisation’s own payment provider. Limit: A summary page of a longer policy; the exemption depends on the organisation’s status. When Should the Ask Be a Nudge? The Effect of Default Amounts on Charitable Donations When Should the Ask Be a Nudge? The Effect of Default Amounts on Charitable Donations · Indranil Goswami and Oleg Urminsky · Journal of Marketing Research, 2016 Abstract reviewed 11 October 2026 Finds “a scale-back effect, in which low defaults reduce average donation amounts”, “a lower-bar effect, in which defaulting a low amount increases donation rate”, and “a default-distraction effect, in which introducing any defaults reduces the effect of other cues such as positive charity information”. A suggested amount changes who gives and how much; an empty field leaves the decision to the giver. Limit: Charity appeals, not church giving; effects vary with the amounts tested. Hey Look at Me: The Effect of Giving Circles on Giving Hey Look at Me: The Effect of Giving Circles on Giving · Dean Karlan and Margaret A. McConnell · NBER working paper 17737, 2012 Abstract reviewed 11 October 2026 A field experiment with donors to a Yale University service club: “charitable gifts increase in response to the promise of public recognition primarily because of individuals’ desire to improve their social image”. Showing givers to others raises giving, and does so through the motive Jesus warned against. Limit: One university club in the United States. 2026 Protestant Annual Church Giving Report 2026 Protestant Annual Church Giving Report · Ministry Brands, 2026 Report reviewed 11 October 2026 Churches that offer digital giving “reported that 41% of their giving came from digital methods”; “Recurring giving accounted for 35% of the digital giving in 2025”. Much church giving is now digital, and a third of it is regular. Limit: A survey of church leaders and data from one vendor’s customers in the United States; the vendor sells giving software. ECFA Standards for Fund Raising ECFA Standards for Fund Raising · Evangelical Council for Financial Accountability · Christianity Today, May 1987 Text reviewed 11 October 2026 Representations “must be current, complete and accurate. References to past activities or events must be appropriately dated”; “Fund raising appeals must not create unrealistic donor expectations of what a donor’s gift will actually accomplish”. A figure about what a gift does needs a date, a source and an honest scope. Limit: The 1987 published standards; ECFA’s current wording is longer, with the same principle. A Statement on the Prosperity Gospel A Statement on the Prosperity Gospel · Lausanne Theology Working Group, Africa chapter · 2008–2009, published January 2010 Statement reviewed 11 October 2026 Defines prosperity teaching as obtaining health and wealth “through positive confessions of faith and the “sowing of seeds” through the faithful payments of tithes and offerings”, and lists among its effects “Replacing the traditional call to repentance and faith with a call to give money”. An ask that promises return for a gift has been named and rejected by evangelical churches worldwide. Limit: A statement from evangelical theologians; it also affirms a biblical vision of human flourishing. Code of Fundraising Practice 2025: table of changes Code of Fundraising Practice 2025: table of changes · Fundraising Regulator (UK) Rule 1.1.2 reviewed 11 October 2026 Fundraising must include “not putting undue pressure on a person to donate, not using unreasonably persistent approaches and accepting a request to end an interaction”. Pressure and persistence are named limits in UK fundraising, and churches that are charities are within its scope. Limit: A UK self-regulatory code; wording is from the 2025 revision. Bipartisan group of state attorneys general and state charity regulators send letter to GoFundMe Bipartisan group of state attorneys general and state charity regulators send letter to GoFundMe · Crowell & Moring client alert, March 2026 Alert reviewed 11 October 2026 Among the concerns in the regulators’ letter: “the application of a default “tip” that went directly to GoFundMe”. A tip added by default to a gift is a regulatory concern, not only a design choice. Limit: A law firm’s summary of the letter; GoFundMe disputed some of the regulators’ points. Publication 1771: Charitable Contributions, Substantiation and Disclosure Requirements Publication 1771: Charitable Contributions, Substantiation and Disclosure Requirements · Internal Revenue Service (US) Publication reviewed 11 October 2026 Organisations that receive “contributions of $250 or more” give a written acknowledgment, which can state that “the organization only provided intangible religious benefits”. A receipt is part of giving; a gift that buys something, such as an ad-free app, is acknowledged differently. Limit: US tax rules; other countries differ. Gift Aid declarations: claiming tax back on donations Gift Aid declarations: claiming tax back on donations · HM Revenue & Customs (UK) Guidance reviewed 11 October 2026 A declaration must tell donors that they need to pay enough UK tax to cover what charities claim, and that “the donor is responsible to pay any difference”. A tick box for Gift Aid needs its explanation, not only a pre-ticked box. Limit: UK rules only. Mehr Spenden in Baden-Württemberg: Kirchen testen digitale Kollekte Mehr Spenden in Baden-Württemberg: Kirchen testen digitale Kollekte · Wochenblatt-Reporter Article reviewed 11 October 2026 Congregations show QR codes on hymn sheets, posters or during the service, leading to the congregation’s online donation form; in Württemberg “knapp 400 Gemeinden und kirchliche Einrichtungen” have set up such forms. In German churches the digital collection is mostly a QR code to a web form, not an app. Limit: A regional news report; church tax still carries most church income in Germany. Givelify Mobile Giving App (App Store listing) Givelify Mobile Giving App (App Store listing) · Givelify · Apple App Store (US) Listing reviewed 11 October 2026 “#1 App to Donate, Tithe & Give”, with 101K ratings, 4.9. The one giving app with reach of its own; most church giving apps are white-label apps in each church’s name. Limit: Ratings show reach, not quality. Led by Dallas entrepreneur, Givelify reports $300 million in North Texas giving, $6 billion globally Led by Dallas entrepreneur, Givelify reports $300 million in North Texas giving, $6 billion globally · David Seeley · Dallas Innovates, 1 October 2025 Article reviewed 11 October 2026 The company says it “has processed $6 billion in donations from 2 million donors supporting 75,000 nonprofits and places of worship”. Giving through apps is no longer marginal. Limit: Company figures, not independently audited. A Spirituality of Fundraising A Spirituality of Fundraising · Henri J. M. Nouwen · Upper Room Books, 2010 Publisher page reviewed 11 October 2026 “Fundraising is first and foremost a ministry”: “a way of announcing our vision and inviting other people into our mission”, and “precisely the opposite of begging”. An ask can be an invitation into shared work, not a transaction or a plea. Limit: A short book drawn from a talk; the publisher’s summary is quoted here. Privacy as contextual integrity Privacy as contextual integrity · Helen Nissenbaum · Washington Law Review 79(1), 2004 Abstract reviewed Proposes contextual integrity as a benchmark that ties adequate privacy protection “to norms of specific contexts”: what is appropriate depends on the context in which information was shared and where it flows. A prayer or confession told to an assistant for one purpose should not flow into recommendations, marketing or another conversation. Limit: A legal and philosophical framework, not a design study. “It’s a fair game”, or is it? Examining how users navigate disclosure risks and benefits when using LLM-based conversational agents “It’s a fair game”, or is it? Examining how users navigate disclosure risks and benefits when using LLM-based conversational agents · Zhiping Zhang et al. · CHI 2024 Abstract reviewed Analysed sensitive disclosures in real ChatGPT conversations and interviewed 19 users: users constantly trade privacy against usefulness; “erroneous mental models and the dark patterns in system design limited their awareness and comprehension”; human-like interaction encouraged more sensitive disclosure. People will tell an assistant more than they intend and misjudge what is kept; show it to them. Limit: General chatbot use; small interview sample. Memory and new controls for ChatGPT Memory and new controls for ChatGPT · OpenAI · 13 February 2024, updated 2025 Announcement as quoted in press coverage (Decrypt, TechCrunch); the page blocks automated reading Introduced memory that people can ask to remember or forget, view and switch off, and Temporary Chat without memory; said it would “steer ChatGPT away from proactively remembering sensitive information, like your health details—unless you explicitly ask it to.” Later updates let people switch off reference to saved memories and to chat history separately. The largest chat product treats memory as something to see, delete and switch off, and holds back sensitive categories; a faith app should do no less. Limit: A company’s description of its own product; behaviour was not tested here. LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection · OWASP GenAI Security Project · 2025 Entry reviewed “Indirect prompt injections occur when an LLM accepts input from external sources, such as websites or files”; hidden text can change the model’s behaviour or leak data. Treat attached notes, pages and files as material to read, never as instructions, and say so. Limit: A security catalogue, not a user study. Code of Canon Law, canons 959–997: the sacrament of penance Code of Canon Law, canons 959–997: the sacrament of penance · Holy See · Code of Canon Law (1983) Canon 983 reviewed Canon 983 §1: “The sacramental seal is inviolable”; a confessor may not betray a penitent “in words or in any manner and for any reason.” The church’s strongest form of confidentiality; an assistant is not a confessor, which is why it should keep confidences it cannot protect as little as possible. Limit: Catholic canon law; other traditions practise confidentiality differently. Confessions, Book X Confessions, Book X · Augustine of Hippo · c. 400 · New Advent translation Chapters 5 and 8 reviewed “There is something of man which the spirit of man which is in him itself knows not. But You, Lord, who hast made him, know him wholly” (X.5); “Great is this power of memory, exceeding great, O my God” (X.8). Only God knows a person wholly; a record of conversations is not knowledge of a person. Limit: A classical theological reflection on memory and self-knowledge. The End of Memory: Remembering Rightly in a Violent World (review) The End of Memory: Remembering Rightly in a Violent World (review) · Miroslav Volf · Eerdmans, 2006 · Themelios review Reviews reviewed Argues that memory of wrongs must be truthful and that its proper end, after justice and reconciliation, is a kind of non-remembrance, drawing on God’s promise not to remember sins. Remembering rightly includes letting go; an assistant should be able to forget, and let people make it forget. Limit: Read through reviews; no quotation from the book used. Gyroscope: AI coach check-ins and the “About You” consultation Gyroscope: AI coach check-ins and the “About You” consultation · Gyroscope · iOS app 11.1, observed 8 October 2026 Used on a member’s own phone with their permission; no screenshots published because the screens hold personal health data Each check-in starts with a switch between “Quick chat” and “Save to history”. What the coach knows is kept as a written profile, “About You”, from an onboarding interview: summary, daily rhythm, food and stress, and a section titled “Internal notes” that the member can read. Corrections go through “Discuss with your coach” prompts rather than item-by-item editing. Asked in chat, the coach recited remembered goals, routines and a health condition, but could not say which screen lists them. The profile also noted church attendance, gathered by a fitness app. A per-conversation “keep or don’t keep” switch is simple and clear, and showing even the internal notes is honest. But a prose profile can’t be edited line by line, and a health coach noting church attendance shows how faith details drift into profiles that were never about faith. Limit: One app, one account; behaviour may differ for other members and versions. Luke 15:1–3, Berean Standard Bible Luke 15:1–3, Berean Standard Bible · Berean Standard Bible (public domain) Passage text taken from API.Bible, 9 October 2026 Provides the wording used in reading-layout and verse-number illustrations. Use real, attributed text to make layout differences legible. Limit: The diagram’s grouping is a design proposal, not a facsimile of this publisher’s interface. Psalm 23, Berean Standard Bible Psalm 23, Berean Standard Bible · Berean Standard Bible (public domain) Passage text taken from API.Bible, 9 October 2026 Provides the wording used in chat, resource and parallel-reading illustrations. Separate quoted Scripture from illustrative commentary and UI annotations. Limit: A text source, not evidence of the proposed interface’s effectiveness. Psalm 23, World English Bible Psalm 23, World English Bible · eBible.org / World English Bible Passage text and edition description reviewed 5 October 2026 Provides the WEB wording used in the comparison illustration. Name each edition alongside the text being compared. Limit: This endpoint is the updated 66-book edition; product availability shown elsewhere is illustrative. John 1:1 Greek text analysis John 1:1 Greek text analysis · Bible Hub The first two tokens, transliterations and glosses reviewed 5 October 2026 Shows the opening tokens with gloss and lexical identifiers. Use a small attributed excerpt to demonstrate token association and on-demand details. Limit: Two-token illustration only; not a complete lexical analysis, alignment dataset or licence for bulk reuse. Neu Bible: navigation features Neu Bible: navigation features · Neu Bible / App Store Publisher description reviewed 6 October 2026 Documents swipe-left chapter navigation and quick search. Separate the reveal gesture from the layout of the revealed chooser. Limit: Publisher description, not a current interactive review or verification of a vertical list. Applied in: Finding passages Read the Bible using Dwell Read the Bible using Dwell · Dwell Historical release announcement reviewed 6 October 2026 Documents a Scripture picker with books and chapters. Treat selecting a passage as part of the reading experience. Limit: Does not verify current category colours or picker layout. Applied in: Finding passages Book identifiers Book identifiers · USFM documentation Identifier catalogue reviewed 6 October 2026 Includes deuterocanonical and additional book identifiers. Build the browser from the edition’s inventory and metadata. Limit: Identifiers do not prescribe one universal display order or genre taxonomy. Applied in: Finding passages Mere Bible: publisher listing and rename Mere Bible: publisher listing and rename · Dwell App, LLC / App Store Reviewed 6 October 2026 The publisher release history confirms the change from Neu Bible to Mere Bible. Use the current name while retaining historical source context. Limit: Does not identify the build shown in the contributed screenshots. Applied in: Finding passages Mere Bible: contributed reader and picker screenshots Mere Bible: contributed reader and picker screenshots · Mere Bible / screenshots contributed by Tobias Treppmann Nine images supplied and reviewed 6 October 2026; capture date and build unverified Shows an in-context chapter rail, expandable book list with inline chapter grid, reading-settings drawer and translation sheet. Compare these observed arrangements with original pattern proposals. Limit: Still images establish visible states, not gesture timing, accessibility, persistence or exact interaction behaviour. Applied in: Finding passages Mental models: expectations of human-like interaction Mental models: expectations of human-like interaction · Google PAIR Human-like interaction section reviewed 6 October 2026 Human-like cues can aid familiarity but create unrealistic expectations when limits are unclear. Evaluate the combined persona, language and interface cues. Limit: Industry framework; not a controlled comparison of faith-app typing indicators. Applied in: How AI comes across Generative AI Profile: Human–AI Configuration Generative AI Profile: Human–AI Configuration · NIST Section 2.7 reviewed 6 October 2026 Identifies risks around human–AI configuration, overreliance and emotional entanglement. Review mistaken identity and dependency risks alongside usability. Limit: Risk framework, not evidence that one visual cue causes an outcome. Applied in: How AI comes across Methods for providing privacy information Methods for providing privacy information · UK Information Commissioner’s Office Layered and just-in-time approaches reviewed 6 October 2026 Describes concise first layers, detailed notices and relevant information at collection. Keep privacy details accessible and surface meaningful data-use changes at the decision. Limit: UK guidance; actual processing and regional obligations require assessment. Information alone is not consent. Applied in: How AI comes across Voice interface discovery references These additional voice design resources are discovery references. Their inclusion does not imply a full review of their contents. Voice Principles · Ben Sauer Orange Voice UI Design System Designing a persona for your assistant · James Walsh Voice UI Guide · Lars Mäder Designing Voice UX collection · nested link chain not exhaustively reviewed Sesame and voice preview · product demonstration, not safety evidence Download the English source register

pages.title: AI agency and care
pages.description: Define permissions, responsibilities and boundaries for personal or consequential interactions.
pages.text: Home / Patterns / AI agency and care A design reference AI agency and care Define permissions, responsibilities and boundaries for personal or consequential interactions. Source grounding, honest memory and reversible action matter in all agentic products. Faith contexts also require humility about interpretation, sensitive data and claims of spiritual authority. Sensitive conversations need more than a UI pattern. Read the health and care evidence and legal research map . 79 · AI agency and care Identify what AI did, where it matters Label the actor, action and artifact at the moment they could be misunderstood. Research-informed design proposal

pages.title: Audio and guided practice
pages.description: Support listening, read-along, stories, contemplation and interruption.
pages.text: Home / Patterns / Audio and guided practice A design reference Audio and guided practice Support listening, read-along, stories, contemplation and interruption. Audio playback, narrated practice and microphone capture are separate activities. Pick a paradigm by the person’s context, the available timing data and the kind of participation intended. 17 · Audio and guided practice The player works without the screen Support listening as a complete mode of use. Research-informed design proposal 18 · Audio and guided practice Playback and reading positions can differ Follow the narration without forcing the reader to follow every movement. Research-informed design proposal 20 · Audio and guided practice Choose a devotional format Compare a continuous reading, a sequence of cards and a chaptered audio session. Research-informed design proposal 100 · Audio and guided practice Bible audio From text alone, through a listen button and read-along, to audio built for a dark screen and fully produced devotionals: decide how much the voice leads, whose voice it is, and how a listening session ends. Research-informed design proposal

pages.title: Conversation and content
pages.description: Keep rich content and long answers readable within a dialogue.
pages.text: Home / Patterns / Conversation and content A design reference Conversation and content Keep rich content and long answers readable within a dialogue. Conversation is one interaction surface among several. Use cards for inspectable objects and dedicated reading or editing spaces when the task outgrows a bubble. 11 · Conversation and content Passage preview opens a full reader Keep long Scripture readable without flooding the conversation. Research-informed design proposal 44 · Conversation and content Intent controls support the prompt Help people express scope through selections and task choices. Research-informed design proposal 52 · Conversation and content Chat contains source objects, not just bubbles Give verses, passages, links and media recognisable identity and appropriate actions. Research-informed design proposal 85 · Conversation and content Show what the chat will use before sending A passage, file, image or link becomes visible, removable context. Editorial design proposal 95 · Conversation and content How human should the assistant appear? Choose social cues deliberately, from names and avatars to typing dots, voice and claims of presence. Editorial design proposal 96 · Conversation and content Explain AI, fallibility and privacy where they matter Layer chat disclosures across entry, composer, response and sharing instead of relying on one disclaimer. Editorial design proposal 97 · Conversation and content Actions on AI answers Copy, share, save, listen, try again, simplify, branch, check quotations, rate or report: choose the actions an AI answer needs and make each one honest about what it does. Editorial design proposal 101 · Conversation and content AI persona From a plain tool with no name, through labelled and named assistants, to personas, companions and chatbots speaking as Jesus: decide how much personhood an AI in a faith app performs, and make what it is as clear as how it sounds. Research-informed design proposal 109 · Conversation and content AI memory From an assistant that keeps nothing, through context the person adds and a conversation they can see, to memory they switch on and can see item by item, and a profile the app builds from their prayers as a warning case: decide what the assistant may use, what it keeps, and whether the person can see and change it. Research-informed design proposal

pages.title: Habits and spiritual formation
pages.description: Support meaningful practice while preserving autonomy.
pages.text: Home / Patterns / Habits and spiritual formation A design reference Habits and spiritual formation Support meaningful practice while preserving autonomy. These patterns are hypotheses and ethical design proposals. Their effects on actual reading practices, motivation and spiritual formation need research rather than assumptions from engagement metrics. These cards are proposed hypotheses. Read the research agenda and study integration method. 38 · Habits and spiritual formation Progress and streaks Choose between a saved place, completion and a shared date. Explain what the record means. Research-informed design proposal 39 · Habits and spiritual formation A flexible reading rhythm Help someone choose a reading rhythm—and adjust it when life changes. Proposed hypothesis 40 · Habits and spiritual formation Return without shame Make it easy to pick up a reading practice after time away. Proposed hypothesis 92 · Habits and spiritual formation Orient within a liturgical calendar Make the tradition, date and observance clear before offering readings or prayer. Research-informed design proposal 93 · Habits and spiritual formation Make room for prayer Compare a prayer text, a guided sequence and a quiet space without requiring personal input. Research-informed design proposal 105 · Habits and spiritual formation Reading plans From a plan tied to calendar dates, through a sequence that waits for the reader and a weekly rhythm, to readings that belong to each day, and streaks as a warning case: decide what a plan asks of time, and what happens when someone comes back after days away. Research-informed design proposal 106 · Habits and spiritual formation Prayer From the received words of a church’s daily office, through guided steps and a list of people to pray for, to quiet prayer with nothing to fill in, and counted prayer as a warning case: decide what each surface asks someone to read, type, share or count. Research-informed design proposal 108 · Habits and spiritual formation Devotional audio From guided prayer with Scripture read twice and room for silence, through a teaching conversation and a one-voice devotional talk, to a sleep story that fades out, and an endless generated stream as a warning case: decide what each format does with Scripture, with the listener’s attention, and with the end of the session. Research-informed design proposal 107 · Habits and spiritual formation Check-ins and assessments From a few setup questions that only shape what the app suggests, through a daily check-in, a gifts inventory and a church survey, to a spiritual score as a warning case: decide what each question is for, what is kept, who sees a result, and how much the result claims to know. Research-informed design proposal 110 · Habits and spiritual formation Sharing with a group From a request kept between someone and God, through one listener they choose, a few friends and a group with a leader, to the whole church and a public wall, with a board ranked by prayer streaks as a warning case: decide who hears a request, what each listener can and must do with it, and what comes back. Research-informed design proposal · draft for review 111 · Habits and spiritual formation Reading together From the same passage on the same day with nothing shown, through a guide for meeting in person, a group with a leader and a plan with friends, to a feed of friends’ activity and a public thread on the verse: decide what the others see of each person’s reading, and who looks after what is said. Research-informed design proposal · draft for review 112 · Habits and spiritual formation First use From opening on a passage, a prayer or a question box with nothing asked, through a first page of places to start, guest use and a short tour, to questions first and payment before the first use: decide what a new person must give, and when, before they reach what they came for. Research-informed design proposal · draft for review 113 · Habits and spiritual formation Children and families From a story read aloud with a grown-up, through family time in a general app, a children’s Bible app and games with episodes, to a youth group app with a leader and a child alone with an AI or a public community: decide who is with the child, what the app collects, how it holds attention, and what happens when a child says something worrying. Research-informed design proposal · draft for review 114 · Habits and spiritual formation Notifications and reminders From an app that waits to be opened, through reminders the person sets, the church’s hours of prayer, a daily word and messages from people, to notifications tuned to bring people back and an AI that writes first: decide who chooses the interruption, how urgent it claims to be, what it says to someone who has been away, and what reaches someone at night. Research-informed design proposal · draft for review 115 · Habits and spiritual formation Giving and offerings From leaving giving to the church, through a quiet way to give, the church’s offering in the app, a regular gift and showing what a gift does, to a gift tied to an ad-free app and, as the warning case, pressure and promises: decide where the ask appears, what is chosen for the giver, and what the app says a gift will do. Research-informed design proposal · draft for review

pages.title: Reading and Scripture
pages.description: Preserve the source text, its structure and the reader’s context.
pages.text: Home / Patterns / Reading and Scripture A design reference Reading and Scripture Preserve the source text, its structure and the reader’s context. Scripture data helps identify meaningful distinctions, but does not determine a single component. Start with what the person needs to read, understand or compare. 03 · Reading and Scripture Footnotes without losing place Inspect a note and return to the exact reading anchor. Research-informed design proposal 05 · Reading and Scripture Editorial distinctions survive reflow Preserve poetry, headings and translation additions without forcing a rigid layout. Research-informed design proposal 49 · Reading and Scripture A reference opens at a deliberate destination Choose the content scope, landing position and temporary cue separately. Research-informed design proposal 51 · Reading and Scripture Change translation without losing the passage Preserve a semantic reading anchor rather than a pixel offset. Research-informed design proposal 76 · Reading and Scripture A bounded passage with a route to wider context Choose the reading unit by the task while keeping its boundaries and context visible. Research-informed design proposal 81 · Reading and Scripture Paragraphs or one verse per line? Compare paragraph reading with a separate line for each verse, while preserving the edition’s poetry and structure. Editorial design proposal 82 · Reading and Scripture Verse numbers that help without taking over Separate locating a verse from the precision needed to select it. Editorial design proposal 83 · Reading and Scripture Finding a passage Let people browse when they do not know a reference and jump when they do. Editorial design proposal 84 · Reading and Scripture Choose a translation with enough context Make language, edition and availability understandable before switching. Editorial design proposal 89 · Reading and Scripture Book and chapter pickers: list, grid or drill-down? Choose the browsing shape independently from the search field. Editorial design proposal 90 · Reading and Scripture How do readers move to the next chapter? Compare continuous reading, explicit buttons and a persistent navigation bar. Editorial design proposal 91 · Reading and Scripture One field for browsing, references and AI discovery Let one input filter books, recognise a reference and suggest passages, while making each result’s origin clear. Editorial design proposal 98 · Reading and Scripture How much text at once One word, one verse, one verse in focus with its context, one passage or a whole chapter: choose the unit of Scripture a reading screen asks someone to hold, and let them move along the spectrum. Research-informed design proposal 99 · Reading and Scripture Numbers, headings and notes From a reader’s edition with nothing but the words, through verse numbers, section titles and note markers, to a full study layout: decide what sits around Scripture, who wrote it, and who can switch it off. Research-informed design proposal 94 · Reading and Scripture Adjust reading settings without losing the passage Keep typography, appearance and text-layer preferences close to the reading experience. Editorial design proposal

pages.title: Study and annotations
pages.description: Make evidence, comparison and personal work inspectable.
pages.text: Home / Patterns / Study and annotations A design reference Study and annotations Make evidence, comparison and personal work inspectable. Study moves between passages, lexical resources, commentary, media and notes. Keep each source and anchor visible so the journey stays reversible. 08 · Study and annotations Original media before synthesis Let readers inspect the source behind an explanation. Research-informed design proposal 30 · Study and annotations Preview before deep study Reveal relevant information from a passage without replacing the reader. Research-informed design proposal 32 · Study and annotations The annotation anchor is explicit Make exact wording and reference-based notes different personal objects. Research-informed design proposal 33 · Study and annotations Overlaps remain legible Distinguish playback, selection, search and saved highlights. Research-informed design proposal 53 · Study and annotations Parallel reading chooses a useful arrangement Compare translations without forcing a desktop layout onto a small screen. Research-informed design proposal 54 · Study and annotations Linked scrolling follows passage identity Let parallel panes move together or independently, with an explicit way to rejoin. Research-informed design proposal 55 · Study and annotations Group editions around a shared verse Use repeated verse groups when matching corresponding passages matters more than continuous reading. Research-informed design proposal 56 · Study and annotations Interlinear rows expose their alignment Distinguish source-language tokens, glosses and translation wording. Research-informed design proposal 78 · Study and annotations Citations in AI answers A citation is a route to supporting material, with source type and limitations visible. Research-informed design proposal 86 · Study and annotations How visible should extra resources be? Compare inline cards, small markers and resources revealed on demand. Editorial design proposal 87 · Study and annotations Keep my note distinct from a shared comment Origin, audience and anchor belong to the note—not just its screen. Editorial design proposal 88 · Study and annotations Mark a passage without interrupting the thought Quick highlighting and deeper organisation can happen at different moments. Editorial design proposal 102 · Study and annotations Translations From one translation chosen with enough context, through switching in place and verse-by-verse comparison, to parallel panes and the Greek or Hebrew under every word: decide how much of translation’s variety a reader sees, and keep them on the same verse while they look. Research-informed design proposal 103 · Study and annotations Highlights and notes From a bookmark that only says “return here”, through highlights and labelled marks, to private notes and notes shared with a group or the public: decide how much a mark says, who can see it, and what happens to it in another translation. Research-informed design proposal 104 · Study and annotations Study helps From a preview card under the verse, through a sheet and a study panel, to a page of its own or help only on request: decide where commentary, cross-references and sermon clips open, how readers find them, and how they get back to the verse.
